R. C. CHILDERS.

parsing_res_list.block_content: # PREFACE.

The Pali language is one of the Prakrits, or Aryan vernaculars of ancient India. It was spoken in the sixth century before Christ, and has therefore been a dead language for considerably over two thousand years. I see no reason to reject the Buddhist tradition that Pali was the dialect of Magadha, and that it was the language in which Gautama Buddha preached. Originally a mere provincial idiom, the Magadhese tongue was raised by the genius of a great reformer to the dignity of a classic language, and is regarded by Buddhists with the same feelings of veneration with which a Jew of the present day looks upon the language of the Pentateuch. A language is generally what its literature makes it. Had Gautama never preached, it is unlikely that the Magadhese would have been distinguished from the many other vernaculars of Hindostan, except perhaps by an inherent grace and strength which make it a sort of Tuscan among the Prakrits. The existing Pali literature is of great extent and importance; it is valuable alike to the philologist, the historian, the student of folklore.

The true or geographical name of the Pali language is Magadihi, 'Magadhese language,' or Magadhabishai, 'Language of the Magadhe people.' The word pili in Sandkrit means 'line, row, series,' and by the South Buddhists is extended to mean the series of books which form the text of the Buddhist Scriptures. Thence it comes to mean the text of the scriptures as opposed to the commentaries, and at least any text, or even portion of a text, of either scriptures or commentaries. Palibhasa therefore means 'language of the texts,' which of course is equivalent to saying 'Maghadi' language. The term pili in the sense of sacred text is ancient enough, but the expression Palibhasa is of modern introduction, and Magadihi is the only name used in the old South Buddhist texts for the sacred language of Buddhism. The English use of the word Pili is derived from the Sinhalee, who use it exactly as we do.

$ ^{*} $ This tradition is generally dismissed in a very summary manner, on the ground that Pali does not possess the phonetic characteristics of Vararochhi's Magudhi. It is curious to see those who are so ready to discredit one tradition accept without examination another tradition resting on evidence not a tithe as good. For that Vararuobi's Magadhi was really a Magudha tornacular is after all only a tradition like the Buddhist one. Considering the great interval that separates Ganama and Vararuchi, the dis

repenancy may be explained in a way that will suggest itself to those who are familiar with the migrations of languages and the names of languages in historical times. Moreover the Magadhas territory may have varied greatly in extent at different periods, and have included several dialects. One of the much-depressed Buddhist traditions is that Ceylon was colonised from a district of Magadhas called Lila, which is evidently meant to be an outlying district, or at least not that in which Geutama preached. If then Pali and Sinhalese are both dialects of Magadhas, we should expect them to resemble each other closely, while at the same time presenting dialectic differences. That this is actually the case I have shown in my Note on the Sinhalese Language, in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society for 1874. So great are the etraits to which those who deny the Magadhases origin of Pali are driven that Karu is compelled to declare Pali a literary manufacture. His argument that the Asoka edicts are not Pali, and that therefore Pali cannot be Magadhas, rests on the assumption that the edicts are Magadhi.

and the student of comparative religion. A considerable portion of it is known to us in outline, but only the merest fraction has as yet been published textually. It may broadly be classed under three heads: first the Buddhist Scriptures, which are the oldest Buddhist writings extant; secondly the commentaries of Buddhaghosha, which date only from the fifth century A.D., but are based upon records of great antiquity; and thirdly, historical, grammatical and other works, varying in date from the second or third century to the present day.

The Buddhist Scriptures are called Tripitaka, “The Three Baskets or Treasuries,” and are divided into Vinaya, Sūtra and Abhidharma, or. Discipline, Doctrine¹ and Metaphysics. The Vinaya Pitaka contains the laws and regulations of the Buddhist priesthood, and forms a great code of monastic discipline; it is besides rich in history and folklore, and contributes innumerable details of the life and ministry of Gautama. The Sūtra Pitaka consists chiefly of sermons preached by Gautama, and in some instances by his apostles,² but it also contains other matter, as the Jñaka tales, the Niddesa attributed to the apostle Sāriputra, and Theragāṭha, a collection of stanzas uttered on different occasions by eminent saints. In the Abhidharma we find metaphysics pressed into the service of religion: it introduces no new dogma, but discusses the various doctrines of Buddhism from a metaphysical point of view, employing a terminology of great wealth and precision.¹ The Three Baskets form a canon of Holy Writ, and are invested by the Buddhists with all the sanctity of a canon. They are reverenced as containing the Word of Buddha, and are the ultimate appeal on all questions of belief and conduct. Owing to their great extent, estimated at eleven times that of our own Bible, they are able to treat in great detail of all the relations of life, and the doctrine they contain is consistent throughout and set forth with clearness and logical accuracy.

Upon the important question of the origin of the Buddhist Canon much has been written, and the most conflicting opinions have been expressed. The time has hardly come for dogmatising on this subject, but the tendency of all recent discoveries is to confirm the Buddhist traditions, which assign to the Canon a venerable antiquity. The Tripitaka bears every mark of recension, and according to the Buddhist historians this recension dates from the 3rd General Council of Buddhism, held under the emperor Aroka in the year 309 before Christ. But even this is said to be a mere revival.

In arguing against the historical reality of the three Councils Kern observes that the name Kālsoks, 'Chronological Asoks', is in itself suspicious. But the Pali spelling with the Vedic | (see Dict.) proves that Kāls in this name means 'black' or 'dark-featured,' and so the argument falls to the ground. In answer to another argument of Kern's I may point out that it is not more wonderful that two Asoks should have held councils than that two Constantines should have held councils.

of the first recension which was made in s.c. 543, just after Gantama's death, when his words were fresh in the hearts and memories of his apostles.¹ These high pretensions have drawn down, as was inevitable, the ridicule of many Western scholars,¹ more than one of whom has held the Buddhist sacred books to be late compilations, scarcely even reflecting the teaching of Gautama. But the question has been placed on an entirely different footing since the discovery last year by General Cunningham of the Bharhut sculptures. These sculptures, which belong to the third century s.c., are illustrations in bas-relief of a great number of Buddhist scriptural subjects, and are accompanied by inscriptions in the Azoka character. Both illustrations and inscriptions are, so far as they have been identified, in perfect accord with the Buddhist Scriptures as we now have them, and in one instance a whole sentence, containing a remarkable expression, which is probably a δωδὲ λεγόμενον, is quoted from the Vinaya Pitaka.

Mahavanna states that the merged books were handed down orally till the first century B.C., when they were committed to writing. This statement has been frequently pointed to as vitiating all the claims of the Tripilipaka to real antiquity. To 1870 I wrote to the Sinhalese priest Subhuti to ask his views on this point, and received from him a letter dated Nov. 25th of that year, from which I translate the following reply: "There is no Sinhalese or Fatji book which tells us anything different from what is said in Mahavanna respecting the time at which they wrote the Tripilipaka in books. But my own opinion is that though all the doctrines of Buddhism and of the Tripilipaka began to be written and used in books in the time of king Vattaganapt, it is not that the doctrines were not at all written before that time. It is said that in king Vattaganapt's time all the sacred books were systematically written down, but it is said nowhere whatever that the doctrines had not been written at all before that period. We are told that at the first Council the pupils of the different Thراas undertook to preserve their respective Nikayas by committing them to memory. They may have done so for the most part, but such as were unequal to the task must have written down the words in books, and used them both privately and even publicly. It is probable that in process of time every one found it was difficult to get on in this way, and then in Vattaganapt's time they all assembled in consultation and publicly entered all the doctrines in books." Now the same difficulty exists with regard to the transmission of the Vedas, and I will place side by side with the above extract a passage from Whitney's Oriental and Linguistic Studies, putting forward an hypothesis identical with Subhuti's: "Thus while oral tradition continued to be the exoticic practice, writing might still be resorted to exotically; collections might be made and arranged, treatises composed, texts compared and studied, by the initiated, while the results were communicated to the schools by oral teaching, and memorized by the neophytes."

or Commentaries,—a whole literature, exegetical and historical, which had grown up around the Tripitaka during the two centuries and a half that had elapsed since Gautama Buddha's death. After accomplishing his mission of converting the island to Buddhism, he proceeded to translate these commentaries from Pali into Sinhalese, and his Sinhalese version continued to exist in Ceylon for many centuries, while the Pali version disappeared. In the fifth century Mahendra's Sinhalese commentaries were retranslated into Pali by the famous divine Buddhaghosha, one of the most extraordinary men that Buddhism has produced, and this third version is the one we now possess, the Sinhalese original having in its turn disappeared.¹ Buddhaghosha did not confine himself to translating Mahendra, but incorporated other old Sinhalese chronicles existing in his time, and added immense contributions, chiefly exegetical, of his own. Much of the matter his commentaries contain is as old as the Tripitaka itself, while like the Tripitaka they are rich in history and folklore, and abound in narratives which shed a flood of light on the social and moral condition of ancient India.⁴

The remaining Pali literature is of very varying interest. The mere tides of the books ancient and modern which it embraces would fill many pages, and it will be sufficient here to mention a few of the more noteworthy. First in importance are the two famous histories Dipavainsa and Mahdainsa, the discovery of which made the name of TURNOU allustrious, and which are almost our only authentic sources for the history of India previous to the Christian era. Next in order of interest should undoubtedly be named the Milinda Paiha, or Questions of Menander. Whatever be the origin of this remarkable work, there can be no doubt of its great antiquity, for it exhibits a familiarity with Greek names and places, and records a religious discussion between the Buddhist divine Nagesena and a Yona' king Milinda, who can be identified with certainty with the Bactrian king Menander. The latter lived towards the end of the second century B.C., and is stated by the Greek historians to have ruled over part of Hindusian. Buddhaghosha's Vinuddi Magga or Path of Holiness is next deserving of mention. It may fairly be called an encyclopædia of Buddhist doctrine, and is a truly great work, written in terse and lucid language, and showing a marvellous grasp of the subject. The Pali grammatical literature is very extensive, and centres around the famous grammar of Kachchaya, which is unquestionably the oldest Pali grammar we possess.

The disappearance of the Binhalese Commentaries appears to me to be easily accounted for. The Malabar princes who invaded Ceylon in the twelfth century, and more than one of whom temporarily obtained sovereignty over the island, were the most determined foes of Buddhism, and are stated to have systematically effected the destruction of all the sacred books they could lay hands on. Among these would be the Tripitaka books, the Fali Commentaries of

Buddhaghosh, and the Binhalam Commentaries of Mr. Hendra. The two first existed in Burmah, and were replaced, as history tells us, from that country, while the Sinhalose Commentaries existed only in Geylon, and once destroyed could not be replaced. All we can hope is that here and there a manuscript may have eumped the destructive fury of the conquerure, and may yet come to light, like a new Goden Sinistics, in some excluded monastery.

though its exact date cannot at present be even approximately fixed.¹ There are probably as many as sixty or seventy standard grammatical works in Pali, and minor ones even now from time to time issue from the native press in Ceylon and Burmah. Dictionaries in our sense of the term there are none, but in Abhidḥānappadīpīkd we have a vocabulary of nouns of the highest authority, compiled on the model of the Sanskrit Amarakosha by a learned Sinhalese priest of the twelfth century. The Pali Tīṭkāʿs, which form quite a literature in themselves, are commentaries, chiefly exegetical, by different authors, and belonging to different periods. They are of unequal authority, but some of the more ancient ones contain an immense deal that is valuable. They comment not only upon the Tripitaka, but upon almost all the standard books, and the Tīṭkāʿs on the commentaries of Buddhaghosha are often of great utility in clearing up obscure passages in those writings. The Pali books on such subjects as prosody, rhetoric and medicine are mostly very modern, and formed upon Sanskrit models. Among doctrinal works may be specially mentioned Sārasaiqaha, a modern compilation very popular in Ceylon, and Abhidḥammatthasaigaha, a masterly analysis or compendium of the Abhidharma, by a modern Burmese scholar named Anuruddha Acharya, whose work shows that the spirit of Buddhaghosha is by no means extinct among his successors in these latter days of Buddhism.

In an interesting preface to his Pali Grammar, Minoyoff says (Fr. ed., p. xiii) that "the early Buddhist literature, orally handled down, must have become modified according to the language of each country." He supports this view by quoting from the Vinaya Pitaka a saying of Buddha that "the word of Buddha is to be understood by every one in his own dialect." Unfortunately the words that translated have an exactly opposite meaning. The passage is a very important one, and Mr. Minoyoff deserves the credit of having first brought it to light, see his Pratimaksha Suture, p. xiii. The following is the correct translation of the whole passage: "Two brothers (some to Gautama and said), 'Lord, at the present time there are monks who have taken orders from various tribes and castes and families, these distort the word of Buddha from its own proper dialect; suppose, Lord, that we render the word of Buddha into Sankrit' (chandana droposma). Here the comment says, "Chandana droposma means, Let us adopt the practice of recitation in the Sankrit language (Sakhtabhadgi), like the Vodas." Buddha replies, "Priests, the word of Buddha is not to be turned into Sankrit, let him who so turns it be guilty of an offence: I command you, priests, to learn the word of Buddha in the own dialect." The comment adds, "Here its own dialect (said niraṭi) means the Maqadha venacular as broken by

Buddhism" (see art. Neruti). In proof of his statement that "the word of Buddhis long remained oral and was transmitted from mouth to mouth to different countries not in one particular dialect, but in several dialects simultaneously," Minesyell places side by side a number of stanzas from Mahrivanta, a North Buddhist Sanskrit text, and corresponding stanzas from the Fali Canon. An examination however of the two texts makes it quite clear that the Mahrivanta stanzas are merely clumsy translations of the Pali ones, made at a very late period by men who in some instances did not understand the expressions they were translating. Thus unable to make anything of the purely Pali word something, the translator turns something na keybird, "lot him not be justful," into at�atam na gache (); again he adopts wjjupafewe unaltered, and the exigencies of metre force him to admit such a monstrosity as cilavantaya (p. xxx). But the question was practically long ago not at rest when Burnouf in his Lotus de la Bonne Loi printed a number of parallel passages from North and South Buddhist texts (p. 850); with regard to which I have only to repeat what I have said under my art. Patiesmbhidd, "No one can doubt that one set are translations of the other, and I have difficulty in understanding how any one can believe the Pali to be a translation of the Sanskrit." They comment not only upon the Tripitaka, but upon almost all the standard books, and the Tīṭkāʿs on the commentaries of Buddhaghosha are often of great utility in clearing up obscure passages in those writings. The Pali books on such subjects as prosody, rhetoric and medicine are mostly very modern, and formed upon Sanskrit models. Among doctrinal works may be specially mentioned Sārasaiqaha, a modern compilation very popular in Ceylon, and Abhidḥammatthasaigaha, a masterly analysis or compendium of the Abhidharma, by a modern Burmese scholar named Anuruddha Acharya, whose work shows that the spirit of Buddhaghosha is by no means extinct among his successors in these latter days of Buddhism.

The Pali or southern version of the Buddhist Scriptures is the only genuine and original one. $ ^{3} $ To a great pioneer of science, BRIAN H. Hodgson, $ ^{4} $ is due the discovery

It results from all this that Pali cannot be derived from Sanskrit; both, though most intimately connected, being independent corruptions of the lost Aryan speech which is their common parent; but that Pali is on the whole in a decidedly later stage than Sanskrit, and, to adopt a metaphor popularised by Max Müller, stands to it in the relation of a younger sister. If the proud boast that the Magadhese is the one primeval language fades in the light of comparative philology, Buddhists may console themselves with the thought that the teaching of Gauama confers upon it a greater lustre than it can derive from any fancied antiquity.

The parallel between Italian in its relation to Latin and Pali in its relation to Sanskrit, is striking enough to deserve special notice. In the thirteenth century the literary language of Italy, the language of culture and science, was Latin, which however had long died out as the spoken tongue of cultivated society, and was probably reserved for the drama, and for occasions of state and ceremony. The spoken language of Italy was to be found in a number of provincial dialects, each with its own characteristics, the Piedmontese harsh, the Neapolitan nasal, the Tuscan soft and flowing. These dialects had long been rising in importance as Latin declined, the birth-time of a new literary language was imminent. Then came Dante, and choosing for his immortal Commedia the finest and most cultivated of the vernaculars, raised it at once to the position of dignity which it still retains. Read Sanskrit for Latin, Magadhese for Tuscan, Gautama for Dante, and the Three Baskets for the Divina Commedia, and the parallel is complete. There is strong evidence that in Gautama's time Magadha was one of the most important centres of Hindu civilization, and it is far from improbable that its language was the most esteemed of the Prakrits, just as the Tuscan was the most esteemed of the Italian vernaculars. We have seen that historically Pall was a vernacular or language of the people, and this is fully confirmed by internal evidence. A close examination of its grammar and vocabulary reveals all the distinctive peculiarities of a vernacular. At every turn we meet with words like atraja for Sanskrit atmaja, vinnamsá for mimámsá, nissád for drihad, jalábu for jaráyu, párpana for prāvarana, makasa for masaka, aggini for agni, piñja for picocha, bhamu for bhri, sumonára for ssumára,—vocables racy of the soil, and dear to the comparative philologist. Again, the artificial regularity of Sanskrit sandhi finds no place in the free and easy prose of Magadha, and though sandhi is certainly used in Pall it is hardly more used than in Italian or English. Another well-known feature of a vernacular is the frequency of double forms, like duáda and bárasa ‘twelve,’ rami and rami ‘ray,’ pappoti and pápáati ‘to obtain.’ Not uncommonly these divergencies are utilized to differentiate meaning, as in the case of aññatra and aññatha, the former meaning ‘except,’ and the latter ‘elsewhere,’ while their Sanskrit original anyatra has both meanings.⁴ Words in common use sometimes even appear under three or more forms, as when agni becomes aggi, aggini, gini, or svāna becomes sāna, sona, suna, suána and suvána. But by far the most striking evidence of the vernacular character of Pali is its wealth of idiom and colloquial expression. Analog writing which alone can make us acquainted with the inner life of an ancient people. But with Pali the case is entirely different. Here a very large proportion of the literature consists of stories of Gautama's ministry among the people, of narratives and dialogues of the most varied description, of sermons addressed to all classes of men, and abounding in homely yet forcible illustrations drawn from the incidents of everyday life. Whole strata of Hindu life and character are opened up and explored which are hardly more than touched by Sanskrit literature, and the colloquial idiom of ancient Hindustan is for the first time revealed to us.¹

The change which Pali has undergone relatively to Sanskrit, though considerable, is almost wholly confined to the vocabulary. And here the parallel between Pali and Italian stops short, for the latter, owing chiefly to foreign influence, has passed into an entirely new grammatical stage; and even looking only as its vocabulary, it is decidedly in a more advanced stage of phonetic decay than Pali $ ^{1} $. The losses which Pali has undergone are by no means inconsiderable. Its alphabet is deficient in the vowels ri, ri, fi, and fi, the diphthougs ai and au, and the consonants s, sh and visarga. The dual is lost in both declension and conjugation, $ ^{1} $ and two of the senses (the Periphrastic Future and the Benedictive) are wanting. Some of the verbal roots are unrepresented in Pali, of others only traces remain, and a host of verbal forms have disappeared. the elimination of one out of two or more conjunct consonants has brought about a real impoverishment of the vocabulary.¹ But all that Pali loses in one direction, it regains, and more than regains, in another. The dual and the two tenses are easily spared. If some roots are little used, others have sprung into unexpected importance. If many nouns are lost, their place is supplied by a greater number of new ones,² while false analogy has brought into existence new verbal forms that may almost be reckoned by thousands,³ and latitude of phonetic change makes up for all the losses caused by assimilation and other causes.⁴ The softening or breaking up of groups of consonants, the dropping of final consonants, the absence of rigid rules of sandhi, the absence of sounds like ri, s and au,—all this gives to Pali a softness and flexibility for which we may gladly exchange the stately but harsh regularity of Sanskrit.

To the above brief sketch I have only to add that, with the exception of a very few imported Dravidian nouns like chatt and chumba, there is no foreign element in Pali. It is on the whole in the same inflectional stage as Sanakrit, and everything in its vocabulary, grammar and syntax can be explained from the sister tongue. But at the same time it exhibits a remarkable elasticity, a power of enriching itself by throwing out new forms; we may perhaps even detect in it adumbrations of a tendency to pass into a later phonetic stage. What Pali would have become had it run on unchecked in its course of decay and regeneration may be seen from the modern Sinhalese, which springs from an idiom closely allied to Pali, and has long passed into the analytical stage. To a great extent Sinhalese may for practical purposes he viewed as a lineal descendant of Pali, and it has worked out a whole legion of grammatical forms the germs of which may often be detected in Pali, and which make it a rich, though as yet almost unexplored, philological mine.

Sometimes the older or regular form only is in use, as gachati, disenti, dasati, khapati (or koti). Sometimes the regular form is lost and its place supplied by an irregular one due to false analogy, as pachisati compared with pakshati. But in innumerable cases regular and irregular forms co-exist, to the great enrichment of the language, as dakhkati and posissati, dejdit and dadoyya. See examples at p. xiv.

I must of course except an insignificant number of forms like those mentioned at p. xiii, note 1. I have been obliged to leave a considerable number of words unidentified in my dictionary, but as our knowledge increases the list will steadily diminish; and if some words should finally remain unidentified (which is extremely probable) we must remember the vernacular character of Pali, which would explain its possessing many undoubted Aryan words which have not crept into Sanskrit literature. Thus the Pali name for white ant, spaskit, which is almost certainly a derivative of upachi, does not occur in Sanskrit, because, I suppose, the white ant does not happen to be mentioned in Sanskrit literature. See p. i, note 2.

the elimination of one out of two or more conjunct consonants has brought about a real impoverishment of the vocabulary.¹ But all that Pali loses in one direction, it regains, and more than regains, in another. The dual and the two tenses are easily spared. If some roots are little used, others have sprung into unexpected importance. If many nouns are lost, their place is supplied by a greater number of new ones,² while false analogy has brought into existence new verbal forms that may almost be reckoned by thousands,³ and latitude of phonetic change makes up for all the losses caused by assimilation and other causes.⁴ The softening or breaking up of groups of consonants, the dropping of final consonants, the absence of rigid rules of sandhi, the absence of sounds like ri, s and au,—all this gives to Pali a softness and flexibility for which we may gladly exchange the stately but harsh regularity of Sanskrit.

To the above brief sketch I have only to add that, with the exception of a very few imported Dravidian nouns like chatt and chumba, there is no foreign element in Pali. It is on the whole in the same inflectional stage as Sanakrit, and everything in its vocabulary, grammar and syntax can be explained from the sister tongue. But at the same time it exhibits a remarkable elasticity, a power of enriching itself by throwing out new forms; we may perhaps even detect in it adumbrations of a tendency to pass into a later phonetic stage. What Pali would have become had it run on unchecked in its course of decay and regeneration may be seen from the modern Sinhalese, which springs from an idiom closely allied to Pali, and has long passed into the analytical stage. To a great extent Sinhalese may for practical purposes he viewed as a lineal descendant of Pali, and it has worked out a whole legion of grammatical forms the germs of which may often be detected in Pali, and which make it a rich, though as yet almost unexplored, philological mine.

xvii

It now only remains for me to express my thanks to the friends who have lent me their help and encouragement in my studies, and first of all to Dr. Rost, to whom I have dedicated this work, and but for whom I should never have written a line. I am proud to be able to call myself the pupil and friend of that eminent Palist Mr. V. Paushöll. Towards another Dane, Mr. V. Trenckner, a ripe and graceful Palit scholar, I shall ever entertain feelings of gratitude and respect: from the perusal of no single work do I remember to have derived greater advantage at an early period of my studies than from his masterly edition of the first chapter of Milinda Paña, the manuscript of which (still I regret to say unpublished) was in my hands for several months. I owe a debt of gratitude to my friend Mr. N. Trübner for his enterprise in undertaking the publication of my Dictionary at a time when its success was, to say the least, uncertain; and to my friend Mr. Stephen Austin for the ready zeal with which he has all along seconded my efforts to carry the work quickly and satisfactorily through the press. From three Sinhalese Buddhists I have received valuable contributions in the shape of letters replying to questions on points of scholarship and interpretation. They are, first the priest Dhammārāma of Yātrāmulā, whose premature death in January, 1872, deprived the Buddhist Church of one of its brightest ornaments; next the priest Subhūti of Vaskadavā, well known to European Palists as the able editor of Abhīdhānappadipikā; and lastly the Mudliar L. Corneille Vijésimha, a scholar of much learning and originality. During the progress of this work I have received from almost all communities in Ceylon proofs of sympathy and appreciation, but from none more than the Buddhist clergy, a generous and enlightened body of men, towards whom I am under many and deep obligations.
R. C. CHILDERS.

AND THE MODE OF TRANSLITATION USED IN THIS DICTIONARY.

a w á i t i w u w ú e

w k w kh w g w gh w à

q c w ch w j w jh w n

g t g th w d w dh w v

n t w th w d w dh w n

w p w ph w h w bh w m

w y w r w l w v

w s w h w l w m

Pull has not, like Sanskrit, a character of its own, but in each of the countries in which it is the sacred language of the inhabitants, that is to say Ceylon, Birma, and Slam, it is written in the character of that country. Hence it is usual in Europe to print Pull texts in the Roman character, which possesses the advantages of clearness and simplicity, and, compared with the Devanagari, is inexpensive to print. The few attempts that have been made by European scholars to adapt the Devanagari for Pull printed texts have been decided failures, and it is unlikely that they will be repeated. The transliteration of Pull fortunately presents fewer difficulties than that of Sanskrit. The system I have used in the Dictionary is, with a few modifications, that of Fumball.†

These lezars are pronounced as in Sanskrit. At the present time anusvira is pronounced in Ceylon and Birma exactly like the English and German ng in 'hang.' Thus will is pronounced 'shang,' not as in Sanskrit 'sham.' That this was the ancient Magadhese pronunciation is most probable, as the labial nasal at the end of a word has a strong tendency to pass into the guttural nasal, compare for instance the Latin means with the French non.

In the above scheme of translation it must be remembered that c is pronounced like our ch in church, and f like the Spanish f, or the English of in 'minion.' [In the Preface the ordinary English practice of rendering by cb is followed.] The aspirated letters are strictly speaking double or conjunct letters, being pronounced like the simple letter immediately followed by h. So much is this the case that a Sanskrit th or dh is sometimes broken up in Pall into lab or dah, e.g. id-daht from nd-dh, and in Sinhalese we have even such forms as daikom = dharma. It is a mistake to say that the lingual f and d are pronounced like our t and d; the fact is that our t is about midway between the Sanskrit H and Z, if anything approximating, to my judgment, rather to the former than the latter.

In this dictionary the circumflex over a long vowel is only used to express crashes, e.g. dammitN = dammi titi, additi = addiu tti adkhisi = na akdi. Ellalon is marked in the European way, as ehon's no = ekena dno. The hyphen is used to indicate the vowel bias, e.g. vika-nafradi, to avoid the misapprehension that might result from writing vika-mafradi.

It must, however, be remembered that these alphabets are all modifications of the Devantguri, and be the same percentage; I have used the Devantguri in the above table. Mr. Fausboll has lately become conscious of the mistake he made in adopting a stoping line to mark the long towals, and in his last two works has exchanged it for the

horizontal line. This, however, does not improve matters. as the horizontal line is required for proudly, and it is now universally agreed that in transliterating Sanskrit (and consequently Pali) the sloping line should be reserved for account, the horizontal for proudly, and the circumflex for long vowels.

AJJHATTAM (ado.), Relating to the Individual, within the Individual, internally, subjectively [+], Ajihattam ed bahiddod, within the individual or externally to him (Gog. Rv. 40). B. Loc. 827.

AJJHATTAM, Individual thought; an object of sense; an object for the mind to dwell upon, sphere or province of intent thought [WATAN]. At Ab. 1040 Ajjhatta is explained by "sesantine (S. avasantina), visayas, gomera." The first of these words is said by Clogh to mean "the cost of the understanding, the place from which thoughts originate"; but I am inclined to think that the true meaning is "the thought, or reflection, of the individual." The meaning "thought, reflection" is attributed to santana by Clogh in his Sikhalese Dictionary. Ajjhatta in verse 369 of Dharmapada is explained by the comment "goorajjhatasichikta kamsaffadabhadana," which may, perhaps, be rendered "Karmachana meditation, which consists in the application of the mind to an object of thought."

AJJHATTIKO (adj.), Relatifg or belonging to the individual or self, personal, internal, subjective [wnt+]. Ajihattikanattha, object forming part of the body, as the flesh, the eyes, an arm, etc. Ajihattikanadna, a personal or corporeal gft, e.g. the sacrifice of an eye or arm, as opposed to the sacrifices of external goods. Ajjhatti-knurampam, personal or subjective instrument, e.g. the eye, as opposed to BAdirakurapam, an external instrument, e.g. a sickle (Cl. Gr. 133). B. Intr. 501; Dh. 288, 370, 410. See Ayatanash.

At Ab. 1040 Ajjhatta is explained by "sesantine (S. avasantina), visayas, gomera." The first of these words is said by Clogh to mean "the cost of the understanding, the place from which thoughts originate"; but I am inclined to think that the true meaning is "the thought, or reflection, of the individual." ANBUROHETT (case.), To cause to grow or increase; to make much of, devote oneself to [with + cause]. The exact meaning of the expression is difficult to determine. At Dham. p. 270 the comment explains it vैचकान ब्राह्म्यो एड्ग्हेर्यो प्रसोमपिजो शहारयो, "should increase, augment sedition, should live in the practice of it," whence the phrase would seem to mean "devote oneself to solitude." At Dham. verse 75, Fauboll translates "socessum anget," but Max Müller, "will strive after separation from the world"; and the latter rendering seems to accord with the use of the phrase at Raa. 25, ekonatin sumaye vivekam aansrakheto aradiyatamam podiet, which we might expect to mean "on one occasion yearning for solitude he entered the forest." But at Mah. 39 we have eko "a Ahagagamchi pabbate vidiai satiracadini vivekam aansrakhayash," he dwelt alone for seven years at the Aboginigs roonals, devoting himself to reclusion": here Turnour translates "ludging to pious meditation." See Bradiet.

Here pajiservattabo is explained to refer to the four paseamya, addisindartabbo to bent and cold, pariseajjetabbo to dangerous animals, and shodetabbo to lust, heresy, and other sins. I am disposed to think that apassessions represents + + + + +, and to mean "that which should be observed or had recourse to." The comment says apassendti apasoydis (7), and the Tikā apasayjittabbajhena apasaydis.

ÀPATTI (f), Offence, guilt, sin, crime [wiffl]

Pardijkapatti, and pardijkid dp., a Pirajilka offence (Pát. 68). Thullacoydpatti, a Thullacoydoffence. Apatid appears sometimes to be used adjectively in the sense of "guilty," e.g. yo pubbjeyya dpatid dkhafassa, "he who shall ordain such a one shall be guilty of dukka." (A.W. I. 79), and andapati bhikkhus pardijkasa dpatid dkkafassa, "the priest is not guilty of parijilka, he is guilty of dukka." But in both these examples it is perhaps possible to take apart as a noun ("there is the guilt of d.").

Daazikhattush vijáti pi kho pana saikh vijáti otya aviha-tyobbará heza koi, though she has borne ten children abe is as young looking as if she had been but once a mother (Db. 233). Baisháygrawtudwna dukhhitam pi nasadhipoth dukkhápetush, to afflict the monarch already suffering from his imprisonment (Mah. 260). Uparajjash Mahindasso ddakhdmo pi, though saxloas to confer the viceroyalty on Mahinda (Mah. 36). Bea saxti pi, to epithe of this (F. Ját. 7). Ma kaddi pi, never at all (Mah. 158). Apis ca kha pana, however, nevertheless (F. Ját. 9). With fall, nima, Apí asmo, perhaps (Ab. 1191). Apis adma searkpopi rakkhaso, dhamman jheeyya, perhaps even a rakkhasa like this might be acquainted with the Law (Ras. 21).—When followed by a word beginning with a

vowel, Api sometimes becomes App (Sank. apy), e.g. app-eva-noma, “perhaps.” The initial a of Api is sometimes absorbed by mandhi, as ajjapi= ajia api, etpi= ca api, adpi= na api. The final i is sometimes elided, as sabble pi= sabb pi eta (Msh. 33), tatrip/disin= tatra api/disin. The mutilated form Pi owes its origin to the frequent elision of the initial a in such cases as manusso/pi, ed/pi, sabble/pi. — ARAMBHO, Commencement; exertion, effort; mischief, injury [wifw], Ab. 882. Thépdrambho, commencement of the thúpa (Mah. 174). Andramba, free from mischief or danger (Pit. 4). There are eight Arambhasothisi, “martars or occasions for exertion, or for making an effort,” via. when a priest has a duty to perform, when he has performed a duty, when he has a journey to make, when he has made a journey, etc.

— ARÁMIKO, One employed about the grounds of a

Buddhist temple, a temple servant, gardener, etc.

[$\overline{1}$$\overline{2}$$\overline{3}$$\overline{4}$]. Mah. 239; Pár. 9, 63.

ARAMMANAM, Thai on which anything reats or dwells, a support, stay, beats, ground, cause, material, object; an object of sense; a thought, an idea [wong], Ab. 94, 1132. The six Arammanas, or objects of sense, are repass, exid, grandio, raso, phaso, disammo, "form, sound, odour, taste, contact and ideas"; they are thus identical with the Babies Ayatans, and are the objects of the six Ajihatilka Ayatanas or Senses (Ab. 94). Aramama is also used in a more restricted sense, "the object or material of the mind or of thought," "thoughts," "ideas." At Man. B. 408, Hardy defines Ar. as "thoughts that proceed from contact with sensible objects in the mind" (see also p. 500). Cough in his Simbalese Diet defines Ar. as "being affected, reflection, thought; the subject of thought, that which occupies the mind." Ex. Ifhdramamase admanash visajjved, allowing the mind to dwell on a pleasing object (Dh. 111). Citain adma' riash adramamaseu digharataam cirikos cavantam, that mind of his long wandering in many channels of thought (Dh. 405; comp. in the same page poddish dramameas, dwelling on sinful and unworthy thoughts). Ånavs is synonymous with Kliesa. The three Ånavs are knddesao, bkaedsao, avijjdesao, "the lust of the flesh, the love of existence, and the defilement of ignorance" (B. Lot. 823). Atthāya hīidya sukhāya devanamassadni, for the advantage, the welfare, the happiness of gods and men. Budidassa atthāya jīvitam pariceajāmi, for Huddha's nake I will lay down my life (Kuhn K. S. 29). Apprādayaraṃ atthāya rodassa, crying for something that does not exist (Dh. 06, comp. 120). Hidathāya sukhatthāya ca pāpiḷa, for the welfare and happiness of men (Mh. 88). Ropaatthāya, for the purpose of sowing it (Mah. 97). Upacadmatkeras upadakathāya padiqil, sent Upavāna There for hot water (Dh. 484). Phadphalaṭthāya pasash ma pavisaat, does not enter the forest to gather fruits (Dh. 155). Bādaṭṭhāya, on this account (Kh. 19). Kuhn K. S. 29; Msh. 103; Alw. I. 76.

ATTHENA (adv.), On account of, by reason of [ustr.]. Sabbarogdasia miodenaffhisa-phena rogaidasa, because it is the dwelling place of all diseases it is called rest of disease (Dh. 313). Dh. 90, 210, 311, 343, 383, 416.

ATTHETI, To request [wā]. Cl. P. Verba, 18.

—ATTHI, To be, to exist [wū]. The following is the conjugation: Present, 1. Arai, asht; 9. asri; 3. atthi; 4. aroma, aisha; 5. attha; 6. asanti. Preterite, 1. Aeia; 2. asri; 3. asli; 4. delisha; 5. asitha; 6. arash, delishma. Optative, 1. Aronia; 2. asso; 3. assa, slyá; 4. aesthma; 5. asartha; 6. aero, cigrash. Imperative, 1. Ami; 2. dhi; 3. attha; 4. aroma; 5. attha; 6. aero, astema. Part, present Siaia, aandina (see map). For some of these forms

see Alw. I. 57, 89, 60.—Ex. Atti parolino, there is a future life. Rydt ce atti, if there is a king (Mah. 254). Atte buddho adma n' atthi, there is no other Buddha (B. Lot. 868). Parthman n' atthi, there has been nothing entitled (F. Jat. 7). Tammim unduguse drush orti bhikkulayiga, in that assembly there were eighty kozis of priests (Mah. 88). Bhuttank atthi nu no, have I eaten anything (Mah. 158). Attar dhuzino so al, he was very prosperous (Mah. 200). Ahom ami dato, I have come. Nikkhant's anba, we have come away (Dh. 161). Boam asu vacaniyd, they should be thus spoken to (Pit. 100). Ce tamha asattha dandina, if ye were glad. Capidio nies so siyd, he is probably a Capdila (Mah. 24). Posseslon is frequently expressed by Azhil with the dative; Kaifthakhati me atthi, I have a younger brother (Dh. 79); Samti to evaripd daddid, have you got any such diseases as these? (Kamm. 4); Yass mayi sinsho atthi, he who has love for me (Dh. 833); Mama hirafkiss swappah atthi, I have got gold and wrought gold (Pit. 60); Paidgato to mokkho n' atthi, you cannot escape by flight (Dh. 404). Atti with the dative is sometimes used in the sense of "to think" (comp. the phrase etad ohoni): N' atthi paraloko ti itti ce me asu, if I thought there was a future life. The singular atthi is frequently used with a nominative in the plural; Patta m' atthi, I have sons (Dh. 12). Sace ppakad atthi, if there are insects (F. Jat. 57). Ye keei ppabhati atthi, whatever belongs there he (Kh. 15). In some of the forms elison of the initial a sometimes takes place: patto'omi, I have obtained (Raa. 18); dguto'mhi, I am come (Dh. 88; Ras. 21); samasai'sali, I am a woman (Dh. 155); gato'si, thou art gone (Dh. 97); su'tha= su attha (F. Jat. 8); jito'si= jito dish (Raa. 28); saadd'si= saadd al. On the other hand, before some of the forms beginning with a, the final rowel (whether short or long) of the preceding word is frequently elided: tush'ass= tushil assa (Kamm. 8); dgut'attha = dgatdi attha (Dh. 228); sam'attha= samo attha (Kh. 22).

ATTHI (a.), A home; a kernel or stone of a fruit; a seed [wif], Ab. 278; F. Ját. 13; Kh. 18. Koppdaatthi, a cotton seed (Dh. 301). Used of the stone of a mango (F. Ját. 5). Dh. 27; F. Ját. 15. ATTHI (adj.), Dealrous, wishing for [wif].

Lot. 291; D. 73, 413. Bhavas is one of the links of the Pajicasanappāda. Ab. 177, 768, 807, 1087. Gambhirathava, profundity (B. Lot. 330). Mahabibhav, queen-consortship (Mah. 82). Tittakabhav, bitterness (F. Ját. 6). Bharidya ca putidaṇa ca arogabhadrav pucchi, asked after the health of his wife and children (Dh. 206). Rathassa lahubhavatthash, to lighten the carriage, lit. for the sake of the light state of the carriage (Mah. 203). Majabhavas asampatto, not having attained intoxicating properties, i.e. yet unfermented (Pát. xli). Samsaddiyadabhavan tekan, wishing to be a kinsman of religion, lit. wishing for the state of a kinsman to religion (Mah. 30). Vinicchayaffadam chaddetabbabhavas ppapml, the police court had to be closed, lit. reached the state of having to be closed. — CETOPARIYAÑNAM, and CETOPARIJYAYAÑNAM. The first of these forms is the older. I am disposed to believe that pariya represents the S. y (comp. ekiti = cahyul, majhtmo = madhyama, etc.), so that pariya and pariyaya (y) might very well be used as synonyms. CITTAM, The heart; the mind; a thought, an idea; will, intention [fɪˈvɪŋ]. Ab. 152, 839. Sorrhasa me intarono ma passa citta, you are lord of my body but not of my mind (Dh. 159). Cittahiryd, operation of the mind (Att. 107, 216). Cittais paideti, to have faith in, lit. to cause the heart to rejoice in (Mah. 70: with loc.). Cittapassidaamationa, by faith alone (Mah. 177). Abhijadhi cittodram, ascertain how his mind is disposed (Mah. 246). Thagactiona, with thleviah latent (Kh. 29). Samutthacitto, having a contented mind (Att. 212). Na jadari cittaa elassa, do not you see his object? (Mah. 290). Macchernacitdach sahasawai, a thousand sordid thoughts. Rajjaldahaya cittaompl unappdedod, without giving a thought to receiving the kingdom (Att. 106). Ahas shikkhuisighanis parisianimaiti piapakam cittaus updedod, having conceived the sinful thought, "I will." (Dh. 143, comp. 134). Uparijavaadhaithdya jidacietid niraastarash, continually forming the project of assassinating the sub-king (Mah. 130). Saddikhiakriku spajjhdayumhi pitselittah upaphapeasati, the popl shall look upon his master as a father, lit. "entertain towards his master the idea of father" (Pitt. xx). Gogerty says that as a psychological term "citifial, thoughts, differ from certain, which are thoughts on external objects, whereas the citifian appear to be occupied with lateral impressions, and are identical with the fifth khandha or consciousness" (Friend, Oct. 1838, p. 69). dharmas, having the nature of a man, a mere mortal (Art. 189). Nibbaadhamma, the nature of Nievaqa (E. Mon. 294). Diffho dhamma, the visible condition, the present state of things, this world, this life (E. Lot. 370, comp. Diffhadhamma). Mittadhamma, friendship (F. J4. 13). Sabbar dhammam, in all conditions, in all things (Dh. 63). Asekha dhamad, attributes or properties of a perfected saint (see Asekho). Buddhadhammd, attributes of Buddha (Msh. 108). Sabbarso lokases eadeakassa er'eva dhammo gadidam aniccasi, impermanence is the property (or condition) of the whole world including the devaloka (Att. clxii). The two dhammaes, "conditions" or "qualities," are somathā and vipassand, salm and contemplation (Dh. 69, 188, 425). Firdgo seffho dhamandam, Arhship is the best of conditions or things (Dh. 48). Sabbaṃ saṅkhataṃ dhamand, all things material and immaterial (comp. Dh. 389). Aniced dhamand, transitory things (Das. 9, of the eight lokadhammas). Catidro dhamand dyu vappa sukham balash, four qualities or conditions, age, beauty, happiness and strength (Dh. 20). Ye kecii husaid dhamand sabbe to appamaddamdaikd, all good conditions or qualities have their origin in diligence (Dh. 179). Pdpako dhamma, sin (Sen. K. 322). Pdpakd dhamand, and akumald dhamma, evil states, evil ways, sin (Dh. 43, 371; Sen. K. 319, 322). Ppadhamme, sinful, a sinner (Dh. 54). Pardjiko dhammo, a p. sin (Pit. 85). Tayo dhamand jahid dhamanti sahdyadiffki vieikicchita ca siabbatai ca, three sins or states are cast off (Kh. 9). Hmanis dhamma carati, to follow a low mode of life (Dh. 31). Dhammasi sucariam carati, to live a religious life (ditto). Nattahammo, plous duty to relatives (Kh. 12). Udake hsdahammo, sporting in the water (Pit. 15). Kalydadhammo, virtuous, excellent (Pit. 4). Methuno dhammo, the practice of sexual intercourse. Vasaladhammo, low conduct (Sen. K. 322). Bahmanam dukkhadhammanh paṇikkhato hoti, is exposed to many palatal circumstances. a sermon, to go to church (Db. 308, 366). Dhamma-sikkachd, religious conversation (Kb. 5). Three of the five Khandas, viz. Vedan, Saffis, and Sakkhara are collectively termed dhamad (plur.), "mental faculties," and in the first verse of Dhammapada the commentator takes the word dhamad to mean those three faculties. But this interpretation appears forced and unnatural, and I look upon Dr. Max Müller's translation, "all that we are in the result of what we have thought," as the best possible rendering of the spirit of the phrase manopubbongand dhamad. The meaning evidently is that a man's mental or physical "conditions" or "circumstances" are dependent on the state of his thoughts, or heart, or intentions. Thus, as the verse goes on to say, a man who speaks or acts from a bad heart will be in a condition of suffering or unhappiness. The illustrative stories of Cakkhupala and Matkapupala in the commentary confirm this view, for Cakkhupala's blindness was the consequence of his having acted with evil intent, and Matkapupala's blissful state in the Tāvatihas heaven resulted from his faith (monopassida) in Bodcha. B. Int. 41, 43; E. Mon. 5, 167; Dh. 4, 18, 47, 49, 65, 67.

a sermon, to go to church (Db. 308, 366). Dhamma-sikkachd, religious conversation (Kb. 5). Three of the five Khandas, viz. Vedan, Saffis, and Sakkhara are collectively termed dhamad (plur.), "mental faculties," and in the first verse of Dhammapada the commentator takes the word dhamad to mean those three faculties. But this interpretation appears forced and unnatural, and I look upon Dr. Max Müller's translation, "all that we are in the result of what we have thought," as the best possible rendering of the spirit of the phrase manopubbongand dhamad. The meaning evidently is that a man's mental or physical "conditions" or "circumstances" are dependent on the state of his thoughts, or heart, or intentions. Thus, as the verse goes on to say, a man who speaks or acts from a bad heart will be in a condition of suffering or unhappiness. The illustrative stories of Cakkhupala and Matkapupala in the commentary confirm this view, for Cakkhupala's blindness was the consequence of his having acted with evil intent, and Matkapupala's blissful state in the Tāvatihas heaven resulted from his faith (monopassida) in Bodcha. DHUTANOAM, and DHUTANOAM. The thirteenth Dicalignas are certainly ascetic practices, the observance of which is meritorious in a Buddhist priest. It is not intended that all should be kept at the same time, but of course the more are kept the greater the merit. The word represents the Sanskrit yor or yor + yor, and is explained to mean “precept by which the paselons are shaken or qualled.” The dhutaignas are as follows, parism-kalikrigaas, techarikrigaas, piadapikrigaas, arpadinacdrikrigaas, ekdanikrigaas, pattapiplikrigaas, khalapaechdhattikrigaas, drishikrigaas, rukkhanthikrigaas, obdhokdrikrigaas, saddihongras, yathidanthikrigaas, acajikrigaas (see search sep.). EKAYANAM, The exact meaning of this word (S. U. I am not sure of. Clough in his Shih. Diet. says that it means "the way of Nirvapa." At Pat. xyl we have ekdyaamamaggo, which perhaps means "the only true road to salvation." At Mah. 251 Boddaghsom, after studying the Buddhist Scriptures, says Ekdyaano ayash maggo, which Turnour readers "this is the sale road (to salvation)."

Yodhe dasadas' eheko casatha, seek out each of you ten soldiers (Mah. 144). Ekrekhal landhsi Lomakipesu jadtni, the hairs grow singly in the pores (B. Lot. 571). Ekrekakamaato, successively (Mah. 19, komato = 19). Fem, gen. ekektard (Mah. 163). Mah. 179.

EKIBHAVO, Solitade [qū-tāʾ]. Dh. 387, 407. EKO (adj.), One, single; alone; a, a certain; the same; chief, pre-eminent, unique; general [qū]. Ah. 690, 717, 718, 830. Eko tumheru, one of you (Mah. 89). Ekma'் dno, deficient by one (Mah. lxxvii, comp. Ekēno). Eko pi ndائىنلىقى, not one was able (F. Ját. 5). Ekam pi gótiham nadehi, speak but a single stamam (Ras. 21). Ekabhiikham pi alabhiid, not having received a single means of boiled rice (Dh. 160). Nihass affaim chasaddam pi samamupassdami, I do not know of any one other sound (Dh. 85). Ekashati, one and twenty (Dh. 76). Ekpanādsam, fifty-one (Atw. 1. 104). Ekafisagimo, and ekatimeo, thirty-first (Mah. 193; Ras. 28). Ekapasse, on one side (Ras. 28). Eko 'va, all alone (Mah. 39, 194; B. Los. 332). Eko care, let him walk alone (Dh. 58). Eko ekaya raho nisajjam karryya, should sit secretly alone with her alone (Kam. 37; comp. Ekun amaccah peseri, soot a miulster (Mah. 39). Eko myydnapido digata, a gardener has come (F. Ját. 6). Tasminh kile eho edsijo, at that time a certain merchant (F. Ját. 14). Plor, ehe, some men (Dh. 23; Das. 6). Khori spema, in the same form (Ab. 710). Ekavidhalam akoi, there was a general shout (F. Ját. 17). Gantama, or the Gotamud ecstatic, no doubt because Gantama was the sacerdotal family name of the military race of Cákyas, who being Khatrilyas had no ancestor or totalist salut likes the Beahmans, but might, as the Hindu law permits, have taken the name of the sage to whose family belonged their spiritual guide" (Intr. 155). Clough says, "Gantama, the name of Buddha, which be took from his teacher, a celebrated sage, and supposed by some to be the founder of the芸ay philosophy" (1). It would appear that all the Cákyas of Kapilavasu bore the name of Gautama, so that the phrases Gotama Buddha and Samapa Gotama merely indicated the family from which the Buddha sprang (see B. HEVA (ads.), Quite, just, even. Dh. 225. This is another form of eva (which see). I have met with heva in three passages only, and in each the preceding word ends in a vowel. The first is pupphdmi heva (Dh. 9), the second ashatayobband heva (Dh. 23), the third and heva (Dh. 403). The h is probably like the y in yevra, merely a euphonle addition, but comp. the next article.

HEVAM, In the phrase and N'evank season, "say not so." It is doubtless even preceded by the particle fig. It is true that Hevank occurs in the Dnaull Inscriptions at the beginning of a sentence (comp. Aiw. I. iv), but it is not safe to argue from the Pili of the Inscriptions to that of the sacred books. A phrase and h'evank, "not so," "certainly not," occurs at Gog. Ev. 39, and with this compare so Netash (see Hotash), and perhaps and h'eva (see last article).

IDAM (neut. syraah), This [ᠮᠥᠩn], Idam vadit, spoke as follows (Mah. 170). Idam satthid kothet, this the Teacher said (F. Jt. 1). Adam avoca bhagad, this the Blessed one said. Vattam sabbaam idah, all this has been said (Kh. 21). TeM idanid idah ca vatid, having been told so and so by them (Dh. 180). Idah ca idai co kafresati, will cause such and such things to be made. Idah ca volare, by the byel an exclamation when a thought suddenly strikes one (Att. 100). See Ayarh.

IDAM (adv.), Here, now, even [now]. In the phrase Ekin iddesh samayam, "now I on a certain occasion," there can be little doubt that iddesh is this adverb followed by sham: a comment indeed states positively etike idam el apidassatish; but the virk on the twentieth rule of Kacciyana's Sandhikappa gives it as an example of the change of de to d, resolving it into idha shari (Sen. K. 209; Cl. Gr. 10). Idasi occurs in the words gadidass, tadidam, kimidass, yathayidam, egyadidass. It is possibly also the second part of sayidass in the phrase as-y-idass sukarash oprade qijdeasast, etc., but comp. Db. 163, like 15.
IDÄNI (adv.), Now [ɑːnəˈnɪn]. Sen. K. 308. Idn's son, at this very time, at the present moment (F. Jé. B. 16).
IDAPPACCAYÃ, From an assignable cause, from an ascertained cause [ [ + abl. 1111111111]. At this dispassioned jordensrapont, does deoxy and fethth artist from an assignable cause? Comp. Gog. Ev. 6.

IDATTAYAM, These three [+]. Ab. 100. IDDHI (f), Prosperity, power, majesty; supernatural power, magical power, miraculous faculty; a miracle []. B. Lot. 310, 818; Man. B. 38, 500. There are ten hiddih, each as the power of passing through the air, of taking any form, of creating, or causing to appear (at and from) anything that is required. Iddhi is the peculiar attribute of the Arahia, though it is also possessed by those who have practiced Jhina. Rjiddhidi vrdjonato, resplendent with royal majesty (Mah. 245). Iddhiti elya almanitish, as U created by supernatural means (Mah. 242). Puthijawidid iddhiti, such supernatural power as an unconverted man may possess (Dh. 143, comp. Man. B. 315). Iddhiti parthydited, having fallen away from lddhli, having lost his magical power (Dh. 143). Tush iddhikii sparjdil so dind, the sub-king having seen this miracle (Mah. 34). Nisappatdrid iddhiyo kated, having performed many miraculous acts (Dh. 29). Inatr. iddhiyid, by supernatural power, miraculously (Dh. 35; Mah. 194).
IDDHIMÅ (adj.), Possessed of supernatural power [wifong]. Das. 49; Dh. 249; Mah. 173.
IDDHIMAYO (adj.), Created, or made to appear by supernatural power [ + 124, 315.

supernatural power [ʌnˈtʃɑn+ʌn]. Dh. 124, 315. IDDHIPADO, Constituent or basis of magic power [ʌnˈtʃɑn+ʌn]. There are four iddhipidas, which are means by which iddhii is attained. They are esendo, the will or determination to acquire iddhii, cirryas, the necessary exertion or effort, estias, thought, or the necessary preparation of the thoughts or heart, visomist, investigation. The full text is as follows, outdro iddhipidd, iddhidwao shikkhu chandasamidhipathasawikhadrasamondapatah iddhipidoth shidwoti, cirryasanddhipadhasasakidhrasasamadgotash i. shidwoti, citasanddhipadhadrasasikhadrasasamandgotash i. shidwoti, winakhadpanddhipadhadrasasikhadrasasamadgotash i. Madwoti (Sang. 6.). Here padhona is no doubt used in its Pull sense of “exdion,” but the northern Buddhists, misunderstanding the word, have rendered it by “shandoment,” and so made nonsense of the passage (See B. Int. 625; Los. 810, 311, 312). Att. 57; Max. B. 413, 498; Alw. I. 77; Db. 838.

— INDO, Chief, lord; sking; Indra [], Ab. 20, 860, 1132. Devindo, king of the devra, Indra (Mah. 47). Sakko devdam indo, Sakka the king of the devra (Ras. 21; Du. 185). Indapafo, a statue of Indra (Dh. 194). Manujindo, a king. Leahindo, king of Gaylon (Mah. 07).

— INDRIYAM, An organ of sense; a power, faculty, function, organ; a moral quality; sense, perception, acquisition; sex [f(f)(q)]. Ab. 149, 607. There are three indriys, which are three sorts of knowledge or sense. Firstly, as alliefadichaeans (indri-yani (an-adidites hossedmi ili indriyan)), “the sense which says, I will know what is not known;” this is explained to mean sotapattimagga. Secondly, aisinidriyan (see Aind), “sense of knowledge,” explained to mean the stages from sotapattimagga to arabattimagga. Thirdly, as alididisindriyan (aaddid), comp. huddi), “sense of having thoroughly known,” explained to mean arabattiphalas or Arhatship. The five indriyan or moral qualities (paicindriyan or posee's indriyal) are suchindriyan, striyindriyan, satindriyan, somadhisindriyan, paisindriyan, faith, energy, recollection, contemplation, wisdom (Att. 58; Man. H. 488; comp. Balash). Another set of five are the five organs of sense, eakikhadriyan, sotidriyan, ghadindriyan, jiokhadriyan, latindriyan, the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the sense of touch. A third set of five are five faculties or sensations, sukhidriyan, dakkindriyan, soma-sopindriyan, dosmonastudriyan, wypekhindriyan, ease, suffering, joy, grief, indifference. The six indriyan are, cakkhadindriyan, sotidriyan, ghad

sindriryark, jivihindriyan, kdyindriyan, matindriyan, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, touch, mind (Man. B. 439, 439; Dh. 111, 429). The twenty-two Indriyan, or principles, are cakhmadriyan, soti-driyan, ghdindriyan, jichindriyan, kdyindriyan, masindriyan, ithindriyan, puridindriyan, jilindindriyan, sukhindriyan, dushkhindriyan, sommasindriyan, dosmasindriyan, mpekhindriyan, saiddhidriyan, viriyindriyan, satindriyan, sandhidhidriyan, palindridiran, amandirian, fandini and indiriyan, affindiriyan, alhididindriyan (see Ceylon Friend, Oct. 1838; I have copied the list from Visuddhi Magga).—Indiriyanjaro, subjugation of the senses (Aix. 193). Indiriyagatti, keeping watch over the senses, self-restraint (Dh. 67, 422). Indiriyavidra, perturbation of the senses, excitement, emotion (Dus. 3). Indiriyaman bhivand, and Indiriyahdoand, cultivation or production of the five moral qualities (vir. saddha, viriyas, etc., see Alw. I. I.ix). Tkhisiandriya, one whose organs of sense are keen; madindriya, one whose senses are dull (B. Lot. 808). Dh. 2, 122.

—IRIYAPATHO, Way of deportment [kɑːt + wɑː]. There are four Iriydpathas or postmen, vib. walking, standing, sitting, lying down. Colum irlydpathen viryukarapamshrakito, devoid of energy in all the four positions, viz. In all he does (Dh. III). Iriydpatha Nagacmasa paiditod, pleased with the deportment of Nagacma. Iriydpathasampama, of decent deportment (B. Lot. 297). Iriydpathato mattore arhatton apdpsel, atained arbatship without any of the four usual postures; by this is meant that Ananda at the moment of attaining sanctification was neither sitting, nor standing, nor walking, nor lying down, but in the act of placing himself on his coach; I quote the following from Brahma Jala S. Aith., catertriypathavritakam therasa arhatton, tena imasmih sdesse “entprano envismo affahito acokumanto ko bhikkhu arhatton patto” it evite “Ananda thero” ti vattam vattati (B. Lot. 290, 297; Mah. 13).

ITI

III, and TI, and before a vowel ICC (odc.), Thus [WtT]. Ab. 1158, 1189. This particle is very extensively used in Pill, as in Sanskrit, in cases of indirect narration, or of ennumeration, or of quoting the words or thoughts of others; the full are examples. Manh sandhduya bdaasati fatad, perceiving that he spoke of him, lit. perceiving thus "He speaks of me" (F. Jt. 19). Siko ti saondya, thinking it was a lion, lit. thinking thus "It is a hon" (F. Jt. 15). "Bukhimyad him etan" it paechi, asked her, "Where are you going, what have you got there?" (Mah. 59, comp. F. Jt. 12). "Agind me aitho" ti dho, he said, "I want fire" (F. Jt. 2). Rajosau H c�jula, finding that it was silver (Mah. 167). Ambaphalan ti auted, hearing it was "a mango" (F. Jt. 5). No sechatiti zadusa, finding he was unwilling (Mah. 132). Tattha "abbitharsthti" turitash turtash agham algahs kareyyati attho, here as regards the word abhittha-rtha its meaning is, "Let him act very quickly, very speedily" (Dh. 292). Bittha "sahiton" ti tripokana's Buddhavaense's etam adasm, in this passage the word sahtita is a name for the Buddhist scriptures (Dh. 150). "Ava" Lee etassa okarddeno hoti, the letter o becomes a substitute for ava (Sen. K. 234). Tumu Cuilapalo ti adanak hatod, having called him Callapila (Dh. 78; comp. Ran. 15). Mahaprtes o tccati, is called "a great man" (Dh. 63). Rattakkhi iti vicinto, known as "The Red-eyed" (Mah. 230). Buddha ti vacana rattamati, at thomere sound of the word "Buddha" (A.w. 1. 97). Tatditi vacanena, hearing himself addressed as "Tissa" (Mah. 78). Hatthajdanyyo navjitaayyo mabbidjanyyo khipdeao ti tse catibro phapetod, setting aside these four, the high-bred elephant, the high-bred horse, the high-bred bull, and the Arhat (Dh. 296). Sometimes in an example like the last the noun preceding it is in the same case as that which follows it, e.g. Tsumaha Nigadipake ti cehasi otadresu pakdron ca akdrayi, at these six monasteries, the Tissa monastery, the Nigadipaka monastery, etc., be built an including wall (Mah. 297). Sometimes the verb of saying, thinking, etc., is put first: "Twa' dha Magard" acijfawata loko" ti, therefore has Boddhus said, "The world is shrouded by ignorance" (A.w. 1. 108); "Lakhted" rjjadhidti" ti, inscribing theen on the words "A King's Daughter" (Mah. 131); "Apposi comidpatish" "adroht pitavans me"

It, he ordered the commander-to-chief thus, "Put my father to death" (Mah. 261); Rājdā nasī puchehī "kiāh" iti, the king asked him, "What is this?" (Mah. 157); Rājdīīī Ḵicītāyāʾ "addīhā' yām edma-pero me ghare heusari afmīka," the king thought thus, "This novice will certainly one day be master in my house" (Mah. 23). Frequently a participle "saying," "thinking," etc., is understood: "Udakaṃāko" #1 clearati, goes about (saying) "Water-crane" (Alw. I. xxi); Kākhīi "needense there sildeyya no kho" ti, doubted whether the then would sit on a high seat, lit. doubted (saying) thus, "I wonder if the then would sit on a high seat (Mah. 89); "Tāto pi adkhil ad" ti pabbqijāh yōw rocayī, he resolved on being admitted to the priesthood (saying), "It is superior to the other profession" (Mah. 38); "Sādhāti" bhasejjāḷi samādāhi, said "Very well," and prescribed for her (Dh. 89, comp. 171, and P. Jil. 12); Bhāntā Cakkhupādathāero "sānika-māmi" bāhuāpāka adrīzi, Lord, C. Thurā thinking he would walk up and down has killed a great many lineets (Dh. 88). The following are instances of double quotation: Rājdā, "guechathā tūmādkhāh rājdōmā maṇa vacaṇeā paṇappāna drogāym paṣchītd 'rājdī taṇakhi saddāhi saṭṭabikāmaṇi techāṭti" eadakhīi, "dho, the king said to them, "Go now, and having in my name repeatedly asked your king after his health, say to him, 'The king wishes for friendship with you'" (Alw. 1.7); Bāhkkhā dhāshurā thārassa taṃ dhamasakātpurāsh, "hāhi bhāma āpatthavabito kātuṃ sāanapaggahōm" iti cutis makārāja thēru āhitī so" (li, the priests told him what would induce the then to come, (saying) "Great king, the then will come if you say to him, 'Vouchers, venerable man, to be my support in restoring the faith'" (Mah. 40). Twice in Mah. I find iti placed within the sentence quoted: Diṭṭhā pifṭīti evrīma, saying, "We have seen the last of our enemy" (Mah. 291); "Pajicca-kamwam w'atthīī kīliṭḥam cetumasa vīdu" thēro bodhisat rājānā, the then informed the king, "There can be no guilt without a sinful intention" (Mah. 41). Sometimes iti may be rendered by "namely": Sādkhāfijasastathāsh satākhāsh dāṭupājsam tec addhandāsh kheperot, having passed a whole fortnight, namely a week of solenam jubilam and a week of homage to the relics (Mah. 11); Tassa nūrajsh vīthmalaṃ dhamasakātpurāsh

nirodhadhammas ti, he received the pure and spotless Eye of the Law, viz. the knowledge that whatsoever has an origin has also an end (see Dhawmacakkhu). Is the tenth book of Khuddakan/kāya, and contains five hundred and fifty "jakakas," or tales of the former bluffs of Buddha. These tales, which are placed in the mouth of Buddha, all contain a moral, a warning, or an example, and in each the Bodhisattva plays the best and most prominent part. Jādakash is also one of the nine Aigues, or divulkans of the Buddhist scripturee according to subject, it includes the five hundred and fifty Jādakhas—Jātakhas ca tatth' eos daun, there also were depicted jakakas, via. illustrations of the jakaka stories (Mah. 164). Devadattam rabbha bhāttāni sabbhāti jātakhas, all the jakakas told about Devadattas, vis. all in which D. is represented as playing a part, e.g. the Javasaknapjātaka, in which D. was the ungrateful lion (Dh. 130, see F. Jét. 12). Puñadāddhikāmi pañoqiditakaatāni, five hundred and fifty jakakas. B. fut. 61; E. Mon. 170; Man. E. 08 and foll.; Alw. I. 61; Mah. 74.

JHÂNAM, Meditation, contemplation; religious meditation or abstraction of the mind, mystic or abstract meditation, ecstasy, trance [WT].

Ab. 171. Jhâma is a religious exercise productive of the highest spiritual advantage, leading after death to re-birth in one of the Brihma heavans, and forming the principal means of entrance into the four Parts. The four Jhâmas are four stages of mystic meditation, whereby the believers' mind is purged from all earthly emotions, and detached as it were from the body, which remains plunged in a profound trance. The priest desirous of practising Jhâma retires to some excluded spot, seats himself crosslegged, and shutting out the world, concentrates his mind upon a single thought. Gradually his mind becomes filled with a supernatural ecstasy and serenity, while his mind still reasons upon and investigates the subject chosen for contemplation; this is the first Jhâma. Still fixing his thoughts upon the same subject, he then frees his mind from reasoning and investigation, while the ecstasy and serenity remain, and this is the second Jhâma. Next, his

Thoughts still fixed as before, he diverts himself of ecstasy, and attains the third Jhāna, which is a state of tranquil serenity. Lastly, he passes to the fourth Jhāna, in which the mind, exalted and purified, is indifferent to all emotions, alike of pleasure and of pain. The full is the full text of the four Jhāna: Ikh'dema bhikkha elivice' evaṃkamaṃ elivicea akusalaṭṭh dhammahi savitakhamā saీvedraṃ elivicānaṃ pitirukhānaṃ paṭikamājiṃ maśapasampajja viharati; elivicakavicīdrāmaṃ upasamāda ajīkhattāsh saispandāsmā cetao ekodibhidāmaṃ avatakhamā avidraṃ samādājajāpiilmakhāmi dhtigayjjhāmaṃ upasampajja viharati; pitiyāda evaṃdgi spekkāmaṃ paṭiratiṃ saṃ campajādo sukhāri ca kāyena paṭisaumecdell yan taṃ ariyā dicikkhamā ti upaṃkāho saṭīndī vihakavīdhāti ti tatiyajhidmaṃ upasampajja viharati; sukhassa ca paṭand dukkhassa ca paṭand pubbe ca samanassāda manasamā vihagumā adikkhāmi arukhāmi spekkāsiṭpdrissiddhā coatthajjhidmaṃ upasampajja viharati. They are summarized thus: Vitakma vichraptisaṃ khecaggadaṃ tiham paṭhamājiṃ maśapasampajjhi, pitirukhēkaṃ gagdaṃ tiham dushiyajhidmaṃ, sukhakgagdaṃ hitaṃ atiyajhidmaṃ, spekkakaggattamā catutthajjhidmaṃ. Each of the first three Jhāma is subdivided into three, the inferior, the medial, and the perfect contemplation (paṭakamajhidmaṃ parittash, paṭhamajhidmaṃ maqīkhāma, paṭikamajhidmaṃ paṭitam, dushiyajhidmaṃ paṭitam, and so on). Those who have exercised Jhāma are reborn after death in one of the first eleven Rūpa Brahma beavens, the pardoular heaven being determined by the degree of Jāṃasa stalled. Those who have only reached the initial contemplation of the first Jhāma are reborn in the Brahmapلام্বāja heaven, the medial contemplation of the same Jhāma secures admission to the Brahmapழo-bita heaven, while the perfect contemplation is an introduction to the Malidbrahma beavens. Thus the three lowest Rūpa Brahmalamakas are peopled by those who have stalled the first Jhāma. The next three are peopled by those who have stalled the second Jhāma, the next three by those who have attained the third Jhāma, and the tenth and eleventh (Vehaphala and Asadbasarta) by those who have attained the fourth Jhāma. Lastly, he passes to the fourth Jhāna, in which the mind, exalted and purified, is indifferent to all emotions, alike of pleasure and of pain. The full is the full text of the four Jhāna: Ikh'dema bhikkha elivice' evaṃkamaṃ elivicea akusalaṭṭh dhammahi savitakhamā saీvedraṃ elivicānaṃ pitirukhānaṃ paṭikamājiṃ maśapasampajja viharati; elivicakavicīdrāmaṃ upasamāda ajīkhattāsh saispandāsmā cetao ekodibhidāmaṃ avatakhamā avidraṃ samādājajāpiilmakhāmi dhtigayjjhāmaṃ upasampajja viharati; pitiyāda evaṃdgi spekkāmaṃ paṭiratiṃ saṃ campajādo sukhāri ca kāyena paṭisaumecdell yan taṃ ariyā dicikkhamā ti upaṃkāho saṭīndī vihakavīdhāti ti tatiyajhidmaṃ upasampajja viharati; sukhassa ca paṭand dukkhassa ca paṭand pubbe ca samanassāda manasamā vihagumā adikkhāmi arukhāmi spekkāsiṭpdrissiddhā coatthajjhidmaṃ upasampajja viharati. They are summarized thus: Vitakma vichraptisaṃ khecaggadaṃ tiham paṭhamājiṃ maśapasampajjhi, pitirukhēkaṃ gagdaṃ tiham dushiyajhidmaṃ, sukhakgagdaṃ hitaṃ atiyajhidmaṃ, spekkakaggattamā catutthajjhidmaṃ. Each of the first three Jhāma is subdivided into three, the inferior, the medial, and the perfect contemplation (paṭakamajhidmaṃ parittash, paṭhamajhidmaṃ maqīkhāma, paṭikamajhidmaṃ paṭitam, dushiyajhidmaṃ paṭitam, and so on). Those who have exercised Jhāma are reborn after death in one of the first eleven Rūpa Brahma beavens, the pardoular heaven being determined by the degree of Jāṃasa stalled. Those who have only reached the initial contemplation of the first Jhāma are reborn in the Brahmapلام্বāja heaven, the medial contemplation of the same Jhāma secures admission to the Brahmapழo-bita heaven, while the perfect contemplation is an introduction to the Malidbrahma beavens. Thus the three lowest Rūpa Brahmalamakas are peopled by those who have stalled the first Jhāma. The next three are peopled by those who have stalled the second Jhāma, the next three by those who have attained the third Jhāma, and the tenth and eleventh (Vehaphala and Asadbasarta) by those who have attained the fourth Jhāma. The remaining five Rāpabrahmalokas are peopled by those who have entered the third Parbh (Anāgāmimaggya, see Bāṅmi). The attainment of the fourth Jhāma

KAL

KALO (adj.), Low, soft, indistinct [adj]. Ab. 137. KALO, Time; right time, due season; meal time; death [adj]. Ab. 404, 1682. Gacchante, Idle, as time goes on, in course of time (Alw. 1. cvil, 74). Uttarakido, future time (Ab. 86). Kaladdahُam, time and distance (Sen. K. 342, see Addendum). Ettakao, all this time (Dh. 123; Mah. 246). Taomim, Idle, and tema Idlema, at that time (F. Jat. 18; Sen. K. 359). Páha-maahdaigiltikde, at the time of the first great rehearsal, Dhammaim impoate kijam oitindmeti, spends his time in hearing the Low. Klayutta, timely, appropriate (F. Jat. 19; kdayittah at Alw. 1.92 seems to be an adv. meaning "for a time, temporarily"). Attano vacomakle appatte, when the time for him to speak has not come (F. Jat. 50). Yaddahkilou apekkhauto, waiting for the right time to begin the campulgo (Mah. 64). Kdie akde, id, in season or out of season (F. Jat. 50). Kdlockam, a gift given at a particular season (E. Mon. 62). Kdima, klam, from time to time (Dh. 153; Alw. N. 36). Klaza'ca ufjhaya, having risen between (Pst. xx). Low, Idle and lastr. kdena, at the right time, in due season, in due course (Mah. 23, 46, 70, 198; Kh. 5). The loc. kile at the end of a compound may often be rendered by "when": Attano corakile, when he was a robber, lit. at his time of being a robber (Mah. 209); Tasa, daharkide, when he was an infant, in his infancy (Ras. 72, Alw. I. vii); Tasa, bahigarakide, when he was gone out (Dh. 300); for other examples of this consideration see Dh. 60, 68, 176, 180, Dua. 3. Mayd lakhdakdila paffhya, ever since I go it, lit. from the time it was obtained by me (Dh. 109). Upardjana, pabbqjikdila to pa-ahmi, ever since the sub-king embraced the sacerdote life (Mah. 36). Klam droeti, and bhatakdla droceti, to give notice that a meal is ready, to announce a meal (Bl. Lot. 362; Mah. 7). Dinner seems to have been announced by merely saying kdo, "It is dinner-time." Klam ghati, to sound the call of refection, to proclaim in a loud voice that the priests' meal is ready (Mah. 167, 195). Dhammaim oavomakdlah or dhammakdloa ghati, to sound the church call, to proclaim that it is time to hear the Law (Mah. 81). Klam karoti, to die (F. Jat. 2; Dh. 08; Alw. I. xlv). Kdakhiriyd, death, Kdakato, dead (perhaps also klam, kato or kdakikato, see Dua. 30).

KÀI O (adj.), Black, dark blue, dark [wūng]. Ab. 90. Fem. kāfi, kājd. Kājapahkhō, the dark or moonless fortnight of the month (Ab. 74). Kāfa-kōhile, the black cuckoo (F. Ját. 40). Huh kāfoh nādhu wūkdiwappam, pray is it black, or is it blue, or some other bright colour? (Dh.193). Frequently spelt kôla; for kōja see Dh. 102 (kūjiyakihipi), 118, 140, 232 (kūjiya), 340 (kūjakihpi), Ab. 302, 461, 641, 657; at Mah. 16, 19, 21, the Iud. Off. MS. reads Kūjifooka.
KALUSIYAṄ, Pollution, obscuration [ᠮᠥᠩᠭᠥ], Att. 102.
KALUSO (adj.), Polluted, turbid, impure [adj. Ab. 600. Next. kalusak, impurity, sin (Ab. 1103; Alw. I. 111).

KALYÃO, and KALLANO (adj.), Fortunate, blest, happy; beautiful, charming, pleasant; good, virtuous [ἀγαθὸ]. Ab. 694, 1074; Sen. K. 518. Neut. kalydram, a virtuous action, virtue, a beauty or charm (Ab. 88; Dh. 21). The paisa kalydram, or five feminine charms, are kassakalydam, maushak, affihik, charik, voyak, fine hair, red lipa, pearly teeth, a blooming complexion, and youth (Dh. 233; Man. B. 231). Ma mark dysamanto hinci acoacttha kalydram od pdpakami od, do not, etc., say anything to me, good or bad (Pit. 5). Kalydra smito, and kalydramito, a good companion, a virtuous friend (Dh. 14, 67, 272, explained by sappartia). Kalydramito sometimes has the technical or semi-technical meaning of "spiritual counsellor" (see B. Int. 284). Thus the kassakafthmoddyaka is called kalydramito; and I find the full, quoted as Buddha's words, maash ki Ananda kalydramittam dgamma jididhamma sattid jidiyd parimmccanti, "for by coming to me as their spiritual guide, Ananda, beings subject to re-birth are released from re-birth."

KALYATA  $ (f_{*}) $, State of being ready [ + 11].

Cittakalyut, planey of the heart, readiness of

the heart to receive the truth (Tea Jit. 16).
KAM, see Ka.
KAM, Water; the head [w]. Ab. 601, 1198 (it may be used as an indeclinable).
KAMABHAVO, Sexual existence, Le, existence in the Kamaoka or world of sense [+]. The eleven Kamaibhavas are existence or birth in the eleven Kamaolkas (Man. B. 445; E. Mon. 808).

KAMACCHANDO, Wish for sexual enjoyment

[ɑːrɪn + ɑːrɪŋ]. See Nardapais.
