39). Kamamash koroti, to work, to labour (Dh. 800, 422). Kamamashi akarada, were hard at work (Mah. 153). Kamamakuropadi, work, service, labour (comp. kamakidro). Hatthakumawai, manual labour (Dh. 198, 237). Kamamodi dredpated, having caused the works to be commenced (Mah. 103). Kated kamadai citwidi dukkaradai, having executed many difficult works of art (Mah. 242). Ayokamawai, ironwork (Mah. 152). Suddhakamawai, clunam work (Mah. 250). Pejiakamawai karati to practise as a physician (Dh. 80). Balikamawai, making offerings to spirits (Mah. 59). Kamamai is an ecclesiastical term, meaning an act, or function, or ceremony performed by a chapter of priests. These kammas are of two sorts, gapakamawai, an act performed by two or three priests, and smighakamawai, an act performed by four, five, ten, or twenty priests. Thus we have spasothakamawai, the act of general confession, spasompadikamawai, the rite of origination, abdhakamawai, apalokusakumawai, and many others (see Pit. x, 69 and fol.). See Kamamovied. Dhamnikamah kamamawai chaudad, dated having given his consent to orthodox ecclesiastical acts (Pit. 18). Kammappatin, attending the ceremony (Pit. 9). As a religious technical term the word kamamai is of great importance, the doctrine of Kamma, or the efficacy of good and bad works, being inseparably bound up with that of transmigration or renewed existence. Every being who is not immediately qualified for Nirvipa by the attainment of Arhatship is necessarily reborn after death to another world, and what that world is, and his state thereid, depends on his kamma or actions in previous existences. Broadly stated the doctrine is that the present condition of every soulment being is determined by the aggregate of its actions in previous states of existence. Sometimes a good or bad action meets with its appropriate reward immediately and in the same existence, sometimes to the next existence, but its consequences may be indefinitely delayed, and an action performed countless ages ago may be working for a man's good or evil at this moment. Works are of three sorts, kusakakamawai, good works or Merit, akamakamawai, evil deeds or Demerit, and cyokakamawai, indeterminate or neutral actions, i.e. such as are either meritorious nor demeritious, and therefore have no influence
### KAN

on the future state of their agent. The actions of a being are the cause of its rebirth, and consequently of its continued existence, and hence the whole existing universe of sentient beings has its origin in Kamma. The cessation of existence can only be obtained by the destruction of its cause, Kamma. And this destruction is effected by Sancificalion, viz. entrance into the four Paths, and especially the fourth, Arthoship, after entrance into which Kamma is immediately and wholly extinguished, the Arbat when he dies causing to exist (see Maggu). It will be seen from the above that Kamma has at least three shades of meaning: first it is merely an action good or bad; then the effect of that action, the merit or demerit which lives on after the action has been performed; lastly, viewed as an abstraction, it becomes a potent Cause or Energy, whereby the multitudinous beings that people the universe are brought into existence. Sangiti S. enumerates four Kamma, kamman kapham kophavipdhami, kamman sukkah sukkahupdhami, kamman kaphasakkhah kaphankkhahupdham, kamman akaphah sukkah sukkahupdham, sukkahupdham, sukkahupdham, sukkahupdham, sukkahupdham, and actions which have a bad result, good actions which have a good result, mixed actions which have a mixed result, neutral actions which have no result. Deeds are of three sorts, kdyakamman or action, oackamman or speech, mopakamman or thought; all three originate to stand or the will (Man. B. 266, 267). There are eleven sorts of Kamma or moral merit, diffadhammavedamyakammam, Karma manifesting itself in this life, appajjavedamyakammam, Karma manifesting itself in the next existence, apardiparyavedamyakammam, Karma manifesting itself at a period subsequent to the next excellence, yaddasamakammam, appljahakammam, apathamhahakammam, etc. (Man. KAMMATTHANAM, Beats of action [ᠰᠠᠭᠠᠨ + ᠪᠷᠠᠭ]. This term is applied to certain religious exercises or meditations, by means of which Samsdhl, Jhins and the four Parbs are attained. Each of these is based on a certain formula or rite, also called kammattham. Alabaster says, "Kammattham is one of the modes of Boddhat meditation, and may be called analytical meditation. He who exercises is first his mind on any one element, and reflects on it in all its conditions and changes, until, so far as that element is concerned, he sees that it is only unstable, grievous, and illusory. To aid this kind of meditation there are formulas, some people incorrectly call them prayers, in which a list of the elements is repeated" (Wheel of the Law, 206). The ten Asubhas are given as follows: uddhu madtakam, vinilahah, opudbakam, viechiddakam, vikkhdyitakam, vikkhitfukah, katavikkhittakam, lohitakam, pulavaah, afikham. The ten Anussatis are buddhismati, dhammadmasati, nishidmusasi, rildmusati, odgmusati, decaldmusati, marapmasati, ktyagutati, dadpmasati, wpasammusati. The four Brahmaivikras are metti, karupd, madita, spekkha. The tour Aruppas are dhadmadaikydatanah, vihidpaiidyaatanah, dkincaifidyaatanah, mvasasifidindimidyaatanah. The Safida is dһире paikkulasaimid, and the Vavatthina is casmadhatawasthamam. Ten of the forty Kammaqlianas, via the two last and eight of the Aussatis (hayagata sati and dadpmasati being accepted), are productive of Upacira, the remainder are productive of Appani. See E. Mon. 267, 269, for a full account of the dadpmasati-kammaqliamah, which exercise consists in fixing the mind intently on one's own breathing in connexion with cerials set subjects of reflection (sixteen in number). The aridhakammaifidak is described at E. Mon. 268, and consists in contemplation of the impurity of the body as illustrated by the sight of a putrefying corpus. The formula for karmasthina, and instructions for practising the rise, are obtained from the skariya or spiritual teacher, who in this capacity is called kammaifidmaddiyao, and must be a kaly�damitto, viz. either he must be walking in one of the four Paths, or if he be a puthujana he must be of eminent plenty and learning. The person who obtains karmasthina from his skariya is said kammaifidam, gakhi or eggaheti, "to receive" or "to learn it."—Ex. Saittha sonNha kammaifidam gakhet, having obtained instruction in karmasthina from the Teacher (Dh. 196, 210, 328). Tathagatma disass dhtikammaifidam, the Dhatu karmasthina gives him

by Buddha (Dh. 125, this must be the exhalad-tuvaatthasa). Kammaftham add theo pabb-jeted yathdrakam bdoamam asuyanjauto aelrema mahdmati sotdpatiphalam patto, the elder having admitted him to the priesthood duly taught him karmasthina, and devoting himself to its reall-sion the high-minded youth are long attained the same tification of the first Path (Mah. 39). Iti pi so bhagavd sammdeambuddho ti dlikam budikha dhammaarighdmausatikammaffhasah niifhya, having gone through the formulas of medication on Buddha, his Law and his Church, beginning with the formula "Behold the Blessed One endowed with true and supreme knowledge" (Dh. 346). Kammaftham me kathethath ath' asa suthd yava arahatid kammafthasam katheri, "teach me karmasthina," and Buddha taught him the karmasthina rites up to Arhatship, viz. taught him all the rites by which mystic meditation is produced, up to the highest and most difficult of all, the successful exercise of which results in the attainment of Arhatship (Dh. 80, comp. 196). Mar-fakmaafthahah bdivento, exercising mirage-meditation, i.e. meditating on the resemblance of the body to a mirage (Dh. 210). Kammaftham's asuyadjati, to practise k. (Dh. 394). Kammaftham's manasikarochi, to devote oneself to k. (Dh. 175, comp. 423). Kammafthne kammah karonto, exercising himself in k. (Dh. 422). From all the above it will be seen that kammaftham is a term of wide significance, embracing a succession of rites and exercises, which form the basis or frame-work of all those modes of mystic meditation by means of which sanetification is attained. Thus, to give an instance, the first Jham is a state, the ten Asabbas with kdyagald saft, are the kammafthane, "rite," or "practice," by which that state is sal-lulud. E. Mon. 353-373; Alw. I. xxi, 88; Dh. 151-339. See drammam.

proved by a k, and so on. The fol. specimen of a kammavdi 1 take from Brihna Jala 8. Aṭṭakala: Sundra me dvarā evigho, yadi evighassa pattakailank saṅgho tindāi pañca bhikkhuṣatāti samamneyya Rājaqahe vassām vassant dhammañ ca vimayaṃ ca saṅgyattun na āśnehi bhikkhāti Rājagahe vassām vassitābin ti, ed fatti : sandtu me dvarā evigho, imāni pañca bhikkhuṣatāti samamnaṭṭī Rājagahe ... vassabba ni, yaṃ dyaṃato khamati imesāni pañcaṃnati bhikkhuṣatāniṃ samnati Rājagahe ... vassabba ti so tuṭā' asso, yasa no kikkwati so bhāsyya; samatāni saṅghena imāni pañca bhikkhuṣatāni Rājagahe vassām vassant dhammañ ca vimayaṃ ca saṅgyattun na āśnehi bhikkhāthi Rājagahe vassām vassitābin ti : khamati saṅghassa tarud tuṭā' exam etah dhrayāmi, "Let the assembly hear me, if all is ready for taking the vote let the assembly decide whether these five hundred priests shall spend the rally season at Rājagula and rehearse the Doctrine and Discipline, and whether all other priests shall be precluded from passing the rally season at Rājagaha, such is the resolution I have to propose. Let the assembly hear me, the modon is that these five hundred priests shall, etc.; those who are in favour of the motion are to keep silence, those who are against it are to speak. (I now proceed to put the question) Does the assembly decide that these five hundred priests shall spend the rally season at Rājagaha and rehearse the Doctrine and Discipline, and that no other priests shall be allowed to pass the rally season at Rājagaha? The assembly approves the resolution, it therefore keeps alliance, so I understand your wish. The above form is used at all Kammavdi, see Kamm, 6, 7, Res. 69, 89. Kammavdi karotti, or sāfieti, to hold a k., to propose a resolution (Pit. 30). A Kammavdi is of two sorts, hatidutiyā, where the question is put to the assembly once, as in that given above, and fotticatutid, where the question is put three times, as in the ordination service.

Anakbeynyakappa contains twenty Antarakappa, an Antarakappa being the interval that elapses while the age of man increases from ten years to ten asakheyya, and then decreases again to ten years; this period is of immense duration, see Yugam. A Kappa is either sufakkapp, in which there is no Buddha, or sufakkapp or buddha kappa, in which one or more Buddias appear. There are five sorts of Anakibakappa, sdrakapp in which one Buddha appears, maddahapp in which two appear, varakapp in which three appear, sdramakibakapp in which four appear, and Shaddakapp or mahabbaddakapp in which five appear. The present kappa is a Bhaddakappa; of its five Buddhas four have appeared, viz. Kakamuratho, Kondagamano, Kassapo, and Goramo (Cikyamuni), the fifth Mettegyo has yet to appear. By the word Kappa standing alone a Mahakkappa is meant. The interval of time which elapses between one Buddikappa and the next varies from one Mahakkappa to so vast a number as an asakheyya of Mahakkapp. The names of the last twenty-seven Buddhas are preserved. Of these the four first, Tashankaro, Medhankaro, Sarasankaro, and Dipaskaro, belonged to a Sammapdakappa the date of which was four asakheyya of Mahakkapp plus a hundred thousand Mahakkapp ago. Dipankaro, the last of these four, was the first of the twenty-four Buddhas (see Buddha). Since his kappa there have been eleven Buddhakappas, the present one being the eleventh. The interval between Dipankaro's kappa and the next Buddhakappa was one asankheyya of Mahakkapp (Sahmakapp). Twenty-nine Suhakkappas elapsed between the present kappa and the last Buddhakapp, which was a Mardakappa of two Buddhas, Sikh and Vemash. Kappasataahakaddhhkini estidi asakheyydai, four asankhayya of Kappas plus a hundred thousand (Dh. 79). Ehatimes to kappa, in the thirty-first kappa from Dla time (Ras. 29). It does asankikapp, ninety-two kappa ago (Dh. 127). Man. B. 1, 5-8, 25-36, 94-97; Dh. 116, 128, 287; Mab. xxvii, xxii, xxiii, 80; Ras. 15; B. Lot. 314, 324-329.

Kasalukmasolahammakarapan, dolng right and wrong actions (Da. 69). Thópasoo karopoo, building the Dagoda (Mnh. 107). Ifhalakharapook, brick-making (Ditto). Okdeakarapoo, making room. Abhisapakarapah, renovation. Karapah is the name of the instrumental relation (see Krahash).

KARANAM, Motive, cause, reason, means; thing, matter, case, event, substance; destruction [ᠲᠠᠠᠭᠠᠨ]. Ab. 91, 1187. Kīn su kho karapam, what can be the reason? (Dh. 213). Kīn su kho etika kōrapam, what can be the cause of this? (F. Jii. 6). Tutti's diganassakrapam, the object of her coming there (Mah. 121). Aparam pi kōrapam otiM, and I have another reason beides (Dh. 234). Tena kōrapama, for this reason, on this account (Dh. 393, comp. 898, 407). Kena kōrapama, on what account? (Dh. 348). Nihon enfima karapama gadi, this was my sole object in going (Dh. 249, comp. 238). Inan kōrapam nedeikht, did not tell me this matter (Dh. 212). Brithamara ekam to kōrapam kahemi, Brnhim, I have somewhat to tell thee (Dh. 163). Tutha kōrapam partyesitabdom, then the matter is to be investigated. Kroasan te fidam agamane mayd, your case became known to me as I approached (Mah. 243). Dakkhakakrasimai, palufal circumstances (Dh. 396). Khippam eva imam kōrapam akikoyya, would soon teach him this thing (Dh. 400). Akroama, unreasonable, groundless. For all, kōrapam, see separate article.

KARANDAKO, A box [$\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi$]. A1w. I. 74; F. J44.5; Mah. 161.

--- KARANDAVO, A sort of duck [ɑːˈdʒuːk] Ab. 428.

KARANDO, and DAM, A basket, a wicker-work box [$\sqrt{a}$]. Ab. 817; Mash. 258.

KARANIKO (adj.), Investigating, judging [1-11-11]. Ab. 728. One of the guardians of hell is called kdropiko, "the judge" (Ab. 658).

KARANTIYO (p.p. korovi), That ought to be done or made [māʾāʾiā = ʔi]. Ab. 779. Use this karaspyo, effort must be made (Kamm, 8). Añjaliharaspyo, to whom salutation should be made, deserving salutation (Aiw, 1, 79). N'atthi hassalharaspohami kamasehi karaspoyani, there is no use in doing good or bad actions. Next, karaspoyami, that which ought to be done, duty. Saṅgha karaspohami koroti, to perform ecclesiastical duties (Dh. 348). Catidri karaspohami catidri alaraspohami, four things to be done, four things to be avoided (Kamm, 8).



KARANJO, The plant Pongania Glabra [Ab. 567.

KARANO (adf.), Maklog, causing [ []. So-maggharapo, causing reconellization (Mah. 6). Fem, -gf.

KARÃO, see Karoth.

BARANTARIPHALO, The Jack-tree or bread-fruit tree, Artocarpus Integrifolia. Ab. 569.

KARAPALIKA (☐), A wooden sword, a cudgel [w pifw]. Ab. 392

KẮRẠPANAM, Causing to be made. Dh. 250.

KARĂPETI (cause, karoti), To cause to be made or done. Dh. 242; Sen. K. 438, 487. P.p.p. kadripto (Mah. 158).

KARAPUTO, The cavity formed by joining the bent palms of the bands  $ [\overline{q} + \overline{q}\overline{z}] $. Ab. 238 (same meaning as orijali).

KARASAKHλ (f.), A anger [π + π]. A5. 200.

KARAVELLO, The plant Momordica Charantia

मारशि]. Ab. 596.

KARAVIKO, The Indian cuckoo; name of one of the Kulacuna. Ab. 28, 226; B. Lot. 565, 560. See Kuraviko.

KARAVIRO, Oleander or Neslum Odorum []. Ab. 677.

KARAVO, see Káru.

KARENU (m. und f.), An elephant [āŋʷŋ]. Ab. 866 (note). See Kaperu.

KAREHI (m.), The tree Capparla Trifolista Ab.53.

KARETI (cause. karoti), To cause to be done or made, to make, to perform [काएपि = 1]. Ben. K. 467. Rajjain k., to reign, to rule (K.I. 1.73; F. Jat. 16). Abhinakini kreted, having caused himself to be mangurned king (F. Jat. 5). Yoggani k., to make fit (F. Jat. 9). Palmidya akdrayi mayin taṃ maganam, caused this jewel to be made into the eye of a statue (Mah. 243). Sippinggavisham akdrayi, taught him accomplishments (Mah. 60). Kdayamāmo, causing to be made for himself (Pit. 4). Prafjikema dhammaṃ kōratabbo, is to be treated according to P. rule, convicted of a P. offence (Pit. 7). With

KARI (m.), An elephant [anfəng]. Mah. 103
KARL (adj.), Dolag, rcting [rɪˈfɪŋ]. Pipakri, a sliner (Dh. 8). Dh. 52; Ben. K. 512
KÄRIKA (f.), Work, action; a memorial verse, a metrical explanation [arffart]. Ab. 1105. Dukkarakö-likun karad, having performed difficult deeds (Alw. I. 77). See also under Kiraka.

KARIRO, The plant Capparls Aphyla [].

Ab. 500.
KARISAM, Excrement [αα]. Ab. 274, 005.

KARISAM, A superficial measure = four Annmap.

Ab. 197, 996; Mah. 61, 168; Dh. 135.
KARISAPANO, A KARISAPANO []. Ab. 481. See KARISAPANO.
KARISAM, see Kவர்த

KARITO (p.p.p. krwrti), Caused to be made or done, made, constructed, performed [=]. Alw. I. x; Db. 78, Kim me rejjena krritena, what's the use of my relgufug? (Db. 406). Next, krritach, the causal form of the verb (Sen. K. 436). KARIYA, see Krwrti.
KARIYA, KARIYATI, see Karott.
KARIVO (p.f.p. kerovti), That ought to or can be done []. Ab. 1037.

KARO, The hand; no elephant's trunk; tax, toll,

revenue; a ray of light [wʌn]. Ab. 64, 265, 255,

1047. Karasis gepháti, le collect the revenue

(Mah. likxyl), Dackhlapis karash add, offered

his right arm (Mah. 41). Karasis ruójio dlambidó,

holding the king's hand (Mah. 41, coup. 23).

— KARO (adj.), Malking, causing, doing [adj.]. Only as the latter part of a compound: Pailifakure, doing good works (Mah. 132); shukkoro, difficult; Aitakaro, a benefactor (Mah. 20); paadassasayaka-karo, causing pleasure and pain (Mah. 1); daomakaro, causing joy (Mah. 12); bhedakaro, causing discord; paahamara, one who answers satisfactorily questions put to him. Comp. Bhayamikaro, Disakaro, Madukaro, Nakkaro, Sakaro, Kierakaro, etc.

KARO, Making, action; a person; the tree Caethian Parviflorum; a song of psalm [ᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ]. Gaishakire, book-making (Alw. I. x). See Ahaikidro, Ahaikidro, Balakhidro, Sadhukidro, Kiro is used after letters to form their name: abiva, the letter a; didra, the letter d; kashididro, the letters k and the rest (Sen. K. 201); ahakulard, the letters o and a (Sen. K. 206). Ab. 1011; Db. 274.
KARO (adj.), Making [ɑːŋt], Rathakdra, a coach-maker, Rathakdro, a cook. Ben Andialdro, Camalakro, Cittakro, Swappakro, etc.

KAROTTI, To not; to do; to cause; to cause to become, to render, to make; to perform [W]. Bidsott ed. kavesi ed, speaks or acts (Dh. 1). Tathed katesd, having done so, having acted thus (Dh. 156). Bd som abathha, do not do so (Dh. 80). Kish kated, having done what? by what means? Yes kitee kared, by some means or other (Dh. 156). Ahas pi kiteid eos hariesfui, I too will do something or other (Dh. 108). Iddwi bis karemi, what are I to do now? (Dh. 157). Kisiot akroesf, having done nothing, without doing anything (Alw. 1.99). Yatid manh na meafati fatid kitesa saffati, I nani manage that he does not diamiss me (Dh. 156). Yatid so nigeoechati tatid hariesfui, I'll take care he does not come. Diao disain yas isah isayird, whatsoever an enemy would do to an enemy (Dh. 9). Na te labbed kiteid kitesa, it is not allowed to do anything to them (Alw. 1.79). Kisi so bleate katshi isin karemi, pray, kr, what do the elephants do to you? (Dh. 154). Natake siga akati, treated them like relatives (Dh. 240). Te atvino dcerdi itin kariesanti, what will they do with their own clothes? (Dh. 174). Tesam andgamraati harisefui, I'll prevent their coming back. It, I will cause their non-return (Dh. 154). Akariya jiwakhedasi, without causing human suffering (Mah. 215). Lemahakeshik, to cause amagazent (Mah. 167). Karoti so tash'atidrom yatid sash kehatt dles, be makes himself what his enemy would with him to be (Dh. 28). Eotodus makatish Sihataealii, having made B. bis queen (Mah. 46). Ratheim k., to build a chariot. Eatomamufliim k., to convert into a handful of sabes (Dh. 364). Tatididipani mirtoa istush, to make such a man one's friend (Alw. 1.76). Daikhaik. bandhuvasi, makes the fetier strong (Dh. 63). Ujush k., to make straight (Dh. 7). Upahik k., to best (F. Ját. 57). Naggaish

k, to strip naked (Mah. 261). Uyghurman ramaspiyak skidi, rendered the garden delightful (F. Jit. 6). Parmash samash kated, making the earth smooth (Dh. 154). Khetamr dee kujthae kated, having divided the field into two, lit, made it into two portions (Dh. 125). Harthagatah k, to make one's own (Dh. 229). Visadam k, to make friends with (F. Jat. 17). Agghak, to make a fire (F. Jat. 2). Vahramk, to trade (P. Jat. 14). Karis k, to till the ground (F. Jat. 9). Aftash k, to go to law, to bring an action. Kumici diayash akutod, not feeling desire for anything (Dh. 291). Akated ratim akkharen, not delighting in syllables (Kh. 21). Sitam k, to smile (F. Jat. 10). Kidash k, to die. Mhasasik k, to resolve (Mah. 78). Okasam k, to make room for. Paribagash k, to use (Dh. 100). Pucuggamamash k, to go to meet (Dh. 231). Samadassik k, to pay honour to (Mah. 241). Sakkrom k, to entertain bospitsibly. Ausifash k, to permit. Hattam k, to show friendship to (Kh. 6). Siddhyo k, to work miracles (Dh. 200). Sllabhedash k, to commit a breach of morality (Dh. 150). Sakgittish k, to hold a rehearsal (Mah. 11). Sdkocehash k, to converse (Dh. 121). Narash k, to make a man into his power (Dh. 9). Desdash k, to inflict punishment (Alw. I. 00). Disdishdash k, to take one's midday rest. Abskashk, to make a bet, lay a wager. Ksalahk, to quarrel. Popidshim or patthassah k, to make an aspiration for, to pray for. Saddokh k, to make a noise, to shoot. Pufidshik, to do good actions. Kamamk, to do a deed, to perform an action. Pucatish k, to establish (Mah. 68). Parmashtishik k, to establish one's dynasty. Upamash k, to make a comparison (Dh. 24). Opamash k, to give a smile or illustration (Alw. I. xtil). Sokash k, to mourn (Dh. 300). Piyagich or diappash k, to make an effort, to exert oneself (Mah. 13; Dh. 310). Pudsham k, to fight, to make war (Mah. 153). Purapaghatam akutod, without mentioning llshaughter (Alw. I. exriv). Attoma ghare akdal, kept them in his own house (Alw. I. 78). Batthe kurted, having placed it in his hand. Vime kaufithak kated, placing his sister on his left side (Mah. 44). Papparch ucehaige kated, having put the letter to the fold of her dress (Dh. 221). Bahi mals kurtisad, I'll put him outside (Dh. 84).

Ekata k., to pat together (Mah. 140). Purata k., to pot in front (Mah. 233). Dorald k., to divide. Arhattha k., to pat elsewhere (Alw. I. 68). Tolo amacea katadna, naxi in order posting the ministers of state (Mah. 233). Zhanai karoti or memesikari, to attend to (Mah. 158, Dh. 401). Patid of dhansou ed tabanim amayie khn eva karitamati, when that time comes what good will sons and relies do to you? (Dh. 258). Jythena khi karisadmi, what is the use of living? lit. what shall I do with life? Karoti is sometimes compounded with a non or adj., the short s of the nominal base being first changed to f: dalikharoti, to make firm; kharmikharoti, to reduce to sabes; arathikharoti, to render helpless (At. 207); complikharoti, to provoke. The present tense of karoti is as follows: karroti, karosi, karroti, karoma, karroha, karroti. Pres. firm. 3rd para. karate (Dh. 9, 39; Mah. 219; Sen. K. 462), barbari, barbara (Sen. K. 463), pl. kubbarit. Opt. kayyad (Dh. 8, 10, 19; Mah. 244; Des. 6), kayyadha (Dh. 8, 22, 55; Kh. 14), barbetha, karo (Dh. 8, Sen. K. 465), karryya (F. Jat. 2; Sen. K. 466). Imperat. 2nd para. karw (Mah. 18, 61), karahi (Dh. 42); 3rd pers. karw; 2nd pers. pl. karotha (Sen. K. 436); 3rd pers. pl. karonim, Fat. karisami (Sen. K. 429; Db. 186; F. Jat. 12). There is also a contrasted form of the fat, of which the 1st pers. in kdhani, 2nd kdhari, kdhani, 3rd kdhati, kdhiti, 1st pl. kdhana (Sen. K. 452; Dh. 28, 123, 329; Mah. 49). Aor. akrdi (als in the usual form in prose, Sen. K. 465, F. Jat. 6, Mah. 72, pl. akdama), akd (Mah. 93, 37, pl. akarwa, 2nd pers. pl./akatha), akari (Sen. K. 455, F. Jat. 13, Mah. 13, 72, Db. 129, pl. akurah, akurina). Aor. 1st pers. pl. with itm. term. akaramhase (F. Jat. 13). Inf. katas, katam (Sen. K. 512), kalave (Mah. 217, Sen. K. 455, 503). Ger. katad, katadwa, katidwa, katama, karited, kariya (Sen. K. 466, 503, 510, 512, Mah. 194, 215 akariya, comp. Att. 214 abkinukhi-koriya). P.pr. kubbavi (Dh. 10; F. Jat. 13), kubbanto (Sen. K. 433; Mah. 244), karanto (Dh. 21), karab (Dh. 25; Mah. 137, das. karato), karammo, karammo, karidwa, kubbino. Part. fat. karisash (Cl. Gr. 120). KASINO, and -NAM, This is the name for one of the divisions of the Karmashana, and is a process by means of which mystic meditation may be induced. There are ten sorts of Kanalpa, pofha-kuipash, dyokariipash, tyokariipash, vdyokariipash, mikaasipash, pitakasiapash, lohtitakasiapash, oddita-kanipash, dikaikasiapash, paricchihadikasiapash, earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, light, and the sky seen through a narrow aperture (E. Moe. 252). The word keispa is the Sank. and this rite is I think so named because in practicing it the mind is wholly absorbed or engrossed in one predominant idea on which it is intently fixed. In Pufakashasina a circle (kasipas-maqala) a few inches in diameter moulded of earth or clay in placed upon a low frame. Seen at a short distance the priest must fix his eyes upon the circle, and concentrate his mind upon the idea of the element of earth, inwardly repending its various names, and dwelling on the thought that the particles of his own body are composed of this element. He must continue this exercise until his mind attains a state of absorption or measure the manuscripts, when Nuitta will be produced, the circle being seen when the eyes are closed as clearly as when they are open (see Nuitituk). In Apokاسpa the object contemplated is a bowl full of water, in Akkakasipa a circle of light thrown upon a wall, in Pariechimaskedasina a portion of sky seen through a hole in the roof of a hut. In Nuitasipa some object of a blue colour is used, as a piece of blue cloth, or some blue flowers, or a blue circle painted on a wall; and so with the remaining Kanalpa. Saigiti S. numerates ten Kasipasmanas, pafavikaspash, dpoek., tejak., vdyok., mlak., piak., lohtak., oddita, didask, viindpasastash. E. Mon. 212 and foll.; Man. B. 10; Dh. 131, 270. KHANDHO, The shoulders; the trunk of a tree; a multitude, quantity; one of the five elements of being [egg], Ab. 364, 548, 630, 851. Harthikkhandho, the back of an elephant (Msh. 88, 45; Raa. 17). Nakkdhaya tan khandha, the elephant placing the king on his back (Msh. 217). Of a hem's back (Mah. 44). Rakkkhakkhandho, the trunk of a tree (Dhi. 165). Tildman khandAd, the trunks of palmya trees (Mah. 141, comp. 113). Dushkhakkhandha, aggregation of sufferings (Alw. N. 38). Pwissakkhandha, accumulation of merit

(Ait. 106). Taoukhkondhosa deufé, abrouded in thick darkness (Alw. N. 98). Mahadi tejokhankdhoa, by this vast accumulation of heat. Mahastam bhogakkhandhas pahdya, leaving behind him a great store of wealth. Mahikhondho, a magie jewel (F. Jat. 3). Khandha is one of the technical terms of the Buddhist philosophy. There are five khandhas, "elements or attributes of being," repakkhondho, vedandkhondho, acindkhondho, samikhakkhandho, vifidakkhandho. They are also called ropapoddmakkhandho, oedamupddakkhandho, sufipapddakkhondho, samikhapddakkhandho, vifiduppddakkhondho (see Upddam). Separately they are repass, oedam, saifad, samikard (pl.), vifidpank, or Forra, Senaathon, Peroepikon, Discrimination, Consciousness. For a full description of each khandha see the sep. articles Rapakkhandho, Vedandkhkhandho, etc. Khandha in this connexion probably means collection or aggregate, for Rapakkhandha, or the organized body, is an assemblage of twenty-eight elements and properties, and Viffigakkhandha has no less than eighty-nine subdivisions, and Sankhira fifty-five. The five khandhas embrace all the essential properties of every seat that being: some belongs possess them less completely than others, and the jahabitants of the four Arúpbrahmalokas do not possess the first khandha (ripa) at all. When a man dies the khandha of which he is constituted perish, but by the force of his Kamma a new set of khandhas instantly starts into existence, and a new being appears in another world, who though possessing different khandhas and a different form is in reality identical with the man just passed away, because his Kamma is the same. Kamma then is the link that preserves the identity of a being through all the countless changes which it undergives to its progress through Satinira. Though the khandhas perish at death there is practically no break in the line of organized existence, for the formation of the new khandhas follows instantaneously, and without appreciable interval, upon the dissolution of the old. When by the attainment of Arhatship Kamma has been destroyed the potentially for re-birth conveyed by Kamma ceases, and the death of the Arhat is the annihilation of a merely of his khandhas but of his existence. KILAMATI, To be tired, worn out, troubled, ex-banated []. Dh. 76, 154; Alw. I. 101. Caus. AriLamdjpetL P.p.p. hilanto.

KILANJO, A mas, matting []. Ab. 455; Mah. H2; Alw. I. 78.

KILANTO (p.p.p. kilamat), Wearied, exhausted [= 🚫], Maggakilanto, tired with his journey (Dh. 210), Ndedkilastadehatto, from their bodies being exhausted with the sea-voyage (Mah. 217). Usha kilaste, in this exhausting heat (Mah. 183). Mah. 182.
KILASO, A cutaneos complaint, dry leprosy [ཁུགས]. Kamm. 4. Yildino H na bhijjasmakim na paggharapakim padmapupdarikuvaapans kujthain yena gunnadi otya tubalain sarirain hoti.

KI,ATI, To play, to sport [ ]. Sihakijash kifim, gunbolled as lions will (F. Jt. 47). Migacam kifitasi agd, went forth to enjoy the sport of the chase (Mah. 78). KILESO, Sin, depravity, corruption, biman passion, moral defilement, last [ʌn]. The ten Kilesan, or evil passions, are lotho, doso, moho, mimo, diffit, viciktechá, thimash, uddhaccam, ahiriká, amettappash, deaire, bale, ignorance, vanity, heresy, doubt, loth, arrogance, shamelessness, hardness of heart (B. Lot, 444, comp. Man. B. 417, 418). Kleça or moral depravity being the cause of sinful actions is therefore primarily the cause of re-birth or continued existence. Arhatship consists in the amhillation of Kleça (B. Mon. 281, 288, 290). The five Klesas are probably lotho, doso, moho, mimo, uddhaccam. At Dh. v. 88 the commentator explains etitakled by the five vivarapas. Kilesturo, love-alek (Ten J. 51). For Kilesakdmo see Kamo. Dh. 138, 277, 278, 280, 432. See Kiconani.
KILINNO (μ.p.p.), Wet [f+]. Ab.753.

KILISSATI, To suffer, to be injured; to be deprived [ʃʷʷʷ]. No kiliseyya, let him not allow himself to be diagnosed (Dh. 29, 320). Vatthimi kilisanti, one's clothes get dirty, P.p.p. kilittho. KILITAM, see Kiljari.
KILITO (p.p.p.), Bound [$\tilde{a}$ = $\tilde{a}$]. Ab.747. KILITTHO (p.p.p. kilisoti), Afflicted, suffering; deprived, alnful, polluted, vicious; soiled, dirty;

KILOMAKAM, This word is +: It is explained by Vlaudchi Magge in the following words, kilomakers papicchannakrizomakash kada ya'a cakka' ca partodretod appapicchannakizomakash sakalasarire eamassa keffhato masasach parigomandhitod fitash, which appear to mean "Of the two k.s the inermost k. surrounds the heart and kidneys, the outer k. envelops the flesh below the skin throughout the whole body." From this it would appear to indicate some membrane, as the pleura.

KIM (adv.), Why? Pray! What! [fug], This word must not be confounded with bism the neut. along from ko, for the use of which see under Ko. Ab. 249, 1138, 1139. Kim dqato 'si, why are you come? (Mah. 103). Na klijepanti kish bhikkha, why should not worky amuse themselves? (Mah. 33). Kim evoh sodei, why do you say tha? (Dh. 189). Ichokiloharamdpanno samuho kim shavisati, can a man be a Gramupa who is full of last and covetousness? (Dh. 47). Kim Jomodo na ppahoti, what is Jnanda not qualified? Kim no bhoute hatthi kish karonfi, pray, sir, what do the elephants do to you? (Dh. 184). Rosappadema tam'eva ktn piremi manorathais, can I fulfil my wish by getting sugry with him? (Mah. 261). Godrabhikam save attham kish jomdi, what I do you know the hidden meaning in the bray of an nas? (Mah. 250). Kim ayam makardjd gaho paiko elys dhaseti, why there's a king running like an ordinary householder! (Dh. 224). Samma Sujida kish unmattako 'st, why, friend Sajta, are you mad! (Das. 31). Kim mahdrijas aisinamid dqato 'riti dosa bhente, pray, great king, did you come here without having any rest? Yes, lord (Dh. 401). Kim kafirah, is it black? (Dh. 103). Kim taas' eva disunah makappaham omdikam pi disunah makappaham eva, of course alms given to him have a great reward, and alms given to us have a great reward also (Dh. 838). Kim shamle magthakamamh katoi, well, sir, did you use my remedy? (Dh. 83). With foll pama: Kim poma nappah bhdeitha, did you really prame? (Dh. 896); Kim poma so tumhati mderato ditha, come? did you see him kill them? (Dh. 89); Kim poma Rifagule tuto adhikash ratanagni atthi, let me see, is there no treasure in B. greater than shla? With full, so: Kim su kho rogo na vapa-santo, how is it the disease is not cured? Kim su ma'sa exampalyo, of course these are plus cuns (Ph. 89; Gen. next, hiss. Plur, kx. Gen. and dat. pl. kessam. Instr. and abl. pl. keki. Loe. pl. kess. Neut. pl. kchai. Ke'ei, who are you? (feu. kdi'ei, Dh.180,103). Ko pama toash, who are you? (Dh.192). Ko jndti him p' eea karisati, who knows what this follow will do? (F. Jst. 12). Ko ciraturam ke sigkataram, which of the two (is born) later, which sooner? (Alw. I. xiii). Ke'e eiroomati, who are these screaming? (Dh. 194). Ko dikkaro, which of the two is the more difficult? (Mab. 41). Ke'm drabba, about whom? (Dh. 77). Khi drabba, about what? Tinh ko adma no jdnayya, who could fall to recognize him? Ko adma toash, who art shon? (Dh. 99). Ko adma te spajhdyo, who is your spiritual master? (Kamm. 5; comp. Dh. 134). Kdi adma' and mtingd-maa vign kiyid, what a woman-like proceeding I (Dh. 159). Ke attha, and khi poryejamah, what is the use or meaning of? (Sen. K. 202, 478, followed by instr.). Kim akdi pufisani, what good deed have you done? (Dh. 99). N' doahati kas admaatthani, what evil does it not produce? viz. it produces much evil (At. 183). Kena's auloua loko, by what is the world shrouded? (Alw. I. 106). Khi, what is this? (Mah. 167). Khi idam, what is this? (Db. 300). Idam khi, why is this? why so? (Dh. 160). Khi etach or khi adma etau, why is uila? what is the meaning of this? how is this? (Mah. 156; F. Jst. 49, 57). Khi pema wa kho etam, cow what on earth can it be? (Alw. I. 101). Ayam to brdhamao khi koti, what is this brahmin to you? (F. Jst. 10). Tsumdhikah ettha khi, what's that to you? (F. Jst. 17). Khi to dukkkok, what is your all meat? (F. Jst. 12). Pitund visaditash khi kini eva, what were the several acts of destruction committed by my father? (Mah. 238). Khattiyd khi agghasiti, what are khatriyas worth? (Dh. 352). Idini khi karomi, now what am I to do? (Dh. 157). Khi su kdtabbasi, what is to be done? (Mah. 153, 343). Khi su kho karisadma, what shall we do? (Dh. 231). Khi kafad, having done what, by what means? (P. Jst. 17). Gehe khi karisadmi, what can I do at home? i.e. it is no useliving at home (Dh. 313). Pardnabismath-arajad khi kurissouti, what do they do with the old carpen? (Dh. 174). With instr.: Jeideua khi karisadmi, what is the use of my living? Etitakehi khi karisamha, what will you do with all these? (Dh. 174). Khi su kho pesemi, what shall I send? (Alw. I. 75). Khi su kho etha

Krasna, what is the cause of this? (F. Ját. 6). Kassa indul, whose are these things? (Dh. 803). Kessa vuttash, by whom was it said? (Ahw. I. xxi). Kessa phalash adni etam, what is this the fruit of? (F. Ját. 5). Kessa te attho, what are you in want of? (F. Ját. 2). Kissa hetu, on account of what? why? Kessa hatund, and karad hetund, on what account? why? The gen. neut. kissa, instr. kissa, and abl. karnd, are used adverbally in the sense of "why?" Kissa pama thero often's month adel, now why did the sider omit one? Kissa visad attāman spadpaye, why should the wise man distress himself? (Das. 5); Ken' ambo kajulapphao, why has the mangu birter fruit? (F. Ját. 7); Teoth kendel kiso, why are you thin? (Mah. 33); Karnd man parehari, why do you ask me? (Dh. 96); Karad esma kurasi, why do you do so? (Dh. 333); Karnd pass teath bhikkhu bhushkho jido, how is it, priest, that you have got so much property? (Das. 38). amphallopelopoeusae, amobhijik, oeydpoo, sammaddijhi, "refraling from killing, from stealing, from impurity, from lying, from slander, from harsh language, from frivolous talk, freedoms from covetousness and from mallee, and orthodoxy" (Raa 15).
KUSALĄKUSALAM, Good and bad [+], KensilAhmpolakamash, doing good and doing evil, merit and demerit (Dh. 89).

KUSALATA (f.), Skill, knowledge [y]

Apattikendatid apattitestphdemaakendatid, skill In

discerning what is sinful, and skill in discerning

what leads to slu.
KUSALATTAİ, Skilfulness [可[ +]. Dh.231.
KUSALI (adj.), Prosperous; morturious [ɒrɪˈfɪər]. Cl. Or. 29.

KUSALO (adj.), Skillful, expert, clever; lucky, happy, prosperous; good, right, virtuous, meritorious [ʃɑːrɪn], Ab. 730; Dh. 9; Kh. 15. Ce sommier Shāriyānou taṃ paṭisalayyāya ice etāṃ kusalou, If being adonebled he forsake it, well and good (Pli. 5). With gen. kusalo naccanglassa, skilled in dancing and singing (Cl. Gr. 145, xiao loc, see Ben. K. 345). Adraramaia, skilled in right conduct (Dh. 67, comp. Att. 212). Vied kaud, appropriate, happy, well-timed speech (F. Já. 18). Kusalaṃ kasamam, and kusalaṃ kamamam, good actions, meritious Karma (Dh. 86; Man. B. 445; B. Mon. 5; see Kamamam). Neut. Kusalaṃ, health (Ab. 331), luck, happiness, good fortune (Ab. 803), a good action, good works, merit, meritorious Karma (Dh. 10, 33, 845; Ab. 85). Kusalaṃ khatiyā, doing good actions. With dad kusalaṃ khatiāo hotu, health to you! good luck to you! (Sen. K. 329). There are three Kusalaṃ khatis, “elements of goodness or merit,” they are nekhkamamodhat, aeydpaidaṃda, arishikhadhat, self-abnegation, benevolence, humanity. The three Kusalaṃ khats, “roots of goodness, or groundwork of merit,” are alabho, adoo, anaba, freedom from covetousness, from anger, and from ignorance. The three Kusalaṃ kaṃ, or meritorious ideas, are nekhkamamodhat, aeydpaidaṃda, arishikhadhat. The three Kusalaṃ kaṃ, or meritorious thoughts, are nekhkamamodhatka, aeydpaidaṃka, arishikhadhatka. The three Kusalaṃ kapas, or meritorious resolves, are nekhkamamodhat, aeydpaidaṃkappa, arishikhadhat, aeydpaidaṃkappa, arishikhadhat. The dasakramam and dasakramam are appears to be identical with the ten Pudha-kityapatthas (Att. 56, 200, 204, 212). Kusalaṃ cetam, virtuous or meritorious thoughts (Gag. Ev. 68). Kusalaṃ takam, virtuous or meritorious slate of roud (Man. B. 448, see Lokattaro), Kusalaṃ vipika, the good result or reward of a good action (see Kamamam). Kusalaṃ vipika (adj.), having a good result or reward. Kusalaṃ takam, accumulation of merit.
KUSESAYAM, A water-lily or lotus [yāu]. Ab. 684
KUSI (n.), One of the four cross seams of the robe of a Buddhist priest. Ab. 296.

BUSINARÃ (S), A town in Índia, the capital of the Malas [the Sanak, name is or

Ab. 201; B. Int. 85, It was at K. that Buddha died (Man. B. 843; Mah. 11).

KUSITO (adj.), Slothful, inert, indolent [suff] Dh. 2, 21, 49, 289, 383. There are eight Kuala-vathus, “occasions of Icdolence,” vis. when a priest has a duty to perform, when he has performed a duty, who he has a journey to make, when he has made a journey, when he has failed to obtain food in alms, when he has obtained food in alms, when he is attacked by illness, when he is recovering from an illness: in each of these cases the slothful man lies down and rests instead of exerting himself (comp. the Arambhavathus).
KUBO, A blade of grass; the sacrificial grass, Pom Cynosuroides [གུ་]. Ab. 602, 1079; Dh. 55.

KUSSURAHAM, A small pond, a puddle [ʒʌd].

Gog. Ev. 15. Comp. Sabbah.
KUEOLO, A granary []. Ab. 459.
KUSUMAM, A flower; the menses []. Ab. 545, 1105; Mah. 63.
RUSUMBHAM, Safflower, Carthamus Tinctorlus [3].
KUTADHÁRIKÁ(f.), A meld-servant, lit. "she who carries the water-jar" [$\frac{3}{4}$ + $\frac{1}{2}$ + $\frac{1}{2}$ +], Ab.233.
KUTAJO, The plant Wrighta Antidysenterica [34]. Ab. 573.

KOTAMAM, A heap, a mound; a peak  $ [\frac{3}{4}d + \frac{3}{4}] $.

Ab. 224; Mah. 4.

LAC

LABBHÃ (indecl.), Allowable, possible [qūng].

Daa. 87; Cl. Gr. 73. With Inf. Idash sa labbhd

each kdtush, the thing cannot be done in that way

(Dh. 212). Na te labbhó kūtel kdtush, it is not

permitted to do anything to them (Alw. 1. 72).

Comp. Labbhó. For the origin of this form see

Sakhd.
LABHANEYYO (adj.), Obtainable.

LABBHATI (pos. labhati), To be taken, to be received, to be obtained; to be permitted [=]. Mah. 177; Kh. 14; F. J4.13, Labhatate (Ben. E. 44). Mayd vutto mistakennego na labhati, the mixed course I spoke about is inadvisible (Pht. xvi).
LABBHO ( $ p_{i}p_{j} $. labhasi), Obtainable, attainable; proper, right, suitable, admissible [=]. Ab. 1066. Asoinalabho, not obtainable by others (AH. 190). Comp. Labbhd.
LẦNH, toe Labho.
LÄBHAOGAM, Hlghest gain [π+]. Dh. 121, 305.
LABHANAM, Taklag, receiving, acquisition [qian], Dt, 129, 150.

— LABHATI, To obtain, to get, to acquire; to meet with, to find; to receive; to take; to obtain permission, to be allowed; to receive an opportunity, to get a chance, to be able [wɑː], Laddish samathapasie, taking with him competent men (Mah. 220). Tittahm I., to reach port (Mah. 69). Accetam I., to find a teacher (Dh. 121). Nadawan I., to assume the yellow robe (Dh. 114). So rifi deviy land ekad alabhi diltaran, the king had a daughter by this queen (Mah. 43, comp. Dh. 78; putam I., "to give birth to a son," may also be said of a woman). Nodawan I., to receive an asylum (Mah. 209). Pijash I., to receive honour (F. J41. 7). Abram I., to take food. Sakhani I., to obtain happiness (Dh. 34). Vacanaam I., to get a word said to one (Dh. 156; comp. Mah. 31). Gobbahani I., to conceive. Saco Labritha mupakani saidyaam, if he obtained a prudent friend (Dh. 58). Pabajid laddish naffati, the accetellife ought to be adopted, or accetidram is the right blung to take up (Dh. 121). Pas'laikhhasamagama no sakki laddhum, such an assemblage cannot be met with again (Mah. 49). Afino kaci daffun na labhati, nobody else gets pernuSelon to see him (Aiw. 1. 80). Pabajitun sace laekchani, if I am allowed to enter the priesthood (Mah. 110). Geha baht mikhhamitun mishanto, not being allowed to go but of the house (Dh.401). With da' Labhrypima... semadya, may we be allowed to hear (Dh.107). Sakhena sayidam labhiandui, I shall be able to sleep in peace (Dh.176). Saithirash daffun na labhimha, we were not able to have an interview with the Teacher (Dh.105). Pres.am. labhate (Dh.24). Imperat. labhain. Opt. labheyya. Opt.am. labhetha. Fut. lacchati (Dh. 86, 324; Mah. 104, 122), labhimanti (Sen. K. 404; Dh. 121, 129, 130). Aor. alattha (Sen. K. 457, Mah. 31, Alw. I. 83, Dh. 240; 1st pers. alattha, 2nd alattha), alabhi, labhi (Mah. 31, 208, Alw. I. 60; 1st pers. labhish). Cond. alabkiad (Sen. K. 439; Dh. 292). Inf. laddish (Dh. 114, 160). Ger. laddid (Kb.8; Mah.200), labhimang (Mah.69), labhited (Dh.160; Ras.19). Abaddid, not having obtained (Dh.28). P.pr. labhanto, labhamono (Dh.108, 180; F.J41.7). Pass. labbhati, labbhate (see sep.). P.f.p. laddhabho, labba. P.p.p. laddho.
LÄBHI (adj.), Possessed of [ɑːfɪˈpɑː]. Uposampoddidkh, an ordained priest (the termination belong to the whole compound).

LÁBHO, Receiving, getting, acquisition, obtaining, taking; gun, receipts [WTQ]. Db. 14, 87, 48. \Lá-

høssakidro, guin and bonour (Dh. 143, 238). Devad

dattoesa kedeaidbo, D's assumption of the yellow

robe (Dh. 112). Apparididho, anquisition of dem

merit, guilt (Dh. 55). Appaldsho (adj.), whom

guins are small (Dh. 66). Soighas' appaunaldho,

the gains of the priesthood, i.e. charitable gifts

(Mah.87). Ovaraldsho, receiving a robe (Pst.

106). A datidho (for idhiya, comp. parisonildho,

abhind) is used adverbially with foll. gentitive:

Idhho cata no, this is for our advantage (Dh. 149);

Idhha cata me, this is all gain to me (Dh. 129);

Idhhá cata me yam mama santikao samendam-

buddo mphadahasa atthdho sarakam padisi, how

forteante I am in that the supreme Buddha has

sent a vessel to my humble house for hot water

(Dh. 434); comp. the similar use of atthdya, e.g.

atthdya me bhavisati.

[w]]. Ab. 570.

(para as opposado to the assayfijanalskkhapas). There are three lakkhapas (tilakkapasa), or properties of all existing things, aniccans, dakkham, smalltash, impermanence, suffering, unreality (Man. B. 405; Dh. 292). Ithilakkhapas, characteristics of female's beauty (Mah. 223). Dhainialakkapasa, poussing personal characteristics Indicalive of future good fortune (Mah. Ixxviii). The essential property of a thing is called lakkhapas, e.g., the property of pathavidhatu or earth is lakkhalattain "solidity," that of dpodhatu or water is paggharapash "fluidity," that of dadsadhatu or space is asaphuftham "intaugibility," that of sahad or sense is sajdhanam "perception," that of marapass is cuti "disappearance." Salionsaggalakkhapo padddo, sloth, the characteristic or evidence of which is indifference (Dh. 334, comp. 311). According to P61, xli to be a visayatharo a man must possess three lakkhapas or qualifications, he must be thoroughly vermed in the contents of the Visayn Pipaka, he must be a steadfast observer of the Visayn precepts, and he must have thoroughly mastered the devilayapassapard. At Dh. 163 a brdhman woman is represented as versed saakkhapamantdam tipam oddman "in the three Vedas and the lakkhapasmantras"; the latter appear to be memorial verses enumerating the outward signs by which character or fortune may be known or predicted; on the same page will be found a pdaialakkhapamanto, or gichr describing the different sorts of footprints left by men of different characters. Asakha is applied only to the Arshartaphalatha. Arshartaphala, the biggest degree of sanctification, is also called kilesapartibedman (or kilesambodman), and spatiasomibidman, and even simply wibdman. All those who have not entered the Paths are called Pathujjana, "unconverted," lit. "ordinary men." When a man has once entered one of the four Paths he can never fall away, his salvation is assured, he must ultimately attain Nirvaga. Of the four Paths the last alone brings immediate release from existence. When a man has attained Arshartiph he ceases to exist as soon as the natural term of his life has expired, that is in a few years at most. With the other three Paths the case is different. When a man attalos the state of Soti panas be is far from being wholly freed from human passion, and must pass through a period of probation, before he is qualified for Nirvapa by the total extinction of Impurity and of Kamma; he must be born again seven times, in any of the worlds except the four Apiaya, from which he is exempted. The Sakadigamin, in whom a larger portion of human passion is destroyed, has only to pass through two more exciences, one in a devaluka and one in the world of men. The Angagmin is not reborn on earth or in a kamaloka, but passes to one of the five highest Rupabrahma-lokas, and the once atsinus Nirvapa. B. Int. 290-298; B. Lot. 520; B. Mon. 6, 250-291. Naggu-brahmacariyama, the life of one who is walking in one of the four Paths (Man. B. 492; Du. 379). See Phalan. For further details respecting the Paths see Nibbassah.
MAGGURO, A sort of fish [ 777]. Ab. 671.

MAGHĂ (f.), Name of a Nakkhatta [ทหาร].

Ab. 59.

— MĂỊH ĐẠTO, Non-slaughter, Interdiction of slaughter [ẨT + ẨTn]. Măghdatam rabbale dipe kderni manajiddhipo, the king interdicted the destruction of animal life throughout the whole island (Mah. 215).
MAGHAVĂ (m.), Indra [왜다], Ab. 90; Dh. 6; Sen. K. 273, 274.
MẠGHO, Name of a month [wɪŋ]. Ab. 78; Sep. K. 302.
MÁGHYÁM, The blooms of the many-flowered jasmine [H]. Ab. 578.

— MAGG, A deer or antelope [彐]. Ab. 617. See also Migo. Comp. Magnoiro.

MAHÃ (adj.), Great. This nominative is sometimes met with, e.g. at Mah. 132, tost' diddho mahd ahw, "a severe illness befell him," and Dh. 298, camayassa Gotamaesa idbhankkdr mahd hutod nibbatti. It may be the Sanskrit nom. m, from m, or it may be the Vedic adj. mT, or it may arise from a misunderstanding of the true nature of the base mahd-. How easily the latter may be mistaken for a nom, can be seen from such compounds as mahd-uggkkhandho (Aiw. N. 36, where D'Alwla prints mahd as a separata word). That mahd-aggkkhandha is really a compound is evident from the comparison of words like mahd-apisikda and mahd-araniam. The nom. masc. of mT is rarely found in Pili, its place being generally supplied by the base mahd- forming the first part of a compound. When it does occur it is almost always in the form mahamto (which see). At Ab. 413 occurs a nom. plur. mahd, which perhaps should be referred to the Vedic mT (iti yag mahd ime).

MAHÃ-, Great. This is a Vedic adj. much used as a substitute for WWH in the formation of compound nouns and adjectives. Mahdawigrodho, a great banyana tree (Dh. 105). Mahdawidho, a great warrior (Das. 7; Mah. 194). Mahdawwad, great compassion (B. Lot. 376). Mahdeeffi, an eminent or very wealthy se若hi (Dh. 239). Mahdawam and mahd-arafinam, a great forest (Raa. 18; Dh. 606). Mahd-updeik, an eminent female devotee (Dh. 107). Mahd-agglikkawidho, a great mass of fire (Alw. N. 38). Sometimes prefixed to a proper name in the sense of "eminent," to disintegrish its owner from others of the same name, e.g. Mahdawasapo, Mahdhaecodyano, Mahdmaggaliama, names of eminent disciples of Buddha. Mahdawidhavo, very wealthy (Das. 24). Sometimes compounded with an adj. as mahdavidho, very broad (Att. 201).

MAHĀATTHAKATHĀ (f.), The Great Commentary [ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠨ + ᠪᠣᠶᠠ + ᠪᠣᠶᠠ]. The Mahā-afthakathā was the oldest and most important of the commentaries upon the Tipijaka. The tradition is that it was rehearsed at the first Council, and brought to Ceylon by Mahinda, who translated it into Singhe-lese. Buddha’s commentaries appear to have been briefly compiled from it (Pālīīī).
MAHABALAM, Great strength [ʌʃɪt + ɑːr]

MAHÃ (adj.), Great. This nominative is sometimes met with, e.g. at Mah. 132, tost' diddho mahd ahw, "a severe illness befell him," and Dh. 298, camayassa Gotamaesa idbhankkdr mahd hutod nibbatti. It may be the Sanskrit nom. m, from m, or it may be the Vedic adj. mT, or it may arise from a misunderstanding of the true nature of the base mahd-. How easily the latter may be mistaken for a nom, can be seen from such compounds as mahd-uggkkhandho (Aiw. N. 36, where D'Alwla prints mahd as a separata word). That mahd-aggkkhandha is really a compound is evident from the comparison of words like mahd-apisikda and mahd-araniam. The nom. masc. of mT is rarely found in Pili, its place being generally supplied by the base mahd- forming the first part of a compound. When it does occur it is almost always in the form mahamto (which see). At Ab. 413 occurs a nom. plur. mahd, which perhaps should be referred to the Vedic mT (iti yag mahd ime).

MAHABRAHMA (m.), The archangel Brahman, also called Brahma Salhampati [阿勒特 + 库拉].

Mahābraḥmā, or as he is also frequently called Braḥmā, is the ruler of the Brahma heaven, and therefore the greatest of all the devas or nagels. He holds the same place among the Brahma angels that Sakka and Marā hold among the angels of the Kāmādevalōka. It is of the greatest importance not to confound the Buddhist Brahman with the Brahman of the Hindu triad. Mahābraḥmā is merely a powerful angel, and vastly inferior in power to Buddha. Every cakkhavela has its Mahābraḥman as the ruler of its Braḥmaloka, so that in reality Mahābraḥman is not one but many, for the universe contains an almost infinite number of Cakkhavīlas, and consequently of Mahābraḥmans. Moreover, the term Mahābraḥman in truth designates rather an office (the sovereignty of the Brahma angels) than an individual, for the same person only remains Mahābraḥman for a limited period, as the expiration of which he enters upon a new existence, and is succeeded in the Brahma sovereignty by another. According to Man. B. 109 Cākyanmui when a bodhisattis was four times born as Mahābraḥman, I find it started in a comment that the Mahābraḥman of Gāப்ama's time had been a monk named Sahakma, who under the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, by the practice of Jhāna, attained the sovereignty of the Braḥmadevas. Mahābraḥman is represented as continually exercising good will towards every being. He sometimes descends from his celestial above to interfere for good in the affairs of men. Thus when after the attainment of Buddhabod Cākyanmui hesitated for a while to communicate to mankind the truths he had discovered, we are told that Brahman quitting the Brahma world appeared before him, and loosing his robe from one shoulder in token of respect, and falling upon one knee, implored the sage not to keep back from man the knowledge of the way of salvation (Gog. Ev. 8; Man. B. 164). Again, at a critical period of the fortunes of the Buddhist church, Mahābraḥman is represented as appearing to the Thora Sāḥa to confirm his wavering faith (Mah. 17). Mahābraḥman was present at the birth of Cākyanmui, and received the infant in a golden net (Man. B. 145). One of his insignia is a silver chatta or parasol, which he carries as the symbol of his sovereignty (Mah. 180; Man. B. 173). On certain occasions the Mahābraḥmans of other Cakkhavīns are represented as coming to this earth.

Unmatatoa eau maine, why the man must be mad! (Dh. 608). Appamaññati, to despise. Bahmañati, to honour. The phrase yassa dañai kiltah maññati is equivalent to our "I want your pleasure." When Jivaka in Sāmañāphala S. gets ready the king's elephants to pay a visit to Buddha he says, kuppidut kho te deva katthiyandini yassa ddi kilaṃ maññati, which the comment explains thus, upacadravacasanat etah: idam vattah hoti, yan tayd Ḥattam taṃ mayd katāsh, idal yassa team gumsassa ed agassanassa od kolati maññati tad eva attēvo raciyd karokiti, "this is a courteous expression by which is meant, I have executed your orders, far whatever coming or going you think the right time has come, do it as suits your convenience." In Brahmalyn S., when Uttara tells Buddha that Brahmalya wibes to see him, Badha replies, yassd idni madavako Brahmalya brdhasapo kilaṃ maññati: here the use of the 2nd pers. is peculiar, but the idea is, "I will see Brahmalya whenever you like;" it is explained thus, mapavaka Brahmalya-brdhasapo yassa daṃanaṃ kāmo tassa daṃanaṃ iddi tuāhi kilaṃ maññati dassavāya dgammaṃ aṃ patakkalla ti atthe. nlmmltavassavttiddemoloks), and divides with Sakks (Indra) the sovereignty of the Kinnavacaredevaloka. Like the other two archangels Sakka and Mahabrahman he is possessed of vast power and reigns with great magnificence in his devoloka. He owes his exalted position to having in a former existence exercised in a high degree the virtue of Dina or charity, but he is nevertheless a wicked angel, and his pleasures are those of sense. Like Mahabrahman and Sakka he often descends from his celestial abode to interfere in the affairs of men, but unlike his brother archangels he always acts for evil and not for good. Thus by various articles he endeavoured to deter the young Siddbatths from devoting himself to the ascetic life (Man. B. 157, 159), and when at last he saw him on the eve of ataining omniscience he brought against him all the host of his evil angels, to endeavour to conquer him by forces (Man. B. 171). When a holy ascetic enters a village to ask for alms Mira will sometimes harden the hearts of the villagers so that none will give (see Man. B. 892; at Db. 352 this happens to Buddha, and at Db. 160 to a Paccika Buddha). At Db. 255 he is represented as endeavouring to prevent Godhika There from attaining Nirvāya, but his wiles are overcome by Buddha. He sometimes tempts a holy ascetic to enter a village for alms, and then controls the bodies of the villagers by a sort of Satanic possession, so that they are forced to insult their visitor with mocking gestures (Dh. 160, 352). Mira has three daughters Tapi, Rati, and Arati, or Concuplence, Love, and Anger, who tempt men to sin (Dh. 164; see Ragd). His army (undrabalai) are the Paranimmilavassatti devas over whom he rules (Dh. 118, 319). He is called Papina and Kapho "the Evil One," and Paranttabandhu "the Tempter" (Ab. 48, also Papidati and Namaci). By the word Mira is generally understood the being described above, whose full name is Paranimmilavassattimara. But the term has really a far wider signification, that of the Evil Principle, of which the sinful archangel is merely one of the manifestations. From one point of view Kieya or original sin is the evil principle, the mira or hindrance to the attainment of Nirvāya. Again, from the Buddhist point of view that existence is an evil, the Skandhas are a mira, because so long as they continue to exist Nirvāya cannot be at

Lained, So again Death (maero, marapath, entako) and Karma (abhiskakhdro, see Saskikdo) are manifestations of the Evil Principle. Thus we have five Miras or biendrances, khasdhansdro, kilesandro, maceasudro, abhisankhadramdo, devapultamdro, continued existence, xlo, death, Karma, and the sinful angel or Templar. The close connection of the four first is obvious from the consideration that re-birth necessarily involves previous death, and that wherever there is continued existence there must be Karma and Klega, which are its abiding cause. The realm of Miras (mdrodheyya) is the realm of sin, of Karma, of death, of re-birth; it is therefore the whole sphere of sentient existence, and it is opposed to Nirvipa or Annihilation, in which sin, death, and birth are alike unknown. The four Miras are khasdhansro, kilesandro, abhisankhadramdo, devapultamdro. The three Miras are kilesandro, marapandro, devapultamdro (Dh. 409, 434). The angels of Miras's heaven, the paronimitavasavettidred, are called Miras. The term appears to be sometimes extended to the inhabitants of the four highest Kimpavacmardvalokma, since, in the eight Parasis, the inhabitants of the whole deva world are classed as Catummahardjika-parial, Tivatinasparis, Miraparisi, and Belaimaparisi, "the host of Catummahardjika angels, of Tivatinasa angels, of Miras angels, and of Brama angels" (comp. B. Lot. 396).—Dh. 2, 7, 8, 9, 11, 19, 39, 48, 49, 111, 197, 200, 201; B. Int. 133, 398; B. Lot. 90, 395, 396; E. Mon. 82, 133, 251; Man. B. 151, 336, 382.

down knee deep (Muh. 107). Addhamadamatam elindameri, spent a period of half a month (Alw. I. 90). Yagamattam pekkhatt, be looks forward to the distance of a yuga. Addamattapaudpato, a droga measure in amount (Mah. 108). Vidathimattapathulo, a span broad (Alw. I. 76). Kicimattash addri, gave him a little of it (Mab. 280). Pariandoyamattam gahetod, taking with him only his water-strainer (At. 212). Gehagopakamattah thapeetod, leaving none but the housewatehers behind (Dh. 215). Pallmatam kh'du'tam, the text only was brought here (Mah. 251). Etisad adiko kunjikamattam pl labhisati, that lady's husband will get nothing but rice-gruel to eat (Dh. 233). Mama sarre kmakdampattam pi wabam katim nsaakkhi, it was unable to beat so much as a pore of my skin (F. Jat. 57). Pdo-porapamattam, a mere expletive (Ab. 1187). Tattha nas ti nipdiamattadi, here "nash" is a particle (F. Jat. 15, at Dh. 286 nipdamatt). Sdagarm H sacamamatena, by merely saying welcome (Dh. 392). Masopandamattam' eoa, by faith only, by a mere exercise of faith (Dh. 98). Muhuttamatt' eoa, in a moment (Dh. 133). Avalakhamatema, by a mere look, by merely looking at a thing. Pdhkarapamattma, by mere talk (Dh. 47, comp. 48). Agatigomazadod mutta-matena, merely by being released from the sin of walking in the agnils (Mah. 129). Niruddhi admit outhatmatte yeva, the moment it was sold, she is dead my lord (Dh. 307, comp. the use of vutter). Buddha ti vacame smamatte, the instant he heard the word Buddha, or at the mere sound of the wood Buddha (Alw. I. 97). Tomura nikhamatamati, at the moment of departure (Mah. 253). Solena mighafliamatte yeva, as soon as ever it comes in contact with the ear (Alw. I. civil). Sometimes the compound with -matia is used adjecively: Moyd khittamattam jilam addiga, taking away the net as soon as it is thrown by me: Rjpen' ummadayi rare difthamold 'va ad yato, because she meddened men with her beauty as soon as she was seen (Mah. 56); Sakrama vattamato so Loskam dgramma, he, the instant he was spoken to by S., having come to Ceylon (Mah. 47); Hatthato muttamattad ed, the branch as soon as it was liberated from the hand (Mah. 118); Hatthe makkhittamatio' ea hoti, the hand is merely amearad (Dh. 269). See Matid, Mottakmi.
MATTANNO (adj.), Moderate, temperate [mod+adj. Bhojismahi m., moderate in eating (Dh. 2).
MATTAŃUTĄ (f.), Moderation [ᠪᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ + ᠪᠠᠭᠠ], Dh. 34, 345.
MATTASITÀ (f.), Moderation in eating, temperance [$\pi\pi\pi+\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi+\pi\pi\pi$]. Alw. I. xxiv.
MATTEYYYATA (f.), State of being a mother, maternity [m+q+]. Dh. 59, the comment explains it to mean dutiful conduct of a son to his mother (Dh. 408).
MATTEYYO (adj.), Maternal [可[可+可].

MATTHAKO, and -KAM, The head; top, summit, end; excellence, eminence [egm], Ab. 256; Db. 146; Kh. 3, 19. to utter speech (F. J. 19). Imash musiciya atk' asado, benides this mangu is there any other mango, lit. setting said this one (Mah. 79). Man musiciya, except me (Mah. 154). Yathā man sa musicati, that he does not abandon me (Dh. 156). At Dh. v. 359 musicati with foll. dat. appears to mean "to throw oneself upon, to attack"; the commentator however takes it in the sense of "to be angry with," Aor. musici. Inf. musicituh. Ger. musietud (Alw. I. xxi), musiciya.—Pass. musceati, to be loosed or unfastened, to be released, to be emitted, to escape. Dukkhaldya m., to be released from suffering (Alw. I. 108). — MUTTO (p.p.p. musicati), Released, delivered; free, free from; discharged, shot [ᠰᠠᠭ = ᠪᠷᠭ].

Ab. 1013; Dh. 61. Ahāʾcʿamki mutto loka ca amuta, and I am delivered but the world is not delivered (B. Lot. 878, viz. delivered from transmigration by the attainment of arbustship). Beakusto jilamutto na, like a bird escaped from the source of the fowler (Dh. 82). Abādā mutto wa cowdind, like the unclouded moon, bit. free from cloud (Db. 31). Jordurjaddimuto, free from decay and pale and other ills (A/w. I. v/l). Jidqumtuudhanus, a bow with the string loosed, an unstrung bow (Mah. 217). There are four sorts of weapon (dyudha), podimuttais, a hand missile, as a javelin, yomutumash a machine missile, as an arrow, amutass, a non-missile weapon, as a knife, mutimutass, a weapon which may either be thrown or retained in the hand, as a bludgeon (Ab. 388, 387).

Tama cuhayagami na oaddmi, I cannot get a pair of wheels for it (Dh. 95). Na jondari, do you not know? (Dh. 103). Nididre alcodegama, neither too far off nor too near. N' ev' atthi na n'atthi paro loko, there neither is nor is not another world. Na tidn' eva pubba pi akatahhia gena, not only now but formerly also ongainful (F. J41. 12, 8). With foll. hi: Na hi verena verdni samnanti, for wrath is not appeared by wrath (Dh. 2); Attibi koci satto go imenshed kyd atish kdyah saiko-maiti F na ki madhrija, la there any being who iresunigrutes from this body to another body? No, great king (Gog. Ev. 44). Na sometimes forms the first port of a compound: nasikdmoaseyyd, an un-comforzable bed (Dh. 5); mappardope, abundant; adgamamam, non-arrival (Mah. 3, 8, but perhaps the reading should be 'adgamame); naehikkhu, a non-priest; nasiyo, a non-sanetlied man; neko, several; nejo, stless; napadsha, neuter; nadryo, irreslatible; nache, short; madaponto, silent; nicehandnako, unwilling; nadidere is sometimes a compound (see sep.). The toll are instances of sandhi: n'era = nasso (Mah. 254); n'etam = na etam (F. Ját. 14, comp. n'atthi, n'eva), udlah = na aloi, ndpi = na apl, edyan = na ayam (Dh. 87), ndha = na aksh (Dh. 193), udhi = na ahost (Raa. 22), uáéco = na afino, uádoes = na addasa (Raa. 22), ndaakhi = na asakhi (Dh. 195; F. Ját. 8), udam = na asa (see sep.), netaro = na idaro (Raa. 22), nereri = na lresi (Dh. 24), nopeti = na speti (Raa. K. 206); Mah. 194), napagaechithha = na spagaechithha (Mah. 29), na ppahoti = na pahoti (Dh. 314), similarly na ppasahati, na ppandati, na ppajinandati, na ppacatiati (Dh. 2, 23; F. Ját. 9, 47), na kkhamati = na khamati (Kaw. 8), na-y-ime or na yime = na tmo (Alw. 1, 73), na-y-idah or na yidam = na idah (see sep.), na-y-imassa or na yimasa = na imasu (Sen. K. 217), na-y-ito or na yito (Pél. 78, for the y in these examples comp. yeva, and viya = giva).

The niga tree is a fine forest tree the wood of which is excessively hard, its flowers are fragrant (Ab. 579; Raa. 28). In the Buddhist mythology the Nagas are represented as hooded snakes with three (sometimes seven) heads, or as snakes with human heads, or as human beings with the hood of a cobra. B. 189, 309), but they were often friendly to Buddha and his velegton, and great numbers of them were converted to Buddhism (B. Mon. 274; Maa. B. 303; Mah. 6, 72, 81). NAMARUPAM, Name and form, mind and body, the individual [+]. The term Namarupa designates the individual sentient being viewed as an aggregate of certain mental and physical elements. By ropa is meant the ropakhandha, or assemblage of the material elements and properties which constitute the body, while name includes the three mental khandhas, cedand, saifad, saiskhad, or, adding vindhadh, the four mental khandhas, cedand, saifad, saikhad, vindhadh. Namarupa is therefore identical with the four or the five khandhas. Ev. 68, 69. Sabbaradmarapamala yassa n' atthi mamayitara, in whom there is absolutely no elinging to his own individuality (Dh. 68). Dh. 422.

Nekkhamma is one of the Paramitas, and consists in the complete abandonment of allмерations and objects of desire (Han, B. 109). Nekkhammae disashao, the blessings of self-abegation (Pli, xxii). At Dh. 270 kiyaceloke is explained to be the act of coxaikittakiyadach sekkhamaddikratasam, “those who practise bodily retirement from the world, who delight in seclusion.” Nekkhammae dassame rad, delighting in the peace of emancipation (Dh. 83, the comment at 343 says it means Arhatabip, “that Nirvipa which is the cessation of human passion”), At Dh. v. 379 the comment explains sekkhamma by the enjoyment of the state of anagamin. Nekkhammao pattikya, from the time he gave up the world (Dh. 155). B. Lot. 532; Dh. 137; Pli. 29. Nekkhamma represents a Sanskrit form of the soothing and having nothing to do with the impossibility of identifying it with the latter word becomes obvious, when we consider that in the Baddhlet system caraciness, seal and energetic action are the very basis of all holiness (e.g. witness the well-known formula for best would disarmed sabble to appassad dassakd, “all good qualities or conditions have their root in diligence,” and comp. the eight Armzhavathus). As neikkamma is sometimes opposed to kima (see the articles Akkadodikta and Kusala), it might at first sight appear also to represent a S. form but in the first place (comp. nikkamin, “free from desire”), and secondly since abandonment of the world involves abandonment of all objects of desire, may well form the antitheals to kima.

NIBBANAM, Extinction; destruction, annihilation; annihilation of being, Nirvana; annihilation of human passion, Arhatship or final sanctification [f]]. "Existence is suffering." This is the first of the four Ariyassaccal, or Sublime Truths, upon which the religion of Buddha is founded. But a creed which beglas by saying that existence is suffering, must end by saying that release from existence is the highest good, and accordingly we find what annihilation is the goal of Buddhism, the supreme reward held out to the faithful observer of its precepts. There are several words in Pill by which the annihilation of being is expressed, but the commonest and best known is widdog or extinction, a word which conveys in a vigorous metaphor the fullest idea of the cessation of existence. Ever since Buddhism has been known in Europe great diversity of opinion has existed among European scholars as to the true nature of the Buddhist Nirvana. This disagreement is due to the fact that in the Buddhist texts two sets of expressalions are used with reference to Nirvana, the one implying bihafal existence and the other annihilation. According to the relative importance attached by them to these expressalions scholars have variously held Nirvana to be a state of biliefal immunity from human passion, or the total extinction of being. In 1869 Dr. Max Müller advanced a theory of Nirvana which was, as far as I know, the first attempt ever made to grapple seriously with the difficulties of the question, and to account in a scholarlike manner for the apparent co-existence of two irreconcilable doctrines of Nirvana. His theory is that the two opposite sets of expressalions represent two phases of the doctrine, the one ancient and the other modern. Of these the original doctrine taught by Buddha is that of "the entrance of the soul into rest," while the dogma of annihilation is a perversion introduced by metaphysicians in later times, and finding its expression in the Abhidharma. But a fatal objection to this view lies in the fact, which was unknown to Dr. Max Müller, that the doctrine of the Abhidbarma is identical with that of the other two Pippas, and that the expressions relative to Nirvana used in the Abbidharma are in reality taken from or authorised by the Vignya and Sūtra Pippas.

true explanation of this great question must be sought elsewhere. In Trübner's Record for July, 1870, I first propounded a theory which meets all the difficulties of the question, namely that the word Nirvūya is used to designate two different things, the state of blissful sanctification called Arbatship, and the annihilation of existence in which Arbatship ends. In my subsequent reading I have met with the most abundant evidence of the truth of this view, which early in 1871 was further strengthened by the publication of Mr. James D'Awlm's important essay "Boddhist Nirvāya," in which the author, writing independently of me and in ignorance of my theory, arrives at precisely the same conclusions as myself.

Having made these preliminary observations I will now proceed to state, as clearly as I am able, the doctrine of Nirvāya. Every being born into the universe is subject to transmigration. Death is everywhere followed by re-birth in a new existence, which may be one either of misery or of happiness. The insect crushed beneath the foot may be re-born as a radiant angel, or by the potent force of Karma an angel may be harled at death into the nethermost hell. Thus all is unstable, all is uncertain, present happiness is no safeguard against future misery, and even the bliss of heaven has its alloy; the whole sum of sentient existence is Suffering, and release from suffering or from the prospect of suffering can only be obtained by release from existence. The cause of continued existence is sin, remove this and you strike at the root of existence. Bin is removed by the Four Paths of Sanctification, and to these entrance is obtained by the “Sublime Eight-branched Road,” which is a life in accordance with Buddha's commands. By the practice of charity and other good works, by purity in word, thought and dead, and by the exercise of religious meditation, the disciple of Buddha is enabled to enter the Four Paths, and by so doing to escape from the misery of existence. The Four Paths are four stages of sanctification, ending in Nirvāya, the fourth immediately or to the course of a small number of years, the other three after various intervals, but all with absolute certainty, for he who has entered the Paths can never fall away, but is certain of attaining Nirvāya. Since the first three Paths all end in the fourth we will pass them by at present, and devote our attention to the fourth and highest, which is called arahatta or Arhatali, “the state of being salty.” Arhatship is final and perfect

sanctification, it is a state in which merit and demerit, original sin, devils and attachment are rooted out, in which all that blends man to existence, all that leads to rebirth or transmigration, is wholly extinct. The Arhat is still a man, be is subject to temptations, he is subject to physical suffering, and his life is not prolonged beyond that of other mortals. But he is a man purified and exalted. However greatly tempted he cannot sin, for his heart is purged from every taint of human passion. Freed from the trimmels that bind men to earth he traverses the air and works great miracles. He scans the thoughts of others, he can recall his own past life in countless exsistence, he bears the sounds in distant spheres, he beholds with the divine eye the beings that people the universe dying and being re-born. And in all the vclossitudes of life his mind preserves its even tenour, serene and tranquil be lives out his speed of life rejoining in the ever-present consciousness that he has triumphed over man's great enemy Existence. Death comes at last, but the seed of existence has withered, the lamp of life has burnt out, the Arhat is reborn no more again, he has attained Nirvana, he has crossed to exist. A great number of expresalons are used with reference to Nirvana which leave no room to doubt that it is the absolute extinction of belong, the annihilation of the individual. Thus Nirvana is called the Void, the Unconditioned, the Abstract, the Uncreate, the Infinite, the Eternal, the Formless, the invisible, and so forth, and its common synonym is Nirvada, “cessation” or “destruction.” It is described as “free from all trace of the elements of being.” and in scores of places the death of an Arhat is likened to the extinction of a flame, the strongest possible way of expressing annihilation intelligibly to all. Those who maintain that the goal of Buddhism is a state of blissful exemption from human passion, in other words that it is Arhatship, are as once confronted by an objection so formidable that its mere statement is sufficient to show how untenable is their theory. The objection is simply this, that Arhat, as is well known, die like other men. The Great Arhat himself died at the age of seventy-nine, and the deaths of all his great disciples and apostles are recorded; it is not even said that their lives were prolonged beyond the natural term of man's exist

The doctrine of Buddha on this subject is perfectly explicit, he even predicted his own death. Now to be the ultimate goal of Buddhism Arhatship must be an eternal state, for if it be not eternal it must sooner or later terminate either in annihilation or in a state which is not illusful, in either case it is not the goal of Buddhism. But since Arlaus die Arhatship is not an eternal state, and therefore it is not the goal of Buddhism. It is almost superfluous to add that not only is there no trace in the Buddhist scriptures of the Arbat consolidating to exist after death, but it is deliberately stated is innumerable passages, with all the eclasse and emphasis of which language is capable, that the Arhat does not live again after death, but ceases to exist. There is probably no doctrine more distinctive of Cikyamuni's original teaching than that of the annihilation of being. To suppose that the Buddhist Nirvega is the blissful repose of Hinduism is to suppose that Cikyamuni is a leading question of religious philosophy, that of a Future State doctrine, would content himself with borrowing from the creed which it was his mission to subvert. In point of fact we find that while he adopted many of the technical terms of Hinduism he almost always gave them a widely different or at least greatly modified meaning (see for instance BrAdAmo, Mahabrahmi, Sakka, Devadivo, etc., and comp. Alw. L xxxv).

The time has now come for the consideration of a point which it is of the utmost importance to clear up, since its misunderstanding has given rise to the erroneous view of Nirvāga held by so many scholars. The difficulty is this. It is true that many expressions are used of Nirvāga which seem to imply annihilation, but on the other hand other equally numerous and equally feasible expressions are used which clearly point to blissful existence. Thus Nirvāga is called Freedom from human passion, Purity, Holiness, Bliess, Happiness, The End of Suffering, The Cessation of Desire, Benze, Cakso, Tranquility, and so on. How is this discrepancy to be reconciled? I reply, the word siiddoa is applied to two different things, first that annihilation of being which is the goal of Buddhism, and secondly the state of illusful sanctification called arakatta or Arhatship which terminates in annihilation. This fact at once explains the apparent contradiction. The proof that Arhatship is called Nirvāga has first in the deliberate statements to that effect which abound in the sacred

texts, and secondly in the fact that all the names of Arhatship, such as saoti, viraddhi, daapakkhaya, eirdga, etc., are also used as names of Nirvāya. To distinguish them the two Nirvāya are called anupaddisevanibodman and samupddisevanibodman, the former designating annihilation and the latter Arhatship. Upddi is a name for the five skandhas, and anupaddisevanibodman means annihilation of everything except the five skandhas, while unupddisevanibodman means the extinction of being. From another point of view the two Nirvāya are distinguished as kilevanibodman or hilevparisinibodman, "the extinction of human passion," and khandahavibman or khandkapriinibodman, "the extinction of being." At first sight it may appear inexplicable that the same term should be applied to two things so different as annihilation and blissful existence, but I think I am able to show that after all the phenomenon may be easily accounted for. To the first place the ideas of Arhatship and of the annihilation of being are inextricably bound up together, there being no annihilation without Arhatship, and no Arhatship that does not end in annihilation; and thus there is an instinctive tendency to treat them as one and to designate them by the same name. Secondly, both Nirvāya involve the idea of annihilation, Arhatship being the annihilation of suffering, of original sin, of karman, of everything except the skandhas, while Nirvāya is the annihilation of every conceivable attribute of being. Thirdly, in a great number of instances the use of the word Nirvāya involves the designation of both Arhatship and annihilation. Thus if we say "Nirvāya is the reward of a virtuous life," this may strictly speaking mean that annihilation is the reward of a virtuous life, but since annihilation cannot be obtained without Arhatship, the idea that Arhatship in the reward of a virtuous life inevitably presents itself to the mind at the same time. Fourthly, when we consider how leader is the tie that binds the Arhat to existence we can understand how easily the word Nirvāya might be extended to include Arhatship. For what is left to the Arhat?
