In point of fact we find that while he adopted many of the technical terms of Hinduism he almost always gave them a widely different or at least greatly modified meaning (see for instance BrAdAmo, Mahabrahmi, Sakka, Devadivo, etc., and comp. Alw. L xxxv).

The time has now come for the consideration of a point which it is of the utmost importance to clear up, since its misunderstanding has given rise to the erroneous view of Nirvāga held by so many scholars. The difficulty is this. It is true that many expressions are used of Nirvāga which seem to imply annihilation, but on the other hand other equally numerous and equally feasible expressions are used which clearly point to blissful existence. Thus Nirvāga is called Freedom from human passion, Purity, Holiness, Bliess, Happiness, The End of Suffering, The Cessation of Desire, Benze, Cakso, Tranquility, and so on. How is this discrepancy to be reconciled? I reply, the word siiddoa is applied to two different things, first that annihilation of being which is the goal of Buddhism, and secondly the state of illusful sanctification called arakatta or Arhatship which terminates in annihilation. This fact at once explains the apparent contradiction. The proof that Arhatship is called Nirvāga has first in the deliberate statements to that effect which abound in the sacred

texts, and secondly in the fact that all the names of Arhatship, such as saoti, viraddhi, daapakkhaya, eirdga, etc., are also used as names of Nirvāya. To distinguish them the two Nirvāya are called anupaddisevanibodman and samupddisevanibodman, the former designating annihilation and the latter Arhatship. Upddi is a name for the five skandhas, and anupaddisevanibodman means annihilation of everything except the five skandhas, while unupddisevanibodman means the extinction of being. From another point of view the two Nirvāya are distinguished as kilevanibodman or hilevparisinibodman, "the extinction of human passion," and khandahavibman or khandkapriinibodman, "the extinction of being." At first sight it may appear inexplicable that the same term should be applied to two things so different as annihilation and blissful existence, but I think I am able to show that after all the phenomenon may be easily accounted for. To the first place the ideas of Arhatship and of the annihilation of being are inextricably bound up together, there being no annihilation without Arhatship, and no Arhatship that does not end in annihilation; and thus there is an instinctive tendency to treat them as one and to designate them by the same name. Secondly, both Nirvāya involve the idea of annihilation, Arhatship being the annihilation of suffering, of original sin, of karman, of everything except the skandhas, while Nirvāya is the annihilation of every conceivable attribute of being. Thirdly, in a great number of instances the use of the word Nirvāya involves the designation of both Arhatship and annihilation. Thus if we say "Nirvāya is the reward of a virtuous life," this may strictly speaking mean that annihilation is the reward of a virtuous life, but since annihilation cannot be obtained without Arhatship, the idea that Arhatship in the reward of a virtuous life inevitably presents itself to the mind at the same time. Fourthly, when we consider how leader is the tie that binds the Arhat to existence we can understand how easily the word Nirvāya might be extended to include Arhatship. For what is left to the Arhat? Karma and Upddi, the causes of existence, are gone, Kleya or original sin is rooted out, Kama or sexual pleasure is extinct, the mind is freed from all that is gross and earthly, nothing separates the Arhat from extinction except the narrow film of human life which a breath can take away, and which cannot be prolonged beyond a few here

years, a term which dwindles into nothing by the side of the eternal death which follows. Fifthly, since Arhatship is necessarily followed after an insignificant interval by Nirvana, to say that an Arhat has attained Nirvana is merely to say that he has made sure of Nirvana, that he has made Nirvana his own, it is a figure of speech examples of which are to be found in the literatures of every religion. Other instances of this anticipation may be adduced from the Buddhist texts, as the passage at Dh. v. 418, where the Arhat is called by anticipation "free from upadhi," although upadhi properly includes the skandhas from which the Arhat is not yet free; and at Ras. 30 an Arhat says, "I have obtained (i.e. made sure of) Nirvana, in which there is no decay and death."

The term Nirvāya then was originally limited to the extinction of being, but by the operation of causes like those just enumerated came to be extended so as to include Arhatship, and the terms suopaddisansibodna and suopaddisesanibbāna were afterwards coined to distinguish the two Nirvāya when logical precision was required, or where the context did not clearly determine which Nirvāya was meant. An extraordinary error, originating I think with Burnouf, and repeated unsuspectingly by several eminent European scholars, has done much to involve the question of Nirvāya in needless doact and obscurity. It is the belief that there are three degrees of Nirvāya, viz. nibbāda, parinibbāda, and mahdāparibādna, “ordinary Nirvāya, complete Nirvāya, and great complete Nirvāya.” This idea is strangely wide of the truth, for parinibbāda means merely Nirvāya, or the attainment of Nirvāya, and mahdāparibādna means nothing more than the death of Buddha. Another error results from mistaking Savaga or heaven for Nirvāya. We have seen that none but Arlusta attain Nirvāya at death, and an ordinary Buddhist if questioned by a European as to the reward of a virtuous life will generally answer by depicting the sensuous joys of the Kāmāycaradevaloka which is the reward he immediately looks to; the questioner then is apt to come hastily to the conclusion that this blissful state is the famous Buddhist Nirvāya, and proclaims to the world that the modern view of Nirvāya makes it a sort of paradise of sensual delights. In some Buddhist countries the doctrine of Nirvāya appears to have participated in the general degradation that the whole religion has undergone in those countries, and which has produced such monstrous as the Adi Buddha, the Dhyani Buddha, the worship of Amitabha and Avalokteyara, the doctrine of the perdition of women, and many other fantastic modern innovations.

I have shown that the goal of Buddhism is annihilation, and that Nirvāpa is a brief period of bliss followed by eternal death. It is of course conceivable that Gākyumuni should have made Arhatship the maximum δḤomāni held out to his discipline. It may even appear incredible to some that having imagined a state of blissful parity resulting from a virtuous life, be should have made it end in annihilation. That he did so is however certain, and it must be remembered that his denunciations of the evil and suffering of existence are levelled not merely against transmigration but against all existence whatever, and that the bliss of the Arhat is chiefly based on the consciousness that he has rooted out Karma and may any day cease to exist. It is not my intention here to discuss the ethical aspect of the question of Nirvāpa, and I shall content myself with observing that Christianity with its doctrine of everlasting punishment can ill afford to reproach Buddhism with a doctrine of annihilation.

I now proceed to give a few details respecting the Four Paths which properly belong to the article Maggo, but which as bearing closely on the question of Nirvaga I have reserved for this article. The first three paths all end to the fourth (Arhatshp), and consequently in Nirvapa. The lower paths lead into the higher. For when a Solapanna has passed through five of his existences he has but two more, and then would naturally be a Sakadigamin; the next birth would make him an Anagamin, after which he would be re-born only once again and again Arhatshp. To obtain the higher grades of sanctification it is necessary to pass through the lower: thus a man cannot become a Sakadigamin without having first been a Solapanna, or an Arhat without having been a Solapanna, a Sakadigamin and an Anagamin.

But a man who has attained Sotidpatti can, by a successful exertion of the necessary means, pass onward before his death to one or more of the higher steps. Thus he may either attain Sakadagamiship and stop there (in which case he will have to be re-born twice), or he may attain in succession Sakadagamiship and Anagadimship and stop there, or he may pass successively through the first three paths to Arhatship and so attain Nirviqa when he dies. The first two paths will be further considered under the words Sotidpasno and Sakadagam. The Anagamin when he dies is reborn for the last time in one of the five highest Erbma heavens (suddAdedas), and there attains Arhatship and Nirviqa (suddAdassam wibbattled tatth' eva arakhatas papapilt portabbayati). that be who realizes the unabstαιtiality and impermanence of the body "will pass beyond the key or reach of the king of Death," viz., as the comment says, will become an Arhat (khāṣrāma bhikkhāry). At Db. v. 85 Nirāfa is spoken of as pāra, "the Further Shore"; pārma is given as an epithet of N. at Ab. B, and this passage of Dhammapada shows the origin of the metaphor; this shore is continued existence (maccakheyya), to obtain Arhatship and thereby escape from continued existence is exceedingly difficult, is is like crossing a rushing river, but once you have crossed, once you have obtained Arhatship you are safe, your release from existence is secured. The last verse of this chapter is a very important one, "Those whose mind is rightly developed in the seven branches of spiritual knowledge, who freed from upshاśma delight in the abandonment of assessment, such men, enlightened and with human passion destroyed within them, attain Nirāya." I have Islī lokə untrawlśrā: I at one time though that is qualified partalbūmā and that like partilbūmā meant "even in this life they atāsu Nirāya," but further consideration has led me to abandon this view. For the commentator says that both Nirāya are meant (is uses the words exaspā-diēsa and amypridēsa, and adds that "they attain con-existence, like the flame of a lamp when the oil is exhauṣmād)." The fact is that lokə is constantly used in a very vagus manner without giving any definite additional meaning to the passage, and to lokə parimidāmi probably means merely "they may be said to have attained Nirāya." If however lokə here means "in this life" (imasmih lokə), the sense of the passage would be that those who have got rid of attachment attain Arhatship (followed by extinction) in this life, namely, that they do not stop at Anigimship, to which ease they would have to be re-born, and attain Arhatship and extinction in a Brahma heaven, but that they reach Arhatship in this world of men. The next chapter of Dhammapada, the Arahaotavagga, consists of ten verses taken from different parts of the Tiptaka and descriptive

of Arhatship. Of these the most important are verses 90, 93, which express the idea that the Arhat passes away, leaving no more trace of existence than a bird leaves of its passage through the air. Vinokha yammy guearo means, I think, "whose heart is set on Emancipation from existence (viz. khasdhaparissiddha or amhiliation)"; the comment says turn drammaram kated, which is strongly in favour of this view. Sufiato amimitta, "the Void, the Unconditioned," are adjectives qualifying vimokho: in the article Garoo I have readored vismakho by Arhatship, taking gocaro in the sense of "sphere" or "domain," but the epithets suzilata and amimitta make this very improbable; though it must be observed that there is a tendency to reflect back upon Arhatship the names properly applicable only to amhiliation. At Dh. 114 we have apasam amalam padam, "not beholding the eternal lot (viz. aupdad) daraamiddha or amhiliation"; to see Nirvaga, or to realize Nirvaga (subdam sachkharoti), means to atain Arhatship or to be an Arhat (E. Mon. 282): for the word amata see the Letter part of this article. At Dh. 120 it is said that "some are born as men, evil doers go to hell, good man to heaven, while Arhats asma Nirvaga"; here the Nirvaga meant to oumpiddiesamiddha or amhiliation. At v. 134 it is said that the man who has made himself as noiseless as a broken gong (viz. completely sullied his passions) has attained Nirvaga (viz. Arhatship: for an explanation of the simile see Kassio). At v. 154 occurs a very important passage, visakidharagatan cittas taphdanah khagam qijhagi, "my soul, arrived at the gates of amhiliation, has attained the destruction of human passion"; the comment explains tapAdama khaga by "Arhatship" and vismakha by "Nirvaga," and says that the mind by dwelling on amhiliation has gone to it or gone up to it (comp. my remarks on verses 90 and 92). The next mention of Nirvaga in Dhammapada is at v. 184, khanti paramas tapo tikkhad, niddama paramam sodamti badakha, "patience, which is long suffering, is the best devotion, the Buddhas declare that Nirvaga is the best (of things)"; this is the rendering of the commentator, and it is quite impossible to take the passage in any other way: of course both Nirvagas are meant. Santam, “the Tranquil,” belongs to both Nirvāya; senti in its sense of “calm” to Arhatship, so its sense of “cessation” to annihilation. Saccon, “the True” or “the Truth,” means, I think, that the doctrine of Nirvāya is the cardinal truth of Buddhism. Several words implying eternity are applicable only to annihilation, since Arhatship is as I have shown a very brief state; such are akkhasam, “the Imperishable,” anatash, “the Infinite,” dhuvam, “the Eternal,” accutam, “the Everlasting” (explained at Dh. 385 by sassatem). The word amatam as an epithet of Nirvāya I believe to mean “the Deathless,” or “the Eternal,” and to designate anupaddisesanihodma. From Dh. v. 114 it is clear that amatam as a designation of Nirvāya is an adjective, and not a noun, so that whatever it means it cannot well measure immortality. The commentators generally explain it to mean “free from death” (Dh. 290, Alw. N. 133), which cannot be said of Arhatship unless by anticipation; comp. the passage at Ras. 30, where an Arhat says he has attained Nirvāya, free from decay and death, and tranquil (ajardmaram sittikam patto niddassam), meaning that he has made sure of it, that he has made it his own (I have also met with ajdam as an epithet of Nirvāya). Too much stress should not be laid on such expressions as “diving into the Amata” (Kh. 8, Dh. 73), which may very well be anticipatory; comp. the expressions “to touch Nirvāya or annihilation,” “to see Nirvāya,” “to know Nirvāya,” which mean to attain

Arhatship, Asonikhatam, "the Immaterial," nippanis, "the Abstract," asickhatadhatu, "the immaterial element," and akutam, "the Uncreate" or "Uncaused," are epithets of anupdidiserasidbima, and so probably are anidassomank and apalokitas, which appear to mean "the Useen." Sududdasah, pardyanati, hevalah, prami belong to both Nirvipas. Nibbati is its sense of "tranquility" designates Arhatship, in its sense of "extinction," Nirvipe. Virappas, "freedom from transmigration," would apply to both Nirvipas: probably also dakkhakikayo and ayapigham. Sivan, "bliss," can be used of both Nirvipe, for we have shown that Arhatship is a state of bliss, and from a Buddhist point of view annihilation can perfectly be spoken of as "bliss," for it is a "happy release" from the suffering of existence: comp. Dh. v. 203, niddam paramath smikham, "extinction is the highest bliss." The same remarks will apply to yogakhemo if we take it in the sense of bliss, but it is interesting to see that the comment on Dh. v. 85 explains it as "exemption from the four Yogma" (kama, bhava, ditthi, amjida, the pleasures of sense, existence, false doctrine and error), and seems to restrict it to an updidiserasidbima; should this etymology be Buddha's, it affords another instance of the way in which, in adopting technical terms already in use, he was accustomed to modify or alter their meaning and application. Although expressions like "extinction is bliss" may sound strange or even ridiculous to us, who have from our earliest infancy been taught that bliss consists in eternal life, to a Buddhist, who has always been taught that existence is an evil, they appear perfectly natural and familiar: this is a mere question of education and association; the words "extinction is bliss" convey to the mind of a Buddhist the same feeling of enthusiastic longing, the same consciousness of a sublime truth, that the words "external life is bliss" convey to the Christian. There are many other names and epithets of Nirvipe besides those enumerated in Abhidhnappadipik, as seppo = "bliss" (Sen. K. 235), fstikkayo, "end of birth" (Dh. 75), vaffappachedo, "cutting short of transmigration," accentam, "the Endless" (astana pariyadamam anikkhatatid acoantam), anakkhatam, "the Ineffable" (Dh. 39), appavatti, "non-existence," appavattam, "the Non-existent," amarapan, "free from death," asokam, "the Borrowless," anappddo and apafisandhi, "absence of re

The remarkable expression ab freepa, "City of Nirvipa," involves a bold metaphor, Nirvipa (ambigation) being compared to a city, which is the goal of the pilgrimage of existence. How far back this metaphor can be traced I do not know, but I have met with it in Buddha's com- mency on Mahāparinibbāna Sattā. Comp. andur' etain amatassa dedrāth, unlock the gate of Nirvipa (Ahw. N. 138). The question of Nirvipa is discussed with great ability by Burnoff in his introduction, 18–20, 516–522, 580–594: I think I may say that he is decidedly in favour of the opinion that the goal of Buddha is annihilation. Hardy's testimony is very clear: thus at S. Mon. p. 5 he says, "the path that leads to nirwāna or the cessation of existence:" at p. 6, "at his death the rahat fuvariably attains nicwāna or ceases to exist," (these words are repeated at Man. B. 38); at p. 20, "the priesthood is to be sought in order that existence may be overcome, and that nirwāna, or the cessation of existence, may be obtained;" see also 15, 229, 291–308. Agāni, in his Legends and Theories of the Buddhists, p. xivi, he says, "be attains nirwāna, after which he will never be re-born, but will cease to exist;" and at p. 173 he distinctly grasps the true meaning of the terms comp- paddisnu and sappiddisna, for he uses these remarkable words, "It is said to be sawpuddindam, as having the five khandas. This is the state of the rahat, and is one view of nirwāna. It may be said of the rahat that he has attained to nirwāna, though he still lives. He who is anupaddisna has not the five khandas." In D'Aiw's Buddhist Nirvipa there is abundance of valuable matter, but one passage is of such great interest that I cannot forlear quoting it. The author says, p. 52, "We need only remark that the Nirvāna which Gotama attained before death, and which according to Buddhism man must procure in this very life, is savupaddissemibāna, or 'sivāna with a remnant of the elements of existence.' This lot is called Nirvāna from there being as impediment from thence to the commuion of the reality itself," and, as Muller says, 'it means the extinction of many things, of selflessness, desire and sin, without going so far as the extinction of consciousness, and even

It would also seem to be a condition in which 'all wishes and dealers are subdued, in which there is indifference to joy and pain, to good and evil, and a freedom from birth in the circle of existence'; and although all the causes which led to the last birth before the settlement of savopiddisannibbana have been destroyed by the achievement of this condition of existence; yet there is in it a remnant of Upadil. That remnant is Existence itself; and its final destruction by death constitutes what is called par excellence the Nirvapa, or anupiddisannibbana, or parinibbana, or Nihilism." Nothing can be more clear or positive than this, or more completely in accordance with my own conclusions published in 1870. It is, however, much to be regretted that both Mr. D'Alwis and Mr. Harly should have dismissed this part of the question in a few times, apparently quite unaware of its extreme importance.

My task is now at an end. It is true that it is in my power to offer abundant further proof of my statements from unpublished texts which I have transcribed or indexed, but many of my readers will consider that this exposition has already exceeded the legitimate limits of a dictionary article, and but for the extreme importance of the subject I should not have ventured to deal with it at so much length. The Labour spent in obtaining the present results is simply rewarded if, as I sometimes allow myself to hope, I have succeeded in withdrawing the Buddhist Nirvaga from the category of disputed questions. At any rate I feel confident that time is on my side, and that the researches of future students will only confirm the general accuracy of my conclusions.

NIDAHATI, and NIDADHATI, and NIDHETI, to put down, to lay aside; to deposit, hide, to bury; to enshrine [fɪˈstʌri]. Bhāmiṇyasi w., to hide in the ground, to bury (Dh. 408, comp. Kh. 12). Sabbau bhatien nidhdya daqdais, merciful to all creatures, lit. having laid aside severity to all creatures (Dh. 28, 72). Nidhadakdmo janatdem dhaumasi, desirous of enshrining the Truth in the hearts of his people (Att. 201). Pres. nidahati (Dh. 408), nidheti (Kh. 12). Ger. nidhdya, nidahited (Das. 30). Inf. nidhadwim, Pass. niddhyaeti (Kh. 19). P.p.p. nhito. Caus. nidhdpeti, nidhadpeti, to enshrine, to cause to be laid up or deposited or buried (Mah. 123; Ten J. 52). For the form nidheti comp. deti, to the analogy of which it perhaps owes its origin.
NIDAM, see Niddham.

- NIDÂNAM, Primary source, origin, cause; cause of a disease; introduction [frʌːtʃər]. Ab. 91; B. Int. 50. Pafhamassa Pirdijkassa vathum pi pucchi niddamus pi pucchi prggalam pi pucchi, inquired the subject of the first P., the causes that led to its enactment, the person concerned (Bruhmajala S. Attb.). Rijá middamu tama pucchiya, the king having acquired into the cause of his disease (Mah. 244, comp. Dh. 181). Tato middamu, in consequence of that, on that account. N'atthi tatv, middamu ppapus, there is no guilt from this as a cause (see B. Lot. 453, line 8 fr. bottom, the stth says tato middamu ti mathakhalakarama niddamu). N'atthi to uto middam bhayam, you have nothing to fear from this (Jit. 26). Tuto niddamu labhetha pndqijom, he would on this account experience pleasure (see B. Lot. 473, line 8, nth says tato middamu ti dndqyaniddamu): the construction in pecullat, one would expect taand siddato. In the Tipijaka the narrative of the circumstances under which any sermon of Buddha was delivered is called its middamu, “cause, or raison d'etre.” Evam me suam ti delikath dyasmotd Amdendema pafhamamahdanigtilikile vattam niddamu did, the passage beginning exam me sutash, spoken by A. at the first Great Rebearmal, is the

"Cause" or "Origla" (Brahmajala S. Aith.). Hence any preface or introduction to a book or compilation is called sidama, e.g. the reading of the matter prefatory to the rules of Patimokkha is called sidawadasa (Pit. 3). The introduction to the Járaka book is called Jidakamiddwah, but I am not quite clear that in this word it remains the original meaning of "cause." It deals with the tipi middhadal or three epochs into which the life of Gotama Bodhisatta and Buddha is divided. They are called dàresiddawah, aviddremiddawah, and santikemiddawah, "distant Epoch, middis Epach, and near Epoch." The first extends from the Bodhisatta's resolve to become Buddha (4 saak-kheyas and 100,000 kappas ago) to his birth in the Tusila heaven; the second from the latter period to his attainment of Buddhahood; and the third from his attainment of Buddhahood to his death. I have followed Vijesinha in calling these "Epochs," but in the present imperfect state of our knowledge of the Játaka I feel unable to give a decided opinion as to their meaning.—The twelve Nidamas or Causes of Existence are avijid, saikhadra (m.pl.), viñidpan, mimarúpas, sajdayatasa, phaso, sedand, taḥad, upddamah, bhavu, jāti, jardmarapah sakapartiradakkhadomanasupydad (pl.), "Error, Karma, Consciousness, the Individual, the six Organs of Sense, Contact, Sensation, Desire, Attachment, Existence, Birth, Suffering" (for detailed account see Paticcataisapppada). E. Mon. 6, 103, 301; Man. B. 179, 391, 432; B. Int. 59, 483, 634, 638; B. Lot. 380.

Pafhamassa Pirdijkassa vathum pi pucchi niddamus pi pucchi prggalam pi pucchi, inquired the subject of the first P., the causes that led to its enactment, the person concerned (Bruhmajala S. Attb.). Rijá middamu tama pucchiya, the king having acquired into the cause of his disease (Mah. 244, comp. Dh. 181). Tato middamu, in consequence of that, on that account. N'atthi tatv, middamu ppapus, there is no guilt from this as a cause (see B. Lot. 453, line 8 fr. bottom, the stth says tato middamu ti mathakhalakarama niddamu). N'atthi to uto middam bhayam, you have nothing to fear from this (Jit. 26). Tuto niddamu labhetha pndqijom, he would on this account experience pleasure (see B. Lot. 473, line 8, nth says tato middamu ti dndqyaniddamu): the construction in pecullat, one would expect taand siddato. In the Tipijaka the narrative of the circumstances under which any sermon of Buddha was delivered is called its middamu, “cause, or raison d'etre.” Evam me suam ti delikath dyasmotd Amdendema pafhamamahdanigtilikile vattam niddamu did, the passage beginning exam me sutash, spoken by A. at the first Great Rebearmal, is the

"Cause" or "Origla" (Brahmajala S. Aith.). Hence any preface or introduction to a book or compilation is called sidama, e.g. the reading of the matter prefatory to the rules of Patimokkha is called sidawadasa (Pit. 3). The introduction to the Járaka book is called Jidakamiddwah, but I am not quite clear that in this word it remains the original meaning of "cause." It deals with the tipi middhadal or three epochs into which the life of Gotama Bodhisatta and Buddha is divided. They are called dàresiddawah, aviddremiddawah, and santikemiddawah, "distant Epoch, middis Epach, and near Epoch." The first extends from the Bodhisatta's resolve to become Buddha (4 saak-kheyas and 100,000 kappas ago) to his birth in the Tusila heaven; the second from the latter period to his attainment of Buddhahood; and the third from his attainment of Buddhahood to his death. I have followed Vijesinha in calling these "Epochs," but in the present imperfect state of our knowledge of the Játaka I feel unable to give a decided opinion as to their meaning.—The twelve Nidamas or Causes of Existence are avijid, saikhadra (m.pl.), viñidpan, mimarúpas, sajdayatasa, phaso, sedand, taḥad, upddamah, bhavu, jāti, jardmarapah sakapartiradakkhadomanasupydad (pl.), "Error, Karma, Consciousness, the Individual, the six Organs of Sense, Contact, Sensation, Desire, Attachment, Existence, Birth, Suffering" (for detailed account see Paticcataisapppada). E. Mon. 6, 103, 301; Man. B. 179, 391, 432; B. Int. 59, 483, 634, 638; B. Lot. 380.

NIKAYO, A. multinde, assemblage; a collection; a class, order, group; an association, fraternity, congregation; a house, dwelling [fautto]. Ab. 208, 632, 1104. Aimaire decanbokya, some one class of devs. Bahá sationikdyd, many classes of beings. Játe andianikáye pi, even when another association of name was formed (Mah. 120). The three federities of priests mentioned at Alw. I. x, xi, are those of the Abhayagiri, Jetavana and Mahāvinára monasteries, all of Ceylon (Sabb.). The name Nikáya or Collection is given to certain divisions of the Tópitaka or Baθdblet scriptures. The five nikáya are the five divisions of the Sutta Pípaka, each containing a certain number of the discourses of Buddha and his apostles (E. Mon. 168, 169, 172; Alw. I. 63). Their names are Dighankidyo, Majjhimanikdya, Samyuttankidya, Aiguttorankidya, Khaddakankidyo. By the four Nikáya are meant the first four of these. Nikáya? —NIKKHAMATI, To go out, set out, start, go forth, go away, depart [fɪˈnɑːtɪŋ]. Used like abhinikkhamati of giving up the world to devote oneself to the successful life (Mah. 10). Nikkhamiturn ndaakkhi, could not get out, or escape (F. Ját. 5; Tea J. 40). Aor. nikkhami (Dh. 108; Ten J. 111; Mah. 204). Ger. nikkhamma (Ma. 139, 233), nikkhamited (Dh. 103, 233; P. Ját. 53). NIKKHEPO, Putting down, depositing, rejection [fng]. Podasiikkhepo, setting down the foot (Dh. 282). Dehaisikkhepotfhoamaki, on the spot where the body was deposited (Att.138; Mah.125).
NIKEHIKO, A royal treasurer or mint-master [@qq]. Ab. 343.

NIEKHIPANAM, Putting down [fəfəqə]. Pa-

dawikhipama, setting down the foot.

NIKHIPATI, To put or throw down; to lay or throw aside; to lay up, deposit, keep [fuhap]. Paddars n., to set down the foot, tread. Pidaamile siikhhipi, laid it at his feet (F. Ját. 5). Dhanamarai ca siikhhippa (grv.), laying aside his bow and arrows (Mah. 78). Khduladondeh sitono apjakaan siikhhipited, having laid her own egg in the nest of the raven (F. Ját. 49). Bhikkund taah ctevaras siikhhipitabkan, the priest must keep his robe by him (Pkt. 8). Atiasa siikhhipited onan bhdeati, means one thing and says another (lit. keeps one thing in his mind). Caus. manijadaya siikhhipápesi, caused it to be deposited in a casket (Ten J. 51).
— NIKKHITTO (p.p. last), Put down, thrown down; laid aside; deposited [fəfə]. Asikkhitta-dkuro, docile, unmanable to discipline (lit. "by whom the yoke, or the burden (?), is not thrown off").

NIKEHO, and NIKKHAM, A golden ornament for the neck or breast; gold; a weight of gold equal to five savappas [fug]. Ab. 480, 888; Dh. 367. A form mekkha occurs at Dh. 41.

NIKEILESO (adj.), Proc from Kilesa [fug]. Dh. 369, 370.
NIKKOSAJJO (adj.), Free from cloth, diligent [f(x) + 5] [26]. Ab. 516.

NIKKUJITO (adj.), Overturned, upside down [fùq + yāqun]. Nikkujito udakumbo, a waterpot upset (Jst. 20). Seyyath pl bhanta nikkujjitan ed akkujjeyya paicchaanash od vica-ryya, 'tIs as If one should set up that which is overthrown or reveal that which is hidden (this formula occurs at the end of a great many sutras). Of the reading kk I think there can be no doubt, I find it in two MBS of Siglovda, in one MS. of Subha Solta, and at the end of Sūmaṭṭhaphala Sutta in two MBS. My copy of the Comment on the latter sutra says nikkujjitan ti adhomakhash faphitan heftdawkhajdtasid. It is true that at Mah. 133 we have nikkujianadoseh ("a canoe which was turned up on the beach," Turnour), but it is clear that in this case the exigency of metre has determined the loss of one h. At Pets. 61 we have a nona nikkujjana, "reversal, upsetting," as if from a verb nikkujjati or nikkujjeti, "to upset," which however I have not met with (patimkkujjanavaena, like the upsetting of a bowl). Ses Nikjjati.

NIKUBRATI, To degrive, cheat, defend, overreach

[fng]. Kh. 10.

NIKUJJATI, To attach importance to, lay to heart. The etymology of this word I have entirely failed to trace. I have met with it only in Simahinnhala Sutta, where the foli, formula occurs six times, anahianandited appafikkostind anatamano anatamassvdeam aslochdretod tam eva vdcani asgaphanto anibujjanto withdgt' daud pakhdasim. "Expressing neither praise nor blame, feeling annoyed yet uttering no word of annoyance, acqu效ing to the words (of the Tirthaka) though attaching not the alghliest value to them, I rose from my seat and went my way." The comment of Buddhaghasa is as follows, asagaphanto is idrato agaphanto anibujjanto to cravasan' eva idam siharasam ayah paramattho ti hadage afthapento ayahijamam pomhema eggaitaa eva nikujitah co (my M8. reads nikk- in this second place); which with Vijesigha's help I render thus: amagaphanto means not going into the master according to its essence but merely acquiesing, anikujjanto means not laying the Tirthaka's words

NIKHIPATI, To put or throw down; to lay or throw aside; to lay up, deposit, keep [fuhap]. Paddars n., to set down the foot, tread. Pidaamile siikhhipi, laid it at his feet (F. Ját. 5). Dhanamarai ca siikhhippa (grv.), laying aside his bow and arrows (Mah. 78). Khduladondeh sitono apjakaan siikhhipited, having laid her own egg in the nest of the raven (F. Ját. 49). Seyyath pl bhanta nikkujjitan ed akkujjeyya paicchaanash od vica-ryya, 'tIs as If one should set up that which is overthrown or reveal that which is hidden (this formula occurs at the end of a great many sutras). Of the reading kk I think there can be no doubt, I find it in two MBS of Siglovda, in one MS. of Subha Solta, and at the end of Sūmaṭṭhaphala Sutta in two MBS. My copy of the Comment on the latter sutra says nikkujjitan ti adhomakhash faphitan heftdawkhajdtasid. It is true that at Mah. 133 we have nikkujianadoseh ("a canoe which was turned up on the beach," Turnour), but it is clear that in this case the exigency of metre has determined the loss of one h. At Pets. 61 we have a nona nikkujjana, "reversal, upsetting," as if from a verb nikkujjati or nikkujjeti, "to upset," which however I have not met with (patimkkujjanavaena, like the upsetting of a bowl). Ses Nikjjati.

[fng]. Kh. 10.

NIKUJJATI, To attach importance to, lay to heart. The etymology of this word I have entirely failed to trace. I have met with it only in Simahinnhala Sutta, where the foli, formula occurs six times, anahianandited appafikkostind anatamano anatamassvdeam aslochdretod tam eva vdcani asgaphanto anibujjanto withdgt' daud pakhdasim. "Expressing neither praise nor blame, feeling annoyed yet uttering no word of annoyance, acqu效ing to the words (of the Tirthaka) though attaching not the alghliest value to them, I rose from my seat and went my way." The comment of Buddhaghasa is as follows, asagaphanto is idrato agaphanto anibujjanto to cravasan' eva idam siharasam ayah paramattho ti hadage afthapento ayahijamam pomhema eggaitaa eva nikujitah co (my M8. reads nikk- in this second place); which with Vijesigha's help I render thus: amagaphanto means not going into the master according to its essence but merely acquiesing, anikujjanto means not laying the Tirthaka's words

disdna, beholding each prognosticatior realised (Mah. 135). Nimittam stank na samazupasrdni, I see no reason for this (B. Lot. 400). Nimittam karoti, to drop a hint. Nimittakammam or nimittakavapank, a hint or inausnion (for a full illustration see Ohdo). Nimittam gapditi or garhati, to fall in love (Dh. 85, 86; comp. Clough's Diet. "nimittagakama, affected by personal beauty, falling in love"). Kilesaparimiddmam/imitam (adj.) khamdhaparimiddmam, annihilation of the elements of existence caused or heralded by annihilation of human passion (Dh. 300). /Animito (adj.) at Dh. v. 93 is I think rightly rendered by Max Müller "conconditioned," lit. "free from marks or attributes;" the comment explains it as "free from the three nimittas, riga, dosa, moka," which indeed are attributes of sentient existence. Animittam anadhtam marodasak idha jevitash, man's life here below is unmarked and unknown (Das. 34). As one of the technical terms of the Buddhist system of ecstatic meditation similar to the first sign of mental illumination produced by the successful exercise of kammathdna. In the haripakammathdna it is said to be established when the coloured circle is seen equally well with the eyes open and shut, the phenomenon of the circle seen with the eyes closed being the almitta, "sign or indication" that supernatural illumination is attained. In the dadsasatikamojfdma the priest with his eyes closed sees a form as of a star or gem or cloud or gurland, etc. (Man. B. 244, 253, 255, 258, 269, 302).

clear (Db. 106, 156).

Subhati sends me the foll. from Niddea Attb., paktipahjattdraampapot atirekaa ramatikmatkkidka yathdraelash drammapam almanhited ramath, tomed almanharratash devdawai sinbultd khad adma, "when they wish to enjoy themselves in a greater degree than the enjoyments (drammapaa, lit. materials of enjoyment) originally prepared for them admit of, they create ad libitum new sources of pleasure and enjoy themselves; accordingly the pleasures of the N. devas are called created pleasures." The explanation given at B. Int. 606 is purely fascful; so also, I need hardly say, is the wonderful etymology given by Clough in his Diet. NIBSAGGIIYO (adj.), That should be rejected, given up, abandoned; to be forfeited [ἐφανέ+v], the corresponding Baskrit word is βανδύγ[]. Kh. 26; B. Int. 302; Pit. 5, 76. The Vinsya treats of thirty priestly affeices called sissaggi and pociittiyidhamand, they are enumerated in Pitiimokibib. It is usual to take sissaggi in the sense of "that should be avoided or rejected," but I have no doubt that the whole term should be rendered "Piciittiya sins accompanied with forfeiture." Sabbhi sends me the full, gloss, sissaggiyanh kofiti sissagittabban kofi sissagikasa od gusapam puggalatao ed, "by a thing being nissaggias is meant that it has to be forfeited to a large or small chapter of priests or to a single individual." He adds, "If a priest has with reference to any article committed a pociittiya offence, he must surrender that article either to the saigha, or to a chapter of two or three priests, or to a bigb priest; this is called Nissaggiya; in giving up the article he must use this formula, idom me khaste efoorash (or patish, etc.) dassdhikkantath sissaggiyanh thath dasshata sissagjhad, Bir, this (exts) role has been kept by me beyond the preserved ten days, it is therefore subject to forfeiture. I surrender it to you." At E. Mon. 9 Hardy says, "Nissaggiat pociittiyidhamand, thirty in number, requiring forfeiture of such articles as the priests are permitted to possess."

similitakamamah karoti, "to give hints and signs," is thus explained in a passage from a comment quoted by Subhati, Yehir khiet kirdpetab

keish yash kiriki kicam ujkanam samad akhathed

yahi khiet updyehl ahidpasam abdaakamam

sultakamamadi adma. "The terms obdisamama

and nimittakamama mean giving to understand by

various devices, and without speaking straight out

and in express terms, that you want some business

or other to be done by some people or other."

Ilhamrashina are then given: a priest who wants

a priada built for him meeting some men says to

them, "Devotees, where do you live?" They reply,

"In a priada," when the priest observes, "There

is no rule against priests living in priada, is

there?" This is an instance of obdisma, then follows

as example of simiti: a priest seeing some

men coming begins sketching out a string and

filing sticks in the ground: "What are you doing,

reverend alri?" they ask; "I am going to make

myself a dwelling," be replies. In the above ex-

tract the compound is treated as a dvandava, but a

tiki makes obdisma qualify nimitta, obdisma imit

takamamam to shadebahtamimittakamam par-

lyattamimittakaramam ti atthe. In Par, E. I find

Ojdihe obdisma kmpramame, "when this broad

hint was given him." And in Vappupatha Jik

taka, Obhdisma mattam of similitomatias of spp

detaia alakakhi, could not get a glimmer or a

sign (of supernatural Illumination, while striving

to attain Jhana).
OCINATI, To gather, pick [wəfɪŋ]. Of flowers (Dh. 298, 269).
OCIEKBATI, To point out, draw attention to []. Db. 271.
ODAHANAM, Depositing, stowlog away (from next). Bhs:618, 817.
-ODAHATI, To pot in, to deposit; to attend, apply [$\sqrt{a}$]. Sothak e., to give ear, listen, attend (Alw. N. 23). P.p.p. ohito.

ODAKANTIKO, A deep pit or hole in the earth. This word is probably a derivative of  $ \frac{1}{2}\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi\pi $ 14 means a pit (an bandi) which goes as far as the water, that is to any, so deep as to reach water (Kh. 12). Or it may be odafo, “water” + antika.
ODAKO (adj.), Belonging to water, watery, aquosite [$\bar{v}$]. Pit. 91. Neut. odaikook, water. Odaikookho, a waterfood.
ODANAM, and -NO, Boiled rles []. Ab. 465; Dn. 224.
ODANIKO, A cook [  $ \hat{a}t{a}f\hat{a}ng $], Ab. 484.
ODÃO (p.p.p.), White; pure, clean, clear [wq- [tU]. Ab. 95, 1068; B. Lot. 563. Oddtaroet, white-shining, an epibet of the moon (Kh. 22).

OPDET, To place, set. This word is used of laying a lower's snares and nets. The scymology is doubtful; Subb. says it is from Di khipane, and quotes from a comment odditas thapitom; Ystrimallé says it is Di vehdeganame with area, he quotes to the place ca jididni ca oddpersi, "then is laid his snares and nets," and attumo odditash jidlo ca pdoon ca poed, "when he reached the net and snare set for him," he adds that Mahsaddanit gives a doktu Di khipanuddaneau, "DI, in the sense of throwing and placing." Trn J. 50, 113.

ODHISO (ado.), At the end of a period, ultimately  $ [\psi(t_{0})+\psi(t_{1})] $. Alw. I. 108.
ODI88A, Δ ger. from (§11 with ∀q; it appears to mean "expressly":�aista tra adita asmásida, without express permission" (?).
ODUMBARO (adj.), Belonging to the unburner tree, made of unburner wood [ʌtʃʌn]. Sen. K. 392. P1. Odontal, name of a people.
OGACCHANAM, Going down (from with par. S.A.)

OGAOHO (adj.), Belonging to, connected with, contained in [w+]. Ab. 742. See Antogado, Yster, quotes from Abhidhasappadipik Vappani, GADHA patifhdaya, auto agddhatiti antogadho, and adds that the is shortened.

OGĦATTI and OĠĦETI, To diva, plunge into, enter [$\sqrt{a}$], Ogħġietet polikharoptiż, diving into the tank (Mah. El). Aor. ogaki (Mah. 152, a perbapa shortened metri caust), Ger. ogugha, ogġħited (Ras. 69; Mah. 59). Anomalous ger. ogayħited (Mah. 201), P.p. oggħento (Dh. 105). Ogħieti at Mah. 118, ogġhetti at Dh. 431, P.p.p. ogġhko, plunging into, fording, entering.

OGĂHO, Flangling into, wading, fording [wãngtng].

Maáámmaddó vóyn dukkkagáka, unfordale as the

ocean (Er. J. S. A.),

OGALHO, see Ogdhati.

OGAMANAM, Ologdowa, setting [สุขพร[+จร].

OGAYHA, see Ogdhart

OHO, A flood, torrent, inundation, overflow; multitude, quantity [wɪtɪn]. Ab. 629, 941. Metaphorically of evils or passions which overwhelm humanity like a flood; in this sense there are four floods, khmagho, bhavgho, ditthagho, avijagho, the flood of sensual desire, the flood of renewed existence, the flood of false doctrine, and the flood of Iguorance (Dh. 432). At Dh. 162 these are called catabidiho kilesogho, the fourfold flood of evil passions. An Arhat is called oghatisgo, one who has crossed the flood, as having escaped from the four oghas (Dh. 68, 421). Jusogho, a multitude of people (Mah. 38, 124). Balogho, a large force of troops (Mah. 36, 124).
— OGILATI, To swallow [ √q ].

OQUNTHITO (p.p.p.), Covered, velled, wrapped up [qqqqqq], Pát. 21.

OHÁRANAM, Removlog (from next). Ab. 798.

—OHÄRETI (case). To remove [caus. wą]. Ke-

samausic o., to cut off the hair and beard (Alw. I.

92; B. Lot. 863). Ohritokesamasus, having the

hair and beard shaved (Dh. 140).

OHARI (adj.), Dragging down [$\tilde{v}$ + $q$].

Db. 62
— OHAYA, no Ojahati.

— OHITO (p.p, odakati), Pat In, deposited; put down, laid aside [$\alpha\beta\gamma\delta$]. Dh. 27. See Komhito. OHIYATI (pas. ojahati), To be left [$\alpha\beta\gamma\delta$]. Opt. ohiyeyya (P4. 07). Aor. ohiyi (Db. 215).

OJÅ (f.), Strength, sap of life, vitality; sap, juice, [E]'. Ab. 949 (the text has ydand, "that which supports life," the Sinbalese translation has Carbaydanaya karassad ruedjas "the ojas jelice which keeps the body alive;" this meaning belongs rather to Saaskrit [D. Dhammo-japassid (Dh. 360, 379) is rendered by Vjlesinha "Wisdom having truth for its essence, i.e. vlpasand." Dibobid, celestial essences (Dh. 139, Sabb. says "divyarana, madhuramunakra"). Pafkasojid, juice or map of the earth (Dh. 974), probably the sweet substance described at Man. B. 64. See Ojadd and Ojo.

OJADIPO, A name of Ceylon [ʒɑːl + ʔɑːl]. An 7: Mah. 93.

OJAHATI, Tu leave, forwake, abandon, renouvelable

[ ]. Ger. schlott, achägu (Db. 98; Sen. H. 504; B. Lot. 863). Pase. ohlyoti.
OJAVÃ (adj.), Juicy, succulent, sweet, lasclons [wã-vãn]. Ten J. 108 (qjavantdi ni sigrndhapak-kdi); Dh. 188 (papildni ojavantdi phaldphaldni).
QJO, Light, splendour; strength, vigour [$\bar{a}$]. A5. 912 ($\bar{a}$ and $\bar{a}$).
OKAM, A house, dwelling; a resting-place, asylum [ᠰᠠᠭᠠᠨ]. Ab. 207, 1060. Okam okon jakanti, they forsake every resting-place (Dh, 17).
OKAM, Water [ωωω]. Okapuppehi elvarehi, with drenched garments (Db. 197). Okamokato, from its watery home (for oka-okato, Dh. 7).
OKAPPANIYO (adj.), Becoming, suitable, proper [from up with up]. See Saddhi.
OKARO, Villeness, worthlessness [from ¶ with wiy, comp, Vokdro], Kindman's oldro, the vanity of sensual pleasure (Db. 79).

OKASAIKO, World or realm of space [+]. This is one of the three great divisions of the universe, and answers to our Space or Ether, being the great void which contains the worlds. Subbati written, "Of the three worlds the safta and sahtikva worlds are contained in the okdas world, which is the empty air (cónya kháça)." Vijalsha says that "the exaltikkhá, being the region of space above the edgu, belongs to okdaoloka." Hardy calls it "the world of space, the empty void, the far-extended vacuum" (Man. B. 3). Vij. informs me that the lines at Das. 45 are from the Mahāmandham Jāśak, and that the idea they contain is "conceive a thousand worlds like that over which the sun and moon revolve, within such a space they dominion extends."

okdoo adma n' istiki, the rest have not an opportunity of saying a word (F. Ját. 16). Majhe thapered okdama, leaving a space in the middle (Mah. 172). Okdama ydcati, to ask for leave (Dh. 128). Okdama kuroti, to give leave, to make room, to find time. When the multitude saw the brabmin Brahmiya approaching—tash okdam karoti yathá tash hitposso yasavino—they made such room for him as was due to a man renowned for his wisdom (Brabumkyu 8). Since me Bhagad okdama haroti paikassa veyyekurampiya, if the Bleased One has leisure to reply to my questious (Slim. 8, comp. Ten J. 12). Amaadattherama okdakaurwattahavi, in order to make room (keep a place vacant) for the Ubers Aanda (Br. J. 8. A.). Katkada, having an opportunity (comp. Hatokahisa). Ano-ikdama, unauthorized (Pitt. 111). Okdama labati, to have an opportunity, to get leave. Siku-piko okdama labhissati, the fowler will have a chance. Okdama labhited, having received permission (Dh. 103). Dubbinicchayam affank vindemchamato okdam alabhited, my time having been entirely taken up with trying a case of great difficulty, lit. not having had any leisure while trying a case very difficult to try (Ten J. 1). Laddokhado, having seized an opportunity (Att. 107), having obtained permission (Att. 108). In grun. okdo is the name of the locative relation (see Harkus).
OKIRANAM, Sprinkling (from next). Mab. 258. OKIRATI, To sprinkle [wɑ+ɤ]. Aor. okiri (Mah. 80). Ger. okirited (Dh. 135). Pass. okirigati. Caus. oldritpeti, to cause to be sprinkled (Dh. 78; Mah. 211).

OKEKO, A proper name [چرش]. Mah. 8

-OKEAMANAM, Descent (from next).

— OKKAMATI, To desecond, step down; to disembark; to fall into, enter or come into [ˈnɪːdɪnɪ] Niddam o., to fall asleep (F. Ját. 3). Niddam smokhamoto, getting no sleep (Db. 81). Strajjam okkami, got into a nervous state (F. Ját. 48). Buddhamah thagwassidam sattem mahdkarand okkomati, great compassion for mortals enters the hearts of the blessed Buddhas (B. Lot. 377). Lajidhamman okkomitod, becoming ashamed (Dus. 44). Maggi (ob.) o., to get off the road, leave the road (Pé. exl; Db. 303), to make way for a person entitled to respect (Db. 403). Sommudd thalom okkomam, came on shore, lit. deseended from the sea on the land (Mah. 169). Mdxkucchinh o., to enter the mother's womb, vlt. to be conceived (see Goddodekananti). Dtpakpimis okkassisham, landed on an island (Mah. 46). Ger. okkamma, okhassitod (Sen. K. 504).

OKKANTO (p.p. okkamati), Descended, entered; embarked [$\overline{+}$ 44]. Mah. 40, 131.
OKKASSA (ger.), Having dragged away or abducted [ger. fr.  $ \underline{\text{wong}} $].
OKKATTHO (p.p. avakad(hati), Lowered, low [$\sqrt{38}$].

OLAMBAKO (adj.), Hanging [ 백속 백칠잔]. Ját.51.
OLAMBATI, To hang down [ʌbˈwɒʃn], Db. 191; Ten J. 114. Cana. olambetti, to suspend (Jét. 9).
OLAMBO, Something hanging, an appendage [wɒŋθəˈʌŋ], Multolambo, hanging festoons of pearla (Mah. 213).

OLÁRIKO (adj.), Large, great; gross, coarse; material [σωματίς]. Appatirúpaš ofdrikasb, a gross impropriety (Dh. 293). Odriko obhdo, a broad hint. Odriko sukhusno, material and immaterial (Gag. Ev. 43, of the body and the mind respectively). The food which we take into our bodies is called odriko or material, as opposed to the subtle Nutiments phaso, masososicetand, and mishasas (see Ahdo).

Mahastash aftisongham ohduy pabbajito, having abandoned a large circle of kinsmen and entered the priesthood (H. Lot. 863). Pabbajitakdato puffdya, from the time he became a monk (Db. 402). Pabytod bhikkhun pabbajito hott, having fled, embraced the ascetic life among the Buddhist priests (Alw. I. 78). Anupabbajitadam, of those who took orders from his example (Mah. 34). PABBAJJA (c.), Leaving the world, adopting the ascetic life; state of being a Buddhist monk or priest, the monastic life; taking the robe, ordination [M] . As a Buddhist technical term pabbqjid means the condition of being a Buddhist monk or non. The ceremony of admission to the priesthood is called pabbqjid or pabbqianam. If viewed as the act of the recipient of orders, and pabbqianam (from the cans.) If viewed as the act of the priest conferring orders. The lyman desiring to renounce the world, having chosen a monastery, goes to one of the upasampanna priesla of that monastery, bringing with him a robe, and asks to be ordained. The priest then invests him with the robe, and makes him repeal the Sarapattaya or Creed, and the Danadla or Ten Commandments, and with this simple ceremony the candidate becomes a member of the sanghe, or chureh militant of Buddha with all its holy privileges (see Sangho). Eight is the lowest age at which the candidate is admitted to the priesthood. Until he receives upasampada or priest's orders (at the age of twenty), he is a Samqamera, "novice" or "descun." Imperat. 2nd pers. pabbaja, pabbajidhi (Dh. 139, 141), P.p.p. pabbajito. Caus/pabbajjeti, to bainah, to put away; to cause or induce to become a Buddhist monk; to admit to the priesthood, to ordain. Riddimalah pabbdjento, putting away the slins of lust, etc. (Dh. 428). Saighamittah Shikkhanish taah pabbdjento elcajjiya, having sent Saighamittah to ordain her (Mah. 111). Mayans attene putta pabbdjema, let us make our sons go into the church (Dh. 139). Ayamed Mahdaca-yano Somra updakaah pabbdjeto, she venerable Mahakassayana ordained the lay brother Sona (Alw. I. 92). PABBAJITATA (f.), State of being an ascate or Buddbiet monk [มรคิสตา + ราคี]. Db. 411. PABBAJITO (p.p.p. pabbajati), Having given up the world, having become an ascetic or Buddhist monk; having taken the robe, ordained [mifun]. Mahastash aftisongham ohduy pabbajito, having abandoned a large circle of kinsmen and entered the priesthood (H. Lot. 863). Pabbajitakdato puffdya, from the time he became a monk (Db. 402). Pabytod bhikkhun pabbajito hott, having fled, embraced the ascetic life among the Buddhist priests (Alw. I. 78). Anupabbajitadam, of those who took orders from his example (Mah. 34). Gaaffito vdd pabbajito vdd, layman or priest (Db. 348). Masc. pabbajito, an ascetic, a Buddhist monk or priest (Ab. 433; Db. 69). PABBAJJA (c.), Leaving the world, adopting the ascetic life; state of being a Buddhist monk or priest, the monastic life; taking the robe, ordination [M] . As a Buddhist technical term pabbqjid means the condition of being a Buddhist monk or non. The ceremony of admission to the priesthood is called pabbqjid or pabbqianam. If viewed as the act of the recipient of orders, and pabbqianam (from the cans.) If viewed as the act of the priest conferring orders. The lyman desiring to renounce the world, having chosen a monastery, goes to one of the upasampanna priesla of that monastery, bringing with him a robe, and asks to be ordained. The priest then invests him with the robe, and makes him repeal the Sarapattaya or Creed, and the Danadla or Ten Commandments, and with this simple ceremony the candidate becomes a member of the sanghe, or chureh militant of Buddha with all its holy privileges (see Sangho). Eight is the lowest age at which the candidate is admitted to the priesthood. Until he receives upasampada or priest's orders (at the age of twenty), he is a Samqamera, "novice" or "descun." PACCATTAṃ (adv.), Slagly, severally, individually [M. 30; Alw. I. 77; Sen. K. 215. PACCATTHARANAM, A cushion or carpet to alt on; the cushions or bedding of a couch [comp. NIRTUT]. Mah. 164; Db. 174, 302.

PACCATTHIKO (adj.), Hostile, adverse [μνυπην]. Das. 25. Paccatthiok jond, the disaffirmed inhabitants (Mah. 1xxvii), Paccatthiko, an enemy (Ab. 344; Jix. 8; Mah. 1xxvi). Atthopsecatthika, friends and foes (Das. 25).

PACCAVEKKHANAM, Looking at, consideration, contemplation [πυρνεῖν]. Dh. 102, 119; Das. 44; Ab. 794. There are five paccavekkhanas or subjects of self-examination for the Sσάρησμα, Bakadágiamin and Augámi. They are the Path, the Fruition of the Path, the pascuales already destroyed, the passions yet to be destroyed, and lastly Nirvipa. The following is the text as applied to the Sσάρησμα. See magnam paccaeekkhati, phalam paccavekkhati, pahaikhelere paccavekkhalil, "tatv isme manna killed avaritthah" ti wparimaggaittayavaijhe kilur paccaveekkhati, avaudus "agaw me dhamma drammaqato patididdha" ti amatavilbódnach paccavekkhati (Vle. Maggu). The Arhat, having no human passion remaining, has only four paccavekkhanas. (I owe the above to Vijesinha.)

— PACCAVEKEHATI, To look at, regard, consider,

contemplate []. Dh. 203.

— PACCAYÄKARO, This is a compound of the adverb paccayd with wīī (compare words like wīī, adduhkāra, yāutī), and is used to designate the Nidānas or the Paticezataumuppida (a cijjīpaccoyd saakhārd, etc.). Pacceydōre (loc.) adipak, knowledge of the causes of existence (Dh. 118, 319, comp. Man. B. 179). B. Lot. 532.
PACCAYIKO (adj.), Trustworthy [nɪˈtʌrˈwɒrɪt]

— PACCAYO, Belief, conviction, trust, faith; ground, motive; cause; a requisite or necessary; in grammar an affix [ʌmʌn]. Ah. 91, 987. Ashash tucash paceeayo patitihá jito, I became their trust and refuge (Dh. 329). Ko Artu lo paceeayo, what is the reason, what is the cause. 7 (followed by dat.). — Ye team paceeayo hoti, he who instigates them, lit. he who is a cause to them (Dh. 90). Kdyavteka 'co estitavokana paceeyo koti, bodily seclusion stands to mental abstraction in the relation of cause and effect (Dh. 370). Kocid vsa paceeyo evdguamandya, any (proper reason) for visiting the army (Ph. 15). Manedash sladdunah saibaititadpaldhdaya paceeyo bhavata, may this offering of my head be the cause of my receiving omniscience (Att. 215). Stod vsa paceeayo karited amofihah, giving this as his only reason, lit. making this thing and no other his motive (Ph. 15, 10). At. Dh. 148, the words dyatihhavassa paceayah kdfxah saikhkaali appear to mean "be will gain assurance of future happiness," lit. "he will make confidence of future existence." The twelve Nidhas are also called Paccayas (khayo paceayah, cessation of the causes of existence, Journ. Ceylon As. 806, 1845, p. 17). Tathárupo paceeyo, a reason of this sort, viz. a sufficient or satisfactory reason (Ph. 15, 27, 90). The four paccayas or neemazetes of a Buddhist priest are cfeasah, piadpda, sendunash, bhesajiam, clothing, food, bedding, medicine (see Catapaccayah). Paccayasantose, contentment with the four requisites, one of the virtues of a Buddhist priest (Alw. 1. 89). Mahagghehi paceeyehi, with priestly requites of a coaty description (Alw. 1. x). Gildapaccayd, requisites for the sick, medicines and sick diet (Mah. 87; E. Mon. 81). Paccayaddaya, one who maintains a Buddhist priest, supplies him with the necessaries of life (Dh. 103). — The abl. paceeyo is used adverbially as the second part of a compound, in the sense of "by means of," "in consequence of," "as the result of." / Tesasi kamma-paccayd, on account of their evil Karma (Kh. 11). Taphdpaceeyd spiddam, from Deire springs Attachment, lit. "as a consequence of Desire (there is) Attachment" (Alw. N. 36; Gog. Ev. 69; B. Lot. 521). Tassa pupphardma caritapaceayd, on account of or as a consequence of his going into the flower-garden (Dh. 228).

PACCEKO (adj.), Each one, single, several [单数]. Paccekabddhsu garetodwa, taking her by each of her arms, viz. one holding her at each side. \ Paccekapathah, each several question (Pat. 2, comp. 8). Paccekabaddiko, or paccekasambuddho, a Pratyeka Buddha, that is, one who has attained, like a Buddha, by his unslded powers the knowledge necessary to Nirvipa, but does not preach it to men (Mab. 5, 27; B. Int. 84, 297, 438; Alw. I. 76; Ten J. 119; Man. B. 87). He is not omniscient, and is in all respects inferior to a sammasambuddho or Supreme Buddha (E. Mon. 290). Paccekabadhisata, one destined to become a Pratyeka Buddha

PACCHĀBHATTIKO (adj.), One who eats afterwards, i.e. after it has become improper to do so [ᠮᠣᠩ + ᠪᠣᠶ + ᠪᠣᠶ]. Vlsuddhī Maggnā saye, pandritena eatā pacchā laddhata bhattanā adma pacchādbhattuā, tasas pacchādbhattasra bhojannat pacchādbhottabkhyanā, tasmin pacchādbhattabkhojana paechādbhattasāᠨnam hatad pacchādbhattash ellam asetti pacchādbhattika. The sevesih Dhutanga precept is khalapacchādbhattikugara, and

the full explanation of it is given by Hardy at pp. 09, 100 of East. Mon., “The priest who keeps this ordinance cannot eat any more after he has met with that which is akapa,” i.e. if he has for any reason to refuse that which is brought to him when he is eating; or if he be presented with that which is improper to be eaten from its loafsomeness or otherwise. He who keeps the superior ordinance may only eat that which is in his mouth and nothing more, although even the first handful of food that he takes is akapa. He who keeps the middle ordinance may eat that which is akapa, but nothing more. He who keeps the inferior ordinance may eat as long as he remains in one seat.” Clough, in his Sinhalese Dictionary under Telesdhátiága, calls it Pacchábhattikaíga, and this word be explains in its place as follows, “Pacchábhattikaíga a. (paccha afier, bhakūka not desired [alc], aṅga on ordinance), an ordinance of the buddhist priesthood enjoining it upon the priests to live on one meal a day, which meal must not be eaten before or after midday.” Vijasinha writes to me, “The sings enjoinus the non-acceptance of a second course in meals: the yogin accepts the first bowl of meat offered, but refuses to be served with any other whatever. Buddha-ghoma thus explains the first part of the compound, khaláti paṭṭhechamatthe updto ... na pacchábhattiko khalapachādhatiko ... paṭikkhitidriritṭahājanam' etam adman, khalu is an indelinable used in the sense of refusal, khalupacchābhattiko is equivalent to na pacchábhattiko, the term is used for one by whom food in excess of what is permitted is refused” (comp. Affiritto). Vij. also quotes from a commentary the foll whimalical derivation, khaláti eko sahwipika, so makhena phalam gahetod temin paṭite pana anāna na khatañti, tādāo ayam ti khalupacchādhatiko (comp. E. Mon. 09). Hardy's explanation above given is undoubtedly the correct one, as the full passage, which I take from Vleuddhī Magga, will show, Khalupacchādhatikaṯam pi “atirittabhojasam paṭikkhipādui” “khalupacchādhatikaṯam samādiyamiti” imissā aññataṇavaṇasena samādinnam hoti. Trua pama khalupacchādhatikaṯava pavaśretud puvabhojanam kuppiyan kreted na bhujjiltabam idam assa vidh

P.A.D.M. (Step, stride; footprint, trace, track, vestige, mark; a foot; footing, station, sits, place; office, rank, appointment; abode, home, lot; Nirvipa; business, matter, thing; subject, occasion, cause; a part, portion; a quarter or line of a steaks; a word; a sentence [ug], Ab. 91, 619. Sattupadam, seven steps or strides (Jit. 53). Dinnam pi alarupapadam direct, seeing the footprints of two people who had gone down to the lake (Dh. 304). Therapaddang, following in the there's footsteps (Mah. 167). Hatthiparlam, elephant's track. Akita padam ni'althi, there are no footprints in the air (Dh. 45). Sakmadash padamikkapo, birds setting down their feet (Dh. 282, this may however be referable to podo). Natkiti padam ni'althi, but never before heard the words "There are none left" (Dh. 139). Abidi-dhammapadadi, sentences or articles of the Abhidharma (Trenckner's Milinda Patha). As the title of one of the Tripitaka books Dhammapadam means "Texts of the Law," or "Religious Sentences," for the sing, comp. Kammandoumi, "Collection of Kammarakis:" the work answers to its title, being a collection of striking verses called from different books of the Tripitaka, and arranged under various beads. In another appillon of Dhammapadam means constituent or basis of Relligham (see the four dhammapadas under art. Dhammapadam). Buddha's sub-artism padam, the well-spoken words, lit. sentences, of Buddha (Alw. N. 68). At Pitz 80 the words Yo sahadram gacchi are called a poda or "sentence." Beavellad alari ovaadadil to delind mayema paratadai gwdagapadadi, words of praise and blame, such as "be had such and such virtues or such and such lives" (Sam. S. A.). Catwro paid, the four sentences in which the four Ariyassas are embodied (Dh. 48, there are many instances of next, nouns assuming a mass, form in the plural). Akkharapaddai, letters and words (Alw. I. xvl). Pividham padam, various grammatical forms (Ditto). Pappuns veccamodam pi montapadah vattah asakkomain, unable to say a word of the spell even when it was repeated for her (Dh. 189). Akkadpa-padam, a verb. Nipatapadam, an adverb. Amat-thapadain athapadass, unprofitable words and profitable words (Dh. 19, 285). Padam delim, the word "dvim" (Alw. I. vll). Ehrinavilapado, containing twenty-one words, Padai vyanijadai

words and letters (Mah. 303). Appañado amato-padas, diligence in the way of Nirvings (Dh. 5, here the commentator says padan ti updya maggo, pada is 'measas', 'way'). Sampuapado, complete in all its parts (Mah. 230). Pada is used like pada for a quarter of a slaman. At Alw, I. 100 the four parts of an anashubb stanza are called bndini cattēri padini. At Pat. 84 we have tattha padan ti eko gáthpādo, "here by pada is meant one quarter of a stanza," and further on masopubbingand dhamd is called a pada. Padadasyah, a hemlstich (Dh. 123). Catuppadik gdhid, and catuppad gdhid, a stanza of four members, a complete verse (Raa. 18, 67). Amatash padani, the eternal lot (Dh. 21). Santasi padan, the tranquil place or lot (Dh. 61). Sukhapadam, hilafal lot (Alw. I. will, p doubled metri caus). Padam is the sense of "the Lot" is one of the names of Nirvings (Ah. 8). Adipidapadam dated, malgaling him the post of Adipida (Mah. Ixxvii). As an epithet of an Arhat spade means "free from occasions, or conditions, or attributes." The phrase apodah kema padama wessatha at Db. 33 is difficult to translate because it contains a play upon two different meanings of pada: "the Truchless by what track will ye lead him" is very inadequate. Here apodo means devoid of conditions for rebirth, such as human passion, desire, karma, klege, etc., and kema padama wessatha means that the Buddhar's track or passage through Samasira has come to an end, and cannot be prolonged through any new existence, but at death he will come to exist. As the title of one of the Tripitaka books Dhammapadam means "Texts of the Law," or "Religious Sentences," for the sing, comp. Kammandoumi, "Collection of Kammarakis:" the work answers to its title, being a collection of striking verses called from different books of the Tripitaka, and arranged under various beads. Catwro paid, the four sentences in which the four Ariyassas are embodied (Dh. 48, there are many instances of next, nouns assuming a mass, form in the plural). Akkharapaddai, letters and words (Alw. I. xvl). Pividham padam, various grammatical forms (Ditto). Pappuns veccamodam pi montapadah vattah asakkomain, unable to say a word of the spell even when it was repeated for her (Dh. 189). PAHENA KAM, and PAHINA KAM, As offering, a present, especially of food [H]]. I believe this word to be a derivative of praHI and not proHIL, the S. prahegka and prahela h"sweetments" being identical with it, while prahela "a riddle" is really from HIL. The form pabi-ka strengthens this conclusion, while for the a comp. prahet, prahetri. The original meaning is "something sent, a present," and the meaning "sweetment" is a secondary one, and arose from sweetments being one of the commonest forms of a present. At Ab. 835, 256 pakeaka is given as a synonym of spadd, pahala, epdyana, ukkoca, and pappukara, all of which mean a present generally. At Db. 113 the present is tailed rice (bhikkhādi). The secondary sense of a present of sweetness is probably intended at Pit 89, where we read paceh adma pahaṅkattāḥya pafiyattā, "pāva is anything prepared as a present:" the fīkā however explains pahaṅkattāḥya by pappudhr-atthya. In Sām. S. A. I had Autunī pakaṅkaṇkādru.

PAHINATI, sed PAHETI, to send [HfU]. Aor. pákes (F. Jit. 5, 26; Mah. 81, 131, 167, 200), pohipi (Ten J. 41, 51; Dh. 107, 139, 140, 162, 434), pákií (Mah. 130). Fut. pakipissati (Aw. I. 76; Dh. 84, 101). P. pr. pakipasslo (Dh. 23). Ger. pakipistó (Dh. 133). From the false analogy of the nor. páhipi we have an opt. pálikepya at Pit. 83. But a far more remarkable instance of false analogy is the present pákiti "ba senda." This form is dedicated back by false analogy from pákií, which of course is the regular S. nor. WT. But looks as though it pointed to a present pákit, in the same way that the nor. bhdesi points to a present bhdesi. Dotom pákita, "send yo a messenger," occurs in Hillinda Path, and at Pit. 28 we have pakietabo. P.p.p. pahito, sent, despatched (Dh. 82, 139, 167). / Pahitato at Dh. 254 means resoluta, latent (prahita + stman); Sabb, says, vitiyahorapidilion pahito pesito aíld yassa so pakitatto.
PABINO, PAHIYATI, veo Pegajati
PAHITO, see Patriot.
PAHO (adj.), Dismissing [from W]]. Aghappaha, "sin-scaring" (Ahw, I. vli).

In exactly the same way, and comp. the use of Tantra and Sūtra in Sanskrit. The word piltikhad, which we render "Pali language," really means "language of the sacred texts" and the geographical name of this language is Māgadhā, "Māgadhāese," or Māgadhakhadā, "Māgadhā language." As, however, there are two or three dialects of Māgadhase, the term piltikhad, or "Language of the Buddhist Scriptures," is really the most accurate, specifying as it does a particular dialect of Māgadhā originally obscene and ignoble, but rendered immortal by the peerless literature of which it is the vehicle. The term pilt is a name for the Buddhist scriptures was of late introduction, probably dating from the first or second century after Christ. Gotama Buddha's name for his teaching as committed to memory by his faithful disciples was simply dhammaṃvāsāya, "doctrine and discipline" (yo so Aanda mayd dhammaṃ ca visayo ca desito paṭṭhito se vā man' accoyema satihā, "Let the doctrine I have preached you, the discipline I have prescribed for you, be your Teacher when I am gone," Br. J. S. A.); and this is the only name by which it was known as the first Great Rehearsal immediately after Buddha's death (iddal dhammaṃvinayamigahankara, "now we would make a recession of the Docurine and Discipline," Br. J. S. A.). It will be seen that the foil examples of the use of the word pilt in the sense of "sacred text" are all taken from late works. Neva piltigavā na apthakathāyaṃ disati, is to be found neither in the text nor in the commentary (Shā, S. A.). Piltigavā poma Buddho ti ken' asthena, but why is he called "the Buddha" in the text? (B. Lot. 71, from Jīna Akkaka). Yo pama atkam eva sappadeti na piltih, he who masters the sense but not the text (Dh. 419). Piltikh piya fau aggaham, held the commentary in the same estimation as the text (Msh. 263). Ptākkattayapādī ca rassā atphakathāś ca, the text of the Triptpaka and its comment (Msh. 207). Theravādāhi pālīhi padehi syvijānī ca atīlathattam adu' eva potthakram pi tów pi, in the three versions there was not the slightest variation from the theravīdas, from the texts of the scriptures, from the words or from the letters (Mah. 262). Piltimattam idh' adu' na' atthi apthakathā idha, the text alone was brought here, we have not got the commentaries

(Mah. 331). Tans avittastathash ayam Cila-oaggapdi, to disprove this there is the following passage from Cülsavagga (Sundesakathi, quite a recent work). Pálim dhādhikhamassa, reciled a passage of the Abkhidharma (Mah. 251). Tardayak pdi, here I may quote the following passage (Pdi. 76, in one instance the passage quoted is not from a Triplipaka text, but from an ancient commentary). Indya pdi, in this passage (Jis. 7, from a Triplipaka text). Pálimattik dhammakathd, a religious discourse not belonging to the sacred canon (Par. A.: Vijesinha tells me that he has found in a Tiki on the Vineya the fol. explanation of this term, asigaha-andriha-pakipakadeasad, "miscellaneous discourses which did not enter into the Recenloss," and therefore do not form part of the Triplipaka).—A grammatical work in the Ind. Off. says saddathash pdiiti pdi, "text is so called because it protects the sense of the words" (1). Cough's contribution to the elucidation of the word is as follows, "a name of the Nagadabhadhar, i.e. the ancient language of South Bahar, or India within the Ganges; it bears this epithet in consequence of the perfection of its grammatical structure" (1 Suhalese Diet. a. v.). D'Alw's explanation, so far as it is intelligible, contains at least the germs of the truth (Alw. I. iv. v). The Sinhalese often write pdi, but this spelling is of late introduction (see Jat. 7).

B. Lot. 514. Mesfakapaṇaṃ according to Vijasinha means a question which places you on the horns of a dilemma; if you say "Yes," such and such as absurdity follows; if "No," another absurdity follows; the metaphor is taken from the fighting of rams. Saigiti S. has the following text, catidro pañhoyykaraṇd; ak㐷maṇeyykaraṇya pañho, albhajayykaraṇyyo pañho, paṭipuekhayykaraṇyyo pañho, thāpanyyo oylikarāyyo pañho; Vij. writes that these are four modes of answering queasoua, ekainsa "direct," vbhajja "qualified," paṭipucchā "after further questioning," thapaniya "not to be answered, setting aside"; be adds the following: Interesting explanation from a comment, taltho eakkhuāmiணccan? It puṭṭhena dma aniccau ti ekainsaṇayykatabbam, aniccau adna cakkhuāmi ti puṭṭhena pana na eakkham eva satam pi aniccau ghamamp pi aniccau ti evaṇ vishajitod ydhakabbam, tutkhākin cakkhuāmi ti puṭṭhena kenī affhena pucchaṭti paṭipueehited amiccatthena paechdmīti vuttā dmatī ydhakabbam ayam paṭipuekhaydkaraṇyyo, tam jīpasaṃ taṃ saṃran? It ddai puṭthena pana ayakhatam etain Bhagavatt thapetabba esa paṭihona oydkatabba ayam paṭihot thapastyo, which I translate, "A man who is asked, Is the eye impermanent?" should reply with certainty. Yes, it is impermanent; but if he is asked, Is that which is impermanent the eye? he must return a qualified answer. Not merely the eye, but the ear is impermanent, the organ of smell is impermanent. Agala if he is asked, What is the eye? he must first retort. Why do you ask? and when the other says, I ask with reference to impermanence, be must reply. Yes: this is called a question to be answered by a counter question. Again, if a man is asked, Is this the life? is this the body? and so on, the question must be set aside with the reply. Buddha laid down no rule on this subject, the question must be set aside, the question must not be answered.
PÂNI (m.), The hand; a wooden hand or truwel

Yes, it is impermanent; but if he is asked, Is that which is impermanent the eye? he must return a qualified answer. Not merely the eye, but the ear is impermanent, the organ of smell is impermanent. Agala if he is asked, What is the eye? he must first retort. Why do you ask? and when the other says, I ask with reference to impermanence, be must reply. Yes: this is called a question to be answered by a counter question. Again, if a man is asked, Is this the life? is this the body? and so on, the question must be set aside with the reply. Buddha laid down no rule on this subject, the question must be set aside, the question must not be answered.

ing, but the form pirsmid is generally used at the end of a compound. The data pramiyo or "Ten Perfections" are the perfect exercise of the ten principal virtues by a Bodhisattva, as a preliminary, and indeed a condition of his amazing Buddhahood. They are as follows, dinaspramitid, siapdramitid, usikkhasampdramitid, pindapramitid, virtyapdramitid, khantipramitid, sacaprapramitid, adikthidampramitid, mettipramitid (or mel-di-), spekhapdramitid, perfect exercise of silm-giving, morality, abegation of the world and of self, wiadom, energy, patience, truth, resolution, kindness, and realignation. Each of these may be subdivided into the ordinary, the inferior, and the unlimited perfection of the virtue, thus, dinaspramitid, dhasapramitid, dhasapramatthapramitid, siapdramitid, and so on, making thirty in all. Clough says (Binhalese Dlet.), "daspdramid expresses the duty to general terms, and signifies acts of shacity, or making offerings, without any reference to their nature or value; dhasappramid signifies presenting gifts of an inferior kind, as gold, silver, robes, treasures, etc.; dinaspramitid signifies expressing religious offerings or gifts of the biggest order, as the gift of wife and children, the gift of one's own body, flesh, bows, blood, and sinners, as well as the soul or principle of life, when required." Each of the pramitidis is exercised by a Bodhisattva to the three degrees. At J61, 25 we are told that the simple dinaspramitids are aigapricage, "sacrifice of limbs," the upapramitis didirabhadaparicage, sacrifice of external goods or property, and the parasmatthapramitid is jivitaparicego, "sacrifice of life." The period during which any paramitid is exercised is called paramitabhumi, and is of vast extent (Msn. B. 103). The attainment of Buddhahood with all its superhuman attributes (e.g. omnidence) is the result or consequence of the vast accumulation of merit during the exercise of the thirty paramitids in anterior births. The Jataka and the Cariyapitaka are full of tales of the exercise of the paramitids by Gautama Buddha when a Bodhisattva (Att. 60, 64). Upakkhāpdramittus gustaf, having attained the perfection of indifference (Jit. 25). Akhitānīdu pramatid gate, having attended perfection in the Abhijīti (Jit. 17). Khantipramit, perfection or supreme exercise of Long-suffering (Att. 38). Prasāmiṇyā pérvi, to accomplish the

pdranitía (Dh. 79; Ras. 64), Desapralmyo preted, havlog fully exercised she ten Perforions (Ahw. I. 77). Paridapranat (m.), one who has exercised a pramiti (Ten J. 119). Samotihas-pramyo preted, having fully exercised all the thirty Perforions (Ras. 23). Sabbatist data-pramidhid, onnsience or Buddhabood acquired by the ten perfect exercises (Att. 202). Parami is declined like nad, e.g. gen. pdramiyd (Att. 202), pl. pramiyo and prami (Mah. 2): In composition generally parami-, e.g. pram-japan (Dh. 125, 134).

PARANIMMITO (adj.), Crented or brought into being by others [+]. Paranimmitokmd, pleasures procured by others. The paranimmitasarattidod are the inhabitants of the highest of the Devalokas. I am indebted to Schhati for the foll-qolation, attono ajjhdosyanatad pareht niumite drammae sevanti (attono vase vattenti), tasmid tesani kind parnimmitokmd adma, "knowing their own inclination, they indulge in pleasures (lit. materials of pleasure) created for them by others," etc.; comp. Nimmaruti, and see Miro. Man. B. 25, 189, 171; B. Int. 608.

PARANTAPO (adj.), Tormenting others [ˈpɑːrɪntərˌʌpərˈkʌm], The bither and further shores, the far bank and the near bank [ˈfɑːrɪkɪt]. This word and araphrask, which is its exact homonym, are used metaphorically in a theological sense. The first occurs at Db, v. 388, where it is said that the true brahmapa (i.e. Arhat) is he for whom neither the bither nor the further shores exist. It is clear that the pára and the apíra are two divisions of some condition or quality release from which constitutes Arhatship; this might be, for instance, Káma, or Kleça, or Karma. The commentator on this passage takes it in the sense of the outer and inner Aysanas, meaning thereby that the senses of the Arhat are stilled, and his passions extinguished. In the Urgasantia (Ram. 77, 88) the Arhat is said to leave the near bank and the far bank (oraphra), by which the five orambhágiyasmayojanas and the five uddlambhágiyasmayujanas are evidently meant, freedom from the ten samayujanas being one of the conditions of the Arhat. The comment, which is a modern one, and not the work of Baddhaghose, takes are in the sense of the orambhágiyasmayojanas, but mistakes the meaning of pára, explaining it by fira, or bank generally, and giving to the whole compound the sense of "the near bank"; whereas the whole Sottas refers to the Arhat, and Arbatship is release not from the five lower samayojanas, but from all the ten

In the Urgasantia (Ram. 77, 88) the Arhat is said to leave the near bank and the far bank (oraphra), by which the five orambhágiyasmayojanas and the five uddlambhágiyasmayujanas are evidently meant, freedom from the ten samayujanas being one of the conditions of the Arhat. The comment, which is a modern one, and not the work of Baddhaghose, takes are in the sense of the orambhágiyasmayojanas, but mistakes the meaning of pára, explaining it by fira, or bank generally, and giving to the whole compound the sense of "the near bank"; whereas the whole Sottas refers to the Arhat, and Arbatship is release not from the five lower samayojanas, but from all the ten
