PARICCHEDO, Division, separazione, discriminazione; exact determination, definition; exact discernment, decision, judgment; limit, boundary, termination, extent; divisions, section, region; chapter of a book [qū]'. Andhiparicche dothompidis, an adverb with the meaning of "limitation," "definition" (Dh. 369). Gaspandya paricchedo paripashi na bhdeita, the exact number is not stated by the old writers (Mah. 179). Vaffadikhshana entush paricchodo us kurtantha, ye will put an end or term to the suffering of transamigation (Dh. 389). Anapandiddadni ca parichedo wa vijati, his gifts of food and drinks and so forth it is impossible to determine exactly, lit as to his gifts of food, drink, etc., there is no determination of them (Mah. 287, or perhaps "there was no limit"). Jysparichedo, extent or duration of life (Dh. 344; Daa. 2). Attuno dysparichedash pechedid, asking how long he should live (Daa. 2). Ponsedapariochedo pi c'ettha w' atthi, in this case there is no measure or limitation (Pit. 66). Sabbismana parichedodna catidro, four in number at the very least, lit. at the very lowest limit (Pit. 2; Dh. 319). Trwasn wickadnan parichedo, the limits or extent of these Epochs (Jit. 2).

PARICCHINDATI, To limit, define, mark out, determine, determine, fix accurately [1].

At 216. Pass / parico-injurit. At Db. 80 an snombleo passive of the passive paricochijlyati. P.p./paricochino, detailed, distinct; circumscribed, limited, small; limited by, extending to. Pumattano pours onipni sporicchimati appimattosa paricochimae, now the transmigrations of the slothful man are unlimited, while those of the diligent man are limited, i.e. the man who is indifferent to his spiritual welfare may go on transmigrating indefinitely, whereas he who is zealous in working out his salvation, and enters the Paths, will attain Nirvapa within a determinate period (Dh. 179). Pitodamhatias anso-majjhaothens paricochinnas, the time of eating the morning meal is limited to the period before noon (Br. J. 6. A.). Salamans paricochimae, speech limited by, vis. extending to, a thousand words (Dh. 88). Sattidias cutiappitis adma Buddha/pensa pi apariochismo, the deaths and rebirths of mortals cannot be defined even by a Buddha's knowledge. Le. they are infinite (Vij. Dh. 183).

Ims said over sukhit atidam parishart, may those beings, free from malice and full of happiness, preserve their lives, lit. keep themselves going. log [next + ☐]. Kiyaparidrikani elvaram

kucchiparidrikia piqlapdito (S.8).

— PARIHÃO, Attention, care, honour, pomp, state, ceremony, rite; keeping, preserving, guarding; forsaking, avoidance [ἐπίσημα]. Ab. 1009. Imassa ruħħassa pordsakapardħrato paritham n'attit, of the usual care bestowed on this trans notblog has been wanting (F. Jst. 7). Vajandya vijtoparithram hardpenis, I caused the mare to resolve the attentions required by a mare that has loiled (Db. 249). Kusadraparithrena vajdhitattd, from bis being brought up with royal state (Db. 328). Mahatid parithrena vajdhihmu, were brought up with great state (Msh. 135). Cetiyam tattha karevi parithram oddat ca, "built a tomb there,

and ordained that it should receive honours" (Mah. 155, Turour adds from the Thik "like unto those conferred on a Cakkavatti"). Mitaridiakakatdya tamd sontraparidhrakilated, when his mother died, having paid the last honours to her remains (Das. 22, comp. 1). Mahald parihdrenna mahesitte 'bhiscayri, with great pomp invested her with the queenship (Mah. 53, comp. lxxix). Paridro mahd dis paridro 'va (ca 7) rfdino, great was the retinue and the pomp of the king (Mah. 205). Tassa parisana mahantah ghasmi kated mahdparidhram karatha, build this person a large house, and treat him with great distinction (Raa. 36). Attano parishdrenna Mahtach tassa addapayl, caused food to be served to him with the same ceremony as himself (Mah. 139). Tint bhadiri dupparidhrakil, these things are difficult to use or keep (Subh.). In the frequently occurring phrase tamd gabbhavapidhram addai (Dh. 78, 120, Das. 2, 22) paridra, according to Subhati, means "protection," though in what the protection given to the bebe in the womb consisted it is difficult to say. The context sometimes seems to imply that on the wife being discovered to be pregnant some ceremony was performed which was supposed to be a preservative to the child. Subhati (who explains the phrase by "garbhusakhadina") quotes the fall. passage, tassa accucha-atietta-at꜀aibidiparibhagadh vajjetao sukhena gabbhaim pariharyasad, "being tended with great care and kept in comfort on account of her unborn child, avoiding the use of food and drink too hot, too cold or too sour for it." On the other hand, Vijesinha writes to me, "Gabbha-parihara is explained in our commentaries as cedes outtaagena gabbhasa didabbaparidro." If this explanation be correct, I must leave the question to Vedic scholars. Ab. 1008 gives also to this word the meaning of rajjana, "avoiding," as in Seukrit; but of this I have not as yet met with any example.

PARINĀYAKO, Governor, chief, prince [ʌfɪˈwɪtɪŋ]. Mah. 63. The eldest son of a Cakkavetti monarch in called a parindyaka, and is one of the seven ralans of the empire (B. Lot. 580; Man. B. 187). Sagkhapariniyako, a chief of the priesthood, an aged or eminent priest (Par. 5).

PARINETI, To lead, guide, rule [φ(φ)]

PARINIBRANI, Attaloment of Nirvapa, extinction, annihilation [qūrīqāy]. This term is used only of the attainment of khandhoniddasa, or the annihilation of being (see Nidbhash). When used with reference to an Arhat, it may be translated by "death," since the death and the annihilation of the Arhat are one and the same thing. Parisinibbnamaicamhtwipawolokhandyakn, when the lord of all worlds lay on the bed of death, or the coach on which he attained Nirvapa (Mah. 47, 108). Parisinibbnagato pi, even after his death, lit. even when he had attained annihilation (Mah. 109). Parisinibbnakdie, as his death drew nigh (Dh. 378, comp. 333). At Dh. 308 the Arhat Santati says to Buddha, parisinibbnash me osujadakha, "allow me to die." At Dh. 399 the great Arbat apostle Moggallana's death is called parisinidma. Attic dasame vasse Kifabokana refino saobaddikapardabibdad evam vassatam aA, thus at the end of the tenth year of king Kifasoka a century had elapsed since the death of Buddha (Mab. 15). The Buddhist era is reckoned from the death of Gotama Buddha, B.C. 543; thus the present year (1674) is the 2417th of the Buddhist era. For the terms kilreaparinibbda and khandhaparisinibbda, which mean "annihilation of human passion" and "annihilation of being" respectively, see art. Nidbhata, pp. 267 (2), 373 (1), and Dh. 350. Mahaparinibbmaa means the death of Gotama Buddha. See Parisinibbdayi.
PARINIBBÄNIKO (adj.), Tending or conducive to Nirvéps (last + ✗).
PARINIBRÀPETI (est. parifibbodyati), To cause to attain Nirvāya (B. Lot. 876, here it is used of Arhatalp).

PARINIBBĂYATI, and PARINIBBẠTI. To be extinguished; to attain Nirvāya or the extinction of being; to attain Ardhispip [ᠰᠠᠭ + ᠰᠠᠭ]. Yatīḥ sarapam additional ordind parinibbaye, as a burning house may be extinguished with water (Das. 8, opt. partialböye with d shortened metal cause). Used of the death of an Arbat (see Partialbāsnam). Partialbāstí andand, Arhats are freed from existence (Dh. 23). At Db. 333 Buddha says, Shikkhavā ito cutumāucageyra parindbdy-tsami, “priests, at the end of four months I shall attain Nirvāya.” At Dh. 299 the Arhat apostle Moggallāna says to Buddha, Shante partibbādyisadi, “Lord, I am going to die.” Of the Arhat Sāno (Dh. 403). Of the Arhat Santall (Dh. 309). Of the Arhat nun Saṅghaṇittā (Mah. 126). The death of Buddha is sometimes spoken of in the following words, amputandaya atabbadādtdayd parisinibbādi, or parisinibbāto, he attended the extinction of being through that element of Nirvāya in which no trace of the skaudhas remains (B. Lot. 335; J42. 28).

PARINIBBÄYT (adj.), One who attale Nirvāgs or the exduedon of being [uʃ + fʌʃ + ʌʃ]. Antarparisinibdyt is an Anāgāmin who, having been re-born to the Suddhāvasa beavens, dies (and attale annihilation) before half the term of his life as a Suddhāvasa is completed: antarparisinibdyt ityattha kaṃthaci suādadhvambhao vappajjited dyaṃvaṃajthain appatod parinibdydati (Vij.).

PARINIBBUTO (p.p.p.), Eating finished, extinct; having attained Nirvipa or the annihilation of being, (of an arhat) dead [uf+fim]. This word is regularly used as the p.p.p. of partibid-yati, partly from a confalon between the roots and y, and partly no doubt to reserve the form parisinibdna exclusively for the noun. Lokondtha saitidhopartinibbute, when the savlour of the world had been seven days dead (Mah. 11). At Mah. 38 it is said of the arhat Tisan, dkdsumhi niedited tejodhatavasena so yathdr-eith adhifthya ear-nata parisinibmto, seated in the air, by the power of fire kammaqthana, having willed his body as he pleased, he attained the annihilation of being; Sabh. sends me the Tik'a's comment as follows: tejoharihadramaapaddakahonavaena attono sairasa yathdrachna masiddbal jhdyanta na afthai evae adhifthya parisinibmto ri attha, "by the power of jhna based on the foundation of tejokariisa (see Kasipe), having willed his body as he liked, saying, Let my flesh, muscles, etc., be consumed, and not my bones, be attained Nirvipa."

Attic dasame vasse Kifabokana refino saobaddikapardabibdad evam vassatam aA, thus at the end of the tenth year of king Kifasoka a century had elapsed since the death of Buddha (Mab. 15). The Buddhist era is reckoned from the death of Gotama Buddha, B.C. 543; thus the present year (1674) is the 2417th of the Buddhist era. For the terms kilreaparinibbda and khandhaparisinibbda, which mean "annihilation of human passion" and "annihilation of being" respectively, see art. Nidbhata, pp. 267 (2), 373 (1), and Dh. 350. Mahaparinibbmaa means the death of Gotama Buddha. See Parisinibbdayi.

PARINIBBÄNIKO (adj.), Tending or conducive to Nirvéps (last + ✗).

PARINIBRÀPETI (est. parifibbodyati), To cause to attain Nirvāya (B. Lot. 876, here it is used of Arhatalp).

PARINIBBĂYATI, and PARINIBBẠTI. To be extinguished; to attain Nirvāya or the extinction of being; to attain Ardhispip [ᠰᠠᠭ + ᠰᠠᠭ]. Yatīḥ sarapam additional ordind parinibbaye, as a burning house may be extinguished with water (Das. 8, opt. partialböye with d shortened metal cause). Used of the death of an Arbat (see Partialbāsnam). Partialbāstí andand, Arhats are freed from existence (Dh. 23). At Db. 333 Buddha says, Shikkhavā ito cutumāucageyra parindbdy-tsami, “priests, at the end of four months I shall attain Nirvāya.” At Dh. 299 the Arhat apostle Moggallāna says to Buddha, Shante partibbādyisadi, “Lord, I am going to die.” Of the Arhat Sāno (Dh. 403). Of the Arhat Santall (Dh. 309). Of the Arhat nun Saṅghaṇittā (Mah. 126). The death of Buddha is sometimes spoken of in the following words, amputandaya atabbadādtdayd parisinibbādi, or parisinibbāto, he attended the extinction of being through that element of Nirvāya in which no trace of the skaudhas remains (B. Lot. 335; J42. 28).



PARINIBBÄYT (adj.), One who attale Nirvāgs or the exduedon of being [uʃ + fʌʃ + ʌʃ]. Antarparisinibdyt is an Anāgāmin who, having been re-born to the Suddhāvasa beavens, dies (and attale annihilation) before half the term of his life as a Suddhāvasa is completed: antarparisinibdyt ityattha kaṃthaci suādadhvambhao vappajjited dyaṃvaṃajthain appatod parinibdydati (Vij.).

PARINIBBUTO (p.p.p.), Eating finished, extinct; having attained Nirvipa or the annihilation of being, (of an arhat) dead [uf+fim]. This word is regularly used as the p.p.p. of partibid-yati, partly from a confalon between the roots and y, and partly no doubt to reserve the form parisinibdna exclusively for the noun. Lokondtha saitidhopartinibbute, when the savlour of the world had been seven days dead (Mah. 11). At Mah. 38 it is said of the arhat Tisan, dkdsumhi niedited tejodhatavasena so yathdr-eith adhifthya ear-nata parisinibmto, seated in the air, by the power of fire kammaqthana, having willed his body as he pleased, he attained the annihilation of being; Sabh. sends me the Tik'a's comment as follows: tejoharihadramaapaddakahonavaena attono sairasa yathdrachna masiddbal jhdyanta na afthai evae adhifthya parisinibmto ri attha, "by the power of jhna based on the foundation of tejokariisa (see Kasipe), having willed his body as he liked, saying, Let my flesh, muscles, etc., be consumed, and not my bones, be attained Nirvipa."

Parisatteted, turning the honeycomb over (Dh. 107). Bihikkamiyad anddhish cforash pariestotted, exchanging diseases with another pilestes (Ph. 102, 82). PARIVATTHABBO (p.f.p.parivarati), That must dwell apart [qf( + quan)]. Tena shikkhund parivatthabdom, parivana must be undergone by that priest (Pit, 6).

PARIVATTO, Change, exchange, return [qīqun].

Return of a deposit (Ab. 472). Lahkparinattain

kho citlam vattain Bhagantd, the Blessed One

has declared the heart to be easily perverted

(Pát. xxxii).

—PARIVATTO, Circle, succession, revolution [uffi-

qf]. Mahantaod hatiiparivaftah pahdya, for-

saking a great circle of relatives (Dh. 892). Ydoa

sattamá kataparivaftá, for seven generations back

(Dh. 190; Ras. 72). Cha rójaparivaftá gotá, alr

successive kings passed away (Ten J. 51, 114).

PARIVENAM, A hermit's cell, the cell or but forming a mouk's private chamber in a Buddhist monastery. Saighamaajhd apakkamma atana parivepam agamdei, departing from the assembly retired to his own chamber (P. Jat. 46). Mama vihdro mama parivepam, this is my monastery, this is my cell (Dh. 281). Pildro ddodasaparivepaho, a monastery of twelve cells, viz. accommodating twelve moku (Mah. 206). Silapassaya parivepma Thesdme mopathahum, nursed him at the Thesdrama monastery in the Silapassaya cell (Mah. 192). Parivepaelidro evideally means a monastery provided with cells for the monks (Att. 201). I see no reason for supposing with D'Alwla that parivepa ever means a college (Att. 64, 115).
PARIVESANAM, and -NÃ (f), Distribution of food; attendance, surrounding [φ(φ)]. Mah. 94; Dh. 168. Buddha's partisane, in attendance on the Buddha (Ját. 26).
PARIVES90, A halo round the sun or moon [φ]. Ab. 65.
PARIVETHETI (cause.), To envelop [φαῖη], PARIVIMAṇSATI, To examine, search. Dh. 634.
PARIVIBATI, To present, offer food, wait upon [qifq]. Pasiten' dkdrema parisisedit, serving him with avoury food (Dh. 81). Sakkaceath pari-
viti, showed him every attention (Dh. 99). Dh. 136, 169, 244.

PARIVITABKETI, To reflect [φ(r + φ) + π].

Db. 14A

PARIVITAKKO, Thought, reflection [φί +

[γ + πη]. Ten. J. 55./Cetoparivitaliko, mental

reflection. Eoam etaso parivitaliko udapadi, a

consideration presented itself to my mind as follows

(Alw. I. 83).
PARIVUTO (p.p.p.), Surrounded, attended, accompanied [qicqun]. Alw.1.74; Dh.94; F.Jét.17.

PARIVUTTHO, and -TTHO (p.p.p. parivosati),

Dwelt apart [p.p.p. ☐ + ☐]. Parivutthopari-

vão, one who has undergone parivisa (Pét. 6).

PARIYĀDĀNAṃ, Taking up, adug up, finalbling [ᠮᠥᠩᠭᠥ], Puritnasr upādmasas pariyādādā, from the original fuel being used up (Alw. N. 37). Uddham jīvitapārisiddād, after the term or end of life (Alw. N. 51). Yaṃkiñetti amavassapariyādnuasacanaṃ, yaṃkīhi is a word that includes everything (Dh. 988).

PARIYĂDỀTI, To seize, lay bold of [u:t], At Dh. 86 it is said of woman's voice, partassa cittam pariyddya tifthati, "it makes a deep impression on men's hearts." Fydddo cittam pariyddya tifthati, malice possesses his heart. Inf. pariyddum.
PARIYANKO, another torn of polliniko. I have only met with it at Sen. K. 333.

PARIYANTAVĄ (adj.), Discrimination, accurate [adj.+ [adj.+], Pariyantavati oded, discriminating speech (comment on Br. J. B. A. says precheckedon dassertd dassertd yathd 'sa paricchede parksyati evam bksati).

PARIYANTO, Boundary, border, limit, term, end [ᠮᠥᠩ], Ab. 714. Vlayapariyantoh gusad, proceeding to the frontier of his dominious (Alw. I. 79). Parisapariyants (see) mindi, sat down in the outer circle of the congregation (Dh. 70, comp. 412). Bhasapariyante jhi, standing at the utmost verge of existence, viz. about to attain Nirvaga or the extinction of being (Ten. J. 119, of an Artist). Sabasapariyante, at the end of all, lastly (Alw. I. 80). Sapariyante apariyanto, limited and unlimited (Man. B. 492). Samsaddopariyanto, ocean-girt (Mah. 85, comp. B. Los. 581). Udaka-pariyantush kafed mahdpathavki kampi, the great search quaked to its ocean boundary.

rafiroach, further shore or bank (Ab. 665). Paradish, the welfare of others (Mai. 209), Paraddiro, neighbour's wife. Na paro, no one else (Mah. 154). Eo paro, who else? (Dh. 20). Na paro paramikmbetha, let not one defraud another (Kh. 16). Parassa shagdash gapAditi, takes the property of another (Kh. 29). Pare bhikkha, the priests of the opposite party (Mah. 237). Mase, Paro, an enemy (Ab. 344). Paro loko or paroloko, the other or the next world, the next state of existence (Dh. 31). Paro saro, the following vowel (Sen. K. 206). Sare paro (loc. abo.), when a vowel follows (Sen. K. 205). Yosty apare param, the rest refer to what follows (Alw. I. vii). Pl. paro, other men (Kh. 15). At Dh. v. 6 I think Mex Miller is right in rendering pare co na vijandanti by "some do not know." Paraparaipard, the night opposed to the full moon, viz. the night of the new moon (Ah. 73). N'atthi santiparash sukham, there is no blise but Nirvipa (Dh. 36). At the end of a compound para frequently denotes having anything as the highest object, devoted to it, filled with it: Daydparo, devoted to mercy, compassaloute; Kaddparo, famished (Raa. 85); Dhammaparo, devoted to religion, devout (At. 165). Nent, parash, Nirvipa, i.e. the acme or goal of existence (Ab. 6; Mah. 47). Adv. parash, beyond, after, With abl, Parash samaddato, from over the sea; Parash marad or param marad, after death (B. Lot. 866). Parash Jatiyagakham, beyond Jotiyagsha (Mah. 67). Tato parash, next, afterwards (Mah. 169). Adv. paro (loc.), afterwards. With abl. Tato paro, thereafter (Mah. 8). PARO (adv.), Beyond, more than [TTH], Paro ankasah, more than 1000. Paroahassah kho par' asas patid Maseuti, be has more than a thousand sons (B. Lot. 581). PARUPANAM, and PAPURANAM, Dressing, putting on a garment; a covering, mantle, clank, upper roles [πήγιση]. Paprasas chaddoted, throwing off his upper roles (Dus, 88; Dh. 803). Isola pitupdrupasma kambalah, this blanket which your father wore as a clank (Dh. 157, 154). Nindmauprasma-stitharasvasma, as inner and outer garments and coverlets (Dh. 115, comp. 309). The two forms are about equally common: paprasma occurs at Psk. 103, and at Dh. 290, where Fassball has wrongly altered it to paprasma. The s of paprasma is due to the greater proximity of the s. A Tika says soriam septetod pdrupyanti paprasad. In bad Burmese M98, we sometimes find pdrupasma and pdrumpart. See next.

PARUPATI, and PAPURATI. To dress, put on an outer garment [[111111]. Saghhitim p., to put on the upper robe (Dh. 204). Saghakoh p., to put on a cloak (Dh. 290). Sarleish p.p.p, having wrapped himself in his upper robe, head and all (Dh. 288). Haas nidestabbak soak pdrupitabbak, the inner garment is to be worn in this fashion, the outer in this fashion (Dh. 371). Gadrobahk elhacammena pdrupited, dressing up the ass in a lion's skin (F. Jat. 14). Fuk pdrupisatt (Pat. 20). Ger. pdrupited (Mah. 7). Pass pdrupityati, P.p.p. pdruto, covered, dressed; put on, worn (of clothes); shut. Pdrutapafah vito akkhipt, the wind blew up the robe she wore as an upper garment (Dh. 841). Pdruto sihacammena, dressed in a lion's skin (F. Jat. 15). Apdruladodro, one for whom the gates of hell are not about, i.e. a slomer. Dupprato, badly dressed (Dh. 156). Pdrupati is only a metathesis of popurati, which represents the Sanskrit pbrvarali from Ptq: I have met with popurati in Sutta Nipati: a curiously similar metathesis occurs in Sinhalere, where the Sanskrit vijapurs, "citron," has become bijurraps instead of bijupurad. PASADANYO (adj.), Causling happiness [

PASADHANAM, Decoration; ornament, parure; wenrig ornaments [ᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ], Ab. 259, 688; Dh. 178, 234. At Dh. 237 there is a description of a magnificent set of jewels, constituting a dress of honour, given by the wealthy Dhanajara to his daughter Visakhā on her marriage; it is called mahidatpaddhanam, and is said to have cost ninety millions of kahāpaṇa (see Man. B. 223). Sabbiriyāpaṭesaṇa paṭṭhāṇanayoggāts paṭṭhāṇanāsh, a parures or dress of honour fit to be worn on all occasions (Dh. 245).

PASADHETI (cause.), To put on or wear ornaments [net]. Etirad hi garriyans paoddhanash niccolam paoddhetum na sakkd, for chla lady cannot be always wearing a very heavy dress of honour (Dh. 245). P.p.p. paoddhitio, dressed up, wearing fine clothes or jewels (Mab. 170; Dh. 247).
PÁSÃO IKO (adj.), Pleasing, engaging, amible, gracious [U1111111]. B. Lot. 407; Ten J. 48; Dh. 314; Alw. I. 93; Raa. 36. Phialottel ratri, a delightful evening (Sam. S.).
PASADO. The spotted antelope, the porcine deer [yun]. Ab. 619.

PASÃO, Brightness, clearness; favour, grace; refreshing, joy, serenity of mind; faith [naig]. Ab. 54. Pasdajasnako, causing joy (Mah. 1). Tax ented Abhayo there tenis disadasayam evo so ruubio ciclapaadatthak ashoaypuri asskndid, hearing this, the thera Abhayo, in order to rejoice the soul of the (dying) king, extolled those two gifts in many ways (Mah. 107). The words pasnddo, cittapassdo, and manopassdo are constantly used in the sense of faith in Buddha, lit. "rejoiting," because of the joy or peace of mind which belief in Buddha brings with it. Bornout wrongly throws doubt on this use of the word, observing that "in connexion with Buddha prasida is the favour with which He receives those who come to him" (Int. 108, comp. 383). The syntactical use of pasdo in this sense refutes this view; the following are instances, where it will be seen that the word for Buddha or his religion is in the localis case: Beats Tathagate yeva pasaddo hi mahapphalo, thus faith in Buddha has a great reward (Mah. 178); Citappassdamattena Sugate gati uttand labbhati, by a mere act of faith in Buddha is the happiest future state atalaed (Mah. 177); Pabbajisra pasddena Sammdeam buddhardane, took orders out of faith in the religion of the Supreme Buddha (Mah. 74); Satthari pasddeno Tbatisabhavane nibbati, through his faith in the Teacher was re-born in the T. heaven (Dh. 109); Mayi citta pasddmo, through faith in me (Dh. 94, Gotama Buddha speaks). See also the examples under Paridali. Pariplavaparddo, a man of wavering faith (Dh. 7, the comment says saddhd). Attano dupporipastiyd teants manusad nasi pasddam vindeti, by his own immorally destroys the peace of mind of these men (Pit. 74). Te labhati mhatitthigem paridbdjakeem pasdani, these men take pleasure in the heretial devoteem (Pit. iii, or pus faith in them).

PÁSADO, A building erected on high foundations, and approached by means of step, a terrace, tower, palace, masson [TET]. Ab. 208. It is four-sided (Ab. 210). Peinéptoddam dryha, climbing the terraced belights of stadom (Dh. 6). A king's palace is generally called a pédda, it may have several stories (B. Lot. 627; Alw. I. 78). Péddd otuvins, they left the palace, lit. descended from it (Das. 2, 40). Dh. 117. PASÃO, Brightness, clearness; favour, grace; refreshing, joy, serenity of mind; faith [naig]. Ab. 54. Pasdajasnako, causing joy (Mah. 1). Tax ented Abhayo there tenis disadasayam evo so ruubio ciclapaadatthak ashoaypuri asskndid, hearing this, the thera Abhayo, in order to rejoice the soul of the (dying) king, extolled those two gifts in many ways (Mah. 107). The words pasnddo, cittapassdo, and manopassdo are constantly used in the sense of faith in Buddha, lit. "rejoiting," because of the joy or peace of mind which belief in Buddha brings with it. Bornout wrongly throws doubt on this use of the word, observing that "in connexion with Buddha prasida is the favour with which He receives those who come to him" (Int. 108, comp. 383). The syntactical use of pasdo in this sense refutes this view; the following are instances, where it will be seen that the word for Buddha or his religion is in the localis case: Beats Tathagate yeva pasaddo hi mahapphalo, thus faith in Buddha has a great reward (Mah. 178); Citappassdamattena Sugate gati uttand labbhati, by a mere act of faith in Buddha is the happiest future state atalaed (Mah. 177); Pabbajisra pasddena Sammdeam buddhardane, took orders out of faith in the religion of the Supreme Buddha (Mah. 74); Satthari pasddeno Tbatisabhavane nibbati, through his faith in the Teacher was re-born in the T. heaven (Dh. 109); Mayi citta pasddmo, through faith in me (Dh. 94, Gotama Buddha speaks). See also the examples under Paridali. Pariplavaparddo, a man of wavering faith (Dh. 7, the comment says saddhd). Attano dupporipastiyd teants manusad nasi pasddam vindeti, by his own immorally destroys the peace of mind of these men (Pit. 74). Te labhati mhatitthigem paridbdjakeem pasdani, these men take pleasure in the heretial devoteem (Pit. iii, or pus faith in them).

J. 46), Inf. daffhuis (Dh. 84, 105, 107, 320; Ten. J. 34; Mah. 41; Alw. I. 80), pashtuhi (Dh. 375; Mah. 10, 139), dakhkhituh (Sam. S. A.). Ger. died (very common), pasiya (Mah. 177; Sen. K. 504), pasited (Mah. 29, 56, 165, 262; Alw. I. 73; Dh. 223). P.pr. pasata (Dh. 21, abl. and instr. pasatid, dat. and gen. pasato), pasasato (F. Jat. 4; Mah. 89). Pasain is sometimes used absolutely in the sense of seeing or understanding aright, discerning, wise (Dh. 44). Pas. disati, disate (Sen. K. 439, 448). Pass. sor. adast (Mah. 142), adassatha (Mah. 199), dassithha (Mah. 114, 110). Pas. p.pr. disawadwa. P.f.p. daffhabbo. P.p.p. dittho. Caus. daseti. Pasitebna sildya-pom, noticing the since pillar (Mah. 165). Sapiam sa pomi, dream a dream (Ten J. 112). Passe ce sipulah sukhah, if a man sees the prospect of a great advantage (Dh. 51). Picintiya Patheyyaha dhammapddi iti pasri, reflecting whether the P. were orthodox, came to the conclusion that they were (Mah. 17). Catdari arhyasaeedni pasati, clearly understands the four great truths (Dh. 36; Kh. 8). Gauted manna sahdyah pasitsdmi, I'll go and see my friend (Dh. 153). Pasat Loikissarah, presured herself before the King of Cylon (Mah. lxxxvll). Tush ahah dafftham gacchami, I go to visit him (Ten J. 54). Revataitheraum addasuh, called on the thera Revia (Mah. 17). Saitdhram daffhuh na labhimho, we could not find the Teacher, lit. could not get to see him (Dh. 105; Alw. I. 80). Parisee na pasahaw, found him not in his cell (Mah. 255). Pathamapodam addahardid anastaram na pasal, having repeated the first hemistich could not recollect the next (F. Jat. 46). Mutiddhrath addises, could not find his necklace (Mah. 39). Yo unutiddhrath pasati, whoever finds the necklace (Ditto). Pas. disati, to be seen, to be known, to appear, to exist, to be found, to occur. Dibadeho adasatha, appeared in his celestial form (Mah. 199). Samantato disaudama, conspicuous from every side (Mah. 163). Adisamandmo, invisible (Mah. 60, 106). Adisamandmardhi (f.), having invisible joints, i.e. so graceful and well-built that she appeared to have no joints (Mah. 25). Disasmi applied, there are

some whose terms of life is short, lit. some are seen whose .. Tumhdhokn janapade t(ai ratamdi disanti, are the Three Jewels known in your country? (Alw. I. 76). Dissanti upajjhyd bdid, we sometimes meet with foolish pastors (Pat. xiv). Na dissati, not to be seen, to disappear, to be shant (Du. 53). Sdayan ehe na dissanti pato ditjhd ba hujfaad, many are not seen in the evening who were seen in the morning. Le. they are dead (Dua. 6). Kis nu kho updaika indal diwaadai na disasi, how is it, devotes, that you have not been seen these last days? (Das. 7). Kahah twahs ine divase na disatha, where have you been away all this time? (Alw. I. 74; comp. Dh. 226). For dasetti see sep. article.
PASSÄVI (adj.), Seeing. Sen. K. 31. Comp. Dawdi.
PASSÃO, Urine [πεπυ], Ah. 275. Puede-mago, urethra (Ab. 848).

PASSAYO, The compound shikkhnipassayo, "sunnery," occurs several times in Mab. (see pp. 110, 120, 210). It either represents a possible Bank form ἀριθμός, or is a sandhifor shikkhnif-mpassayo, the is being first elided and then the (shortened. At Mab. 132 we have alapassayo, "rock-sell."

PASSO, and PASSAM, Side, flank [ʌtʃɪŋ]. Ab. 284. Tash passena slpajdpetod, making him he down on his side (F. Jst. 12, comp. B. Lot. 343). Dakhkhinapasse ninnam aggaadvakam Nisabhatthrum dantesti, spoke to the chief disciple N. who sat at his right hand (Dh. 135). Uttarapamak, north side (J4. 73). Vebhraselasa passe, on the slope of the V. mountain (Mah. 12). Maggassa ushou passena afthomix, they stood on both sides of the road (Dh. 288). Ubhatopase, on both sides (Mah. 213). Purassa ekaposamhi, on one side of the city (Mah. 120). Purapassumki dakhkipe, on the south side of the city (Mah. 216). The loc. passe, passamhi is sometimes used prepositionally, "near," "close to," "by the side of," "at." Sayomassa sropasse, at the bead of the bed (Mah. 125). Ddrakokthakapassamhi, near the porch (Mah. 5). Pithipasse, at the back of, bebied. Ehena pasanna gentuh, to go on one side, so slink away (Ten J. 13).
PASU (m.), Cattle; an animal, beast; a goat [qū], Ab, 1111; Dh, 51. Pl. poraco (Ab. 620). Pumpolonai, tending cattle, cattle farming (Ab. 446). Pumpat, Civn (Ab. 16).

Tumhdham pidesu pdtesdni, I will make him throw himself at your feet (Ten J. 20). Kuldoudi (ahl.) pdtesi, threw him out of the nest (F. Jat. 49). Pdtesi bhamiyam (loc.) lekhah, dropped the letter on the ground (Mah. 131). Siee pdtesi, let it fall on his head (P. Jat. 4). Accad kyddi pdiyah, bears worked the hammers, caused them to fall on the anvils (Mah. 22). Asdam p., to lay an egg (Ten J. 111). Rukhham p., to throw down a tree (Dh. 331; Mah. 141). Dakhhipodakom pdited, having poured out the water of donation (Mah. 160). Garaham p., to cause blame to fall on a person (Dh. 220). Ger. pdited (F. Jat. 12), pdayited (Mah. 244), pditya (Mah. 217). P.p.p. pdito, thrown down, cast off (Dh. 72, 266).

PATHAMAKAPPIKO (adj.), Belonging to the commencement of a Kalpa [மகனா + காசா]

I learn from Subhuti that by pathamakappikd massand, are meant those human beings who first make their appearance on the cakikavils when it is renovated (see Kappo).
PATHAMAKO (adj.), First, previous [un],

PATHAMO (adj.), First, foremost, earliest, previous, principal, chief, best [ทมิฬ]. Ab. 715, 833. Pathamid shóai, first floor (of a palace, Mah. 164). Pathamena vayad, in the prime of youth (B. Lot. 863, Siddhartha was then about eighteen). Pathanagdaoi, preceding (Dh. 90). In gram. pathamo pariso is what we call the "3rd person" (Cl. Gr. 100). Fem. pathand, the nominalive case (obhatti understood). Adv. pathaman, first, previously (Kamm. I). Pathamid shisambuddho, when first I attained supreme Buddhaship, immediately after I became Buddha. Saco midma katham pathaman exditi, if he bears his mother's speech first (A.w. I. civil). Pathamanic coa, first of all (F. Jat. 4). Ferom pathaman katom, the enmity originally felt (Mah. 153). With abl. Saighaannipidato pathaman, previous to the assembling of the priests (P6t. I). Ahaim pathamam aham pathaman, I'll go first, I'll go first! Pathamoladdho, first received (Ten J. 84). Comparative used averbially/pathamataram, first of all. Aiw. I. 74; Db. 142, 920.
PATHATI, To read, recite [ч].

PATHAVI, and PATHAVI, and PUTHUVI, and PUTHAVI (f). The earth [giant, giant]. Ab. 181, 182; Dh. 8, 9. Pathavitalach, the surface of the earth (Mah. 68). Pathavishago, region of the earth (Dh. 295). Pathavisaro, pathacisaro, king (Att. 196; Mah. 93). Pathavism, lord of the land, king (Mah. 235). Pathavilampa, pathakampanash, earthquake (Mah. 173; Ját. 96). Mahdpathavil, the great earth, the world (Dh. 129). Gen. pathaviyid, pathaviyid (Mah. 19), pathaviyid (Dh. 32). Loe. pathaviyid (Ten J. 118), pathaviyak (Att. 8), pathaviyash (Gog. Er. 8). Pathavi is the usual form, but the others occur not unfrequently, e.g. pathavi at Mah. 66, 98, 173. Ját. 25, 29, Sep. K. 233, and in Suiciloma Butta.
PATH$\lambda$vI (m.), A traveler [$\alpha$ + $\beta$]. Ab. 347.
PÁTHETI (cause. pathati), To cause to read, to teach [paːdʒaːnɪtɪn]. Sen. K. 335.

PÂTHEYYAM, Provisional for a journey [].

Ab. 380; Dh. 42. Also p(theyyakam (Pát. 89).
PATHIKO, A traveller [yifang]. Ab. 347.
PATHINO, The fish Silurus Boatle [φατίση]. Ab. 674.

PATHO, Path, road, way, course, reach [ʌm].

Ab. 180. Anicchau took patham, disliking that path, unwilling to enter by that passage (Mah. 159). Cakkhupatho, path of the eyes, range of the vision. Rdgapatho, path of sensuality. Kammapatho, course of action, mode of merit. Gopamapatho, senikhydopatho, range of calculation. Manusmapatho, path or haunt of men. Manusmapatho vasati, to dwell among men (Ten J. 112). Kasma akhlpah

Tumhdham pidesu pdtesdni, I will make him throw himself at your feet (Ten J. 20). Kuldoudi (ahl.) pdtesi, threw him out of the nest (F. Jat. 49). Pdtesi bhamiyam (loc.) lekhah, dropped the letter on the ground (Mah. 131). Siee pdtesi, let it fall on his head (P. Jat. 4). Accad kyddi pdiyah, bears worked the hammers, caused them to fall on the anvils (Mah. 22). Asdam p., to lay an egg (Ten J. 111). Rukhham p., to throw down a tree (Dh. 331; Mah. 141). Dakhhipodakom pdited, having poured out the water of donation (Mah. 160). Garaham p., to cause blame to fall on a person (Dh. 220). Ger. pdited (F. Jat. 12), pdayited (Mah. 244), pditya (Mah. 217). P.p.p. pdito, thrown down, cast off (Dh. 72, 266).

PÂTAYAỐM, Skill [v1d4]. Alw. I. vH, 112.

termination-męsen in sahavyotd, dăsava, + 71].

Pát. 12, 85.

PATAYO, see Pati (1).

[π.]. Pit. 82, 84.

PÁTETI, seo Potati.

PÁTHÃ (f.), The plant Clypes Hernandifolia [VI71]. Ab. 582.

PATHADDHI(f.), A thoroughfare, street. Ab. 202. I cannot explain this curious form, it is not a misprint.

PÁTHAKO, One who reads or recites or studies [418]. Thutipáthako, a panegyrist (Ab. 390). Aignalakkhapapáthako, one who reads or studies the linements of the body, a fortune-seller (Att. 100).

PATHAMAJJHÀNIKO (adj.), Connected with the first Jhán ( [x+]+ [x]+ [x]).

PATHAMAKAPPIKO (adj.), Belonging to the commencement of a Kalpa [மகனா + காசா]

I learn from Subhuti that by pathamakappikd massand, are meant those human beings who first make their appearance on the cakikavils when it is renovated (see Kappo).

PATHAMAKO (adj.), First, previous [un],

PATHAMO (adj.), First, foremost, earliest, previous, principal, chief, best [ทมิฬ]. Ab. 715, 833. Pathamid shóai, first floor (of a palace, Mah. 164). Pathamena vayad, in the prime of youth (B. Lot. 863, Siddhartha was then about eighteen). Pathanagdaoi, preceding (Dh. 90). In gram. pathamo pariso is what we call the "3rd person" (Cl. Gr. 100). Fem. pathand, the nominalive case (obhatti understood). Adv. pathaman, first, previously (Kamm. I). Pathamid shisambuddho, when first I attained supreme Buddhaship, immediately after I became Buddha. Saco midma katham pathaman exditi, if he bears his mother's speech first (A.w. I. civil). Pathamanic coa, first of all (F. Jat. 4). Ferom pathaman katom, the enmity originally felt (Mah. 153). With abl. Saighaannipidato pathaman, previous to the assembling of the priests (P6t. I). Ahaim pathamam aham pathaman, I'll go first, I'll go first! Pathamoladdho, first received (Ten J. 84). Comparative used averbially/pathamataram, first of all. Aiw. I. 74; Db. 142, 920.



PATHATI, To read, recite [ч].

PATHAVI, and PATHAVI, and PUTHUVI, and PUTHAVI (f). The earth [giant, giant]. Ab. 181, 182; Dh. 8, 9. Pathavitalach, the surface of the earth (Mah. 68). Pathavishago, region of the earth (Dh. 295). Pathavisaro, pathacisaro, king (Att. 196; Mah. 93). Pathavism, lord of the land, king (Mah. 235). Pathavilampa, pathakampanash, earthquake (Mah. 173; Ját. 96). Mahdpathavil, the great earth, the world (Dh. 129). Gen. pathaviyid, pathaviyid (Mah. 19), pathaviyid (Dh. 32). Loe. pathaviyid (Ten J. 118), pathaviyak (Att. 8), pathaviyash (Gog. Er. 8). Pathavi is the usual form, but the others occur not unfrequently, e.g. pathavi at Mah. 66, 98, 173. Ját. 25, 29, Sep. K. 233, and in Suiciloma Butta.

PATH$\lambda$vI (m.), A traveler [$\alpha$ + $\beta$]. Ab. 347.

PÁTHETI (cause. pathati), To cause to read, to teach [paːdʒaːnɪtɪn]. Sen. K. 335.

PÂTHEYYAM, Provisional for a journey [].

Ab. 380; Dh. 42. Also p(theyyakam (Pát. 89).

PATHIKO, A traveller [yifang]. Ab. 347.

PATHINO, The fish Silurus Boatle [φατίση]. Ab. 674.

PATHO, Path, road, way, course, reach [ʌm].

Ab. 180. Anicchau took patham, disliking that path, unwilling to enter by that passage (Mah. 159). Cakkhupatho, path of the eyes, range of the vision. Rdgapatho, path of sensuality. Kammapatho, course of action, mode of merit. Gopamapatho, senikhydopatho, range of calculation. Manusmapatho, path or haunt of men. Manusmapatho vasati, to dwell among men (Ten J. 112). PATI (m.), Master, owner, lord, chief, ruler; husband [qf]. Ab. 840, 725. Yakhkopati, a yaksha chief (Mah. 50). Loikdpati, ruler of L�iké (Mah. 155). Pl. patayo (Mah. 253), patino (Mah. 153). Comp. Patimنئد, Disampati, etc.

—PATI, and in composition generally PATI (prep.), Towards; back, in return; against [ท้าท], Saigamam pati pihd, louging for union (Ab. 103). With abl. Buddhism pati Sāriputto, S. takes the place of Buddha, viz. is nearly as great as he (Sen. K. 318). Ghatam aso telormd pati ddditi, he gives him ghs in return for ol (Ditto). Much used as the first part of a compound, when it generally takes the form pati, but there are many exceptions. Instances of the latter are patirépo, patikritiha, patikutjha, patikriyd, pǎtimakkhā, patimāqditu, patimāmeti, patimanteti, patisailjma, patitelbati, patisata, patisaya, patitjha, patidisati. We have patidissam but patidaddati, and of the Pall derivatives of those which have gg, as patiggahetod, pafigguha, take f, while those that have a single g, as patigankeyya, patigashisami, take t.
PAT1 (f.), Coarse cloth, canvas [vdt].
PÂTI, To protect [ụ]. Sen. K. 447, 468.
PÂTI (f.), A vessel, bowl, dish [qɪʰt]. Ab. 443; Mah. 41, 61, 175, 244.

PATIBADDEO (p.p.p.), Bound, obstructed, dependent [māʾtāʾ], Mama pabbajid tuva patibaddh, my taking orders is dependent upon you; i.e. my taking orders is conditional on your taking them (Dh. 141). Daqjawapabaddhe, dependent on meditation (Gog. Ev. 2). Paṭibaddhaeito, paṭibaddhamano, whose heart is bound or obstructed by passion or attachment (Dh. 50; P8. 69). Kime (loc.) appafibaddhaiteito, whose heart is not in bondage to lust (Dh. 89). See Ját. 8. Siddhatthakumādo mayt paṭibaddhaeito, Prilace 8. is in love with me (Jit. 61). Parapatibaddhaid, dependence upon others (Jit. 8).
PATIBAHANAM, and PATIBAHO, Warding off, repulsion (from next), Vajjman patibdhaya (das.), to repel the Vajjian princes (Par. B.). Ját. 90.

PATIBAHATI, and PATIBAHETI, To put away, reject, avert, repel [ทิท + ติท]. Tinh rjdá patibdhayi, him the king rejected (Mah. 174). Sabbasah tank patibdhiya bhishwam, baving averted all these terrors (Mah. 73). Apafibdhited, without contradicting (Pht. xvi). Inf. patibdhitw. /Pax. paqtbhiyati. P.l.p. paqtbhiya. Pdpakamawas appapibdhiyadhvam fiatd, knowing that the demerit could not be removed (Dh. 523). Mah. 533. Patibdhati (Dh. 290).

PATIBALO (adj.), Able, adequate, competent [with.

[with]. Pit xiv.
PATIBBATÃ (f.), A devoted or faithful wife [qif-wn]. A6. 234.
PATIBHÃO, One who belongs to the opposite ska, an enemy [πιασμα]. Ab. 1077.

PATIBHÃOO (adj.), Equal to, similar, resembling [π/π] Sd abhtrápá akoni devaceharapapi-bAdg, she was lovely as a celestial nymph (Dh. 102; Raa. 86). Sabbazito Kedemkâpapifâdgw varavárgso, a noble elephant entirely white, like the peak of Kailâs (Db. 158). Ab. 529, 1077; F. Já. 2; Dh. 284.

PATIBHÂNAM, Understanding, intelligence, wisdom; readiness or confidence of speech, promptitude, wit [mʌtʃɪtɪŋ]. Ab. 153, 971; B. Lot. 839; Mao. B. 409; Pát. 65. In its sense of “readiness of speech,” “ready wit,” it is sometimes wrongly spell patibhāna as if from mʌtʃɪ. Both meanings are easily traced to mʌtʃɪtɪŋ. Ab. 971 says pati-bhāma is used for wisdom and for ready speech. —PATIOCA (ger.), Following from anything as a necessary result; by means of, on account of, by reason of, through, by [ger. Wf]. Amddayum p., out of compassion (Dh. 178). Nibdmark p., on account of, for the sake of Nirvipa (Dh. 278). Tash p. patia ed dhitt ad no appajism, to him, lit. by means of him, no son or daughter would have been born (Dh. 325). Aya kim p. titthati 9 dyu mmanh p. tiffhati, what does life depend upon? life is maintained by heat (Vl). Chordidilakhthapah p. pasidonti, they are converted to consequence of . (Dh. 314). Dismach hiddamh gupamahomatah p., on account of the greatness of the virtue of the two families (Dh. 78). Etah (sarapam) p., by means of this refuge (Dh. 346). Vedamath p. taphit, from sensation results desire, or through sensation there is desire, or desire is the consequence of sensation. Mahdma-Aindattherah p. Sihalodipa, edanath suppatifth-ta, by the there Mahinda religion was firmly established in Ceylon (Handass Kath). Akhamahipah p. sahite dhamma pppideri, produces conditions connected in the way of mutual dependence (B. Lot. 538, lit. connected as a consequence one of the other). A tikk in the Ind. Off. Library explains parecaya thus, patteca etasod etti paccayo, "a suffix is that which proceeds from a word following from it." Patteca hammamah m'atdhiti hilliphah cetamah and, without an evil intention there is no resulting karma or demerit (Mah. 41). Patteca hammappama, arisen as a result, having its origin in a premeding cause.

Truths of Buddhism. The Paticcasannappada forms a chain of causal sequences, the first link of which is Error, and the last Suffering. I have endeavoured to show elsewhere that the sequence is occasionally somewhat arbitrary, but on the whole this formula is characterized by much philosophic insight. Beside the chain of causation there is also a circle of causation (paticcasannappadaakkom), in which five of the Nidānas are made mutually dependent on each other, so as to form an endless chain. The text is as follows: viñdā-appaccayad phaso, phasappaccayad nedand, vō-danappaccayad tanīd, tanāappaccayad serikidra, sanikidrapappacayad viñdāpaus, viñdāappaccayad phaso, and so over again ad infinitum; "Contact is caused by Consciousness, Sensation is caused by Contact, Desire is caused by Sensation, Karma is caused by Desire, Consciousness is caused by Karma, Contact is caused by Consciousness, etc.;" and thus existence rolls on in a vicious circle of cause and effect, till cut short by entrance into the Paths. Truths of Buddhism. The Paticcasannappada forms a chain of causal sequences, the first link of which is Error, and the last Suffering. I have endeavoured to show elsewhere that the sequence is occasionally somewhat arbitrary, but on the whole this formula is characterized by much philosophic insight. Beside the chain of causation there is also a circle of causation (paticcasannappadaakkom), in which five of the Nidānas are made mutually dependent on each other, so as to form an endless chain. The text is as follows: viñdā-appaccayad phaso, phasappaccayad nedand, vō-danappaccayad tanīd, tanāappaccayad serikidra, sanikidrapappacayad viñdāpaus, viñdāappaccayad phaso, and so over again ad infinitum; "Contact is caused by Consciousness, Sensation is caused by Contact, Desire is caused by Sensation, Karma is caused by Desire, Consciousness is caused by Karma, Contact is caused by Consciousness, etc.;" and thus existence rolls on in a vicious circle of cause and effect, till cut short by entrance into the Paths. PATIPADĄ (f.), Ingress, access, way, step, course, progress, practice, conduct; the first day of a lunar fortnight, especially that of the moon's increase [มิติบุตร, มิติบุตร]. Dulkkahtrodbagd. mini papipad, the steps or way or practice leading to the cessation of suffering, i.e. ariya affhangikamaggo (B. Lot. 480, see Ariyassacon). Tash dhamamak sutod tadosucchrikam papipadod preted, having heard this doctrine and fulfilled the duties or course of action consent therewith (Dh. 277, comp. 437). Appomddapatipadam papitappij, walked in the path of diligence (Dh. 194). Candopamapatipaddya pamurito, "I was commanded for my progress (in grace) like the progress of the moon" (Br. J. S. A.). Papipaddipank, "knowledge of what is necessary to be done in order to atxala felicity" (E. Mon. 193). The four papipadks, or modes of conduct when an exertion has to be made, are akkhand patipadd, khamad p. damd p. sand p., want of endurance, endurance, self-control, equanimity. Here the forms damd, samd, are by attraction for damo, samo, Subh. quotes the foll. gloss, pakkamakarpakdis siddhini na khamati na sakhati akkhamid, khamati sahati khamad, indriydamah damamah damd, uppamamah khamatikam makhidendhi dhad sayena vitakkamamank spamamamah samd. There are also four other papipadks, dukkhd papipodd damdhdhind, dukkhd p. khippdhhind, suhd p. damdhdhind, suhd p. khippdhhind, which seems to mean "painful practice resulting in knowledge slowly acquired, painful practice resulting in knowledge quickly acquired, pleasant practice resulting in knowledge slowly acquired, pleasant practice resulting in knowledge quickly acquired. Subh. quotes, hetuhditi papipodd dukkhd phalabhad abhind pi dandhavasena pamdavaena mathavaena njihati ad dukkhd papipadd damdhdhind. Tashh etuhbhidd p. dukkhd phalabhad abhind righavasena sudaravasena sijjhati ad dukkhd p. khippdhinid, and so on. Other four papipadks are the four methods adopted for the attainment of the paths satapanna and sakhaddigimii; they are chamaddhipotepyash, viryddhipateyyam, citddhitapayyam, and vimashaddipateyyam (see Pagolo).

PATISAMBHIDĄ (f), Discrimination, analysis. After much study I have come to the conclusion that this compound is, as at first sight it would naturally appear to be, a derivative of the root with the whole containing the idea of "breaking up in detail, dislocation, discrimination, analysis"; comp. "separation, distinction," "distinct," etc. There are four Patisambhidła or analytical selences, being four divisions of the supernatural knowledge of the Artat, viz. althapatisombhidid, dhammapapisambhidid, siruttipapisambhidid, papibhspatisambhidid. Sānkybártha Prakāca (a modern Sinhalese work) explains these to mean respectively "knowledge of the meaning, knowledge of the text (pdi), knowledge of the origin of the words, and fourthly certain or determinate knowledge, together with the accurate discrimination of the first three, artha, dharma, and nitrukti." At Lot. 839 Burnout translates from Jindlaikāra (a modern Pali work) a fuller account, which probably gives to the four terms a more comprehensive signification than they originally possessed. It includes under all the everything spring from a cause, Kamma and its consequence, Nirdpa, and the sense or true meaning of the word of Buddha as opposed to its form. Under dhamma it includes "the cause which destroys the results of Kamma, the Arfym

magge, the word of Buddha, virtue and vice, and the five elements." Niruti is described as the explanation of what is obscure in attha and dhamma, and as resulting from the perfection of interpretation. The explanation of paṭiskhāna, as translated by Burnouf, is somewhat obscure, "knowledge of the three sciences possessed by one who, making science the object of his mind, has in view the triple science (tāṭjīd, see Lot. 372):" the omission by Burnouf of the Pali text is much to be regretted, but the passage appears somewhat to hear out the statement of Sādākhāryātha P. that Paṭibhāna includes the discrimination of the other three paṭisambhādās. See also the comment at Dh. 414, which speaks as a wisdom which includes the three first paṭisambhādās and the dākkhandhas, etc. (atthādhāzaṃsairttāpaṭimaṃ bīkhidnuh atākkhandhādissā ca parigdhikā paṭid), referring probably to paṭidhāsa. Cough in his Sinh. Diet, has the fall. article, "Paṭisambhādiya (paṭi before saṅbhādiya discrimination), universal knowledge, ability to explain terms respecting all subjects of art or science:" and under "Sivalpiliśimbiyā" (the Sinhalese equivalent of satupatissambhād), be says, "the four attainments peculiar to the highest order of Rahata, via a knowledge of ethics, of dharma or religious doctrines, of grammatical comments and expositions of the dharma, and a supernatural discrimination." Niruti, the power of the Buddha to perceive all truth intuitively, without study, and without the teaching of another; 4. occur at all in classical Sanakrit. In Pall we have from pattisamBHID the isolated derivative pattisambhidd, but from pratisainVID the foll. Important derivatives of frequent occurrence in the oldest texts, pappisambidito "having informed," pappisambodeti "to feel, experience," pappisavodin "feeling, enjoying." In North Buddhist Sanakrit we have from pratisainVID the fem. noun pratisavhid (used as the equivalent of pattisabhidid), and the adjectives pratisainvadsaka "informing," and pratisainvedin "enjoying." Now my own view, is that the North Buddhist Sanskrit texts are founded on older Pall texts (the texts in fact of Southern Buddhism), of which they are in some cases in great part literal translations. I suppose then that the North Buddhist translators, being fully familiar with the derivatives of pratisamVID in the Pall texts before them, and meeting with the isolated form pattisambhidid used in a sense which implied discriminate knowledge, jumped to the conclusion that it was also traceable to pratisainVID, and coined, to represent it, a fem. noun pratisainvid, correctly formed according to well-known analogy. I have elsewhere pointed out several other of these North Buddhist adaptations, some of which are very curious and interesting (see art. Opadttik, Pattimakkas and Notes on Diammapada in Journ. Roy. As. Soc. 1871). The question may possibly be raised as to whether pattisambhidid can be a dialectic variety of pratisainvid. The existence of forms like pattisavodeti and pattisambidito is perhaps not of itself necessarily fatal to such a theory; but I may observe that there is in Pall, I think, only one instance of a Sanskrit in pasing into (not mbh but) mbl, vis, samhadana = samvshana. In one case a Pall 84 represents a Sanskrit, with the example in no way affects the present argument, onomatopoeic roots like shthiv being very unstable in their form, comp. Pall papphido with papphusa, and the Pall KHIP, "to come," with KSHU, KSHIV, KSHIB, KSHBV. Lastly, the regular Pall expression for

having attained the four patisambhids is patisambpatisambhido (Alw. I. xxix; Mah. xxvi, 82, 42), where the root fig is repeated (I think pabhinna is here used particularly, and not adjectively, the compound meaning "one by whom the analytical knowledges are discriminated," as in such compounds as parisambhapariada).—I have met once with an adj. patisambhido "having the patisambbhids." At Alw. I. cvil we have patisambhidappatto, having attained the patisambhids (quoted from an atth.).

— PAVATTATI, To arisa, beglo, take place; to start, set out; to roll or flow onwards; to become, be, exist; to go on, to proceed, to be kept up [hŋ], Mahdadi pazatti, a great river arose, or was set golog (F. Ját. 5). Mayl asante jia lokitamadi pamittisatha, but for my presence this day a river of blood would have been set flowing (Dh. 352). Akkilhi qassai pavattimar, the tears began to flow from her eyes (Dh. 329). Khiradhárd pavatitishm, streams of milk began to flow (Ját. 68). Jayanddo pavatitha, a shout of victory arose, or was set up (Ma. 150). Unname madakini paffam yahid alinnam pavatitari, as water rained on a beight flows down to the valley (Kh. 12). Celukhepasahardai pavatitishm samantato, thousands of warfugs of cloth went on on all alden (Ma. 113). Satidahk pavatitati tas eAmam, that festival is kept up, or goes on, for a week (Mah. 49). Dodasa qassadi pavatitisati, twelve years will pass (Das. 2). Devatdi amahdi pjdit nekd pavatti, "innumerable offerings were kept up by innumerable davas" (Ma. 116). Silahafhakuthd.. Silahesu pavatitati, the Sinhalese commentary is extant among the Sichalese (Mah. 351). Kazikamamah na ppavattati, the plougbing does not get on, or no plougling goes on (F. Ját. 9). Avicchimno pavatitati, let it continue unimpaired (Alt. 216). Bhand orkand pavatitishm, severe palms set in (Dh. 279). Iddini pavatitamam kamash, merit now going on, viz. now being accumulated (Kh. 23). Siddhukdrassahm pavatitishm, thousands of cheers arose, or went on (Dh. 266). Diddhini amagidini pavatitati, celestial hymns arise. P.p.p. pavatto.

PAVATTIATI, To revolve, whirl round [ʌʃʌ]. JL. 23.

PAVATTETI (cross, last), To cause to arise, or to flow ownride, or to proceed, to set going, set on foot, establish, produce, make, originate, begin [ἀγαθῆς]. Mahogham parattetod, producing a great flood (F. Ját. 3). Lohitanadim p., set flowing a river of blood (Dh. 224, 361). Mahd-diwan p., to set abundant almsgiving going, to carry on almsgiving on a great scale, to keep open house for the priesthood (Mah. 133, 214; Dh. 136). Pdardam parattetii janassa, provided breakfast for the people (Mah. 117). Vfiecha-yash parattetii, “re-established the administration of justice” (Mah. 1xxvii). Mettam p., to keep up friendly feelings (Dh. 172). Devandawad siddhukdram pavatessah, angels and men raised a shout of adho (Mah. 100). Dhammacakham p., to set on foot the supremacy of the Truth, to laungurate the reign of Law (Dh. 110). Dibbaragitini pavatayimam, set up celestial chants (Ját. 70). Tattha pavatayii aljkdyakammam, thereby be regulated, lit. kept going his actions (Atl. 102). Gambhram mdtikhm pavattest, made or ran a deep channel (L. de Zoyam). Mahduddam p., set up a great shout (Ját. 17). Celakkhepddal pavatentid, keeping up waving of cloth and other manifestations of delight (Ját. 54).

PEYYALAM. This word answers to our Eicetera, or to the dotted line used when words are intrationally omitted. The etymology is exceedingly doubtful. Burnoff (Lot. 388) hesitatingly resolves it into pe-alam, pe being taken as no abbreviation of purvs; but this fails to account for the long st. Subh quotes from a grammatical work, peyyah alam peyydah, ppapah peyyah, alak tiyattah, which, though it guides us as to the meaning, falls to supply no etymology. D'Alwin says that peyydah (not as he reads it peyydia) means "Insert, in the sense of Pill up the gap" (Alw. I. B3). I am disposed to think that peyydah means "to be supplied, or filled up, or read in full." Assuming the latter part of the word to be alak, the remainder peyya will probably have to be sought for among the derivatives of y, q or yt, eg. , or we might perhaps suppose a p.f.p. from IT. Another suggestion I venture to offer is that the word represents IT or IT+ (for the e comp. jeyyo = jydya, seyy = cayy). I have found in a MS. of Sarattha Jallif in the Bodleian the following curious passage, in which peyya is referred to "to preserve":

Adyantamattun dassetod majhe pana adipanaith

Majhepergydiakain nada, ito seseso ayah noyo.

Adyantamajhapergydiak sabhopeyydlahoth tathd

Peyyalan tu catabbhahsh, tam viññahi pakdślaan.

Pátu alash ti pegydlah vitkháretus alash thand

Peyydlasso vacanattho veditabba vibhdvind.

Which I interpret thus, "Exhibiting the beginning and the end of the sentence while in the middle there is a suppression is called majhepepydia, and the same principle applies in the other cases. Pepydia is of four sorts, ddipeydia, antapeydia, majhapepydia and sabbapepydia (omission respectively of the beginning of the end, of the middle, and of the entire passage), this has been declared by the learned. Pepydia means able to preserve, or able to give in full, thus in the meaning of the word pepydia to be understood by the wise man." In a quotation at p. 389 of the Lotus pepydia seems singularly enough to be used to designate the unabrevisted passage itself, so yeva parimapepydlena vitthretabbo, "this passage is to be expanded or supplied in full by the aid of the previous unabrevisted reading," but whether this is what is really meant cannot be determined without a knowledge of the context, the quotation being too brief.—As we shorten "etcetera" to "etc," so pepydlam is usually shortened to pe, and in Bormese MSS. even to the letter p or l (Alw. I. 93), comp Skrattha Jalin: Tres majhamhi pepydia po d lo vd thaplyati.
Tam tam dịch 'ca viết cụp thợ pryytálan pi edkh-máti.

PHAIAM, Fruit, a fruit, grain, crop, produce; result, consequence; reward, profit, advantage; a testicle [wng]. Ab. 273, 540, 851; F. Ját. 6. Sipphaphaism, produce of industry. Saddhammaicane phalam, my delight or reward is in listening to the Truth (Ras. 28). Pintakammassa phalam, reward of good works (Mai. 199). Phalam sukaadakkudman, the fruit or result of good and bad deeds (Ten J. 116). Natosma abhisekuphaton, knowing that her coronation would be the result of the journey (Mah. 85). Tsera classa phalaena, as the reward of that devotion (Dh. 193, comp. 161). Phala is used as a technical religious term, each of the four paths (see Naggo) being subdivided into the path and its phala or fruition. Vjesinba writes to me as follows, "Between the maggruffha and the phalaffha there is scarcely any difference but of priority. First the yogins practises the amZomazdna, by which he attenuates and finally expels passion. Directly he has done this he is supposed to have a particular bent given to his mind called getraakzada. As soon as he has attained this all his thoughts hang on Nirvāyn,

and he becomes a Soldpatittmaggafftha, and instantly receives two or three phalacittdni (des thpi phalacittdni uppajjanti).” At Dh. 180 is the full passage bearing on this subject, due phausand fdsapphusand vipdhaphmaand ca, tattha cattäro maggd fdsapphmaond admo cattāri phaldni vipdhaphmaand adhippetd, “there are two attainments, the attainment of knowledge and the attainment of the result; by attainment of knowledge is meant the four Paths, by the attainment of the result is meant the four Fruitions.” I think it worth noting that a Sihulese gloss is my possession states that the difference between the Magga and Phala is that in the former the process of destruction of passion is going on, while in the latter it is consummated: thus the Soldparilmaggafftha is accomplishing the annihilation of difthi, retkichd and slbbatapardmasa, while the Soldpatitphala las acomplished it. The sottāpatitphala is sometimes called pathamaids phatoids (Mah. 83), or pholaṃ ddikha (Mah. 72). At Dh. 175 the askedgāmpheis is called dutyaphalam, and the anigimphala is called tatiyaphalam. Arhatia-phala or Arhatship is called ariyaphalam (Dh. 180), or aggaphalam (Mah. 109). Maggaphalidni is a dvadva compound meaning “the paths and the fruitions” (Dh. 316; Ten J. 31; Dua. 21). Maggaphalad appears to be sometimes a dvandva (Dh. 109; Mah. 74), and sometimes a tappurisa, “fruition of the Paths” (Dh. 108; At. 185). Agataphala, one who has attained the fruition of the Paths (Mah. 80).

PHASSITO, This is I suppose a derivative of  $ \pi $, perhaps  $ \frac{1}{2\pi^{2}} + \pi $, hardly I think the p.p.p. from  $ \pi $. At Dh. 212, 340, we have suphasita, as an epithet of the Ups, apparently meaning "soft, delicious." Subh. tells me that Siddhposita at Mnh. 124 should be addhemphasitan, and quotes from the commentary addhemphasitan ti esphassitau, doplyd spari plddawh esphassitddrewa thapetod. Turnour translates it vaguely "superb," probably referring it to  $ \pi $.

PHASSO, Touch, contact [wɪtʃ]. Ab. 149. Phasta-ampanno, (of a blanket) soft (Alw. I. 75). Phaso or Contact is one of the terms of the Buddhist philosophy (see Aharo, B. Int. 500; Mao, B. 400, 489). Gogerly says there are seven, “receiving impressions from external objects by the eye, ear, pose, tongue, body, mind, and lastly knowledge or mental consciousness (mamoivihādadhātuqam-phasso).” There are six Phassakāya's, cokkhusamphasso, sotaas, ghdwas, jichde, ktdyaas, manos. (Sang. 8.).

PHASU (adj.), Enviable, agreeable, pleasant, easy, comfortable (Ab. 88, see note stating it to be an adjective). Phidugamanana, easy or pleasant journey (Mau. 16). Phiduvidra, comfort, ease, well-being. Dothanam aggasidhadnam phaduvidram pucchito, questioned as to the welfare of the two chief disciples (Dh. 114). Bhikkhaam phaduvidardya, for the comfort or pleasant living of the priests. Saphadavidratthdya, for his own comfort (Dh. 106). Na me tayd saddhim kathad ed nisajid ed phdru hoti, talking or sitting with you is not pleasant to me (Ph. 15). Neut phdau, comfort, ease, convenience (Ab. 88). Bhikkhaam phadukrapass, for the accommodation or comfort of the nuns (Mau. 123). Adv. phdru, and phdawn, pleasantly, comfortably. Phdau viharati and phdau such viharati, to live pleasantly or comfortably (Pur. 8. 6). The Northern Buddhists render phdau viharati by sukhasapavihara (B. Lot. 426). The fact is that meeting with the Pali word phdu, and unable to make anything of it, they took as its equivalent what they conceived to be the word most nearly approaching it in form. That phdu is not sparca is obvious, first because phdau is an adj., secondly because sparca does not mean "pleasure" or "ease," thirdly because we already have in phassa the true equivalent of sparca. Any one of these three objections standing alone would be inconclusive, but taken together they are irresistible. I feel little doubt that phdu is the Sankrit (sparha). Spk would become phk, and the r would be dropped: this would leave phdau, which being very difficult to pronounce, would easily glide into phdes, the a being supplied from the recollection of the lost initial s. In one other instance, golua = golina, a Pali r corresponds to a Sank. h. For the change of the final a to a we have a parallel in words like sababina = sarvajia, and vedagu = vedaga. See also Phadsha.

Nídsaphdruko (adj.), pleasant to live in (Nid. 9).

PHÁSULIKA (f.), A riú (Ab. 278). For pådækkkd.

PINDAPATIKO, One who keeps the P�dāpādikāḿn [fugāṭīfā], Pīpāpātīkaḷigam is one of the Dhātnāgs ordinances. The priest who undertakes to keep it must obtain food only by going to person to the houses of the faithful and receiving it by having it placed in his bowl. He may therefore not receive sāldhādhatta, aṇigha-bhatta, etc. (see E. Man. 07). B. Inst. 309.

PINDAPATO, Food received in the alms-bowl of a

Buddlist monk [fugya]. B. Int. 309; Dh. 274. I find in Vis. Mingga; bhikkhadakkhididnash

pasa dminapipdmath pito pippapato, parshi diman

maam piadmanat patte nipatant vattas hoti,

from which it is clear that pippapata is a restrictive term specifying that particular sort of alms

which consists in the food being placed or thrown

into the bowl of a monk while on his round.

Thus malkabhatta would be alms, but not pippapita alms. Soyam pippapitash addya, having

themselves gone and begged alms (Du. 84). Antismase pippapidamattas pi, even if it be merely

food thrown into his alms-bowl (Pit. 11). Pippapidapakkanta, having returned from seeking

alms, vis. from the daily pilgrimage to beg food

in the village (Dh. 183, 232, 369), Vij. observes to me that pacechabbattan piqapdtapaplikhanto (see Dh. 175) is a vortepov potepov, as it means "having returned from his rounds, and then made his meal (on the food outlined on his rounds)." bapiṭṭhā khipṭitā, browling the body behind a bush (Dh. 239). Vāthkapittāha nipajī, lay down on the sand (Dh. 192). Kalatapittāha, on the mud (Ten J. 36). Piftham is little used, the fem. form pifthit usually representing prishṭha, Hatthipittāhi, elephant's back (Dh. 157). Asapittāhi, and asapittakāha, horseback (Jit. 63). Diṭṭhā pifthīti ti zerino, we have seen the enemy's back, viz. we have seen the last of the enemy (Msh. 230). Bhikkhuṃ maṃ pifthipase, behind the news (Dh. 315). Pifthimaskiko (adj.), luckbiting. Vādi pifthit, surface of the water (Mah. 72). Pādaṃpittāhi, back or upper surface of the foot (Dh. 237, 340). Pifthiyam like pifth the may be used prepositionally: Therasa danapitthigam jhiio, standing behind the thena's chair (Pit. xvi). Pifthi appears to have the Vedic meaning of "the vault of heaven," for I and In Br. J. 8. A. okkhartkd vuccati ddedo od pifthiyam vā akkharajānasakjīd, "akkharikā means the game of recognizing letters in the air or firmament."

Rjd kathtti prachited, the king having asked, Where? (Mah. 12). With occ. and iti: Kin te dukikan ti tam pucchi, asked him, What all you? (F. Jat. 12, 17; Mah. 157, 248). Evan paiko pucchiabbo, the question must be asked thus (B. Lot. 514). P.p.p. pitho, pucchito (Alw. I. 106; Ten J. 53). Toush ayyadjido ti putho, being asked, Are you the gardener? (Jil. 6). Rajaparisehi pucchito, interrogated by the king's officers (Dh. 291). Satthard divinash agga-svakdanam phaviviharam pucchito, belong questioned by Baldha as to the health of the two chief disciplines (Dh. 114). [Fqun]. Ab.570; F. Ját. 7, 30. PUQALIKO (adj.), Connureted with an individual [q+]. Pát. 103.

PUOALO, An individual or person as opposed to a multitude or class; a creature, being, man [yua]. Ab. 93, 1065; Man. B. 424; B. Int. 501, 508. Tam puggalam eva pasatha, behold that man (Dh. 61). Nidduam pi pucchi puggalam pi pucchi, he asked the circumstances under which the discourse was spoken, the person to whom it was spoken (Br. J. S. A.). Sanghe ed puggalod, in the whole body of the priesthood or in a single member of it (Kh. 13).—The three puggalas are sekho puggulio, azekho puggalo, nevaekha-ndeekho puggalo, the sekha, the azekba, and he who is neither the one nor the other (vis. the pulhujama or unconverted man). The four puggalas are samasamacalo, samasapadumo, samasapundariko, samasapukhumido, by which names are designated the sotdpanno, sakaddgdm, and gdmi, and arahd respectively. Another classification of four is tamotamaparayano, tamajotipardyano, jotitamapardyano, jotijotipardyano, which Sabb. explains to me to mean, “the man who is poor and miserable on earth, and who on dying passes to a miserable state of existence (apdy), the man who being poor and miserable on earth passes to a devaloks,” and so on. Another is puggalo attahitdya patipamno no parahidya, p.

parahidya pajipanno no atitahidya, p. w'eva atitahidya pajipanno na parahidya, p. atitahidya c'eva pajipanno parahidya ca, "the man who acts for his own advantage and not for another's" and so on. Another set of four comprises the man who torments or mortifies himself, the man who mortifies others, the man who mortifies both himself and others, the man who mortifies neither himself nor others, but free from longing, serene and calm, and experiencing a sensation of bliss, dwells with his soul exalted and purified (id'e) e'eucco pugalo atantapa holi attaparitdpanduyogah anuyutto, idha pun' e'eucco pugalo parantapo holi... etc.). The satta puggalid dakkhirigyá or seven persons worthy of gifts are ushatohdaga-vinuttz, panhidvimutto, kiyosakkhli, diffhipatto, sadihdivimutto, dhammansudri, saddhaumdr: the two last mean "walking according to doctrine, and walking according to faith"; dth-hippatto is thus explained, dithantam patto idassamosekhidtasa sotpatinoggafidpassa anastaram patto ti vattam hoti (Subh). I am indebted to Vijiezinha Mudliar for the following enumeration of them. He writes, There are three Solipaunas, vix. ekabiji, klasikolo and sattakkhatiparamo, and three Sakadagimis, vix. kdmabhavadhigatephaio, rapabhavadhigata-phalo and arapabhavadhigataphalo. These six are multiplied into twenty-four by the four methods adopted for the attalament of the states, vix. chandakipateyyam, wiriyadhipateyyam, cittdhit-pateyyam and elmasandhipateyyam (these are called the Patlipada). Then there are two Arshantas, vix. smikhavipasako and samathaydmik, and four Maggnithas. Adding up the above we have

kiriyavattha or pattakriyalavithu (n.), cause, occasion or material of acquiring merit or doing good works. There are three, dhamayash pattakriyalavithu, silamayash p., bhvaadmayash p., almagiving, moral conduct and contemplation. There are also ten, dhamayash p., silamayash p., bhvaadmayash p., apacittashagatah p., veyyd-vaccamhagatash p., patti-amyppedamah p., abbh-antamodand p., daudindmayash p., savanaamayash p., dittkhijikamamash p. (Sabb., Dh. 87). Of these abbhamayash means the acceptance or use of merit made over by another (see Patti, Subh. quotes yema krsach dinnasso pahana adhama citena patiggahapash); dittkhijikamamash is making one's views or faith straight or firm (Fig. 1), Subh.); dattndmayash, and savannaamayash p. are teaching and hearing the truth.
FUNO, see Pans.

POPIYO, A cake-seller, confetioner [ụ̣ng + ự].

Ab. 511.
POPO, A cake, sweetment [qu]. Ab. 463, 511. See also Popo, which is the usual form.

PUPPHAM, A flower; the menses [3], Ab. 238, 543, 1091; Ten J. 49; Db. 49. Pupphada de, see Diedgajo. Pupphachaddako, a low-caste man whose occupation is removing dead flowers (from templea, etc., Ab. 508; P64. 83). Pupphadao, wine made from flowers (P64. 90). Pupphaydash appears to be a ledge or a star in a temple on which flowers were deposited as offerings (Mah. 178, 179, 201).

PUPPHI (adj.), Bearing flowers [yfiəˈwɪ].

Ab. 198, 1060; Mah. 166.

a human being gave sims in various towns, hence he is called Town-giver." There is no Sanskrit a well-known epithet of Indra that "destroyer of towns," and at p. 409 of his Kacclyanappakarapa Mr. Senart identifies perisrada etymologically with it, rendering parisrada "destroyer of fortresses." This identification is inadmissible, and Mr. Senart's criticism on the scholinist is based on the assumption that the Hindu Indra and the Buddhist Indra are the same in every respect. This is far from being the case, the Buddhist Indra (see Sakko) being a mild and beneficent archangel, for whom the epithet of town-destroyer would be quite inappropriate. The simple explanation is that Gotama Buddha unwilling to part entirely with the name Purandara modified it to Parindada, thus removing its inappropriateness and bringing it into harmony with his narrative of Indra's origin.

PURISAJANNO, This word has nothing to do with

way, but is a compound of yoy with dyaria,

and means a man of noble birth, a superior, dis

dnguished man, a man who is to other men what

the thoroughbred racer is to other horses. At

Dh. v. 103 a Buddha is intended, as the comment

states and as the title of the chapter shows. At

Mah. 139, parijojaiya ayak, "this is a remark-

able man."

PURISATTAṃ, Manhood, virility [ᠰᠢᠷ + ᠪᠠ].

Man. B. 389.

PURISO, A man; a male; a person, individual; an ardentant [ʃʌn]. Ab. 227, 1046. According to the Sāikhys philosophy the human soul or life-giving principle (Ab. 93, "paraparkialplāttma" says the Sinhalese gloss). Itthi period, a woman or a man (Kh. 13). Purisēni are you a male? (Kamn. 4). Purisāghūto, homekida (Dh. 298). Purisādhamo, a vile person, a bad man (Dh. 14). Purisattuma, an excellent man, a good man (Dh. 14). Purisamedho, human sacrifice (Ab. 413). Yamapurid (pl.), the servants or ministers of Yama (Dh. 42). Purisadriyan, male principle, virility (see Indrysēni). The aftha parishāḥāmyō or eight stages of man are, mandabḥāmi, Ḫidādḥāmi, elman-sanobḥāmi, Ḥingatabḥāmi, sekhabḥāmi, samasabḥāmi, jīnoshāmi, panasabḥāmi, the first days of semi-unconsciousness after birth, the period of tears and laughter, the first lottering attempts to walk, the dine when the child can walk firmly and straight, the period of schooling or education, the period of embracing the ascetic life, the period of matured knowledge, and the period of decay (?) The last of these I am in doubt about, the words are, bhikkha ca panasaka jino na kuiel dhati evaṃ alabhiṃ samasāha panasabḥamīti vadeti (Sam. S. A.). Purisathāmo, manly vigour. Karam pariaikicchai, performing his manly duties (8lg. S.). Saṃasaparis (adj.), having 1000 attendants (Msh. 40). The epithet of a Buddha's/parism-damasabrahi means either "guide of men whose passions have to be quelled" or "trainer or breaker-in of the human steer." the unconverted man being likened to a refractory bullock: Sikkha-tabaparis in visatabapariet Buddha's dhamamade-sama ented as a traded sotapati-dimaqgaphaida-sama pipa-paita-damaṇasadayo (Snhh.). Purisadomme alrefiti parisadamasadrahati, dameti viseriti vattam hoti, tattha parisadamadti adamid dametam yutid tiracchapariad pi manasaparid pi (Vij.). Vij. also quotes, Ahaikh Kest parism-damame saghaena pi vinemi pharusena pi vinemi saphapharusena pi visemi, O Keslo, I trala men who have to be converted by gentleness, by severity, by a mixture of gentleness and severity.

The above forms are all to common use, and it will be observed that among them are not found any of the forms given by Kaccāya which presuppose a base T, as rajena, rajāma. The explanation of this, as Saddanīti points out, is that Kaccāya has mixed up the forms of the simple word and the compounded word. When rjdā is the last part of a compound, it follows in the oblique cases either the declension of buddho or the declension of the uncompounded rjdā. Thus we have gen. and dat. morardjams (Ten J. 114), Int Eldarājino (Mah. 155), and Bdrānasirāhī (F. Jat. 8); instr. makārājma (Mah. 195), but Vīde harāfīd (Ten J. 55); acc. makārājma (Mah. 105), devardjām (Dh. 184), but morardjāṃ (Ten J. 114); pl. ndagārā (Mah. 6), but pardākarārājino (Ten J. 107). In the nom. sing. alone there is no upion, the farm-rdjā only being used; e.g. manhārjdā, ndagārjdā, devardjā, Konstardjā (Ten J. 1), morardjī (Ten J. 121), and so on in every instance. RAJÁPATHO, A narrow dark place where dust accumulates (lit. "dust-path"), a dust hole, cellar [탄수 + 탁]. The foli. formula occurs in Sám. S. and elsewhere, saddadho ghardasoo rajidpatho, abdhokdo pabbajid, "the life of a householder is a confined one, a hole and corner life, whereas acceti- claim is free as the air of heaven." The comment here says rajdpatho ti radgarjiddnash withdmathdman ti mahd-afthakathdyan cuttasi, dgmamapath to pi pattari, "it is said in the Great Commentary that rajapatha is a place in which the dust of evil desire and the other passions originates, we should add that it means also the path by which they enter." It was inevitable that the commentator should take the word reja in its moral sense, but I think it is clear that here rajdpatho is used in its ordinary acceptation, and is a strengthening of saddadha, "house life is narrow or crowded, it is like living in a dust-hole." I owe to Mr. Trenckner the following interesting quotation, rajdpatho ca manh alkhipoyyan, rajdpatha ti rajapathe ayam eva ed pdhho rejoima dgramamathdnavishdnathdne "va hejdhmanace ed thusakopthake ed bhjanantare od yatika rajema abrhystifi attho, which I render, "And should cast it into the rajapatha... here the words in the rajidpatho mean in the rejaapatha (this is an optional reading), in a place in which dust accumulates or arises, either under a bed or in a baro, or in a jar, where it gets covered with dust." The long dis, I think, an attempt to preserve the a of the original th; while compensating by length for the loss of the visargn. According to analogy we should have rajopatha, but comp. antepura, purecara.

RAJOVAJALLAM, Dust and dirt (Dh. 25). This word is a compound of with, and a Pali word jalla, and should be divided rejo + avajalla. A compound rajojalia occurs in Beahamya S. (no ca photo Gotamassa kaye rajojallas Han pat) and is rendered by Hardy "dust and mud." At B. Lotus 569 we have, sakAamatta Aaviyd rajojaliai kaye na spaliippati, "from the smoothness of his skin the dust and dirt does not adhere to his body" (Burnout wrongly refers jalla to). In Amagandha S., Coomansawamy renders jaddjallam by "matted hair and dirt." To answer to my question, Solub. writes that rajonqjalla means being covered with "rajas" and "dali." This Solhalese word dali is the phonetic equivalent of jalla, and is given in Clough's Dict. with the meaning "soot, charcoal": perhaps it should rather be "smuts" (comp. on the same column dali-kuna "grime"). Subh. says that anajalla is a compound like avamayaru. He quotes adaka-jailokan ti madkolakshmi. That it is the Sanskrit jhalta there can be little doubt, for in Sutta Nipata I find kdayamkad sedqajalika, where arda is the, and jailikl can only be "dirt rubbed off the body in shampoolag."

RASAOGASÃ (5), A nerve of sensation [ʌʃ+ʌʃ]. Ab.279. Buddha is said to be among the most popular things, having the nerves of sensation meeting at the top." The expression is somewhat elliptical. The compound consists of rasaggand + ʌʃ + ʌʃ. Hardy says, "The seven thousand nerves of taste all beat towards the tongue, so that he was sensible of the slightest flavour" (Man. B. 369). Babh. quotes from a comment, rasaggadass aggdu ranggaagggd gydys jhidni, tdii aaa atdhft rasagggaaggt. But not quotes the foll. gloss, niddagganna rasaharagiyo g�dya jidtimi honti exmabihidhiwya, which means, I think, "there are nerves of sensation to his neck all converging upwards" (I am not sure of the significance of niddagganna here, it ought to mean "when be is in an upright pustion"). It is clear from B. Lot. 566 that the North Buddhist translators have fallen into their usual blundering with regard to Pall words which have no equivalent in Saakrit (see Pataambhidd). The noun rasaharagsi in the gloss given above means also nerve of sensation: like rasaggand it is unclassical.

RUPAKAM, A figure, image, representation [qun]. Mah. 154, 163, 183; Db. 217; Das. 7. RUPAM, Form, figure, shape; Image, representation; the body; in gram. a verbal or nominal form; beauty; natural state; characteristic [qx]. Ab. 825. Sihayagghadirāpāni, representations (bas
