SA, A prefix much used as the first part of compound adjectives and adverbs, and generally conveying the idea of possession or similarity [q]. Some of these compounds are peculiar to Sanskrit, asग़ce, asstikash, asyyakid, asakubam. Most of the compounds with so-will be found separately. I here give a few others. Sabdho saardasmo, with his bow and quiver (Raa. 28). Sabajjo, ashamed (Dh. 403). Saphalako, shield and all (Msh. 154). Sakharo, boots and all (Jit. 9). Sasmo, with an army (Att. 107). Sakatthi, with his elephant (Msh. 153). Sabhariyo, with his wife (Alw. I. xlv). Sabondhano, together with its ligaments (of the tongue). Sasambhoso, with great confusion (Mah. 31). Sapariggaho, having a family. Sakadiliphalidhi saadphalini, various fruits, including banana fruits, etc. (Dh. 108). The compound saddithi, "with her handmaidens," at Dh. 240 is interesting, but I have met with no other instance of this use of so, and it may after all be an error of the copyist for saha dasthi.—In Pali, as in Sanskrit, the opposite of words compounded with the private a- is either the simple word or the word compounded with so-. Thus of the former we have amariyo "ignoble" and ariyo "noble," caddha "bad" and addha "good"; and of the latter ashadipaku "unconscious" and saadishako "conscious," aphalo "fruitless" and saphalo "fruitleful." But in Pall the case of so is sometimes extended beyond what would be admirable in Sanskrit, for the sake of emphasis or forcible antithesis. An interesting case will be found at Dp. p. 10, where saphold hoti sakubbato is opposed to aphalid hoti akubbalo. Here we should properly have simply habbata as the opposite of akubbalo, but so is pleonastically added to make the antithesis and rhythm complete. Mr. Fansbell is wrong in supposing sakubbas to be for sakubbas (from gq); the use of sakulacorn by the commentator is either a coincidence or an etymological error. A still more remarkable instance of this anomalous use of so is to be found in ace "lf." At first sight it appears impossile to account for the addition of so to q, but when we find it opposed to noce "if nos," as at Dh. p. 58, we see at once that it was added, as in sakubbas, to obtain a complete antithesis.

SACCAKIRIYA (F.), Truth, act, asseveration [+ fig1]. Hardy says, "A reelation is made of acts done either in this or some former birth, and by the power of this merit, when the reelation is truthfully made, the effect intended to be produced takes place, however wonderful its character may be" (E. Mon. 273). The first of several instances given by Hardy is that of an uplaska is Ceylon, whose mother being ill he went to her and solemnly asseverated, "I have never knowingly taken the life of any creature whatever from my childhood until now," whereupon she instantly recovered. At Mah. 151 we are told that when king Dujfash gamani was waging war with the Tamils he made the solemn declaration, "This war is not for my aggrandizement, but for the re-establishment of religion; if this assertion is true may the armour of my men flash in the day of battle" (tam fath's eco tadd ahs, adds the chronicler, "the same day it came to pass accordingly"). In the Mahimorajaka the converted fowler by the truthful asseveration that he has attained paczekahdhlfaga otalats the instantaneous miraculous release of all animals kept in confinement in India (Ten J. 120). The saccaliriy of king Dhe mmésoka recorded at Mah. 113 la wrongly rendered by Turnour: It should be "If I am of undeviating faith in the commandment of Buddha, and if it, the great Bo-tree, is destined to go hence to the island of Lanká, then let, etc."

Siddhurapo, good, or (perhaps) comely, fair (Db. 47). Siddhukhanah or siddhukfijash, sacred festivity, holy jubiles (Mah. 11, 124). Siddhuddo, saying siddhu, assent, approbation (A. 129, 105). Siddhupofid, truly wise men (Mah. 213). Siddhusomnati, kind permission (Sen. K. 329). Siddhussomnato, entered a good man (Alw. I. x). The neuter siddhu is much used as an interjection, well I good! (Ab. 1144). Siddhiti vared, saying, "Very well" (Mah. 231). Siddhu siddu, very well, my son (F. Jix. 10). Tena hi siddhu, very well, then (F. Jix. 9). Siddhu damidri, very well, I'll give it you (Dh. 139). Siddhu siddhiti adhiod-seri, assented, saying, "Good, good" (Dh. 163, comp. Alw. I. 93). Siddhu raffis darikam dassdmi, Yes, I'll give the king a damiel (Dh. 216). Siddhu mayadi lishayydma, please let us receive, we would much like to receive (Dh. 107; Pii. xxii). vilas. A thousand cakskavalas are called sahasikakhadhu, a million are disinahasil, a billion are tisahasil, or mahasahashel. These must be compound words, for at Dh. 94 we have dasahasakakrodje (loc.), "In ten thousand worlds." The following are further instances: Sahaladasasakaslakakhadhu, the whole of ten thousand cakksvalas (Jat. 51). Dasasahasilokhadhu (Jat. 17, 82, the first being shortened in accordance with frequent practice in samasese). Dasasahasilokhadhu (Jat. 28). Vasudha dasahashati pakampatha, the earth shook in ten thousand worlds (Jat. 25, comp. puthad dasasahasri, Jat. 29). Sometimes samadha is omitted, and dasahashati is treated as if it were a fem. noon; Dasasakashati pakampata, ten thousand worlds quahse (Jat. 18); Vireca dasahashyora, shive in ten thousand worlds (Jat. 27). Judging from these examples we should say that sahasat was a fem. adjective. But in the example above given from Dh. 94 it cannot possibly be fem., and at Jat. 17 it is used as a pk. masc., Katajajali na- masasanti dasasakashel sadevakda, "with uplifted hands the lehalitants of ten thousand worlds, including the deva, worship," while at Jat. 19 we have dasasahashasam, "of the inhabitants of ten thousand worlds." At Jat. 18, Niraya dasasakasaggi nishiyari, the fire of ten thousand bells died out, it appears to be an adj. mase, unless we read dasasahashel-aggi, as a compound. At Jat. 17, instead of sahasilokhadha we have sahasiko toko, "the universe of a thousand worlds." In two instances I find sahasa instead of sahasal in connection with cakkavalas; the first is dasasahasakakhaddead, the angels of ten thousand worlds (Dh. 118), and the second is dasasakasakadharasem, in ten thousand worlds (Jat. 51).

Those who have attained the path are called makaddagminmagguffho, and those who have attained the fruition are called makaddagdimphalaftho. Hardy says, "The path sakradigimi is so called because he who enters it will receive one more birth. He may enter this path in the world of men, and afterwards be born in a deva-loka; or he may enter it in a deva-loka, and afterwards be born in the world of men" (E. Mon. 280). Allahaster says, "There will be only one birth among men or angels before reaching Nirvana" (Wheel of the Law, 171). The fact is that a man who has attained Sakaddagdimship is re-born twice, once in the deva world and once in the world of men. His name implies that he returns to the world, and consequently he must in the interval have been in another world. This is I think proved by a passage in Par. 8, in which Buddha says of a devout disciple who had recently died, Sadatto Aanda updisako tipam rasyajasdamaiparkkkayd radgudamamahasmantid amkaddagini sakid eco imam lokami agwated dakikhasantash korimati, "O Aanda, the updaika Sadatta by the destruction of the three Samiyojanes, by the attenuation of lust, hatred, and ignorance, having become a Sakaddagim, returning once only to this world will make an end of suffering." The Sakaddagim has entirely got rid of the three Samiyojanas (sakkkadattifti, elikicichd, and elabbatupardmaed), and greatly diminished or reduced to a minimum the pastions of raga, dam, and moka. With regard to the expression tametta of the text (see also p. 269, a, of this Dict.) the comment on Par. 8 says, sakaddagdimna hi patthujjaadnam viya abkhassis radgddaye na appajjast, kaddei karahaci appajjastii, appajjandind ca patthujjandam viya bahalabahald na appajjast, mackkhapattam viya tamstankd appajjast, "for the lusts and other passions of the sakaddagim do not arise repeatedly like those of unconversed men, they arise only now and then, and when they arise they do not arise gross and thick as with unconversed men, but they arise exceedingly at-brensted like fishes' scales" (1). A little further it speaks of the seven births of the Soutpanna, the two births of the Sakaddagimin, and of the single birth of the Anagkinin. Burnout takes the right view, for he says the S. is "a being who has yet to traverse sixty thousand kcalpas, to be re-born

once among the devas and once among men" (Int. 293). The sakadagim in may be kdmabhaodN-gataphalo, or rupabhaoddh(gataphalo, or arpa-bhavodigataphalo, according (I suppose) as he is re-born in a kimadevaloka, a rupadevaloka, or an arupadevaloka).

SAKIM (adv.), Once; at once, simultaneously [W-W]. Sakim vijddt, a woman who has borne one child (Dh. 213). Sakim vijddtaapgo, appearance of a woman who has borne one child (Dh. 315). Sakim cedants, speaking to him once (Dh. 272). At the same time, simultaneously (Mah. 108). Sakim yrea, at the very same time (Mah. 84). Tewnik sakik upperank serada na samuati, their wrath when once romed does not pass away (Dh. 100). Sakid eva, at one and the same time (Am. 193), once only (see Sakaddgdm).

BAKIYO (adj.), Own [sæpɪˈɒn], This is the correct spelling (comp. parakiya, datiya, gukita, etc.), salikya at Alt. 216 is merely a return to the Sanskrit. At F. Jat. 18 we have médiya miktiy'oudki, where miktiy is a shortened instr. fam. from sakiyo, and not as at first sight would appear an instr. from an anomalous fem. mikt from sakio.

SÁRIYO, SÁKYO, and SÁKKO, Name of the princely family to which Oustana Buddha belonged [TTI]. Ab. 1001. The Cákyas formed a great elan or people, engaged in agriculture, among whom probably only a very few families were princely (Dh. 851). Their territory seems to have been of some extent. At Ab. 184 Sákká "the Cákyas" is given as the name of a people. At Dh. 801 we are told that on one occasion Buddha was living among the Cákyas (Sakkas ciharonto). In Sutia Nipáta also I fled Khash samayash Bhagavad Sakyesa ciharati. Solydaash Ujamposh adna sigmanah, a town of the Cákyas named Uumpa (Dh. 829). Sákkigo or Sakko, a Cákya prince (Ab. 336, 1001; Mah. 9, 55). Sakyardjido, Cákya prince (Dh. 217). Sakyardjakulach, Cákya royal family (Dh. 117). Sakyardjida, or Sakiyaddrikdi, a Cákya princess (Dh. 218). Mahaddamo Sakko, the Cákya prince Mahaddama (Dh. 218). Suppabaddhaakho, the Cákya prince Suppabuddha (Dh. 296). Sakiyad adma mdmamidid, the Cákya princes are banghy (Dh. 142). Gautama Buddha is sometimes called Bakyputis, son of the house of Cákya, or Cákya prince (Att. 135 fr. Dipavaza, see Sakiyaddikho). Rjdí Schiydamai, the king of the Cákyas (Dh. 222). Sakiyapadho, the royal line of Cákya (Dh. 224). Sakyamani, the Cákya sage or philosopher, is given as an epithet of Gautama at Ab. 5, I have elsewhere met with it only at Kh. 7. I here enter my protest against the continental custom of speaking of Gautama Buddha as "Cákyamen," which is a mere epithet. It is as though we spoke of Jesus Christ as "The Lion of the Tribe of Judah" (Rev. v.), or the "Prophet of Nazareth" (Matt. xxii.). Gautama is the name by which he was universally known and addressed (at Kh. 8 we have even Gotamardamani, "the commandment of Gautama"), and I see no reason to depart in this matter from the practice of antiquity. — SAKKAYO, Own body or person [+]. Kh. 9; Dh. 996. Sakkyadijkh, “the heresy of individuality,” is one of the three satnyojanas, loose from which is obtained by entraces into the first Path (adpatel). Yátr. states that sakkyadijkh is identical with attamido (which see), and quotes, vāsiatāthikid sakkyadijkhā attavadispāśānus. Hardy says, “he also rejects the error called sakkya-dipshti, which teaches, I am, this is mine.” (E. Mos. 229). Sabb. to answer is my question as to the eymology says it means “svikya qarran,” and I have no doubt that he is right. We should naturally expect sabbys, but the k is doubled to compensate for the loss of the v (comp. papildikid; and sabbikass = vāshāyath, where the k is doubled to compensate for the shortening of the vowel). The North Buddhists, passed by the double k, have (as in numerous other instances, see Papisoubhidd) ascribed a wrong etymology to this word, and turned it in Sankrit into sakkyadipkhā, as if the first part of the compound were wīt instead of wē. Bornout adopts this etymology (Int. 263), rendering sakkya by “existing body,” or “aggregate of what exists,” and sakkyadijkhā by “the view that the body is what exists.” From the passage which he goes on to quote from Abdhharma Koṇa Vykhyā It is clear that the author of that work had a correct understanding of the meaning of the term, and was only at fault as to its etymology; the original of the passage will be found at Alw. N. 72, in an extract from Sahyutia Nikiya. Here it is shown that Sakkyadijkhā may be held in twenty different ways (see above alcattakhk). A man may look on Form, the first khandha, as Self (rūpan atate samavapamti), or he may look on Self as possessing Form (rūpavattam atidama), or he may look on Self as residing in Form (attam rūpami), or Form as residing in Self (rūpavattam atidama). If for Ropa we substitute in turn each of the four remaining khandhas we obtain the twenty modes of heretical view as regards the Atid or Self—According to Sangkit S. there are three Antas or goals of doctrine, sakkido as a sakkiyasamadaya as a sakkiyasavodho as to the body or Self, the origination of the Self, and the amihilation of the Self.

SAKKO, Calms or Indra [T] Ab. 1001. When Gautama Boddis deposed Indra from his godship, he made him a powerful archangel ruling over the five lowest kimadevalokas and having his abode in the Tivatilma beavans (see Mdo). He is widely different from the Hindu Indra, though retaining many of his attributes. He is inferior in majesty and power to the two other archangela Mahabrahma and Mira. Like Mahabrahma, he is represented as exercising a heaefial influence over the affairs of men. When a good man is struggling with adversity, the fact is made known to Sakka by the throne on which he sits becoming warm (ugdhabraha dassri, Raa. 16; P. Jat. 54; Dh. 87; Man. B. 50). It is then his wont to take some earthly disguise and demeaned to the relief of the sufferer. When king Dhammasodikha, seeking in vain to obtain a knowledge of the Truth, had given up his throne and resigned himself to the life of an ascetic, we are told that the moment he entered the forest, by the power of his merit the throne of Sakka became hot. At the devar(id) caste and man me popujhambasididomani upham abami, Lin mu kho kropgen? (i) okon okedvated Sakka devarrji Dhammasodikha maddritjana sakajajan badiipam vicimirad sadilhammajjheyyakam alabidi-fed pacitphabdisam addan, "Then the archanged thought, Without my wish my marble throne has become hot, what can be the cause? and gaslag over the world the archangel Sakka beheld the great king Dhammasodikha, who had entered the forest, having sought throughout the whole land of Jambadipa a teacher of the Truth, and having found none." Sakka then assumes the shape of a rakhasa, meets him to the forest and puts his faith to the severest trials. As the last moment he resumes the radiant form proper to him, reveals to the astonished monarch the Truth he was in search of, and restores him to his king-don (Raa. 18, and fall). In the Sakjikaka, Sakka in the disguise of a brahmin tries the faith of the Bodhisattva, and rewards him for his heroic endurance by imprinting the figure of the lara upon the moon as a lasting memorial of his good deed (P. Jat. 54). In the Dadhivahama Jitaka he is represented as bestowing upon three plous hermit's the means of supplying their wants without trouble to themselves (Jit. 9). Shortly after Gautama's attainment of Bodhabod, Sakka went down to meet him in the disguise of a young brahmin and sung his praises (Dh. 10).

What I have said of the personality of Mahibrahma holds good also of Sakka: there is a Sakka in every cakkayita, and the office of Sakka, which is in fact the sovereignty of the Tivatima, angels, and is called Sakkaftam (q.v.), is only held for a limited period by the same individual. The Sakra of the Dadhivilana Jitaka was a plentur bermit of Himaanta (F. J44. 2). The Sakra of Gautama's time had been a young brahmin named Megha, who was re-born as Sakra as a reward for his real is doing good (Dh. 6). And according to Hardy, Gautama Buddha himself was Sakra in twenty of his antecedent births (Mau. B. 100).

Sakka's usual designation is Sakka derdassate (Db. 183), or Sakka decordid (Db. 190, 184, 337, 415). Many of his brabmalical titles are preserved, but always explained to us to harmonize with his new Buddhist characters. Thus he retains the epithet of mahasmutti (Db. 57), or mahasmuttke (Ab. 18), but it is said to mean that he can think of 1000 things at the same instant (Db. 186; comp. the use of personacichthio). He is said to be named Sakka because when a man be additionally exercised the virtue of charity (makkaseeth demakadid I Db. 185). His title of parandra is changed to parisada (q.v.). He is called magkhow because his name when a man was Magha, and he is called Indra because he is telman or lord of the Tivalitima sangla (Db. 165).

Sakika with his consort Sujidi reigns with great splendour in the Tevadinnas heaven situated on the summis of Mount Mero (Man. B. 11). His royal city is called Masakikrasra or Vasspoknares, and his palace is called Vejayanta. He is the Recording Angel of Buddhism, and four times a month, seated to his Hall of Justice called Badhammi, he reads aloud from a golden book a record of good works done by men during the week. Sakika has a splendid car called Vejayanto driven by the charlsteer Métall, an elephant named Erivasa, and a blank or trumpet called Vijayutara, of tremendous power. nor. asakhi and cond. asakhiara are formed, like sakkhisati, from sakkhiti treated as a present. We should expect sakhudti, sakhygya, etc., but the doubling of the k is carried on from sakkoti (= sakkoti), where it is philologically correct. A precisely similar instance will be found in aggimi = agui, and analogous cases in pavilianess = praviqishn, kailahdra = kahlara, sasutika = saqriks, etc. The s is a compensation for the change of W to T, comp. sakhuo. At Mah. 141 we have a remarkable p.f.p. sakhyyeyo. The passage is as follows, asakhuayye padius ucedus catupanicahi ifamāno khipl todd so kifigulale viya, "at that age he could toss about stones which four or five men could not lift, as if he were playing at hand balls." Here asakhyeyo mecdwwa means "unable to be lifted" and the construction is like that of several sentences given under Sakha (e.g. Buddhadasa na sakhed sathena diddhatuai). In one example given under my art. Parmatiko will be found a word asakhyyattam "insability," which is this p.f.p. + W. I have met with asakhyeya in several other places.

The atth. sayu, dolur jihuesu paini pitipharopatid, ilun jihnesu painid sukhapharapatid, paracitte paind cetopharapatid, dibacakkkun doluhapharapatid, tamhd tamhd samddhimkd vuthltasaa paccavekkhapassimittain, “the diffusion of joy is the knowledge obtained by the first two jihans, the diffusion of serenity is the knowledge obtained by the first three jihnas, the diffusion of thought is the knowledge of the thoughts of others (cetaparigaidna), the diffusion of light is the divine eye, and the sign of reflexion is the self-reflexion of one who has risen from one of the states of supernatural absorption.” The samdkhl of ecstatic meditation is of two degrees, the inferior called spacdrasamddhi, and the higher or perfect called appandsamddhi (E. Mon, 357). Saugti S. enumerates four samdkhl bihavans, or attainments of samdkhl; the first leads to blues in this world (diifhadhammaaskhavithera), the second to fagadassapa, the third to satisampaifidha, the fourth to Arhatship. Saugti S. also enumerates seven requisites to the attainment of samdkhl (sarto samdkhlparikkhrda), which are samdkshankappa, samndedded, samndkammonido, samnddjoo, samndedydoo, sammaatj.

mattakaṃ sabbaṃ gaṇeśd kāyaṃ paṭibādhaṃ karūṭaṃ gasehati, "takes all these eight requidities only, and ataching them to his person departs." Kālinga suvaṃ paṭṭhāpiṭadāhaṃ Kurādhammaṃ dīrod samādāya sādāhaṃ pārisi, the Kālinga king having read the Kuru laws brought to him after he had had them written out for him, made it a point of honour to carry them out, and rigidly enforced them (Dh. 417). Pardam Vajjadhammom samaddāya vattanti, scrupulously adhere to the old Vajjian customs (Par. 8, comp. Dh. 306). Generally used of a religious undertaking or vow to fulfil some or all of the religious precepts (akkhāpadas, or alma), either for a time or permanently. Thus a layman may make a vow to keep intact the five precepts, or the eight precepts for a limited period (as a year or five years), or for life. This is frequently done at the present day, the vow being solemnly recorded before a priest. Sikkhāya paddāmi paṭica akhāpadāphillāni samādiyāmaṃ, do thou solemnly undertake to keep the five sikkhāpadas inviolate (Dh. 97; comp. Kh. 17). Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadas, having taken them upon himself he exercises himself in the precepts (Saṅg. 6). Silam s, to vow the performance of the moral precepts (Mab. 249; F. Ját. 53). Aṭṭhōṇaṃsaṃ s, to undertake the eight precepts (Att. 204, 210). Uposathāmi s, to take upon oneself the uposatha vows (Dh. 306). Desaślam s, to take upon oneself the ten precepts (Mah. 110). Pāramisi s, to undertake solemnly to perform a Pāramīṭā (Jāt. 20). Pisaṃ dhammaṃ s, to take upon oneself the whole Law of Buddha (Dh. 47). Pres. 1st pers. samādiyāmi (Dh. 308). Imperat. samādiya (Jāt. 20), samādiguaraṃ (Dh. 07). Gac. samādiya (Mah. 110, 249; Dh. 47, 417), samādiyāti (Jāt. 53; Att. 204, 210). P.p.p. samādinnā. Samādinnāposūṭha (adj.), one by whom the uposatha vows have been taken (Dh. 314). Caus. samādapati, to Instigate, rouse, advise (B. Lot. 431). Sayyām deti param na samādapati, himself gives alms but does not urge others to give (Dh. 112, see also 113, line 16). Attanou spattākkā saṃdapeptet, suborning their own servants (to compass the death of Moggallāna, Dh. 228). Sdnzhian sappundmaths niraydya upahqlhati, monasticism ill handled brings a man to hell; that is a man is not necessarily saved by becoming a Buddhist priest, for if he misuse the privileges of that holy state he is worse off than the worldling (Dh. 35, comment says if he abuse his calling by breaking the sda precepts etc.). First. Nothing shows more strongly the universal veneration in which the Brahmins were held in Gautama's time, a veneration due to their birth and intellectual endowments, than the fact that Gautama, whose mission it was to break down the brahminical system, nevertheless held up the brahmins themselves to the respect of his followers, placed them on a level with his own monks, and even adopted their name into his own system, applying it figuratively to the Arbat, or Buddhist monk who has attained the highest sanctification. Hence we have the word samapadhoamand (pl.), in which brahmins sometimes has its ordinary meaning and sometimes its secondary meaning of Arbat. In Vassals outta we are told that a man is an out-casts who develves a monk or brahmin or other ascetic, or refuses him hospitality (A/w. N. 120). At Dh. 392 we are told that pious monks and brahmins are to be treated with kindness. At Dh. v. 143 we are told that even if a man be gorgieously arrayed (as a king's minister) yet if he be self-restrained, virtuous, and merciful, he is a brahmin, a samapa, a bhikkhu. That is to say, the man who wears the humble garb of an ascetic has not the monopoly of true religion. The comment on this verse tells the story of king Prasenajit's minister Santi, who, on hearing Buddha repeat a religious stams, instantly became an arbast, and stained Nirvaga (by fire kammathhana) while yet dressed in his court attire. The priests ask each other, "Is this man who has attained Nirvaga dressed in his court attire to be considered as a samapa or a brahmin?" The question is referred to Buddha, who makes this reply, bhikkhunī mama putra samago ti vattam vattati brahmapo ti pi vattam vattati, "It is right to call a son of mine (i.e. a convert) both a samapa and a brahmapo." Although Gautama treated caste as worthless from a religious point of view, yet none was more fully alive to the advantages social and intellectual of good birth, and we are constantly told of a man being born a brahmin or kshatriya as a reward of good actions in a former existence, or a low caste man as a punishment for crimes committed in a former existence.

SAMAYO, Agreement, combination; multitude; season; time; custom, rule, religious obligation; order, precept; religious belief, doctrine [[744]]. Ab. 60, 161, 778. Ehem samayam, or skomis samaye, at one time, at a certain time, once upon a time, once (Alw. I. ixix; Kh. 10; Raa. 27). Tena ke paa samayana, now at that time (Alw. I. 92; Dh. 121). Tsumith samaye, at that time, then (Dh. 154, 230, 288). Uphamsayo, time of beat, hot season (Pit. 15; Dh. 210). Majikanti kamsayo, noon-tide (Raa. 32). Syaṃ kamsayam, in the evening (Jit. 9). Pubbaṃ kamsayam, in the morning, Pacatamsayane, at dawn (Dh. 84). Tama marasamayash fated, perceiving that his death-hour was come (Dh. 93). Sitaamaye aggikhated adisi, when they were cold he made fire and gave it them (Dh. 186). Samaye, in due time, in due course (Mab. 134). Samaye papphamti, blossom in season, at the right time (Jat. 27). Hotiki ke yo bhikkhawe samayo, priests, there will come a time when... (Gog. Ev. 14). Ashatra samayid, except on occasion, except under particular circumstances, or at a particular time (Pit. 8, 18). Buddha hada dya samayam okosanto, swalting the time for his becoming B. (Mah. 169, comp. PIL. 106). Brdhmasasamayamin, according to brahmalical observance or custom or views (Alw. I. xiv). Saddhammardjomasayo, the doctrine or religion of the King of Truth (Yak, comp. Mah. 41). Samandhi andamayo, to whom all forms of religious belief were thoroughly familiar (Mah. 260, Turnour says "possessed of great aptitude in attaining acquirement"). Tsumdham jdsama-amayo etika'na, is that all the learning or religious truth you know? (Dh. 121). Akkhara-samayah na jaddit, he was illiterate, lit. did not know the combinations of levers (Alw. I. 101). Samayamara, forelgu usages or politics (Att. 126, 234). Vij. informs me that samaya in maddamayo mesos "a multitude" (see Ab. 778, "samahs"). Thus Mahānaamayanta means the discourse preached to a great company, and on Pit. 14, line 4, he says, "when three priests live by slms, and a fourth comes and there is not enough, the occasion should be regarded as a large company and meals taken accordingly."

SAMMANNATI, To agree to, decide, resolve; to

lanedon, approve, select []. So mahd-

ther... khish saddhammugitinn... bhikhkh

pacicate yea mahkhindave vare sammanni,

this great then authorized or chose (the corre-

sponding word in Br. J. S. A. is meelni) five

hundred eminent Arbal priests to hold a rehearsal

of the Law (Mah. 11). Amandothero pi sammanni

hotuk saugitinn, the thera Kuanda also decided or

chose to join in the rehearsal (Ditto). Tato thero

viseyam pucehamathdya attend ca attdanh sam-

mment Upditthero pi visoijonathdya sammanni,

then the Elder undertook (lit. Itimself chose or

authorized himself) to put the questions on Dis-

riptline, while Upill Thers undertook to make the

answers (Br. J. S. A.). Pacisake ca catro

cature Páheygyaké pi ca sammanni, he selected four Péfnaká and four Páheygyaké priests (Mah. 18), Sammonutid deti, deckes upon giving lit, lit after resolution gives it (Pkt. 67). Sanghe... Shikkhuvn saidkagédkpakah sammanutid, the chapter having elected a priest to act as ticket distributor (Pkt. 63). For two other instances of this word see the extract under art. Kammarid. I find in a comment sammanutid sammanat akid. One would expect sammanutidi, as the simple verb takes the form maññati, but analogous irregularities are not wending, e.g. compare the double forms paññati and paṇpattit, paññad and paṇpada, alifid and did; compare also paṇmarava and paṇpruvati with pañcadasa and pañcadasa. P.p.p. sammato, approved, assented to, authorized, chosen; allowed; esteemed, honoured, considered, regarded. Sammaidai saighena imdi pañic shikkhuatidai... dhammah ca vāmaṃ ca saigāyitwa, is the assembly in favour of these 500 monks rehearsing the dhamma and vinaya? lit are these 500 monks approved of by the assembly to rehearse (See Kommaidé). Kupindā sammato, a landholder of high character (Meb. 143). Daitguamamato azou, the second beat horse, lit. esteemed second (Meb. 134, opposed to enigalapdi, the state charger). Aiatika atjā'amace'ōe mahamaṃ yodhasammatā, galued over eight great nobles, warriors of reputation (Mah. 203, comp. lxxxv). Sādhamammatō means, not "esteemed by good men" (Alw. I. x), but "considered good, excellent, extensible." A comment says, apuh addis appuriso it evam sammato. Seithasammato, considered the best, the most esteemed (Ten J. 109). Thapépeni sammatena amaccena, caused to be laid by a minister specially selected for that purpose (Mah. 173). Sadaishasammatūna rattham, a country rep ated dangerous (Pkt. 107). Saighena sammato, authorized by the clergy, having received permission from the clergy (Pkt. 67, comp. 13, 93). Lokasammatāsh, universally esteemed, held by the world in the highest repute (Jt. 49). Amhā utta mardjalaṃ asammat, we are looked upon as belonging to one of the best princely families. Ratomai of ratamassmatam od, jewels or valuable (Pit. 18, lit. what may be looked upon as a jewel). Mesigalasammato, or abhinagigalaṃsamaṃto, festive, festively arrayed (Mah. 178; Dh. 946; Jt. 53). Comp. Sammanit. Caus./sammanit, to bour

SAMMAPPADHÂNAM, Right exertion [ʌnˈrɪtʃ+ɪnɪt]. There are four, exertion to prevent anful conditions arising, exertion to put away stufol states already existing, exertion to produce meritorious states not yet in existence, exertion to retalu meritorious conditions already existing (Ati. 57; Man. E. 499; Dh. 889; Kh. 37). The text la, idn'd'desse dhikhu anupprandman ppakondma almaelnaah dhamaadna anuppraldya chandani ja-meti ceyamati virigash drabhati clitam paggraphti pedahati, uppasudach ppokindat ak. dhamadmarh pahidya chandam jameti, ete. (Sang. S.).

SAMMASATI, To seise, grasp [græɪŋ], I have only met with this word in the metaphorical sense of seizing or grasping with the mind, gaining a thorough knowledge of, mastering; it is one of the terms of the ecstatic meditation. Yato yato seemament khandadmark edayeyayash, as soon as he masters the idea of the arising and vanishing of the skandlus (Db. 67). Kammafhadmasz, to grasp with the mind and dwell upon one of the forty karmasthanas or subjects for ecstatic contemplation (Dh. 184, 225, 286, see Kasumafhadman). Thakkhasasz, to realise or imbu one-self with the idea of the transdortiness, the evil and the unreality of existence (Ten J. 119, see Lakkhasas). Peesydkhadmasz usulomapplimamgarma z, to cause the mind to dwell successively on the twelve Nidanas to direct order and in reverse order (lit. forwards and backwards, Dh. 220; at Jst. 25 the ten Pramtas are similarly meditated upon). Dh. 139, 134; J4. 74.
SAMMASATI (f.), 100 Suti (1).

SAMMATI, To be appeared or calmed; to cease [晋]. Verdi semmenti, hatred is appeared (Dh. 2, comp. 70). P.p.r. semsemno (Pst. 63). P.p.p.r. semto (Ah. 749, 841). Semen taus semen hoti semt ad, tranquil is his mind, tranquil his speech (Dh. 18, comp. 28, 67; B. Lot. 376). Padani semtani, the quiet place or lot, Nirvipa (Dh. 68; Kh. 15). Sentisdriyo (adj.), whose senses are stilled or calmed (Alw. I. 93). Semen sutt, living a tranquil life (Alw. I. x). Also p.p.p.r. semito (Ab. 749, 841). Semen gemen, a stald or sober gult (Dh. 234). Caus. semeti, to appease, to extinguish, suppress, put a stop to. Tust semetani, to suppress this heresy (Mah. 15, 18; comp. Pit. 62). Lotem semetani, to give peace to the world (B. Lot. 376). Pdpi dni z, to extinguish sin (Dh. 47).

SAMYOJANAM, and SANN, Bond, attachment [shāpiqam]. Dh. 6, 40, 61. In a religious sense samyojasn is the bond of human passion which blade man to continued existence, and the removal of which is obtained by suurance into the Paths (B. Lot. 380). The tan samyojasna (dasavidhasa, Dh. 100, 383, 410) are sakikiyadishii, sikkirichii, sissbopatapardasna, kwardago, paigiko, rapardgo, arpardigo, māno, mādhaasean, avjjd (Vij.). Of these the first five are called paico arwabikiyasangijaadi, and the last five paico mādhaambhāgiyasangiyajandai. The first three (tfiṃ samyojandai) are removed by the First Path (E. Mon. 939). From Dh. 431 we learn that the first five are so called because they cause rebirth in the lower worlds (the spāynas, kimadevaloka, ele.), and are got rid of by the first, second and third Paths, while the last five cause rebirth in the rape and arupadevaloka, and are got rid of by Arhatship. When Arhatship is attained, and human passion is got rid of, there is nothing left to cause rebirth; and when the Arhat dies he is not reborn, but passes out of existence. From Par. 6. 19 it appears that the Solapanna has got rid of the three samynjasas, that the sakadigāmin has in addition reduced to a minimum rage, does and moha, and that the antagāmin has got rid of the fourth and fifth samyanas. I have said in my article Nidāཡམ (p. 269, a) that a man after entering the first path, may pass on through the others to Arhatship in the same existence. I may add that the successive atainment of the paths may either be slow, extending over a whole life, or may be more or less rapid, and even in rare cases instantaneoua, a man being one moment an unconverted man and the next an Arhat, having in that brief interval passed successively through all the Paths and got rid of all human passion. The boy Nigrodha attained Arhatship while his head was being shaved for admission to the priesthood (Mah. 21, 103). Yass entered the first path one night and attained Arhatship next day (Dh. 119). Ananda after attaining Anagamishh remained for many years unable to attain Arhatship, and did not succeed till after Buddha's death (Mah. 13). We often read of a person entering the path, and even reaching the fourth, by merely hearing a sermon of Buddha (Dh. 89, 119), or even a single stanza (Dh. 309).

SANDHI (m. and f.), Junction, union; agreement; a joint of the body [aʃʃn]. Ab. 763; Mah. 25. Maggamndhi, place of junction of two roads (Ab. 203). Chijhandmanu sandhibandhanem, when the ligaments of the joints are being severed (Db. 259). Kifasandhiggahasah, fitting or joining on the peak of a house (Att. 203, crowning the edifice of long-suffering). Sandhim kafutwa, having made a compact (sensignation) with her (Mah. 57). Of the joints of masonry (damiineyyasildandhi ertu). Junction, proper place or interval (Mah. 201, 211, flowers were suspended at suitable places, thimeam, Subh.). In gram. of the euphonite vowel and consonant changes that take place at the junction of final and initial syllables (Sen. K. 200). In Pall external sandhi is comparatively little used. According to Ab. 941 sandhi is also used in the sense of rebirth (pafrandhi). An example of this is found at Dh. v. 97, where sandhichedo, “who has brought rebirths or continued existence to an end,” is explained by the commentator vattasandhim samudrasandhim cheted Jhito. Sandhichedo has a different sense at Dh. 901, 407, where it evidently means housebreaking (comp. Sangk. sandhicaura, sandhiharakn). I render the first passage, “Some such terrible accusation as, ‘This burglaries deed unseen or heard or thought of before (i.e. of unheard-of atrocity), or this state offence (treason), was perpetrated by you;’” and the second, “Discontented with their own property, they attempt burglaries and such like offences.” Ab. 941 makes usdhi fem. when it means rebirth and meac. when it means union. But in the sense of union it is probably common, as Ab. 703 makes it fem. In that sense, and at Mah. 201 we have the fem. loc. sandhigam, where “jancture” is intended.

SANDITTHIKO (adj.), Visible, actual, belonging to this life [sittftem], Ab. 80. At Alw. I. 77 the dhamma or Truth of Buddha is said to be sandifthiko, viz. productive of immediate results, attended with advantages even in this world. Sandifthiko admiapahalam, reward of ascentism even in this life (see Schmafath). When the punishment of a crime (or reward of a good action) takes place in this world, i.e. before death, it is called sandifthiko elpiko, as opposed to punishment in a future state of existence. An example is given at Mah. 201, 202, where a king having been deposed by his rival and put to death by being built into a wall, the chronicler observes that this was the immediate (sandifthika) retribution for his having in the days of his prosperity buried a Buddhist priest alive. SANDHI (m. and f.), Junction, union; agreement; a joint of the body [aʃʃn]. Ab. 763; Mah. 25. Maggamndhi, place of junction of two roads (Ab. 203). Chijhandmanu sandhibandhanem, when the ligaments of the joints are being severed (Db. 259). Kifasandhiggahasah, fitting or joining on the peak of a house (Att. 203, crowning the edifice of long-suffering). Sandhim kafutwa, having made a compact (sensignation) with her (Mah. 57). Of the joints of masonry (damiineyyasildandhi ertu). Junction, proper place or interval (Mah. 201, 211, flowers were suspended at suitable places, thimeam, Subh.). In gram. of the euphonite vowel and consonant changes that take place at the junction of final and initial syllables (Sen. K. 200). In Pall external sandhi is comparatively little used. According to Ab. 941 sandhi is also used in the sense of rebirth (pafrandhi). An example of this is found at Dh. v. 97, where sandhichedo, “who has brought rebirths or continued existence to an end,” is explained by the commentator vattasandhim samudrasandhim cheted Jhito. Sandhichedo has a different sense at Dh. 901, 407, where it evidently means housebreaking (comp. Sangk. sandhicaura, sandhiharakn). I render the first passage, “Some such terrible accusation as, ‘This burglaries deed unseen or heard or thought of before (i.e. of unheard-of atrocity), or this state offence (treason), was perpetrated by you;’” and the second, “Discontented with their own property, they attempt burglaries and such like offences.” Ab. 941 makes usdhi fem. when it means rebirth and meac. when it means union. But in the sense of union it is probably common, as Ab. 703 makes it fem. In that sense, and at Mah. 201 we have the fem. loc. sandhigam, where “jancture” is intended.

SANGHADISESO (adj.), Requiring a saughkanoma at every stage [+]+[20]+[21]. Saughdised dpatti is the name of a class of thirteen priestly offences next in beinousness to the Prajjika spattis. Hardy says, "Saughdisesd,�briean in number, that require suspension and penance but not permanent exclusion" (E. Mon. 9). Burnouf explius It to mean "that which must be declared to the Saugha from beginning to end." The real meaning, if I mistake not, is "an offence dealt with by a Saughkanoma in the earliest (adi) and later (sea) stages." This is pretty clear from the following extracts given at Pat. 68, 89. The first in saughdidiseo ti saigho 'va toad dpatriyd pariodawm deti mldya pofikoasati mndastah deti abdhoti, na sambahid no ekspuggalo, tena vucati saughdidiseo ti, "so called because a Saugha, not a multitude of priests or a single priest, inflicts parivisa for this offence, renews the punishment (If necessary), inflicts mndatta, and reindustes." Here it will be seen that there are three and some times four processes, in each of which a Saughakamna is required. The second extract is, saigho ddiakicva sese ca icchiatabbo asditi saughdidiseo, bidvattam hoti p imam dpatition dpaqjited vaftdudamassa yan taad dpationqftdawm tusa dttmt'eva parivisaaddnatthya didto sese ca saajha mndattaddnatthya mldya pothassawena od saha admataddnatthya aasadsa abdhatathdya ca saigho icchiatabbo, na k'eitha eham pi komumand wind saughena sakkid kdtwn ti saigho ddtmt'eva sese ca icchiatabbo ti saughdidema, "Saughdisess is that for which a Saugha is waited in the first instance and in the remaining instances. What is meant by this? For the man who has committed this offence and wishes to be rehabilitated, for his rehabilitation a Saugha is required; first at the beginning to administer parivisa, and, following upon the beginning (ddite sese), in the middle to administer minatta, or possibly (ed) manatta combined with mldya paikassana, and lastly at the end to reinstate the offender. For in this matter no single ceremony can be performed without a Saugha, and saughdidisea is no called because a Saugha is required in the beginning and in the rest."

Mon. 18). The question before the chapter is decided by vote (see Kommonded). Easily a number of monks assembled together for administrative purposes are called a Sangha or chapter (see Sangha monarch). Hence the term S. may be applied to assemblies of monks varying in number from a chapter of four to the whole body of Buddhist monks, amounting at one time to millions. Saikhyrtha Prakiga observes that there are two saighas, bhikkhausigha and bhikkhausigho. At the present day there are no nuns in Ceyloo, and but few in other countries. Sangha when applied to monks is properly an abbreviation for bhikkhasigha, "assembly of monks," which term is of common occurrence and coextensive in its use with sangha. The senior priest in any assembly of priests is called sanghathera, "elder of the assembly," who generally would be president. Titus Rassapa was sanghathera or president of the first Sangit (Mah. 11, comp. Db. 384). At Mah. 19 we are told that at the second Sangit the there Sahbakhim was paikuviyd sanghathera, the longest erdalsed priest in the world (he had been spaasapana 120 years, he was not however president of the Sangiti). Sanghardja, patriarch or pontiff, is the (modern) title of the principal ecclesiastical functionary in Barmah.
BANOHUTTHO (p.p.p.), Bounded, resounding [qng]. Mab. 09, 170 (mndturiyarighuttho).

SANIGTI (f.), Chanting together, rehearsal [qū-qū]. Dibbaugit, celestial choir (Jāt. 31). The brum S. is given to three great historical convocations or General Councils (saigāfitayos, Mah. 251) of the Buddhist Clergy held for the purpose of fixing the text of the Buddhist Scriptures (Tāplāka). They were called Saṅgit or Rehearsal, because the text was rected, sentence by sentence, by an eminent there, and chanted after him in chorus (gaṇasajbāya) by the whole assembly. The first Rehearsal was held at Rajgaha under the patronage of King Ajātasātru, immediately after Gautama Buddh's death (b.c. 543), the apostle Kassapa preeding, while Upāli was the reclater or precentor for the Vinaya, and Ånsada for the Dhamma. It consisted of five hundred members, and in variously called paṭhamamahdaṃgiti, "First Great Rehearsal" (A.w. i. vi, at Mah. 14 paṭhamadhāmaṃsā), or paṭcatāṭikā s., "synod of five hundred," or therīyā s., "synod of elders" (Mah. 20). The second (duṇiyamaṃkā, saṭasatikā s.) was held at Vesili under the patronage of King Kāṭisoka (the Black or dark-featured Asoka, not as Kern saya, the "Coronological Asoka"1). B.c. 443, and consisted of seven hundred members presided over by the apostle Ravata (Mah. 18-20; E. Mon. 174). The third (tatiyomakā, saṅtakaṃkā s.) was held at Paṭaliputta, under the patronage of King Dhammāsaṃsaka, in the year B.c. 309, and concluded of a thousand members, under the presidency of Tissa the son of Moggall (E. Mon. 174; Mah. 49). At A.w. i. 63 we are told of a heretical synod called Mahāsaṃgīd, "the great Rehearsal" because it was held by ten thousand heretical monks. In Shāhalase the Nāṭayas of the Sātuṇipāka are called saṅgīy's, v.a. saṅgīy's (e.g. dīkaṃgīya + dīghaṃgīti, mīdamsaṃgīya = maṇjikmaṃsagīti, E. Mon. 168, 169). As explaining this use of the word I quote the full passage from Br. J. B. A. Suttasatāpiṃsaka can also soṇāṃītyo, iden paṭhamamāsaṃsagīti? it, dighaṃingīth bhatsā, "In the Sāta Piṃaka there are four rehearsals, of them which shall be rehearsed first? The Long Rebearal, Lord." Here aṇīgīth has the secondary meaning of "text rehearsed."
SANGITO, see Saigdyati.

SANGO, Attachment, bond, tie [T]]. Ab. 789. Generally used in the religious sense of that which attaches men to the world, human passion, desire, etc. The five sings are ridge, deso, meiko, mido, diffi, lost, hate, Irmorance, pride, false doctrine (Dh. 68, 421). There are also seven (Dh. 410). Dh. 31, 61, 71, 78, 337, 498.
SĂNGO (adj.), Together with its Ángas (of the Veds)1 with its divulsions [41]. Ab. 411. Sángpropangu, with its divisions and subdivisions (Ab. 691).

SANHO (adj.), Smooth; soft, gentle, mild; delicate, minute, subtle, abstruse [adj.]. B. Lot. 609.

Saphakarsko (adj.), smoothing, levelling (Ab. 1007). Saphaskhmark at Dh. 80 appears to mean "mightly and exactly." Ahaiko (adj.), very abstruse (Dh. 386, of Abhidhamma doctrine). Saphardco (adj.), of mild or gentle speech (Dh. 185). Na kho pasa man saphena samuddearimati, he certainly won't let me off, will not treat me mildly (Dh. 80). Saphadka = slakshqutvak (Dh. 412). Saphena, "gently, mildly," is opposed to pharma, "barshly" (see Puriso).

— BANKAM (adv.), Slowly; safely; quickly [with or more properly rapid + w]. It is curious that this word, which in S. means slowly, should be Pall mean both slowly and quickly. Ab. 1153 gives it the meaning of sigha. In Beshmayu S. we have aditingham gaochati xátiapikni, where it can mean nothing but slowly. At Ját. 9 it must mean slowly, for we are told that one of the advantages of the bark garment is that sapikani kihasari, "it gets dirty slowly," while one of the disadvantages of the sítaks or linen cloak is that Lakwin kiliasni, "It soon gets dirty." At Db. 107, it certainly means quickly; agdakfui died idni sapikani apometed, "seeing some puppe (in the honey-comb he had offered to Baldha), hastily removed them." At Dh. 856 we are told that the temperate man sapikan jirati, "we are out slowly." At Dh. 176 we have, tamed pachiyomínd na kathesuti sapikani spdyema pacechadmi, if she's asked through intimidation she won't tell, I'll question her gradually and craftily." Ját. 4, sákram middlyantash died sapikani gated mopikkhaudkank gapibitd, "seelug the boar asleep went softly and possessed himself of the magic jewel." At F. Ját. 13 it might mean either quickly or softly. The transition of meaning may have seen in the last two examples: first the word meant "slowly," then "safely, gently, defily," and lastly, since what is done gently and defily is apt to be done quickly, it came to mean "quickly." 261; Dh. 411. Saukhalikdi bandhśrót (Yhtr.). SANKHARAKKHANDHO, see next.

SANKHARAKKHANDHO, constructing, preparing, perfecting, embellishing; aggregation; Matter; Karma; the Skandhas [ʌnʌt]. Ab. 832; B. Int. 503. At Ab. 307, ed. 2001, "performing," is explained by gasundhamdiyddisankhdo, "fitting up or embellishing with perfumes, flowers, etc." (comp. Ab. 259). This passage is probably the origin of the strange mistake by which sankhdo and edand st Ab. 779 are said to mean "perfume," whereas they represent the terms smiskkra and vdsang in their Val-ceshika acceptation (the marginal Sinhalese translation is exaixida = sugandha). Bhāmiasakhāro, preparing or clearing a piece of ground (Ah. 832, see margin). As a technical term Sinhakra has several decided shades of meaning. First from the idea the word contains of aggregation or compustidou, we have it in the wide sense of all existing things or substances, matter, the material universe. In this sense it was no doubt originally used in such expressions as aliced sabbarankhdra, vayadhamand sankhdr, etc. At Mah. 191 we read sabbar pi sawkhdragatam avassah yeva bhijfali omicd sabbaraskhdra iti cutlam hi Satthand, which Turnour translates, "for by our divine Teacher it has been announced that all that is launched into this transitory world will most assuredly perish: the whole creation therefore is perilable." Vij. writes to me, "Sankhara-loka is the world of organic and inorganic matter, I think it includes the Sattaloka." I believe the fact to be that originally the division of the universe was into oldraloko and sankhdraloko, "the realm of Spaces and the realm of Matter," and that the Sankhraloka was afterwards subdivided into sattaloko and sankhraloko, the realm of animates and the realm of laaimates. Hence we have the three divisions of the universe into sattaloko, sakkhraloko and okdaloko (see Man. B. 3, where Hardy says "sanskdraloko, the material world, including trees, rocks," etc.). And thus it is that while to some cases sentient beings are included under the term sakkhra, in others the terms satto and sakkhra are distinctly opposed. For a striking example of this opposition see Dh. 359, where we are told that md piyakii samdgracchi la the text means piyakii satt

eki of saikhdradi of huddacamah ekukkhayama pi na samdgaechegya, "let him never even for a moment associate with objects of delight, whether they be persons or things (estimate or inanimate)." Again at B. Int. 505, we read Buddha it ko satio of saikhdro da, "what being or thing is that which we call a Buddha?" It must be clearly nader-stood that the word Satta applies to the living and moving being as a person or individual only, the separate elements of which the being is composed belonging to the saikhdraloka.' Thus the man belongs to the Sattaloka, while the khandhas of which he is made up belong to the saikhdraloka, being themselves inanimate. At Das. 44, 45 will be found a gloss on the word loka, in which we are told that the sattaloka includes beings in this world and the next, the angels, mankind, etc. (at p. 45, line 3, read Siddha pana sattaloka), and that Sikhdraloka includes Ahara or food, the eighteen Dhatus, the Khandhas, etc. The term Sikhkhara is applied to many things that cannot be brought under our term "Matter," such as qualities, attributes and modes of beings and things. Thus not only is a plant a saikhara but its greenness is a saikhhar, not only is a rock a saikhara but its hardness is a saikhhar, not only is a man a saikhara but his vital principle is a saikhara, not only is the eye a saikhara but vision is a saikhara, and the image depicted on the retina is a saikhara (see the dhātu, which are all saikhharas). In fact saikhara includes every thing of which impermanence may be predicated, or, which is the same thing, every thing which springs from a cause (see Saikhata). As Buddhism does not recognize the existence of a Sprena Being or Creator, there are only two things which are uncaused and eternal, namely Okha or Space (or Extension), and Nibbana or Void (to Néaut, non-entity).

Owing to reflections on the Impermanence of things being so frequently associated with death, the term saikhira came to be sometimes used in the restricted sense of the attributes of living beings, conditions of sentient existence. Thus at Dh. v. 903 we have saikhira paramed dukhd, the elements of being are the greatest evil, or Exist-

since is the greatest suffering, where the comment says that saikhdao means the five khandhas (see Alw. N. 84, and 60 note). So in saikhdao sesatid w'atthi at v. 235 Buddha has taken saikhdrd to the sense of the five khandhas, and D'Alwis renders the phrase "no states of existence are eternal." There is, however, nothing in the context to show that elements of sentient being are meant. At v. 368 the context plainly requires a. to be taken in the sense of the elements of sentient existence (metitohidriyo bhikkhu pasasmo buddhasadrome adigachepadah santos saikhdrapasamah sukhash, see art. Nibbānaṃ, p. 271, a, line 14 from bottom, and Alw. N. 59, see also Gog. Ev. 6). At Dh. 383 it is said that the saint who has understood the destruction of the saikhbaras has understood Nievipa (annibilation). In this case S. might perhaps have its widest sense of all existing things, marker, but the commentator again takes it to mean the five khandhas. In Sasanavahsa, a modern Barnese work, in connexion with the death of Buddha I and the foll. reflection, who vata gechariyo saikhdradhammo, "mysterious, alas, are the conditions of existence," where sentient existence is implied. Another use of the term saikhara is in the well-known formula sabbe saikhdr adiced, sabbe saikhdr dukkhid, sabbe saikhdr amatid, ascrbing to existence or Matter the three characteristics (tilakikhama) of impermanence, evil, and unreality. At Dh. 40 disamnd is substituted for saikhdr in the third formula. The comment takes both saikhdr and dhsuma in the sense of the five khandhas, but the substitution is another proof that the meaning of a wide term like saikhara must not be too closely pressed. We may be right in taking these formulas in the sense of "Life is transient, life is evil, life is unreal," but they may also mean "All existing things are transient, evil, unreal" (aund, Dh. 383, line 8). At Dh. 270, line 6, saikhara clearly refers to sentient existence. At Ten J. 119 we have saikhare parigaphited tilakikhaparamamasato paccahabodhidaparipatijjhi, "investigating the nature of things and mastering the three Characteristics, he attained the knowledge of a Pratyeka Buddha." In Br. J. S. A. I find saikhadram abhianikharapalaikkhapak, the essential property of Matter is Aggregation, or the essential property of the Elements of Being

In Organization. At Alw. I. 108 we are told that the world is oppressed by three sufferings or evils, the evil of pain (dukkhadukkhald), the evil of change, and the evil of existence (sankkhara-dukkhaid). From the first two releases is sometimes obtained during life (as in the case of the Brahma and Formless Angels, p. 111, note), but from the third there is no release but in the annihilation of being (annpdidianed nabbodandha).

By anakhadr (pl.), or Aggregations, as a link of the Paticcasamuppada, is meant the aggregates of those states of the mind which bring about the performance of good and bad sections (see Paticcasamuppada). Practically it is identical with Karma or Moral Merit (see Colebrookea Essays, edited by Cowell, London, 1873, vol. i. p. 433), and is rendered by Hardy (Man. B. 391) and Gogerly (Ev. 68), “Merit and Demerit.” The Saakhadras of the Paticcasamuppada are three in number, pañadābissahidra, apurathibhasichidra and dnesijādhiasihidra, good states of mind, sinful states of mind and states of mind leading to immovability. The first of these causes rebirth in the Rāpaṇrabusiloks, the second causes rebirth in the Kūmaloks (including the hells and the world of men), and the third causes rebirth in the Arāpaṇrabmaloks. Jāseija is only another form of Jāseija (which see), and means immovability or impassibility, and is descriptive of the state of steady and immovable abstraction or trance in which the Farnless Angels live. Sabh, quotes from Vis. M. Tikā, saadahipaccatthikānaṃ atidaraṭāyaṃ na tajati anijānasabhavam abhiacikharat dwejkibhisakikhar. The form daṇajibhatisahidra also occurs (see Gog. Ev. 68), where we have a instead of e. For this change compare kaṇajja from kurita, bāhuaseca from bāhuwata, akhalya from sakhila; compare also maōjanigika with sufinga. In his account of the Nidānas Alabaster, not inaptly, renders saṅkhidā by “predispilion” (Wheel of the Law, p. 230). Prom another point of view the saṅkhāras of the Paticcasamuppada are also three, kāyaṃ asahidra, vācaṃ asahidra and cittassihidra, or state of mind which causes good or bad actions, state of mind which causes good or sinful speech, and state of mind which causes good or bad thoughts (log. Ev. 68). They correspond to kāyaṃ asahidra, saṅkhamash and samakamama respectively.

There is, however, nothing in the context to show that elements of sentient being are meant. At v. 368 the context plainly requires a. to be taken in the sense of the elements of sentient existence (metitohidriyo bhikkhu pasasmo buddhasadrome adigachepadah santos saikhdrapasamah sukhash, see art. Nibbānaṃ, p. 271, a, line 14 from bottom, and Alw. N. 59, see also Gog. Ev. 6). At Dh. 383 it is said that the saint who has understood the destruction of the saikhbaras has understood Nievipa (annibilation). In this case S. might perhaps have its widest sense of all existing things, marker, but the commentator again takes it to mean the five khandhas. In Sasanavahsa, a modern Barnese work, in connexion with the death of Buddha I and the foll. reflection, who vata gechariyo saikhdradhammo, "mysterious, alas, are the conditions of existence," where sentient existence is implied. Another use of the term saikhara is in the well-known formula sabbe saikhdr adiced, sabbe saikhdr dukkhid, sabbe saikhdr amatid, ascrbing to existence or Matter the three characteristics (tilakikhama) of impermanence, evil, and unreality. At Dh. 40 disamnd is substituted for saikhdr in the third formula. The comment takes both saikhdr and dhsuma in the sense of the five khandhas, but the substitution is another proof that the meaning of a wide term like saikhara must not be too closely pressed. In Br. J. S. A. I find saikhadram abhianikharapalaikkhapak, the essential property of Matter is Aggregation, or the essential property of the Elements of Being

In Organization. At Alw. I. 108 we are told that the world is oppressed by three sufferings or evils, the evil of pain (dukkhadukkhald), the evil of change, and the evil of existence (sankkhara-dukkhaid). From the first two releases is sometimes obtained during life (as in the case of the Brahma and Formless Angels, p. 111, note), but from the third there is no release but in the annihilation of being (annpdidianed nabbodandha).

By anakhadr (pl.), or Aggregations, as a link of the Paticcasamuppada, is meant the aggregates of those states of the mind which bring about the performance of good and bad sections (see Paticcasamuppada). Practically it is identical with Karma or Moral Merit (see Colebrookea Essays, edited by Cowell, London, 1873, vol. i. p. 433), and is rendered by Hardy (Man. B. 391) and Gogerly (Ev. 68), “Merit and Demerit.” The Saakhadras of the Paticcasamuppada are three in number, pañadābissahidra, apurathibhasichidra and dnesijādhiasihidra, good states of mind, sinful states of mind and states of mind leading to immovability. The first of these causes rebirth in the Rāpaṇrabusiloks, the second causes rebirth in the Kūmaloks (including the hells and the world of men), and the third causes rebirth in the Arāpaṇrabmaloks. Jāseija is only another form of Jāseija (which see), and means immovability or impassibility, and is descriptive of the state of steady and immovable abstraction or trance in which the Farnless Angels live. Sabh, quotes from Vis. M. Tikā, saadahipaccatthikānaṃ atidaraṭāyaṃ na tajati anijānasabhavam abhiacikharat dwejkibhisakikhar. The form daṇajibhatisahidra also occurs (see Gog. Ev. 68), where we have a instead of e. For this change compare kaṇajja from kurita, bāhuaseca from bāhuwata, akhalya from sakhila; compare also maōjanigika with sufinga. In his account of the Nidānas Alabaster, not inaptly, renders saṅkhidā by “predispilion” (Wheel of the Law, p. 230). Prom another point of view the saṅkhāras of the Paticcasamuppada are also three, kāyaṃ asahidra, vācaṃ asahidra and cittassihidra, or state of mind which causes good or bad actions, state of mind which causes good or sinful speech, and state of mind which causes good or bad thoughts (log. Ev. 68). They correspond to kāyaṃ asahidra, saṅkhamash and samakamama respectively.

This cause is Karma, to which every existing thing is due, Space and Nirvapa alone excepted. Asakhata and Akata as epithets of Nirvapa mean Unmade, Unaggregated, Immaterial (comp. Dh. 60, saikkardman khayas noted akatañni't, having known the annihilation of Matter, thou knowest the Immaterial). Saikkhata saikhatahassod includes every possible conception of the human mind (Ten J. 48). At Dh. 413 the khandahx, dhatus and saytasas are called saikhata.—Saikhato madhupdasyo, rice porldge prepared with honey (Msh. 198). Sasaikkatan rdjagehath, well built or handsome place (Msh. 132, comp. 133). Siddhaiskhato padewa, a well-arranged, viz. de-Igbtful spot (Msh. 118). For saikhatahassodman at Dh. 70, see next.—In the sense of Sa-skrit (language) the word shan becomes in Pali sakkato, in our doubtful instance only have I met with saikhato.

Sanghanandisaikhata Makdkeacydyaso, M. who was called 9. (Alw. I. 104, comp. cxxiv). Yathdhuccabrahmacahdra-artyacahdrasankhadt Mdagdhikabhad, the Pali language, reckoned as the truly sublime and noble tongue (Alw. I. cvil). Thryyasaakhdam at Pit. 3 seems to be used adverbially, and is rendered by Gogerly "with theivish intest;" the comment at p. 66 seems to take saikhata to the sense of clito, "thought, purpose." Saikhadakhammo (adj.), one by whom the Truth has been weighed or estimated, is an epithet of the Arlyapaggalas. It occurs in Khaggaivala 8, where Coomaraaswamy renders it "acquainted with justice," and at Dh. v. 70, where the & is shortened either metri canad, or far more probably by the stupidity of the copylists, who concluded it must be equivalent to saikhatidharma. Ab. 228. Nom. santo (F. Jct. 13). Acc. santoch. Instr. said, santena (Mh. 177). Gen. and dat. sato, santana (dahara't eca sato). Nom. pl. santo. Acc. pl. santo (Ten J. 119). Instr. and abt. pl. abthi (Dh. 28). santohi. Gen. and dat. pl. santo (Dh. 10, 14, 28; Mah. 199; Gog. Ev. 31, m. som. satoam, of those who are men). Loc. pl. santem (Dh. 259). In phrases of this sort with a fem. noun we have sati instead of satiyd. Examples will be found at Pit. 28, dpathtyd sati, and Jit. 4, jdhtyd sati (comp. pucchdya sati, if the question be asked, Ystr.). Loc. abs. pl. Baham pupphera som.tem, when there are many flowers (Dh. 253). Neut. santain, that which is, asantam, that which is not (Kamn. 4). Pl. santa, good men (Dh. 15, 28, 53; Alw. I. 107). 6ATTALOKO, World of sentient being [ᠮᠠ + ᠪᠠᠭ]. This is one of the three divisions of the universe (see Loko, Saakikaro). According to the Buddhist cosmology the universe consists of an infinite number of cakkavillas or spheres,1 sampled by various orders of living beings, to each of which is assigned a particular abode (Loko, Shamsank). Within the cakkavilla, These abodes or worlds are disposed one above another, below, upon and above Mount Meru. [vay], Mah. 2, 78; Alw. I. 79. To s. rjd elappayl, the king himself served them (Mah. 62). S. abhinanda, having learnt by myself (Dh. 63). Soyam eva (Ten J. 115). With a fem. noun (Mah. 113). With a plur. noun S, pabbajhim, they themselves took orders (Dh. 142; comp. F. Ját. 17). SAYAM, see Sigo,
SĀYAMĀSO, Evening meal, supper [ᠰᠠᠷᠠᠨ + ᠪᠠᠷᠠ]. Db. 163.

SAYAMBHſO (adj.), Self-produced, self-sufficient, independent [ᠰᠠᠭᠠᠨ]. This is an epithet of a Buddha (Ab. 4). Bornout says admirably (B. Lot. 330), "This term, which is only an epithet, must not be confounded with the appellation Sya-yambin, which occupies so prominent a place in Brahminical mythology. I imagine that as used by Buddhists this epithet expresses the independent nature of a Buddha, who, as soon as he has attained to a knowledge of the emptiness of all laws and conditions, has no longer any other substratum or raison d'être than himself." He then quotes from Mahavahasa Yika, apt ca yo so Bhagad sayamhā andcariyako publis anannass-term dhammaesu adman saccadi abhiambujhi, and this Blessed One self-dependent, without a teacher, by himself discovered Truth in doctrines hitherto unheard. Vij. writes to me, "Seyambha means one whose knowledge is underlived, self-produced (sagam bhitiya panidya yatto sayambha)." Sayambhadipam, "self-derived or original knowledge," as an epithet of the knowledge of a Buddha occurs in very old texts (see Sikhasshamika). If sayambha, as an epithet of a Buddha, belongs to the earliest age of Buddhism, it affords another instance of the way in which Gautama appropriated the Brahminical terms while materially altering their meaning (comp. Mahabrahmd).
SAYAMPABHO (adj.), Self-resplendeut [สายมหา]. SAYAMPVARÃ (f.), A maiden who chooses a husband [สายพาด]. Ab. 235.

SAYANAM, and SENAM, Lying, sleeping; a bed, couch [沖], Ab. 308, 1121. Bħalda, a large bed, i.e. a bed beyond a certain prescribed width, was forbidden to the plexis. Sayamaahdama, sleeping place (Dh. 83). Attuso sayuagumbe, in the jungle which was his lair (F. Jét. 54, of a jackal). Bħalmaaymak, lying on the ground (Dh. 308). Mab. 83, 194; Dh. 46. The term/sendamaah, = 194 + 194 (once we have sayandana, Dh. 34) appears to mean originally "sleeping and sitting," and hence "dwelling." Rukhhamilasendasossa gatagatafthane suluhataya, from the easy outaiment of a lodging at the foot of a tree wherever you go (Jét, 10, comp. Kamp. 9). D'Alwis renders saoceldhas. at Alw. I. 78 by "nine kinds of habitations adapted to the recluse." Vij. renders sendaanaghako, "steward or housekeeper of an establishment." Sendasa-vottash, "duties of the bed-chamber" (Coruelina Alwis). At Mah. 12 it is used as a synonym for vihara (monastery). It may also mean a bed or bedding (Ab. 1121). Hardy renders sendaanaddam, "the gift of a pallet on which to recline" (E. Mon. 81). Ekamante vicittum kdrtpetod a ddpeai, gave them beds made variegated or embroidered on one side (Ph. 100).

BEKHIYO (adj.), Connected with training [$\pi$]. The seventy sekhiyd disassend are minor precepts regulating the conduct of the priest, and applying to his mode of dress, department, eating, etc. They are also called sekhiyorattah. E. Mon. 9; B. Int. 308; Pát. 20.

— BEKHO, One who is under training [T]w]. This term is applied to the first seven Ariypuggalas, the eighth or Arhat being azekho. It implies that they have still a remainder of human passion to eradicate, still duties to perform, still a probation to be passed through. The seven Sekhas or Sekhspuggalas are sotdpattimagguffho, sotdpattiphalaffho, sakaddqdmimagguffho, sakaddqdmiphalaffho, arshattamagguffho. Of these the first has a maximum of human passion to get rid of, and the last a minimum, being but very slightly removed from the perfect sanctification of the arshatta phalaffho or Arhat (see Maggo). The foll, is Buddhaghosa's gloss on sekho in verse 45 of Dhaomapada, Sekho ti adhisiarikkhd adhislita-sikkhā adhipaṭidikkhā titiadā niem sikkhā sikkhilo sotdpattimaggaffdhank dthāni katedōyāo arshattamaggaffhd satqidāho sekho, by Sekha are menat the seven Sekhas beginning with Sotdpattimaggship and ending with Arhattamaggaship, who are disciplined in these three disciplines, lofty morality, lofty thought and lofty wisdom (Dh. 209). Toat ca sekho sakurapiyho, thou art yet under discipline and hast duties to perform (B. Lot. 227). Appatamiamāno sekho, one who is yet a Sekha and has not attained Arhatship (Dh. 255). Sekhasiam is the moral practice of a sekha, the duties he performs to get rid of human passion (Man. B. 493). Ab. 435; Alw. I. 78; B. Int. 392; B. Lot. 235. Sometimes written

SILAOHATI, To praise [ʌˈtɑːr]. With dat. Had dhasa sildghata, he praises Buddha (Sen. K. 397). SILAḫ, Nature, character; habits, customs, practice, conduct; moral practice, piety, morality; a moral precept [ʌˈtɑːr]. Ab. 178, 430, 1091; Dh. 28, 53; Kh. 13. Silam A etos addhimam, for this is the custom of wicked men (Ras. 88). Hihadafio (adj.), disposed to destruction, mischievous (Ab. 731, comp. 733). \Vddassilo, disputations. Didsoppomasilio, one whose habit it is to sleep in the day-time (Slg. 8.). With affix, akammafittam, laziness (Mah. 138). SilabAedo, a breach of morality (Dh. 158). Silagundho, the fragrance of good works (Dh. 10). Samparmasilo (adj.), moral, virtuous (Dh. 11). Silacdro, the practice of morality. Silamattakuh, a mere question of ordinary morality (Br. J. S.)/Silamattas püretus adakkhi, you could not even keep the precepts, or you could not fulfil the ordinary duties of morality (Dh. 88). Silam rakkhati, to keep the precepts (F. Jat. 59). Adam pl'sa hoti silamut, this doctrine (not to destroy life) finds a place in his morality (see B. Lot. 464, line 3, comment says, idam pi assa bhikkhumo ppudtipidderamapilish alasmish ekam silam hoti). Silakkhanda, body of moral precepts, code of morality. This is given in full in Br. J. S. and Silamfapahala S., and consists of a number of precepts governing the life of the Buddibhat priest. It is divided into cātaḫlam (or cūlaḫ), majikimam and mahālikam. Minor morality, Middle morality and Greater morality. It is strange that we find the position of cūla and mahā reversed according to our notions, the cōlaśila embrading precepts forbidding murder, theft, lying, etc., and the mahāśila dealing chiefly with unworthy employments, such as various sorts of divination, etc. It is difficult to account for this nomenclature; bùbh. says the cōlaśila is so called because it is the easiest to keep. I think there can be little doubt that the three divisions of the sila are literary or recreational (like the bhāpavārs), and

have no reference to the nature of the precepta classified. I have as yet not met with the three terms in a triplitaks text, though they are frequently met with in the commentaries (e.g. see A.W. I. 78; Dh. 258, 407). It is true that the headings ed安市文，etc., are found in the M68. of Br. J. S. and SIm. S., but there is nothing whatever to show that they belong to the original text, indeed the contrary in almost necessarily implied. The text of the sils is translated by Burnoff in the Lotus, pp. 463-471 (in his note p. 465 for mila read edis). The ten Siles are ten precepts regulating the conduct of the Buddhist priest (dasatlam, dasazidham silah, Mah. 110, Jat. 29), respectively prohibiting the destruction of life, theft, imparity, lying, the use of intoxicating liquors, eating at forbidden hours, attending worldly amusements, the use of inguents and ornaments, the use of a large or ornamented couch, and the receiving of money (Kh. 2; E. Mon. 23). The eight Silas (athrognastish, Att. 204) are the first eight of these (Att. 82). The first five Silas (paesatlas) are binding on all Buddhists, and answer to our Deculegue, as they briefly soon up the primary duties of man, A layman may acquire merit by observing the five, eight, or even the ten Silas either for a limited period or till death (thus at Att. 204 a king undertakes to observe the eight precepts, see Samidigati). See Man. B. 489-494.

In some of the oblique cases we meet occasionally with the foli. substitutes when a non already mentioned is referred to (comp. Ema). For the ace. masc. nam, equivalent to task (Tec J. 1; Dh. 1, 99, 153, 177, 299). For the abl. masc. namhd, equivalent to tanhd (Mah. 87). For the nom. and nec. pl. nec, equivalent to te (F. Ját. 17; Dh. 187). For the gen. and dat. pl. nesam (F. Ját. 2; Dh. 192, 153, 299). According to Kacekyna these substitutes may be used throughout the whole declension, in all three genders; and the vriti gives the examples ndya, nash, ne, nem, namhd, udhi (Sen. K. 281).

So samo, he is the true gramma (Dh. 26). Tam me moram madhya piyabhariyad maid, on account of this peacock may beloved wife is dead (Ten Jat. 113). So may sometimes be rendered by "the": Tato ta' c'eva sambuddham Nongadharas... draddhetad, thereafter having supplicated also the Bodbbs K. (Mah. 1, Turnour, however, separates ceva into ca iva, and renders, "as in the case of that supreme Buddha," i.e. Dipankara, but I think his rendering is inadmissible). Sd Hagadhi saidabhad, the Maguddi is the original language (Mah. xxvil). Milindo nama so rjd, the king named Miluda. This pronoun is sometimes added pleonastically to the pronouns alash and team for emphasis. So who alash haite (8km. 8). The abl. tasmd is often used adverbially in the sense of “thereby, therefore, accordingly” (Dh. 65, 69; F. Ját. 3). The base in composition is $\pi\pi$, the final component undergoing the usual sandhi changes. It may stand for the mass, temp, or vent pronoun in either number. Tammajjihagato (adj.), in the midst of it. Tadadikheki, with the halves of them (Mah. 41). Tadassachaviko (adj.), suitable thereto (Alw. I. 99). Tadabhmukhd (adj.) ahesusi, presented themselves before him (Db. 68). Taddahro tadapddamo (adj.), fed upon this, having this for fuel (Alw. N. 38). In one curious instance we find and compounded with a gerund, tadshthya, “arlsing from it” (Db. v. 340, comment says to afshdyo). There is an ludellable or adverb temp = 77, “there, thither, therefore, now, etc.” Tash me midments, therefore let them attend to me. Tash tak namassdmi, therefore I salute thee (Ten J. 47, comment says to and). We have this indeelishable in phrases like yena Muhild tad avasari. With preceding yathd: Yathid took dumnati, like a foolish person (Das. 31, comment says ettha tum ti nipdtamattah). Yathid taxi youd yuvatish, as a youth might (address) a young girl (Pit. 4, here also comment makes the same remark); see a third example under Okam. curred to me (Sen. K. 348). Itihank suchah Bhagazd dyamastaw Ridulah undhi gdhidhi abihinkah oadi, thus did Buddha repeatedly admonish the venerable Rhibula with these stanzas (Rhibula S.; at Dh. 316 read itthah sudah for itthi sudah; itthah sudah, "thus," may be compared with kathah su, "how?"). Tsu-fru sudah Bhagazd Ndlike viharento, at that time Buddha, dwelling at Nidika... (Par. S. 90, comp. Dh. 105; we have also tatra pi sudah, Par. S. 18). Sloce a consonant in Puli cannot stand at the end of a word, an original final consonant is usually either omitted or a vowel is placed after it. Hence feng becomes su or suda, and the latter form is generally strengthened to such by the addition of asuswire (comp. kpanah, kahah, kudocananah, elassanah, sakkuccah). I have once met with the form ruda in a passage quoted by Subh., appafiddi ruddahah bhikkhave padhanah podahami, where suddahah is uda aham. When I wrote my article ASSU, I inclined to the belief that the native grammarists had wrongly evolved a form asu derived from a mistaken view of warda like tayman, kmasan. But we have now positive proof of the existence of asu, for at Jdi. 196 we find is a very old text the word suasaw, which can only be resolved into so asu (comp. suahah = so aham). The comment says asudi wpidamattah. In the same line we have tad asu = tadd asu (comp. tay' asu = tagu asu). Asu points to a form asvld, just as itthi points to a form latri, comp. also asma, ama, "we are," with smas.

TADI (adj.), Like that, such [TADI]. Tyddemaaggajinah nadwata Buddhid, such a man the Buddhas call maggajina. Deed ptassa phayawhtiddino, even the angels envy him being such a man (Dh. v. 84, comment says tathdrapama, comp. v. 85). A curious secondary meaning has been super-induced upon the plain and ordinary meaning of this word. When a Buddha and his arbat disciplines are mentioned together, the latter are often called tiddi, "like him," i.e. like their Master, sanctified, holy. Thus at Mah. 88 we are told that Kakusandhs Buddha was catatjlesahassehitiddhi partdrito, accompanied by forty thousand men like himself, where Turnour has "accompanied by forty thousand sanctified disciples." At p. 91 we have the expressal tishabikkikhsahassehitiddhi partdrito used of KopjagamansBuddhs, Turnour again using the word "sanctified" (see the parallel passage at Jét. 13). Next we have such expressions as supapplitash peveasans arakatschi tiddhi (Jét. 29), where Vijassures me that the word is used absolutely, in the sense of sanctified or tracquil. He tells me that he finds in a Sinhalese Gaphlipada treatise, tiddihlyanu sahalokadharmayeh ekikkaravi, "the word tiddhi means being serene in the eight conditions of life." It will be observed that tiddihaving lost its original consonant term, is treated as a masse in it and declined like mawi. At Dh. v. 85, if we believe the comment, the word is used in both senses, for it explains tiddin the first hemlatych by atthahikodaharmayeh akampiyabdoena tiddi, and tiddino in the second hemlatych by avarapassa. In the next verse D'Alwis says that sponataisaiddiss means "he who is firm and tranquil".

The three Taphás are kēmatapák, rápat, arápat, desire for rebirth in the three forces of existence (see Bhao, Loko). rounds, etc., or the last of the eye, the ear, etc. (comp. Kámaggo, see Db. 410). There are also 106 (aphis, upon which Vij. writes to me as follows: "The six taphis may each be perceived in the light of káms, bhava, and vibhava. a Buddha It means the Belug per excellence, the Great Belug (comp. dipodsttawo, sarastho). The nadie explanations of the term are purely faudful (B. 1st. 75).

— TATHAROPO (adj.), Of such a description, such; suitable, appropriate, adequate [πανέχει]. Dh, 19. Aññatro tathdrāpād paccayd, without a sufficient cause (Pát. 15). Tathdrāpo poppadhro, a suitable present (F. Ját. 16). Fem, tathdrāpí (Dh. 146).

— TATO (ado.), From that place, theace, therefrom; from that time; thereafter, subsequently; further, moreover [ท้าที], T. gasted, having gone thence (Mah. 204, comp. 150). T. cato, having vanished thence, having left that world. T. tatiye vase, in the third year from that time (Mah. 6). Tato paakuti, tatoppahti, from that time forward (Mah. 196, 207). T. adhikami ratamani, a better jewel than this (Alw. I. 75). Papiya tato, worse than that (Dh. 8, comp. 57). T. nikkhami, came out of it, i.e. of the egg (F. Jdi. 49). Dakkhipato tato, to the southward thereof (Mah. 57). T. parad, t. amataram, afterwards. Representing a plural nom. TATO (adj.), Reaperted, dear [TAT]. Tito, a father (Ab. 243). The voc. tita is a term of endearment or a friendly mode of familiar address, "my dear, my good sir." The pl. tido is used when more than one person is addressed. By a son to his father: Tita as elour's era one redid ditto, my dear father, I have only just seen the king (F. Jat. 9, comp. Ten J. 54). By a father to his son (F. Jat. 9; Dh. 128, 303). By an elder to a younger brother (Dh. 79). By a king to his elephant: Rajjati to tito Kapala daomi, I be stow the sovereignty upon you, my good K. (Mah. 152). By Buddha to Niga kinga (Mah. 6). By an Aariya to his disciples (Dh. 132). By King Asoka (before his conversion) to a samspers (Mah. 25). By a young lady of fashion to brahmins (Dh. 234). To a chance passer by (Dh. 113).

TAY

means in past existences (Db. 433, comp. 898, 430, etc.). Tattha is sometimes treated almost as if it were the loc. sing. or pl. of ng, and equivalent to tammis or tesu. Na tattha sineham karoti, puts not his affection therein (Jat. 21, where we might expect taṃmiś); Leithach tattha adcayt, read the writing upon it (Mah. 162); at Mah. 201 we might almost take tattha cetiye as equivalent to taṃmiś cetiye; as Kamm. 8, Tattha te yadajilam usadha karayiyo, in this you must persevere all your life. Tattha avindgakath sucayarajatiddi, of these two the Inanimate is gold, silver, etc. (Alw. I. 76). Tattha kalamad arijid, of these, or in this passage, what is Ignorance (Gog. Ev. 87).
