Tatth' adand sard attha, of these the eight ending with o are vowels (Sen. K. 201). With foll. eva: Tatth' eva matu, died on the spot (F. Jat. 4); Tatth' eva metod, having brought her to that very place (Db. 133). Mah. 87; Dh. 98. With foll. apt, tatthapi, there also (Mah. 86). TATTAKO (adj.), Barling [✉]+ ✉].

TATTAKO (adj.), As many, as great (comp. ettako, kittako). Tatlakni pupphdni okiri, scattered the same quantity of flowers (Mah. 88, 193). Cospdid tatakd, the same number of caqdiles (Mah. 68). Ucato tatako yera, and in height of the very same duneusous (Mah. 163). Yojawadni atak dighad tatakah pathelam tatak, a hundred yojana long and as many broad. Tattakam klan khepetod, having waited all that time (Dh. 129). Tatlakah dhamad dated, paying such an immense sum for it (Dh. 249). See Yattakank.
TATTHA, see Tatra.
TATTO, see Tapati.

TATVAM, Essence, reality [πτῶν], Ab. 1175.

Tutvata, accurately (Das. 1).
TAVA, TAVAỰ, see Toth.

TAVA (adv.), At onea, now, just; really, indeed; yet, still [TTA]. Tifthatha t., stop a minute (Dh. 86). Ahah t. sabbakileshandianahi mito nisesase paca, I indeed am released from all the bonds of human pasdon.., but at my bose.. (Ten J. 120, comp. Dh. 96). Darint t. dardpetha, do you be so good as to have me supplied with wood (Dh. 324). Migdramfthi t.., gantod, M. accordingly having set out (Dh. 238). Katipahani dassah t. demi, let me give alms for a few days longer (Dh. 869). Nahdylaadai t., I'll just have a bathe (Dh. 224). Imath toan dasaman t. dajham hatod samadiya, do you only strenuously take upon you this tenth paramit (Jat. 84). With preceding us: Na thao sitthdi, it is not fulished yet (Dh. 323, comp. Mah. 54, 98). Fakhkhai t. jdaiti mama jdtih, why thla yakkhlni actually knows my rank (Mah. 48). T. often adds very little to the sense, merely emphasizing the sentence (Dh. 99; Aiw. I. 77; F. Jac. 8, 40). With foll. sea, the final consonant being revived for emphoy, tdoad eva, immediately, thereupon, straightway, now, at once (Aiw. I. 77; Jat. 55; F. Jat. 40; Dh. 134; Ten J. 114, 120; Kamm. 8). Tdoade, a shortened form of idoad eva, frequently occurs. It is a curious instance of "forming back," for as thoedea looks as though it might be resolvable into tdoade + eva (tapode 'va), the omission of va gives thode. Nafiso dickkhit tdoade, instantly reported it to the king (Mah. 154, comp. 230; Jat. 18; Cl. Gr. 75). See Ydoa.
TAVATA (ado.), So far, to that extent, on that account [111]. Dh. 47. Comp. Ydoatd.
TÄVATAKO (adj.), So many; so much, so great, so long [+]. Tiegtakd puttaattd, so many sons and grandsons (Dh. 248). Dh. 828. Ben Yénotako.
TẠVẠTIHÁM, see Ydoatihah.

TAYATIMSO (adj.), Belonging to thirty-three. The Tualatim's deed are the inhabitants of the lowest devaloka but one, slimmed on the summit of Mount Meru. They are so called because they form the suite of thirty-three superior angels of whom the archangel Sakka (Indra) is the first (B. 1st, 604; Man. B. 3, 11, 25; Dh. 297, 360). The T. heaven is called Thetishabhaanash (Dh. 94, 107), or Thetishadevaloko (Dh. 102). It is also sometimes called simply Thetishara, the word shavanam being understood (Thetishama guschanid, Mah. 102, Thetishamakhi albhatid, Mah. 178, comp. 181). Thetishamdevagara, the city of the T. angels (Dh. 100). Thetishad sabda, the Tualatima hall of assembly (Mah. 102). Thetishaka is a curious taddbita derivative of swayarlimca, for the change of y to x comp. dudha=wiyaj, and many others. I have not yet met with a list of the names of the thirty-three angels. TAYA, see Town.

Tutvata, accurately (Das. 1).

TAVA, TAVAỰ, see Toth.

TAVA (adv.), At onea, now, just; really, indeed; yet, still [TTA]. Tifthatha t., stop a minute (Dh. 86). Ahah t. sabbakileshandianahi mito nisesase paca, I indeed am released from all the bonds of human pasdon.., but at my bose.. (Ten J. 120, comp. Dh. 96). Darint t. dardpetha, do you be so good as to have me supplied with wood (Dh. 324). Migdramfthi t.., gantod, M. accordingly having set out (Dh. 238). Katipahani dassah t. demi, let me give alms for a few days longer (Dh. 869). Nahdylaadai t., I'll just have a bathe (Dh. 224). Imath toan dasaman t. dajham hatod samadiya, do you only strenuously take upon you this tenth paramit (Jat. 84). With preceding us: Na thao sitthdi, it is not fulished yet (Dh. 323, comp. Mah. 54, 98). Fakhkhai t. jdaiti mama jdtih, why thla yakkhlni actually knows my rank (Mah. 48). T. often adds very little to the sense, merely emphasizing the sentence (Dh. 99; Aiw. I. 77; F. Jac. 8, 40). With foll. sea, the final consonant being revived for emphoy, tdoad eva, immediately, thereupon, straightway, now, at once (Aiw. I. 77; Jat. 55; F. Jat. 40; Dh. 134; Ten J. 114, 120; Kamm. 8). Tdoade, a shortened form of idoad eva, frequently occurs. It is a curious instance of "forming back," for as thoedea looks as though it might be resolvable into tdoade + eva (tapode 'va), the omission of va gives thode. Nafiso dickkhit tdoade, instantly reported it to the king (Mah. 154, comp. 230; Jat. 18; Cl. Gr. 75). See Ydoa.



TAVATA (ado.), So far, to that extent, on that account [111]. Dh. 47. Comp. Ydoatd.

TÄVATAKO (adj.), So many; so much, so great, so long [+]. Tiegtakd puttaattd, so many sons and grandsons (Dh. 248). Dh. 828. Ben Yénotako.

TẠVẠTIHÁM, see Ydoatihah.

TAYATIMSO (adj.), Belonging to thirty-three. The Tualatim's deed are the inhabitants of the lowest devaloka but one, slimmed on the summit of Mount Meru. They are so called because they form the suite of thirty-three superior angels of whom the archangel Sakka (Indra) is the first (B. 1st, 604; Man. B. 3, 11, 25; Dh. 297, 360). The T. heaven is called Thetishabhaanash (Dh. 94, 107), or Thetishadevaloko (Dh. 102). It is also sometimes called simply Thetishara, the word shavanam being understood (Thetishama guschanid, Mah. 102, Thetishamakhi albhatid, Mah. 178, comp. 181). Thetishamdevagara, the city of the T. angels (Dh. 100). Thetishad sabda, the Tualatima hall of assembly (Mah. 102). Thetishaka is a curious taddbita derivative of swayarlimca, for the change of y to x comp. dudha=wiyaj, and many others. I have not yet met with a list of the names of the thirty-three angels. TAYA, see Town.

THA

fasting (Tsu J. 89). Kih tamhadish mama ga-

manathdnama, what business of yours is it where I'm going, lit. what have you to do with the place of my golug? (Dh. 339). Loe, khasa, in certain lastances, in the right place (Sen. K. 213). Ucces phamara thapoted, placing them in high offices or appointments. Aggamakathdnasa, dignity of queen consort (Dh. 160). Sendpatitdhasa, office of commander-in-chief (Mah. 69; Alw. I. 79). Seryasi abodrikathdasa thatodasa, "taking on himself the office of sentinel" (Mah. 117). Dhittdhasa thaperodasa, "adopting her as his daughter," lit. putting her in the post of his daughter (Mah. 222). Tamha ashadkiur pitutdhasa third, you stand to us in the place of a father (Das. 3). Dh. 219; Mah. 3, 118, 123. Sotapattimagayadhasa, the condition of being in the first Path (Dh. 209). Vladikathdanas gaechoti, to come to a state of intimacy (Dh. 216). Gaukhithadasi, knotty points (in the Vedas, Mah. 29). Kankhadhadasi, doubtful points (Trenckner). Pafica okabbafkhindsi, five points upon which there is non-liability. Appamaatara pi thassu kukkuconni karisina, were scrupulous even in the most trivial matters, or on the most trivial points (Dh. 416). Cha asumatifhadasi, six subjects for meditation. Saurato thi thachchi, restrained in three matters or under three heads (kiyama, vdcaya, mangad, Dh. 70, comp. Pita. 108). Etehi thi thaduchi, by three three things (Dh. 40, comp. 23 and 55, where it may possibly be rendered "states," but comment says dukkhakhadrasut). Ucces phamara thapoted, placing them in high offices or appointments. Aggamakathdnasa, dignity of queen consort (Dh. 160). Sendpatitdhasa, office of commander-in-chief (Mah. 69; Alw. I. 79). Seryasi abodrikathdasa thatodasa, "taking on himself the office of sentinel" (Mah. 117). Dhittdhasa thaperodasa, "adopting her as his daughter," lit. putting her in the post of his daughter (Mah. 222). Tamha ashadkiur pitutdhasa third, you stand to us in the place of a father (Das. 3). Dh. 219; Mah. 3, 118, 123. Sotapattimagayadhasa, the condition of being in the first Path (Dh. 209). Vladikathdanas gaechoti, to come to a state of intimacy (Dh. 216). Gaukhithadasi, knotty points (in the Vedas, Mah. 29). Kankhadhadasi, doubtful points (Trenckner). Pafica okabbafkhindsi, five points upon which there is non-liability. Appamaatara pi thassu kukkuconni karisina, were scrupulous even in the most trivial matters, or on the most trivial points (Dh. 416). Cha asumatifhadasi, six subjects for meditation. Saurato thi thachchi, restrained in three matters or under three heads (kiyama, vdcaya, mangad, Dh. 70, comp. Pita. 108). Etehi thi thaduchi, by three three things (Dh. 40, comp. 23 and 55, where it may possibly be rendered "states," but comment says dukkhakhadrasut). Pubbaathdnasa, the first thing, the most important point (Dh. 423). Apprakord thashok, unquestionable things or theses, absolute truth. Duddassom idass thashas, this is a difficult matter or subject for them to understand (Gog. Ev. 6). Thandidhasa, right and wrong thesis, probability and improbability, truth and falsehood (B. Lot. 782-4). Kammathdanam, basis of action. Thona, like pada, of which it is said by the grammarians to be a synonym, sometimes adds little or nothing to the sense when the last part of a compound, as in panda daithasah, "temptation," = panda, unless we take this compound to mean "cause of delay" (Kh. 18; B. Lot. 444). Teki thachchi gabbahara garahastititshaya, by these means women get with child (Saikhiyirtha Praksha). Gastad vitekischafhadad, knots (i.e. knotty passages) the source

of doubt. THERIYO (adj.), Belonging to therms [sahif+

]. The first sangiti was called theriyd, because

It was held by therms (Mah. 14, 20; also therikd,

E. Mon. 177). At Mah. 250 theriyd (maac. pl.)

is rendered by Turnour “the fraterolles who had

composed the theravdd.”

- THERO, An old man; a Buddhist monk of a certain standing, a senior priest, an elder [man]. Ab. 254; Dh. 46. There are sold to be three sorts of them, jitithero, dhammaithero, sammuithero, the first means merely an old man, and the others I think mean respectively, a priest who is venerable for his piety, and a priest who is generally recognized as a thera, that is, has merely attained a certain seniority, without reference to plenty or learning. The term there is a courtesy title given to a bhikkhu who has completed a certain number of years from his upasampadi or admission to priest's orders. The number of years is I think ten (E. Moo. 11; B. Int. 289). Therataro (adj.), senior, older, rather old. Therapdo, a venerable thera (Kb. 24). Therasanah, seal of the senior priest, president's chair (Alw. I. 100; Mah. 12, see Songho). Therakard dhammad, qualities that constitute a thera (Db. 378). There is a thero war, an excellent priest (Mah. 171). Fem. theri, a senior Buddhist nun (Dh. 985). Therugdho, “sluzas spoken by priests,” and Therigdho, “stansas spoken by nuns,” are the names of two books of the Khuddakanikeym. For theraoddo see Vido.

- TITTHIYO, An adherent of a heretical sect or system of philosophy, a sectarian, heretic, uncritudox believer [TTH]. B. Int. 158; Dh. 208; Mah. 20, 30; E. Mon. 179, 303; Man. B. 225. Tithigamata, doctrines of heretics (Kh. 20). In the adj./ofistilithyo, “heretical” (Pit. iii), the term, ya belong to the whole compound, affaittihs meaning “another belief, adverse doctrines” (see Titho). Six tirchlyas or heretical teachers are frequently mentioned as existing in Gautama's time, each with a considerable following (Att. ex; B. Lot. 453; Man. B. 290). They were first, Pirano Kasapio, who was a naked asctic, and who held the doctrines that there is no moral merit or damerit (Karma). Secondly, Mahkhaliigoedo, who was also a naked usetic; he held that the suffering or happiness of beings is uncased, and his doctrine is really identical with Purana's, though expressed in different language. Thirdly, Ajito Kasakambali, a nathhikavdin or nhillat (s'atthi dimam n'atthi hutash, n'atthi makafa-dukkakidnak kommdmak pholam vipoko, n'atthi ayam loko n'atthi paraloko, n'atthi madi w'atthi pitu, etc.; the comment observes that Purana and Makkhal were also practically bilibiliants. Fourthly, Pakudha Kacedyana, whose doctrine as given in Sam. S. is that there are seven great kiyma or elements, viz. Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Good, Evil, and Life, which are "uncreats, barren, stable, immutable, exerting no reciprocal action upon each other." Fithly, Nigaytho Natapatto, who preaches to Ajitatansatto the doctrine of Cituyama samosaro, the first of which was abstinence from cold water (sabbondricritto hoti). Sixthly, Sakijayo Belatihipatto, whose doctrine was the omaravikkhopa.

TUDAMPATI (m.), Husband and wife (Ab. 249). Of the existence of this curious form there can be no doubt, as Kaccayana has the Sūtra, JAYA TCDAM JANI PATIMBI (Ben. K. 884). The Sansk word dampati is rightly referred by the native grammarians to jāypati, but it is in Pall that we find the missing link that connects forms so different. This link is jāyampati, the long a of the first syllable being shortened, and that of the second changed to a (for the latter change we have an exact parallel in Sujampati, "husband of Sujd"). The next change is one of compression, jayampati being shortened to jampati, which occurs in Sanskrit. Lasily, the j passes into d, and we get dampati, which Vij. tells me he has with also in Pall (for the change of j to d comp. daddallati = jāyvalati, Poeradi = Prasunjit, dighaockd = jighataid). The form tudaupati offers considerable difficulty. It is difficult to see how it can have arisen out of jayampati, and it may possibly be a sort of capricious outgrowth of dampati (by reduplication). Or may I hazard with great difference the conjecture whether it might be dissimulated from dudaupati = dvida
paid, dvi being prefixed to show the duality, which is otherwise not apparent in Pall? (dampati in Pall la a masc. sing., for du = dvl, comp. dskak, d-rotata, etc.).

TUDAMPATI (m.), Husband and wife (Ab. 249). Of the existence of this curious form there can be no doubt, as Kaccayana has the Sūtra, JAYA TCDAM JANI PATIMBI (Ben. K. 884). The Sansk word dampati is rightly referred by the native grammarians to jāypati, but it is in Pall that we find the missing link that connects forms so different. This link is jāyampati, the long a of the first syllable being shortened, and that of the second changed to a (for the latter change we have an exact parallel in Sujampati, "husband of Sujd"). The next change is one of compression, jayampati being shortened to jampati, which occurs in Sanskrit. Lasily, the j passes into d, and we get dampati, which Vij. tells me he has with also in Pall (for the change of j to d comp. daddallati = jāyvalati, Poeradi = Prasunjit, dighaockd = jighataid). The form tudaupati offers considerable difficulty. It is difficult to see how it can have arisen out of jayampati, and it may possibly be a sort of capricious outgrowth of dampati (by reduplication). Or may I hazard with great difference the conjecture whether it might be dissimulated from dudaupati = dvida

paid, dvi being prefixed to show the duality, which is otherwise not apparent in Pall? (dampati in Pall la a masc. sing., for du = dvl, comp. dskak, d-rotata, etc.).

If I am right we have only one form to account for, vis, a p.p.p. from a caus. subbilidpeti, pointing to a possible abbilitis which I am inclined to identify with v. comp. (from visq), “to throw upwards” (from visq, comp. visq). On the other hand, assuming abbilid to be an exilating form, it points to a noun abbilita, “elation,” from which abbiliti might be a denominative. This abbilita might be a possible undrilya from v. or odvolla from visq. It would be interesting to know what Pull word is

Ubhatomukho also seems to mean a horse with a mouth at each end (taeso delas pasamwa yapamadi deuti so dolhi mukheki khadati, Dan. 25) or possibly with two heads. Ubhatobhdgavimutto is a technical Buddhist term. I owe to Subb. the full passage from Vis. M., ardayajhdama ceva ariyamaggena ctti ushato-bhigena vimutto it abhatobhdgavimutto, u. means one who is emancipated in two ways, namely by arupajhdana and by arlyamaggga. — UDĂNAM, Upward aspiration, enthusiastic or joyous utterance, expression of intense feeling (whether of joy or sorrow) in words [337]. B. Lot. 892. This term is applied to one or more verses in which a speaker expresses the sudden emotion of his heart on some critical, or mournful, or joyous occasion. These verses are hardened with the phrase it is made as addicted, "breached forth this solemn utterance." The most striking of these definitions is the famous hymn of triumph altered by Gantama Buddha when he stalled onnsilence on the thorns of bodh (ᠰᠢᠷᠠᠭᠠᠨ᠎ᠠᠨᠡᠮ from, etc. Jat. 78, Dh. 29, 319). Another odina of triumph (tulam atulah ca samhassam, etc.), was altered by Gantama three months before his death when he formally resigned his hold upon life (dymaikkidrom osamji). At Dh. 382 we are told that Gantama finding Devadats about to introduce divisions among the priesthood, in the bitterness of his soul atteved the stings, askaram adhaad addisidhu ppema dikkaram, etc., and this is called an adana. At Dh. 251 the udana is a hymns of rejoicing and thankgiving by Vishakha at the fulfilment of her pious wishes. Uddans are not always in verse. At the commencement of Sam. S. King Ajātasatto is seated with his counters on the terrace of his palace, and struck with the splendour of the unclouded full moon, breaks forth into the enthusiastic utterance, "delightful indeed is the night, beautiful is the night, etc." the whole passage being prose. And again in the same Suta, when Ajātasatto reaches the forest glade where by the glare of the torch-light he sees Buddha and his disciples seated to the holy calm of religious meditation, he exclaims with fervent longing, found the spasmoda Uddiyikaddo innumerable as an ungladiato koin, "would that my son Uddiyikhadda might be endowed with calm like this." At Dh. 128 the Buddhist "Gloria," some toma Bhagovato arachato samindasambuddhasta, is called an adasa. One of the angus or divisions of the Buddhist scriptures is Uddan, which is coextensive with the book of that name forming the fourth section of the Khuddaka Nikya (see Tipijakash). Buddha has says, somonsamhadhamaghadthapajisamyattid due-asiti sutustad adamas ti ceditabbam, Udana is to be understood as eighty-two suttas connected with stanzas composed under the inspiration of joy (see Alw. I. 61).

— UDĂNAM, Upward aspiration, enthusiastic or joyous utterance, expression of intense feeling (whether of joy or sorrow) in words [337]. B. Lot. 892. This term is applied to one or more verses in which a speaker expresses the sudden emotion of his heart on some critical, or mournful, or joyous occasion. These verses are hardened with the phrase it is made as addicted, "breached forth this solemn utterance." The most striking of these definitions is the famous hymn of triumph altered by Gantama Buddha when he stalled onnsilence on the thorns of bodh (ᠰᠢᠷᠠᠭᠠᠨ᠎ᠠᠨᠡᠮ from, etc. Jat. 78, Dh. 29, 319). Another odina of triumph (tulam atulah ca samhassam, etc.), was altered by Gantama three months before his death when he formally resigned his hold upon life (dymaikkidrom osamji). At Dh. 382 we are told that Gantama finding Devadats about to introduce divisions among the priesthood, in the bitterness of his soul atteved the stings, askaram adhaad addisidhu ppema dikkaram, etc., and this is called an adana. At Dh. 251 the udana is a hymns of rejoicing and thankgiving by Vishakha at the fulfilment of her pious wishes. Uddans are not always in verse. At the commencement of Sam. S. King Ajātasatto is seated with his counters on the terrace of his palace, and struck with the splendour of the unclouded full moon, breaks forth into the enthusiastic utterance, "delightful indeed is the night, beautiful is the night, etc." the whole passage being prose. And again in the same Suta, when Ajātasatto reaches the forest glade where by the glare of the torch-light he sees Buddha and his disciples seated to the holy calm of religious meditation, he exclaims with fervent longing, found the spasmoda Uddiyikaddo innumerable as an ungladiato koin, "would that my son Uddiyikhadda might be endowed with calm like this." At Dh. 128 the Buddhist "Gloria," some toma Bhagovato arachato samindasambuddhasta, is called an adasa. One of the angus or divisions of the Buddhist scriptures is Uddan, which is coextensive with the book of that name forming the fourth section of the Khuddaka Nikya (see Tipijakash). Buddha has says, somonsamhadhamaghadthapajisamyattid due-asiti sutustad adamas ti ceditabbam, Udana is to be understood as eighty-two suttas connected with stanzas composed under the inspiration of joy (see Alw. I. 61).

— UDDHARATI, To draw out; to lift up, raise [Wg].

Dh. 58. Of catching fish, drawing them out of the water (F. Ját. 53). Dahkkhasm padach u, to lift up the right foot, i.e. to depart (Vj. Ját. 17). Balim u, to raise a revenue, levy taxes (Mah. 185). Pádehi paharited pasahh uddharanti, kick up the earth with their feet (Dh. 154). Karasá (abl.) u, to take out of a box (Sám. 8). Aor. uddhari (Ját. 17; Ras. 30). Oer. uddharitod. Ppr. uddharanto (Dh. 269). Pass. uddharigati, to be formally accepted (of a kathloa, see next). P.p.p. uddhafo, pulled out, extricated (Dh. 195; F. Ját. 55). Neut. uddhafam, pride, arrogance (Ab. 169). Caus. uddharpeti (F. Ját. 8).

UDDHÁRO, Pullag out; debt [ʌlɪt]. Ab. 471, 112). Attihadiddró, drawing out the meaning, explanation (Aix. 1. 67). There is a ceremony called kathiamidddró, which appears to be identical with kathiamidddró, rendered by Gogerly “consecration of the kathina.” The latter is evidently the formal acceptance by a chapter of priests of a robe presented by the lity. The ceremony is a nattidutiyakomna, at which at least five priests must be present (Pét. 114). Ubbdró is a derivative of . At Pét. 79, 114 we have hathinam middariyati, at Pét. 7 mbbhaiasimish kathine, when the kathins has been formally accepted.

UDDHO, and UBBHO (adj.), Raised, erect, bligh [st]. I have not met with the uncompounded adjective, but it occurs as the first part of a compound, e.g. addhalo, addhamukho, whohathako, etc. (see sep. and under Uddham).

UDDHUMĀYATI (pass.), To be blown up, and hence to be swollen [pass. vāʿanā], in 8. it would be vāʰāyāʰ]. Galo addikundyi, his throat swelled up (P. Já. 12). P.p.p.ḷ addikundto, swollen, bloated (of a corpse); with affix ḷ, addikundtdakō (Dh. 315, and see Kasmaffādamā, p. 180, a, line 4).
UDDHUTO (p.p.p.), Shaken [p.p.p.]. Ab.600. UDDHOYATI (pom.), To be driven away. Att. 106. Rendered by D'Alwis, "blown away," as if from additional, but it is probably from addition.

UDDISATI, To point out, to declare; to determine, appoint; to recite [u[]. At Dh. 63 kom addieyyam is explained to mean syahs upajihyo od deariyo vi ti kum xama uddiseyyam, "to whom can I point saying, This is my teacher or master." The meaning of the whole line therefore is, I learnt the truth myself, no one taught me (comp. p. 415, first line, mayhah spajihyo od deariyo od w'atthi). Of reciting the Patimokha (Pat. iii, Dh. 185), Aor. uddisi (Dh. 125). Inf. uddistwa (Alw. I. 103). Ger. uddisa, uddisited, painting out, indicating, etc. (Pat. 77). Uddisa is used adverbially in the sense of "on behalf of, for, on account of, with reference to." With acc. Updakma sadhahm uddisa nishro kárpito hoti, a convent has been built by a plous lsyman for the clergy (Pat. xxx, comp. 8 and 9, line 1). Ját. 55, tak u. smoyhark pabbujid). At Pt. 9 tsuhkhito uddisa tithahmno seems to mean "standing in silence wistfully, or indicating a wish," i.e. not asking for the robe, but standing in an attitude of expectation to remind the donor of his promise. Pass. uddisati (Pat. 17). P.f.p. uddisifabbo (Pat. xxi). P.p.p. uddifthho, rehearsed, recited (Pat. 2, 6).

UKKHEPANIYO, The ukkhepasiyash kamman is one of the Saighhakkamma, and means I think the excommunication of a Buddhist priest for a grave offence [fr. caus. 1]. Dh. 103. One of the offences is dpatityd adasanam, “concealment of a sin” (Pit. 96; Dh. 104). Persistent association with such a person is a parajika offence in a nun (Pit. 95). A monk thus excommunicated can be restored by and brand (Pit. 92, 96).

Sdspikappach ukkhipited, raising the lower edge of the certain (Dh. 159). Jalaus u, seems to mean to cast a net, not to draw it (F. Ját. 5). Mañcen' deldys ukkhipited agamotusew, put them on stretchers and carried them off (Dh. 361). Slaas ukkhipited, raising his head defiantly (Ten J. 14, see Sloan). Ukkhipited deith, brandishing his sward over her head (Mah. 46). To pull a person out of a pit (Ras. 35). Ucchušādrom u, to take up a bundle of sugar-canes on one's shoulders (Pit. xv). To pick up (Dh. 246). To excommunicate (Mah. 16; Dh. 109, 396). Ger. ukkhippo (Ras. 29), ukkhipited (Ten J. 29). P.p.p. ukkhitto, raised, lifted; thrown off, got rid of (Dh. 71). UKKUTIKO (adj.), Sitting on the hams, squatting, crouching, kneeling [ 2023-2024], the corresponding word in S. is [2023-2024]. Ukkufiko hutod, falling back on his hounches (of an elephant, Dh. 246). At Dh. 163 we have rattansa hi ukkufikash padam shave, the footstep of the lustful man would be crooked (?). Subh. quotes ciram ukkufiko ed pi, or sitting on his hams for a long while. There appears to be a fem. noun ukkufik, “squatting,” for at Dh. 300 we have ukkufiki badivena draddha-virjo, “exerting himself by squatting on the hams,” as an explanation of ukkufikappadhuam; here draddha-virjo corresponds to paddhna in the text (v. 141), and Subh. says that paddhna here means utahe. honess (Ten J. 38), but there is another reading

unadentati, "having great fangs." Considered

deri, in the phrase dassenhaatsliokaditutia usand-

dentto, which I think means, "causing all the ten

thousand words to shout with joy" (Ten J. 48;

J4. 63).

UNNALO (adj.), This word occurs at Att. III, where D'Alwla renders it "evil-disposed," and at Dh. 59, where the comment has teamed on a small ship's carapema unafirmant, "to these who are called unanal because they walk uplifting the reed of pride."� Yatr. says he thinks it means "proud, insolent." As we have nalo and nalo, the forms unnalo and unnalo may both be correct.

576. Cause/undermelt, to bend or lift upwards.

UNNATI (f.), Haughtness [빠짐]. Ab. 169.

Ab. 708; B. Lot. 676. Umatatfkhasai, high ground (in a lake or marsh, vix, a bit of land rising above the surface of the water, Ten J. 8). And pftunatfumato (adj.), his joy rose higher and higher, lit. he became more and more elevated with joy (Mah. 87).
UNNO (p,p.p.), Wet [可], Ab.753.

UNO (adj.), Deficient, less [ɑːŋ]. Pit. 8. Éuaiée Aoti, H there is not enough (Dh. 380), Kineé suau adua adaei, was not at all deficient (Dh. 113). Éuaaiatiouau pugalo, a person under twenty years of age (Pli. 16). Éuaaiutiko (adj.), poor, lit. to whom property is deficient (Alw. I. 75). Éuaikkié policassat éke' and, 400 monks, lit. 800 deficient by one (Mah. 11). Ekdya émaisati ko-pyo, 19 kopla, lit. 20 kopla deficient by one kopl (Mah. 161). Ses Ekdwa and Ekdwao. UPA (preu.), Below, less [gu]. Ab. 1185. With loc. Upa khdriyam dopo, a droga is less than a klufr (Sem. K. 350). In composition: Upaskhad, a minor branch. UPACARITO (p.p.p.) Served [qqqqf(n)]. Ab.751.

spaceaged, let not the right moment go by (Dh.

56). Ubho esigam spaceaged, has escaped from

both bonds (Dh. 73).

smile (P. J47 48). Upadkáretka was ti natád, exclaiming, See to her (Dh. 307). P.p.p. upadhá-rida, perceived, observed, understood (P47 113).
UPADHÁVATI, To run after, Lo run up Lo []. Dh. 329; Pár. 2021.

UPADHI (m.), A wheel; the body; a substratum of being [ɒʃuʃu]. From Ab. 968 we learn that there are four substrates of being, and at Dh. 439 we find them enumerated as the Khandhas, Káma, Kilesa and Kamma. Nirupadhi as an epithet of an Arhat means "free from substratum," but not of all the four substrata, since he possesses one of them, Khandha. This is clearly recognized by Buddhaghosa, whose gloss on nirupadhi at Dh. v. 418 is nirupadhin ti nirupakhileam, "free from substratum (bere) means free from Klea." He might have added "or Kima or Kamma," for the Arhat is free from the three last Upadhis. But the whole four Upadhis include every conceivable substratum or condition of being, and when the annihilation of being is intended, we generally have the expression sabbāpadhi, "all the (four) upadhi" (art, Nidbadam, p. 272, a, line 9; Dh. 433, line 11). The term nirupadhi may also be applied to one who has attained anupaddissemnibbāna, who has ceased to exist, and then it of course means deprived of all the four upadhis. (Dh. 270). In one instance I find sabbāpadhi parikkayo applied to the Arhat, where it must I think be by anticipation (see art. Nidbadanai, p. 268, a, line 11); the passage will be found at p. 103 of Coomarmaswamy's Sutta Nipāta.
UPADISATI, To command, advise [wifan]. Att. 215. Aor. wpdisi (Mah. 120). P.p.p. spadifpko, specified (Sen. K. 234).

— UPADISESO (adj.), Having the Skandhas remaining. Updidi is a music, noun formed from the verb STII as upadhi is formed from STII, and is a name for the five khandias (catchi upddachchi upddiyatiti upddi, paicakikhandaesa etam adihacamam). As I have shown in art Nibbann, Nirvipa is of two sorts, upddiswanidibman or Arhatship and acupiddiesomibdman or extinction. These terms mean respectively, “having the Skandhas remaining,” and “not having the Skandhas remaining.” For upddidea we sometimes have a-upddidea or savupddisea. The North Buddhists, puzzled by the anomalous form updidi, concluded it must be a mistake for updadi, and have turned upddidea into sapadhjecta. Hence we have the curious anomaly of the North Buddhists forming the Arhat sapadhjectaah, “having upadhi,” while sirupadhi, “free from upadhi,” is with the South Buddhists a distinctive epithet the Arhat1 (B. fat. 580). See art. Nibbann, p. 207 (8), line 5.

UPADISSATI (pass.), To be seen, discovered

UPADIYATI, To take hold of; to ring to the world, to have upddna or attachment [301]. No ca pdind hanukam upddiyited niddaai, nor dams he sit holding his chin with his hand (Brahmayu S.). Sukke dhamme no upddyait, does not hold fast to good works (Alw. I. 107). Upddnam ahdeena anupddiyit, from absence of the updduas not clinging to the world (Dh. 439). Catáiti upddmahi (teatr.) kiel onupddiyitd, not elinging at all to the world by the four upddinas (Dh. 278). Ppr. upddiyno (Dh. 4), upddyasto (Dh. 151), upddiyamno (Alw. I. 107). Anupdiydo, not clinging to the world, free from attachment. Ger. upddya, upddiyitd, holding; including, beginning with, starting from; on account of, since./Anupdiya, not elinging, free from attachment to the world (Dh. 18, 73, 118). Lesamatian upddya, laying hold of some trifling pretext (Pat. 5). Anukampain u, taking pty, out of compassion, mercifully, kindly (Kamm. 5; B. Lot. 389). Uochurasan u., including or beginning with the juice of the sugar-cane (Pat. 81, I think we have this sense at B. Lot. 30). Bhu mnadava u. tat' sittarim devd, beginning with the terrestrial angels all angels beyond them (Dax. 45). Catummahdrájike deve u. ydoa Tuistidmaí devdainah hidad, the lusts of the devan, beginning with the C. devan up to those of the T. devas. At Dh. 315 upddya seems to mean "in comparison with," I do not see how otherwise to translate dhasah idva amdhakam dhasain u. hiknikafth-niyam than "bis wealth compared to our wealth is n mere trifle." Tadupddya, since then, from that time (Mah. 63). Tadupddya so dri Gojamibarandusko, "from that circumstance," or from that time he was called O. (Mah. 141). Mahantais idas seadhas ti appnnavacamah u. based, lit. which is its groundwork (Dh. 399, comp. 187). Subh. writes to me that arahattasa upamisayo means "the good fortune which is the cause of a man's attaining Arhatship," he adds that upamisaya means bhagya (destiny, luck), and is a synonym of hetu. In this technical use herit occurs at Jat. 44 as one of the eight conditions for the attainment of Buddhahood, and Vij. renders it "power of attaining Arhatship." That he is right appears from a passage from Sarasaingaha quoted at Ras. 62, ketiti arahattasa upamisaya-sampatti, yo hi tasmin attinhdve vayamanto arahattas papanitsum samattho tassa samijhati netarassa, by hetu is meant possession of the faculty of (attaining) Arhatship; for the man who is capable of attaining Arhatship by his exertions in this existence, such a man is successful and no other. Up. may be used of any of the supernatural attainments. At Ten J. 117, we have, Paccakabothindigassa upamisayasampano, possessed of the faculty of attaining Paccakabuddahood. At Dh. 392, Tassa sotapattimagga asu apanissayah divd, seeing that he was destined to enter the first Path (comp. Dh. 358). At Das. 1, Satth paccasasamaye lokasi okwanto tassa sotapattiphalidpasanayah divd, the Teacher early in the morning casting his eye upon the world, and beholding in that man the power of attahing the first Fruition (D'Aiwla has got the correct meaning, for he renders the passage excellently, "Bodha rising at early dawn, looked into the world and perceived that this person was pre-destined to attain the paths," Att. 175, see Des. 20).1 Turnour renders tesath divd pasanayah by "observing their predestined conversion" (Mah. 30). Arahattasa upamisaye sati kurnd andho jito, if he was destined to be an Arhat why did he become blind? (Dh. 89, comp. Das. 21, line 6). By a bold figure this predestination to salvation is likened to a flame burning steadily within a man: Paccakabahavikamattam wa sakki madartah, antoghafe dijo viya hi 'sao hadaye arahattasa upamisayo folati, a man who is lo his last existence

(I.e. who is about to become an Arhat) cannot perish (before attaining Arhatship), for like a lamp within a pitcher the assurance of final sensitification ever burns within his heart (Das. 21). Prieobood (Pst. 83); the passage adds that his moral duties are the observance of the Five Silas, and that his occupation is to earn a livelihood rightlessly and justly, avoiding the five sinful trades, which are caravan trading, slave-dealing, and the trades of hatcher, publican, and polson-seller. UPASAMMATI, To grow calm; to cease; to be settled [ʒʌʃn], Upham upamamani, heat is allayed (Jst. 17). Dh. 1, 19. Ger. upasama, having settled (Msh. 39). \P.p.p. apasanta, calm, tranquil (Dh. 19, 36, 68).
UPASAMO, Cessation; quietude, calm [vʌtʃn]. Dn. 33, 66.

UPASAMPADÃ (f.), Taking, obtaining, acquiring; priest's orders [ᠲᠠᠭᠠᠨ + ᠪᠷᠠ], Dh. 83 (comp. akusaidnam dhammam paidnd kwaadman dhammam upasampaddya). Upasampadd is the fullest possible admission to the privileges of the Buddhist priesthood, and bears to pabbajid the same sort of relation that priest's orders in the Anglican Church bear to demam's orders (see Pabbajid). A man cannot receive the upasampadâ ordination without having first taken deacon's order, but the interval may be very short or very long according to circumstances. Thus, twenty being the lowest age at which a man is qualified for upasampadi, a boy who has become a smaqera at eight will have to wait twelve years before he can receive upasampadâ. On the other hand if a man join the priesthood at or after twenty, if he be otherwise properly qualified he may proceed at once to priest's orders. Full details of the ordination will be found in Dickson's article, "The Upasampadâ-Kamnavád" in the Joarn. Roy. As. 90c. for 1974. See also Spiegel's Kammavākyam, and E. Mon. 44-47. Upasampadā's labhati, to take priest's orders, to receive ordination (Dh. 124). A chapter of priests conferring ordination must consist of at least ten members (Pit. xi). Laddhōpasampado (adj.), having received ordination (Dh. 198, comp. 80). At Mah. 37 upasampadamaqala is reordered by Turnour "hall of ordination." Upasampadak karati, to ordain (with dat. Mah. 103).

[W], Jarouk u., to undergo decay (Dh. 28, comp. 61). Upemi Buddha sarapash, I fly to B. as my refuge (Dh. 97). Nirgash u., to go to hell (Dh. 54). Iddari manh aopali, now he doesn't come near me (Mah. 194). Marasap u., to die (Jat. 20). Gabbahan u., to enter the womb, be reborn (Dh. 58). Fut. 1st pers. spessah (Dhanya S.). Fut. 2nd pers. spekini (Dh. 43, 62). Aor. upagd (Mah. 53, sahaapagd = sahad upagd). Ger. upsea (Mah. 16, 17, 47, 86, 207). Asupocca roash, not giving way to anger (Att. 203). P.p. speta, possessed of. With Instr. upato damacocera, endowed with temperance and truth (Dh. 2). With acc. diasigash u. (Dh. 49). F. Jat. 1. UPOGHATO, An example [پاکستان]. Ab. 115. UPOSATHIKO (adj.), Fasting, keeping the Uposatha vows; betonging to the Uposatha [next to the Mah. 170. Uposathiko Aoti, to fast, keep the Sabath (Dh. 166; F. Jat. 59). Uposathika Maitah (Kamm. 9) is rendered by Dickson "rice offered on the full-moon days."

—UPOSATHO, The Buddhist Sabbath or fast-day; fasting, abstinence from sensual enjoyments; the monastic ceremony of reading the Pátimokkha; the eight Sites; ordination, institution [चक्वा], Ab. 780. The Uposatha day is a day of religious observance and celebrations for laymen and priests, and answers as nearly as possible to our Sunday. It occurs four times in the month, viz. on the day of full moon (pattacadari), on the day when there is no moon (citadadari), and on the two days which are eighth from the full and new moon (attilamif); it is therefore a weekly festival. On uposatha days laymen dress in their best clothes, and such of them as are religiously disposed abetala from trade and worldly amusements, and take upon themselves the uposatha vows, that is to say, go to a priest and make him their witness of their intention to keep the eight Sites during the day (E. Moon. 236, see Silami). Two of the four days, via the etisdodol and pacidadari, are devoted by the priests to the special ceremony of reading the Pátimokkha (pattamokkhaddeno). This uposatha service forms a sort of general confession. Four priests constitute a quorum, but every member of the monastery is expected to be present. The priests being all assembled, the Pátimokkha is read out section by section, and at the end of each section the reader thrives puts the question

whether all present are innocent of the offences just enumerated. Any priest whose conscience reproaches him with having committed one of the offences then makes public confession of it and submits to the necessary presence (E. Mon. 144). These two uposathas are the regular ones, and are called ctduddaiko and pspasaziko (Pit. 27). There is also an occasional one called eimaggi apmatho, "reconciliation-Up," which is held when a quarrel among the fraternity has been made up, the general confession forming as I were a seal to the reconciliation (Pit. 2, 37; Mah. 42). Writing to me in December 1871, Subhiti told me that the two Up. days for that month were Monday the 11th and Tuesday the 20th. If the quorum could not be obtained, and there were only two or three priests, they held a porsimaddhi apmatho, which Vij. explains as "the mutual confession of two or three priests of their innocence of the offences enumerated in the Pithmokkha" (see Pit. 20). The hall or chapel in the monastery in which the Pitimokkha is read is called spasathagqam (Mah. 15, 263; Pit. 1), or sposathagkram (Mah. 232, 249), or sposathagdrash (Mah. 210), or spasathagyo (Mah. 225). The Up. service is called uposatஃakumash (Mah. 96). Uposatash gasechati, to go to the Up. service. Uposatshani kuruti, to hold the Uposatha service (Pit. 36, 97; Mah. 42). The term sposatஃakumash is also applied to the Sabbath duties observed by laymen, at fasting, taking upon one the eight vows, etc. (P. Jit. 52 sposatஃakumash hotod, 58; Ras. 40). Keeping the Sabbath (by laymen) is called uposatshani spasassati (Dh. 404, the p.p.p. is upassatthe),/uposatshavdassat cassit (Dh. 89). The ceremony of a layman taking upon himself the eight siles is called uposatஃakimash adithifkati (Alw. I. 76), or uposatஃakigdni deiyatN (Mah. 86), or uposatshah samddiyatN (Dh. 506), or apthagagilash umiddiyati (see Silous, Samddiyati). At Mah. 230 we have hired apthaguposat, having become an observer of the Up. with the eight Silas. At Mah. 230 I am inclined to read, Uposatshipavdoe co kattabbe 'posathe, and on the Suhahah the Up. fast must be observed.¹ The Up.

Uposathika Maitah (Kamm. 9) is rendered by Dickson "rice offered on the full-moon days."

—UPOSATHO, The Buddhist Sabbath or fast-day; fasting, abstinence from sensual enjoyments; the monastic ceremony of reading the Pátimokkha; the eight Sites; ordination, institution [चक्वा], Ab. 780. The Uposatha day is a day of religious observance and celebrations for laymen and priests, and answers as nearly as possible to our Sunday. It occurs four times in the month, viz. on the day of full moon (pattacadari), on the day when there is no moon (citadadari), and on the two days which are eighth from the full and new moon (attilamif); it is therefore a weekly festival. On uposatha days laymen dress in their best clothes, and such of them as are religiously disposed abetala from trade and worldly amusements, and take upon themselves the uposatha vows, that is to say, go to a priest and make him their witness of their intention to keep the eight Sites during the day (E. Moon. 236, see Silami). Two of the four days, via the etisdodol and pacidadari, are devoted by the priests to the special ceremony of reading the Pátimokkha (pattamokkhaddeno). This uposatha service forms a sort of general confession. Four priests constitute a quorum, but every member of the monastery is expected to be present. The priests being all assembled, the Pátimokkha is read out section by section, and at the end of each section the reader thrives puts the question

whether all present are innocent of the offences just enumerated. Any priest whose conscience reproaches him with having committed one of the offences then makes public confession of it and submits to the necessary presence (E. Mon. 144). These two uposathas are the regular ones, and are called ctduddaiko and pspasaziko (Pit. 27). There is also an occasional one called eimaggi apmatho, "reconciliation-Up," which is held when a quarrel among the fraternity has been made up, the general confession forming as I were a seal to the reconciliation (Pit. 2, 37; Mah. 42). Writing to me in December 1871, Subhiti told me that the two Up. days for that month were Monday the 11th and Tuesday the 20th. If the quorum could not be obtained, and there were only two or three priests, they held a porsimaddhi apmatho, which Vij. explains as "the mutual confession of two or three priests of their innocence of the offences enumerated in the Pithmokkha" (see Pit. 20). The hall or chapel in the monastery in which the Pitimokkha is read is called spasathagqam (Mah. 15, 263; Pit. 1), or sposathagkram (Mah. 232, 249), or sposathagdrash (Mah. 210), or spasathagyo (Mah. 225). The Up. service is called uposatஃakumash (Mah. 96). Uposatash gasechati, to go to the Up. service. Uposatshani kuruti, to hold the Uposatha service (Pit. 36, 97; Mah. 42). The term sposatஃakumash is also applied to the Sabbath duties observed by laymen, at fasting, taking upon one the eight vows, etc. (P. Jit. 52 sposatஃakumash hotod, 58; Ras. 40). Keeping the Sabbath (by laymen) is called uposatshani spasassati (Dh. 404, the p.p.p. is upassatthe),/uposatshavdassat cassit (Dh. 89). The ceremony of a layman taking upon himself the eight siles is called uposatஃakimash adithifkati (Alw. I. 76), or uposatஃakigdni deiyatN (Mah. 86), or uposatshah samddiyatN (Dh. 506), or apthagagilash umiddiyati (see Silous, Samddiyati). At Mah. 230 we have hired apthaguposat, having become an observer of the Up. with the eight Silas. At Mah. 230 I am inclined to read, Uposatshipavdoe co kattabbe 'posathe, and on the Suhahah the Up. fast must be observed.¹ The Up.

— UTTAR[adj.], Superior, highest, best [adj.]. I should be inclined to take the phrase sitarimannassdhammo as meaning “superhuman condition,” the first part of the compound being the adv. altarih. But according to Pit. 67 the first word must be the adj. altari, for the glass says utarimannassdhamman it utarimannassdash jdyilnao'eva ariydnao ca dhammaan, by wit, la meant the condition of the highest men, of those who exercise jhina and of those who are in the Paths (see Pit. 3; B. Lot. 164; Dh. 335). At Dh. 202 we have utarimaggaphalema, by the fraction of the highest Path (viz. Arhatahip). We appear also to have the adj. uttari at Dh. 171, but what the compound uttaridhaigo means I cannot tell.

— UTTARIM (adv.), Beyond, above; further, beside, more, longer [with the last a weakened to 4, comp. uitarilare]. Cuddasa basadai satta ended ca uttarim, fourier years plus seven months (Msh. 204). Mah. 282). Drupah u, appears to mean, to continue till morning, allow morning to overtake you while in some occupation, let the man rise upon you (Ahw. I. 70, Pit. 98, in both instances short a). Aor. uṭṭhārī, uṭṭhātī (Ten J. 114; Mah. 60, 175), anoomakous pl. uṭṭhānā (Mah. 106). Fat. uṭṭhā-hāmi at. 204; Mah. 211, 230). Opt. uṭṭhīthe (Dh. 31). Imperat. Ṣud peru. uṭṭhāna. In. uṭṭhā-hāmi. Ger. uṭṭhāya (Dh. 43, 106; P. Ját. 57; Mah. 154, starting up), uṭṭhākitī (Dh. 288, 870; Mah. 152), uṭṭhīthītd (Dh. 335). Uṭṭhāy' darud, having risen from his seat. Uṭṭhāya astosicosa-nasid pōdi, go4 up and went into the house (Dh. 154). P.p. uṭṭhādo. Anuṭṭhādo, alugāgh (Dh. 49). P.p.p. uṭṭhito, arisen, produced; standing up; striving (Ab. 65; Dh. 88, 198). Mārapatthā'asa uṭṭhītd, those who had risen up to kill, or were exerging themselves to kill him (Ten J. 29). Caus. uṭṭhāperī (comp. spafthāpeti). Causān uṭṭhāpeito viya, as I be was causing the moon to arise (Ten J. 12). Uṭṭhāpetāna yantehī jalam, rulang the water by machloery (Mah. 211). Chaṇam uṭṭhāpetid, having roused Chaṇa (Dh. 118, corp. Mah. 282). Drupah u, appears to mean, to continue till morning, allow morning to overtake you while in some occupation, let the man rise upon you (Ahw. I. 70, Pit. 98, in both instances short a). P.pr. of the caus. pass. (vujthāpyandmo, being roused (Jāt. 10). P.f.p. uṭṭhāponāya, that must be roused (Jāt. 10). When uṭṭhā, follows a word ending in a vowel, and without a pause in the sense, a v is generally prefixed for euphony. Thus we have uṭṭhāy' dead, but ānud uṭṭhākhāh (Jāt. 17; Dh. 403). Other examples are, dpaqjittid vujthāthukmo (Pāt. 69), Saṭchārakṇ vandītd vujṭhāy' deond (Dh. 205), samopatēito vujthāya (Dh. 24, 131), samokirāni puppherī vujthākantasa deand (Jāt. 27, comp. Mah. 7, Art. 8), rjdī vujthādi, na vujthāmd (Mah. 230), patimīldīp vujthīto (Ahw. I. 92), kutham su vujthakanti (Mah. 30), chow su vujthāpetun (Mah. 262), apqijkhaymīti vujthīto (Pāt. xx). At Mah. 30, 00, the euphoule v is used after anuvwra, varasah vujthāya, and samādkhā vujthīto. At Mah. 30, line-9, vujthākanto begins a line.

Nisidauythaham, sitting and standing (Dh. 86). Anutjhadnald ghard, houses are spoilt for want of energy to repair them (Dh. 43, see comment). Bhattufthamjhadnan pi qidansato, not even knowing where boiled rice came from (Dh. 141). With euphole v after a vowel (comp. last): goahha ufthdanah, delivery of a woman with child (Jat. 52, comp. Dh. 240); apattiwythdanah, rehabilitation after an offence (see Soighddisese); adhijhad. navythanah, resolution and exertion (Dh. 343, comp. 291).



UTTHÀNAVÀ (adj.), Strength, active []. Dh. 5.

With eophonic v, vuffápoasm (Pít. 6).

-UTU (m./f.n.), Season, time; a season of the year; (masc.) the mennes [7]. Ab. 79 (where it has said to be m. and f.). 238. The three seasons, of four months each, are hemanta, gimhdna (or gimka), and vasadna (Ab. 78; Pát. 27; Dh. 117). The six seasons, of two months each, are pasanta, gimha, vasadna, sarada, hemanta, siira (Ab. 79). Megha-utw orwpo-utw, time of a storm, and time of sun-rising (Dh. 158). UTUJO (adj.), Produced by the seasons [ 5 +].

Earth, mountains, water, and wind are said to be so produced (Gog. Ev. 31; Man. B. 441).

Mama vacanena Bhagavanto pde sirasd vonda, in my name reverentially salute Buddha (Alw. I. Bl. comp. Dh. 84); Sejthissa vacanena aparam panpan likhi, wrote another letter in the sejthin's name (Alw. I. 102). Buddha vacanain, Sambiddhav, Jinan, Makamusino v., the Word of Buddha (Mah. 23; Alw. I. ix, exlv). Dubbhidain Subhaddama buddhassa v. saram, remembering the wicked words of the dotard Sabbadda (Mah. 11). Amjhaddini bhikkhave . uddisinn H vacanato, from the passage, "I permit you priests to appoint . "(Alw. I. 103). Idam jikdhayavacanan, this passage from the three Tikās. Gdhdbandhadipakdi vacanai, sentences explanatory of the metrical construction (Jst. 2). In gram. number: ekavacanan, singular, bahmo, plural (Cl. Gram. 112), dutiyekao, acrussative singular. Vacana-middganiko, a dictionary (Yair.). V, karoti, to obey: Mama vacanana karonni, they do not my bidding, obey not my words (Dh. 104, 109, 29). Papididnan o. na karosi, you do not follow the advice of wise men (Das. 22, comp. Dh. 97). Also to tell, enjoln: Tar' etah v. karoni, I say this to you, I urge this upon you (Ras. 24); I have met with the phrase sace me v. karegyad, which seems to mean, "if you will authorize me, put the injunction upon me." Annamannavacanan, mutual advice (Pit. 6). Madhuravacanan dapanto, addressing him with a sweet voice, or with kind words (Das. 1). Buddho H vacane satamatte, as soon as he heard the word "Buddha" (Alw. I. 97, comp. Dh. 240). Jaya-namadi-didi-vacanehi, with shouts of Jaya! Nanda! etc. (Jst. 60). Yam kiciti avanasesapariyiddnavacanan, yan kilsei is an expression including all without exception (Dh. 288). Anulih vacane patimantetum, to argue on this matter, about this saying (Alw. I. 1ix).

knit c'voécuolank Jinsudqush, like the great banyan tree the Thera doerline is the best of doctrines, it is the pure commandment of Buddha without diminution or addition. Turnour has for the most part sadly misunderstood the term. At Mah. 20 we have, eko 'vo'e theroddio so didoamate aks adicariyappdd to tolo orom ajdyismin, which Turnour renders, "During the first century after the death of Buddha there was but one schism among the therms: it was subsequent to that period that the other schisms among the preceptors took place." The real meaning is, "In the first century this (orthodox) Thora doctrine alone existed, the other (schismatic) Aorilya doerlines arose at a later date." At page 21, thero-oddema saha to honti dodosa should be rendered, including the Thora doctrine these are twelve in number. At Mah. 207, each to thervaddchi pobhiand bhikkhano deidhd, thus three priests se-ceded in two directions from the orthodox doerlines (viz. made two schisms, the Abhayagirl schlsun and the Dakkhipivihira schism). In the same page, niggatd theroaddola, departed from the orthodox faith. At page 202 thervada occurs twice. In line 2 it is opposed to ajdhakahé, and clearly means the text of the Buddhist scriptures. Line 10 runs thus, thervadddi pdilhi padohi cyojajanehi ca afniathattam abu s' eoa potthakesmi pi tles pi, is the three manuscripts there was no varladon whatever from the orthodox version, in passages (pdilhi), to words or in syllables. The adj. thervaddli (theraddis + w) means holding the orthodox doctrine, orthodox, not schismatic. It occurs at Mah. 250, where Turnour renders it "schismatic," and at Mah. 259, where he has "opponents of the schismatics." In his Glossary Torour defines it, "Discourses of the thgrou, on the schisms in the Buddhist church."

knit c'voécuolank Jinsudqush, like the great banyan tree the Thera doerline is the best of doctrines, it is the pure commandment of Buddha without diminution or addition. Turnour has for the most part sadly misunderstood the term. At Mah. 20 we have, eko 'vo'e theroddio so didoamate aks adicariyappdd to tolo orom ajdyismin, which Turnour renders, "During the first century after the death of Buddha there was but one schism among the therms: it was subsequent to that period that the other schisms among the preceptors took place." The real meaning is, "In the first century this (orthodox) Thora doctrine alone existed, the other (schismatic) Aorilya doerlines arose at a later date." At page 21, thero-oddema saha to honti dodosa should be rendered, including the Thora doctrine these are twelve in number. At Mah. 207, each to thervaddchi pobhiand bhikkhano deidhd, thus three priests se-ceded in two directions from the orthodox doerlines (viz. made two schisms, the Abhayagirl schlsun and the Dakkhipivihira schism). In the same page, niggatd theroaddola, departed from the orthodox faith. At page 202 thervada occurs twice. In line 2 it is opposed to ajdhakahé, and clearly means the text of the Buddhist scriptures. Line 10 runs thus, thervadddi pdilhi padohi cyojajanehi ca afniathattam abu s' eoa potthakesmi pi tles pi, is the three manuscripts there was no varladon whatever from the orthodox version, in passages (pdilhi), to words or in syllables. The adj. thervaddli (theraddis + w) means holding the orthodox doctrine, orthodox, not schismatic. It occurs at Mah. 250, where Turnour renders it "schismatic," and at Mah. 259, where he has "opponents of the schismatics." In his Glossary Torour defines it, "Discourses of the thgrou, on the schisms in the Buddhist church."

VASANTO, One of the seasons, spring [चस्वर], Ab. 79. See U.

VASATI, To dwell, stay, live, abide; spend time [ʌːrˈdʒiːn], Also pres. vassate (Mah. 100). Aor. avar, vīši (Mah. 2, the other part is vacl, 3rd pl. various (Mah. 38), 1st pl. avastma (Mah. 104). Imperat. vasa (Db. 183). Fut. vacchati (Alw. I. 31), vassati (Dh. 153). P.pr. vassamno (Ját. 21; Ten J. 55), vassante (Dh. 153; Ten J. 38). Ger. vaited (Dh. 80). Yuf. vassitni, vattuhni (Ját. 21; Dh. 124; F. Ját. 3, Mah. 52). Idha vassati, lives here (F. Ját. 4). Delathash vassite, having stayed with him two or three days (F. Ját. 4). Vassitni saha shikkhati, were living with the monks (Mah. 35). Vassat v., to spend the rely season. With loc. Eknemish are vassati, lives in a certain pond (F. Ját. 16). Annena vassati seems to mean "he lives for the sake of food," but Cloogh renders it "he lives by means of food" (Sen. K. 339; Cl. Gr. 133). Melaphorically: Yamati na māyd vassati xa mādo, in whom dwells neither decit nor pride (Das. 26). For further examples of the use of vassati, see Vido, Vasso. Pass. vassati (Alw. I. 38), vassati (Sen. K. 493). P.f.p. vattahabbo (Mah. 12), vassitabbo (see Kamma-vedi). P.p.p. vassito, vattu, vattha (Sen. K. 483, the correct reading is in the footnote). Dassablena vassitagandhabuti, the chamber of perfumes inhabited by Buddha (Br. J.S.A., comp. Mah. 12). Uruvelyam vassito, dwelling at U. (Mah. 2). Vattam brahmacariyam, the religious life has been lived, the duties of religion have been accomplished (this is said of the Arhat, who has fulfilled all the duties of religion, and obtained the perfect sanctification which results therefrom, Sen. K. 483). Chraim amhali fumkhāmi santhe vuttham, we have lived with you a long while, lit, it has been lived by us (Ten J. 38). Updaikhāti tāhi... vuttha bhikkhumi passayo, the convent inhabited by these devotees (Mah. 110, comp. 253). Vutthavasso, one who spent the rainy season, lit by whom the rainy season has been spent (see Vasso); Vuttaththama, dwelling-place (Dh. 319). Actively: Andaghare puriso ciravitho, a man who has spent a long time in prison (Ját. 21); Vassam vuttha, having spent the rainy season (see Vasso); Khish vuttha'si, where have you been living? (Dh. 339). Gaus. vassiti, to cause to live or dwell, to lodge (Mah. 56, 139, 142), to cause to stay, detain (Mah.

240). Kieckena paditah rattham, the kingdom established (lt. peopled) by me with great pains (Mah. 53). Assigned as a residence, inhabited (Mah. 203). Also came Vagidpeti. Bkadiotham candipeted, having detained them a day or two (Dh. 235).

Retreat is perhaps the correctest English equivalent. Dickson thinks the Vassa was originally intended as a relief to the monks, who were supposed to live at the foot of a tree; this exposed residence became unhealthy during the rainy season, and Buddha allowed them to build themselves huts as a protection against the indemencies of the weather (comp. E. Mon. 232, B. Int. 255). In a passage from Mahavagga quoted at Pit xxviii the origin of the institution of the Retreat is thus stated. Buddha was living at Rajaguna. At that time the Retreat had not as yet been instituted for the priest, but they went on their travels in winter, summer, and the rainy season. People took offence, 'How is it,' they said, 'that the ascetic disciples of the Sakya prince go on their travels in the rainy season as well as in winter and summer, crushing the tender (springling) plants, and destroying innumerable insects?' To obviate this evil, and silence the gossip of unbelievers, Gotama then instituted the vassallage. During their enforced retreat the priests devote themselves to the spiritual welfare and instruction of the people, who flock to them in great numbers, and who supply them with their daily food and with robes sufficient to last during the year. The robes are finally presented during the clavamisa which follows the last month of the Retreat (see E. Mon. 115). From the next article it will be seen that the vassa may be limited to three months, from the middle of July to the middle of October. Keeping Lent is called vassam as part (Dh. 51, 277, 387; Mah. 9, 12, 103; Pit. 107; Alw. I. 92), or cundadena vassati (Dh. 105). Entering on the Vassa residence is called vassam spagocchiati (Dh. 106, 274; Pit. xxxi), or cassam wpeti (Pit. xxii). Vasshevaso (adj.), having kept Lent, having concluded the Vassa residence (Dh. 80, 84, 107, 199, 277; Mah. 104, read -cosso). Vassam outka, having kept Lent (Alw. I. 92; Pit. 107). Vassipagata (adj.), having entered on the Vassa residence (Mah. 12; Pit. xxxi). Vassodam, keeping Lent, Vassa residence (Pit. xxviii). Vassucchede, breaking Lent (by travelling, etc., Pit. xxxi). Retreat is perhaps the correctest English equivalent. Dickson thinks the Vassa was originally intended as a relief to the monks, who were supposed to live at the foot of a tree; this exposed residence became unhealthy during the rainy season, and Buddha allowed them to build themselves huts as a protection against the indemencies of the weather (comp. E. Mon. 232, B. Int. 255). In a passage from Mahavagga quoted at Pit xxviii the origin of the institution of the Retreat is thus stated. Buddha was living at Rajaguna. At that time the Retreat had not as yet been instituted for the priest, but they went on their travels in winter, summer, and the rainy season. People took offence, 'How is it,' they said, 'that the ascetic disciples of the Sakya prince go on their travels in the rainy season as well as in winter and summer, crushing the tender (springling) plants, and destroying innumerable insects?' To obviate this evil, and silence the gossip of unbelievers, Gotama then instituted the vassallage. During their enforced retreat the priests devote themselves to the spiritual welfare and instruction of the people, who flock to them in great numbers, and who supply them with their daily food and with robes sufficient to last during the year. The robes are finally presented during the clavamisa which follows the last month of the Retreat (see E. Mon. 115). From the next article it will be seen that the vassa may be limited to three months, from the middle of July to the middle of October. Keeping Lent is called vassam as part (Dh. 51, 277, 387; Mah. 9, 12, 103; Pit. 107; Alw. I. 92), or cundadena vassati (Dh. 105). Entering on the Vassa residence is called vassam spagocchiati (Dh. 106, 274; Pit. xxxi), or cassam wpeti (Pit. xxii). Vasshevaso (adj.), having kept Lent, having concluded the Vassa residence (Dh. 80, 84, 107, 199, 277; Mah. 104, read -cosso). Vassam outka, having kept Lent (Alw. I. 92; Pit. 107). Vassipagata (adj.), having entered on the Vassa residence (Mah. 12; Pit. xxxi). Vassodam, keeping Lent, Vassa residence (Pit. xxviii). Vassucchede, breaking Lent (by travelling, etc., Pit. xxxi). Antovassam, during Lent (Pit. 107). Antocassam kadiagash, one day during Lent (Mah. 110).

[φθη]. (Mah. 250); Mohkhadhamash pasa gaosantchi ekal pabbjjd laddhsh caffati, by those who seek final deliverance the ascetic life alone ought to be adopted, or is worthy of adoption (Dh. 121). It will be seen that in the above constructions caffati is used exactly like the indeclinables sakkd and labbhd. With dat. of the person who ought to do the act; Anatra exighammamutiyd shikkhuwa sippaatthuh na caffati, without the permission of a chapter it is not right for a priest to leave home (Sen. K. 299); Buddhamsh xdna ekamin khde nabbddah gastuh na caffati, it is not proper for Buddhas to go constantly to the same place (Dh. 174). Vajfati su kho tunkkhah maddado, now is lying permissible to you, or "worthy of you?" (Trenckser, Mil. P.). The idea "It beboves, It is allowable, it is right," springs from the Sanak sense "to continue, prevall, be customary," since that which is customary is generally so because it is beneficial, what is law is lawful. There are traces of caffati being used like cattati, without the special meaning, showing that in the beginning cattati and caffati were used indiscriminately, and that the differentiation was gradually established. Thus at Ten J. 85 we have ekaise pi caffati yeeg, is also used in the sense of "certain" (the Burness MS. however has cattati, which I am by no means sure is not the right reading); and at Dh. 318, apardparam caffi, she rolled herself backwards and forwards (but should it be caffayl?, comp. Pavajtt). For the differentiated use of cattati and caffati we have an interesting parallel in parattri and pavajtt.

Atha nam Satiki stad azeca, and the Teacher said this to him (Tun J. 1, comp. Dh. 24). With it: Sadhati stated, saying, It is well (F. J4. 17).—Pasa accuti (Ah. 29; Alw. I. 30; Mah. 56, 214), succati (Mah. 64), to be spoken, resorted to be spoken of, to be called, to be meant (pl. succasi, Dh. 304). Sa se bde si succati, he indeed is called Fool (Dh. 12). Pumappana succamdam pi mantapadaim saittah asukkatish, unable to say a word of the mantra though repeated to be over and over again (Dh. 150). Nafadmahi succati, is called by various names (Att. 8). Kahih Asandakoro ti succamama tu kehiel, while it was belog said by some, Where is A. ? (Mah. 13). Jappa nama succati tapid, jappa means last (Alw. I. 107, comp. P4. 93). With acc. of the thing spoken about: Sahadamamijam vucamama, belog spoken to about the S. (Pit. 5). Jisawahs bhante ti succamand, having "Jivatha bhante" said to them (Ten J. 20). P.f.p. vattabba, thai ought to be said; that ought to be addressed, or called, or spoken to. Ahaasama vattabba, when one thing has to be said (Dh. 318). Bhikkheti pi vattabba, ought also to be called a "bilibilihi" (Dh. 310). Jiedti mattabba, be must be said Jiva to (Ten J. 20). Saamam atkhiti vattabba, of any disease you have you must say, "I have it" (Kamn. 6; here emtiabba does not, I thick, agree with saamam or atkhili, but is impersonal). Also p.f.p. maccahye, vaccatiyya. Eochi asa vaccalya, must be spoken to as follows (P4. 5, 96, 100). Attamah asacamamir koroti, refuses to be spoken to, lit. makes himself not to be spoken to (P4. 5). Also p.f.p. edces, in the compound edcoalingo, and also, declinable, adjectival (Ab. 29, 789, 803).—P.p.p. atto, wuta, said, spoken to. Tihi bih idam ti vattd, abs having been mild to by them, What is this? (Dh. 227). Aftahkatabiya vattamayena, as told or said in the commentary (Dh. 418, comp. 3). Vattappakshri dikkhaah, suffering of the sort (above) spoken of (Dh. 308). Vattafhadamakil toki, in the places named by them (Mah. 12, comp. 110). Appam pi vutto samama, being little spoken to. you by your father? (Mah. 280). Loe. absolute: — Eoash exite, having said thus, lit. it having been thus said (Dh. 332). Morapamam bhagemiti outite, on his replying, "From fear of death" (Mah. 33, 80). No ti outite, on being told, No (Mah. 280). With instr. of the person speaking: Satthard hamad evam harwiti outite, the Teacher having said, "Why dost thou so?" It. having been addressed by the Teacher (Dh. 333; Mah. 78; F. Jat. 6, 8). Tehi tathd outite, the message having been thus delivered by them (Mah. 40). Putte myydam phdrukah idi sakhsh vattam mahrdja myydamk yatiphadamkan, on its being said, "Is the garden convenient?" it was said to be delightful, "Great king, the garden is convenient for monks" (Mah. 83). Sometimes the construction is somewhat different, the locative not being impersonal, but agreeing with the person spoken to; Eoash v�tem, on their being thus addressed (Mah. 138); Kdianh vattte, on his being told the time (Mah. 60, comp. akhadhammikarn vaccamdo). — VIBHAJATI, To divide, apportion; to disintegrate, go into details, be minutely accurate []. Khestan vibajfied, having divided the field (between himself and his brother, Dh. 128). Tidha e., to divide into three (Dh. 189). Kammak atte vibajati yadidsh kidnappatatsya, Karma allote being to poverty or grandeur (Gog. Ev. 82). Sankhittens bhatiwa vittadrema attham vibajati, to distinguish or explain in detail the meaning of what is concisely expressed (Alw. I. xxvi). Ger. vibajja. Vibajjavydkarasiyo pino, a question that must be answered after distinguishing, i.e. one that must receive a qualified reply (see Paiho). Bodha is said to be vibajjamdi, which Turnour renders not inappropriately, "of the religion of investigated truth" (Mah. 42); perhaps "religion of Logic or Reason" would not be too free a rendering. I understand the expression to mean that Bodhiem does not deal merely in generalities, like the heretical religions, but both in doctrine and discipline goes into the mintest details, considering a thing in all its bearings, meeting difficulties and providing for contingencies. Subh. quotes from a Tik, vibajja vibajited vadati st-lendi vibajjadddi. At Pat. ix we have, and kun madradja satth khandhaditam vibajitatd vibajjadddi samandambaddho, Great King, our teacher the All-wise Buddha holds a doctrine of distinction, because distinction is made of the Skandhas and so forth. Sasanam ki vibajjadddo, for Bodhidism is the religion of Logic. P.f.p. vibattabdo. Vibattabdo hammath, wealth to be divided (between heirs, Ab. 88). P.p.p. vibhatto. Suvibhatto, well distributed, correctly divided, well proportioned, regular (B. Lot. 575, 583; Dh. 501, of a mapdape, well planned). Sankhittens bhadam avibhattank, concisely expressed, not disintegrated or detailed. Caus, vibadjati.

VIBHANOO, Division; distinction, determination, explanation [faww]. Ab. 1055. Clearus, distribution of robes (P4.100). Daddus, the distribution of Boddha's relics (Mah. 181). Mahdivhago, "Great Division," is a name for that portion of the Vinays which deals with the 227 Pátimokkha precepts (Br. J. 8. A.). The sections of the Vinys dealing with the precepts for mocks and for guns are called respectively bhikkhuvishagno and bhikkhasthe. Vihagan or vihagappakassna is the name of one of the Abbhamma books (for the next comp. kaannadaeam). It contains eighteen vibhanges or disquisitions, the first of which is khandhavidhamigo. E. Mon. 170; Alw. 1. 61.

— VINAYO, Putting away, avoidance; subduing, conversion; training, discipline; name of a portion of the Buddhist scriptures [ཞཡའ], Macchera-eisayo, putting away addishoes (Db. 186, 190, comp. Ras. 84). Sattivinayam kittwa, to effect the conversion of the people (Mah. 88). Gikisayo, discipline or duties of a layman (Sigkovida Sutta is sometimes so called). At Ras. 85 we are told that there are two sorts of inaya or discipline, amicarean, and paddava, discipline of restraint, and discipline of getting rid of (evil states). Visayo is the ecclesiastical code, or common law, by which the Buddhist monks are governed, and is contained in the Vignaya Pitaka (see Tipifakina). The Vignayapitaka

consists of five books, entitled respectively, Pridjiksh, Pācittiyash, Mahidaggo, Cślavaggo, and Puridagoo. Buddha's's commentary on the Vlnaya is called Samastapaddik's, B. Mon. 167; B. Int. 36, 239; Mah. lxrv. Pissagadhara, one who is versed in the Vlnayapitaka (Alw. I. 94; Pát. 17). Pissagadhā, = fayy + ᠮ, knowing the V. (Mah. 13, visyayattinnagagna is the reading of my MS.). There is a division of the Vlnaya called khandakharas, and from Buddha's account of the 1st council it would appear that it is a collective name for the Mahagga and Cślavaggo (comp. E. Mon. 115). It is divided into minor khandhakas, one of which is mentioned at Mah. 103, the passapandiyaksh khandakharas, or section dealing with the mode of commending the Vassa residence. At Pát. 29 the upomshakhandakhas is mentioned. At Pát. 80 we are told that "the parivasaidina, etc., are described in detail in the Samassayakhkandhalam. Subh. writes to me that the dudakikhandakharassatdi are 82 precepts contained in the Kammakkhakra and Parivasa khandhalas. In the terms astiovaya, amishavilaya, I am inclined to think that vinaya means "removal (of blame), acquittal." If so, asifhao means acquittal on the ground of restored sanity." dered by Thought or Mind, the more so as both�citans and monos are more or less accurate synonyms for it. It will be seen further that it consists mainly of thoughts or mental impressions of various sorts. Viñfága as the thinking part of the individual is the most important of the five khandhas, and if any one khandha can be sold to constitute the individual it is this. In Buddha's words, viñfágao sirodáena eth' čtast sparnijhati, by the destruction of Mind the whole being perishes. Of the four mental khandhas the superiority of V. is strongly assumed in the first verse of Dhamupada: Hampobbenigand dhāndmaṃ saṅghā maṃkand, the mental facilities (cedant, saifid and saikhidra) are dominated by Mind, they are governed by Mind, they are made up of Mind (that this is the true meaning of the passage I am now convinced, see Alw. N. 70-75).

As one of the Khandhas and a metaphysical term, Vittagha has no less than eighty-nine subdivisions, which I will now briefly elucidate from Vinddhik Haggas and Abbhadma mithassaugaha. First we have the broad division into korsalovidispach, akusasiv, and asydivastas, mariscerious thought, demitorious thought and indifferent thought. Kusasavidispach consists of 8 kimivacarakusalacitas, 5 rúpavacarakusalactias, 4 arpdvacarakusalclitas, and 4 lokuriakusalacitas. Akusasividispach consists of 8 lobhasaagatalitas, 2 palghasampayattaditas, and 2 momobeltas. Aryakatavidispach has two broad subdivisions into vppaks and kiriyt. To the former belong 7 akusasavipskaltas, 8 kusasavipskahutakcalitas, 8 sahetukakamavcaravipskaditas, 6 rúpavacarakupakacitas, 4 arpdvacarakutakcalitas and 4 lokutakavipakacitas: to the latter belong, 3 ahetukakriyscitas, 8 sahetukakimavcarakriysclitas, 6 rúpavacaraklysclitas, 4 arpdvacaraklyscitas (these numbers added together will be found to amount to 89, which is the number given by Hardy at Man. B. 419). It is impossible in a work of this extent to enumerate the whole of the 89 clitas, but I will give a few as specimens, and add a quotation from Vls. M. which will give a fair idea of the nature of the Buddhist metaphysics.

The full is the text of the seven akma-akvi-paka-ctias, or thoughts having an evil result: Upekkhakagatah cakhavishdapai, upakkhadagatah asovishdapai, upakkhadagatah ghdavishdapai, upakkhadagatah jihodishdapai, dakkahamba-gatah kdyavishdapai, upakkhadagatah sampe-jichamaeitah, upakkhadagatah santirupacittah, eye-coacloanness attended with fudifference (via. attended by neither pain nor pleasure), ear-consciousness attended with laddifference, nose-consciousness attended with indifference, tongue-consciousness attended with indifference, touch-consciousness based on suffering, acquadeclug thought attended with indifference, deciding thought attended with indifference. The five Rāpavacaṅkalasaitas are the good thoughts or states of mind leading to the five Jihanas, visha-vichapritishakhekkagatahkitash pafhama-ajikhas-kasalaitah, viodrapitishakhekkagatsakitash dhtiyajihdakavusilacittah, pitikkhakagatahchiam, tatigayikhalasaitas, suhetikagatahkitash caavishajikhalasaitash, upakkhakagatahka-hitash pahemaqifikhalasaitash. The five Rāpavacaṅkalasaitas are five states of mind in which the five Jihanas result, visakhavidrapitishakhokkagatahkitash pafhama-ajikhas-kasalaitah, and so on as in the last category. The four Arāpavacaṅkalasaitas are four thoughts combined with satia (1) causing birth in the four Arāpa-brahmalokas, disenaficdyatakriydicittah, vichapidiyata-akiyiditash, etc. The four Lokistak-rusa-aciritah are four states of mind leading to the four Paths, and pattimaggactish, sakaddg-mimoggacittah, and gndimaggacittah, oratata-maggacittah. The four Lokitariapikacittas are four states of mind leading to the four Prilitans, and pattipikacittash, and so on.¹

I will conclude by quoting Buddha's brief account in V1s. M. of the eight Kámiavacakusulacūnas, as it affords a good specimen of the practical bearing of Buddhist metaphysics, and of the life that animals compositions which at first sight might be mistaken for lines of barren technicalities. When in the ecstatics meditation a special thought has been successfully grasped, and jihana indoed, this is called visaddhigaume, specific attalament (Db. 197). Alw. I. 108, 107; Mah. 10.
VISAJJANÁM, A gift [f(x)]. Ab. 490.

VISHAJATI, To send forth, emitt, throw, shoot, etc.; to let go, dismiss; to answer; to leave, for-make; to spend [fug], for the double s comp. akkane = avakriebys, soeritka, soppana, ossajjati, etc.]. A form with a single s may perhaps occur as an archaism, but I have only met with it once, in Par. S., visajja (ger.) pallaldai, levling the marshae, where however the metre necessitates a short syllable. The caus. visajjeti with a single s occurs several times in Turour's Mahavanna, but each time meiri cause. Butakam elosajjudes, having set aside or omitted thus much (Alw. I. 63, this is the only place where I have met with the single j, which is probably metri caust). Teani paikami elosajjati, they answer their questions (Dh. 121). Satish elosajji, hurled his spear (Dh. 115). Teo visajjited, levling given it away (Dh. 248). P.p.p. elosajiko, loosed, released, etc. (F. J44. 18 let go; Mah. 64 dismissed; F. J44. 51; Dh. 52, 341). Visajjiko as applied to the human voice probably means distinct, well enundated (B. Lot. 568; Ab. 129). Caus. visajjeti, with same meaning as elosajjati. Suikami elosajjeste, let them (the tax-gatherers) remit their taxes (Alw. I. 74, comp. 78). IppAdraumorpe modassom visajjited, allowing his mind to dwell upon a pleasant object of contemplation (lit. casting or letting loose his mind, Dh. 111). Sidi yogakhetem visajjeti, turns the sea into the rice and barley folds (F. J44. 15). Catapazpadakokhasais elosajjited, having expended 34 kola of treasure (Dh. 78). Dapakama visajjited, letting go the stick (from his mouth, F. J44. 17, comp. Dh. 66). Dachighatus visajjesi, poured out the bowl of curds (F. J44. 5). Tt.. elosajjitedna bhikkhaso, having sent forth those priests (Mah. 2). Lekhamv., to send a letter (Mah. 53, 200). To send a person away, dismha, take leave of him (Mah. 23). Fiasqjiesdmi mas, I'll release him, let him go (Ten J. 115; Dh. 199). Acoro or visajjenti, I be in uncount, they release him (Alw. I. 99). Poishav, to answer a question (Ten J. 12; Mah. 13; Pt. 1, see correct reading class. In the footnote). Poikha visajjited start, dropping its wings, swooped down (Dh. 154). To give away (Dh. 113, 409; Pt. 10). Satish v., to lose one's

memory (Dh. 897). To drop or shed (of a plant shedding its leaves, Dh. 428). Use soraah cissajjiet, discharged an arrow at her breast (Dh. 178). Somodassish vi(s)ajjai, committed her to the deep, "launched her forth into the ocean" (Mah. 181). P.p.p. visajjito. Iwadi caidri paddi tanehi catakli padaki visajijidai, those four lines are answered by these four (Alw. 1. 199, comp. Mah. 13). Kapao tana v., the arrow shot by him (Mah. 143). Plaajjai, with one's meir canak, occurs at Mah. 23, 53, 131, and saajjito at 143. Also caus. saajjidpeti, to cause to be let loose, released, etc. (Dh. 144, 158, 395; Mah. 151). Visajjidpeti adgare, sent them adrift upon the ocean (Mah. 46).

VISUDDHI (f.), Purity, holiness, rectitude, correctness; Nirvita [fuyita]. Ab. 9; Db. 49. Fismiddhimaggo, the Way of Holiness, name of a famous work of Buddhaghons, which forms a sort of cyclopaedia of Buddhist theology (Mah. 282, see a specimen under Vividipass). Vivididibrama, one who is a brahmin (not by birth but) by a holy life, an Arhet (Ten J. 48). Vividididero, one who is an angel by a holy life, an Arhat (Das. 48). Dassimassa v., purity of video, correctness of belief (Dh. 48). Kassava, purity of action, good karma (Dh. 3). Haedy alludes to five risnddhia, of which he mentions three, silaa, diffihiv, eittaa, purity of life, of belief, of mind (Mau. B.414). At E. Mon. 193 he mentions no addition, knikkidhetaropav, magdamaggandpadassava, papiladdhadassava, and hadpadassava (these are the titles of the last four chapters of Vianddh Maggu). According to Hardy visiddhatism means keeping she precepts perfectly, and actisiddhitish keeping them imperfectly (Mau. B. 183).

VISUJJHATI, To be cleansed, to be pure [fug]

Dh. 30. P.p.p\ viesddho, clear, bright, pure, holy, sancilled; correct, orthodox (Alw. I. 64; B. Lot. 800). Caus. visodhet, to cleanse, clear, purify. Tena puffho 'tha vydkari, questioned by him made the following declaration (Mah. 19). Buddhassa viga gamdhraghoatid nait vydkaruhi Buddhaghoati, they styled him Buddhaghoa, from his deep voice like that of Buddha (Mah. 251, vydkaruhi metri caus, comp. vydkari in the same page). Eoach tapam vydkarited, having made this response or prediction to the hermit (a prediction that he would one day become Gautama Buddha, Dh. 135). Tena pathandya samijjhaabdoam, directed vydkari, seeing that his prayer or wish would be realized, made the following prediction (Dh. 130, comp. Jt. 15). Nemitid vydkarum toad sahadasa migiardjiso, fortune-tellers foretold her cobabitingos with a lion (Mah. 43, comp. Art. 190). Ele tayo pi Shaiadipe pathahasard haivassitit attha airiisndnash vydkari, to them sitting there be predicted, "These three will all become Kings of Ceylon" (Art. 196). P.f.p. vydkarasiyo, that has to be answered (see Pahho). P.p.p. vydkato. Further on Rathapdis's mother says to her husband, yagghe gukapati jimeyydai Rathapdo kira kislaputo anappaito, do you know, householder, they say our young R. has come back? —YAKKHO, Name of cartola superhuman belongs [qʷ]. Ab. Li. Some of the yakkhas are attends on Vessavaya, who is called Yakkaddhipo, lord of yakkhas (Ab. 82). The yakkhas are mostly enemies to man, but some of them are harmless creatures, and there are stories of many having been converted to Buddhism (Mah. 3, 48; Kh. 13; Mau. B. 24, 44, 56). Yessavaya is himself called a yakkha (Ab. 909). Yakkkhadjopa, resin (Ab. 304). Fem. gakkh, comp. Yakkkkh. YAM, see Yo.

YAMAKAM, A pair, couple [可] Ab. 629. Yamakatelani, two sorts of oils (Jit. 25). Yamakudidam antare, between two Bal crew (9. Los. 342). Yamakati, or Yamakappakarasak; in the name of one of the books of the Abbidionics (are Yipitakash). It contains ten divisions, the first of which is midyamakash.
