— YATHÃ (od.), As, like, how, when [ʌʃɪŋ], Ab. 1142. Kend to na y. afkashah, your hale is not like other people's (Trenckner). Mida y. niyam pattam... anuraikhke (opt.), as a mother would watch over her own son (Kb. 16). Tan Bhag and na coadati y. Devadattah, Koleligah... blm Buddha does not admanah, any more than D. or K. (B. Lot. 305). Y. parisea kho pama so Bhag-ed sarea alindpeti, when Buddha instructs the assembly with his voice (B. Lot. 509). Nidbani dhra yathā 'yash padipo, the righteous are extinguleled like this lamp (Kh. 10; Db. 36, 53). Khippam dhammah aljadati dabai aparamah ga-tAd, be quickly knows the law as the poon knows the taste of the broth (Db. 12). Opandiy, Shusah, winows them like chaff (Db. 45). In conjunction with fathad: Yathd me dhamahede na hoti tathd karisedai, I'll manage so as to have no expense (Dh. 33, comp. F. Jat. 12; Db. 39; Jat. 8); Ya'th ma'na muficati tathd kritun cojati, I must act in such a way that he does not dismise me (Dh. 156); Tath' attishank nicseyya yathd bharf paraddhati, let him so establish himself that wisdom may increase (Dh. 50); Yatid so idkhag-gappasite hoti tathd akisi, so acted that he became highly prosperous (Dh. 306, comp. Ten J. 49); Kels pasa toah popima tathd aladi yathd 'kash pipidah na lathheyah, what, sinner, did you manage that I should receive no alms (Dh. 333); Bhagad tathd me dhomamah desats yathd althah ajidsyydani, let the Blessed One so teach me the Law that I may understand the meaning (comp. Ten J. 115); Karoti so tath' attishah yathd math lecharf dilam, be makes himself such as his enemy wites him to be (Dh. 29); Yatid ad tathd ed hot, however that may be. smikkhati of asmiikhati of viridge tetank dhamandam aggaon akkhidvati, priests, whatsoever conditions there may be material or immaterial, of these conditions arhatalip is the chief (Db. 882; Pausboll here offers the conjectural amendment ydoomati, nom. pl. from (197), but the reading of the text is correct, comp. ydoond brdhassapagukapatid Zhithidyan polisamut).

YAVATAKO (má), As long, as far, as much, as many (comp. ideatake). Ydatake ass kdo to, as to a case vytmo, as long as his body is so long is the stretch of his arms (B. Lot. 570). Bornout has misunderstood the meaning of this passage, which clearly is that the height of Buddha was equal to the distance between the lips of his fingers when his arms were stretched out. I have more than once been told that in well-proportioned men this is generally found to be the case. Ydatake...

concludish... to take & postfieldputish, to provide as many (novices) as he is able to exhibit (P.L. xlv), Fem; alid; Ydeutik ydassass Shdmi ydassass qumted, going in her carriage as far as there was room for a carriage, or as the ground permitted (Dh. 231, y. of course agree with Shdmi). In one instance (P.L. 2) I have met with a manc form ydastiko.

YAVATATIYAM (ads.), Up to the third time [qun + qiu]. Y. edwind, having thrice endeavoured to prevent him (Dh. 172). Tutid's i.y., this happened three times (Mah. 45). Pit. 5, 66; Das. 4. With affix m, ydostatiyako, a name of the last four Sanghadlaena offences; because before the punishment is inflicted warning must have been thrice given (P64. 6).

— YAVATAYUKAM (adv.), As long as life should last [चम्बिया + चम्बिया + मी], In the phrase y. siiffhati, to live out one's span of life, Le, not have it shortened by evil karma required in the present or a previous existence. When used of a human being it means to live to a good old age; when used of a devu, to live the period allotted to devas of the devaloks in question (in some of the devas lokas life is of enormous length, see Man, B. 90). F. Jét, 8; Ten J. 52; Dh. 117, 252 (y. puffaiz kated), 229, 839 (line 4); Mah. 14 (read -kash).

YĀVATIḫAM (adv.), As many days as [some derivative of qīqīq + qīqīq]. Y. jámāḫ patīṭṭādītā tōqutāḫ... for as many days as he know- ingly conceals his sin, for so many days... (Pāt. 6). YAVO, Ḥarīy [qūy], Ab. 450; F. Jāt. 15.
YAYI (adj.), Going [qīng] [zheng], Sighay, going quietly. Nagaray, going to the city (See, K. 502).

YEAHUYYABIKA (f). Name of one of the Adhikarsapmanathas. It is properly an adj. In agreement with kirgyd undersood. The second part of the compound is  $  \pi^{2} + \pi^{3}  $, while in ye I think we have the relative pronoun  $  \pi^{2}  $. (comp. ergygoth = so-yath). Yij. sends me the full explanation of this term, “It means purdig to the vote and deciding by a majority; this is done by drawing tickets (salddh): a good orthodox priest must be selected as saldkgadhépaka or ticket-issner, who should be careful to have the votes taken when there is a majority of the orthodox (chammanddi).” He quotes, gasad kirgydo dhammaddidno behutard, and gedehyyachammaddino stassa yebhayyadid.

smikkhati of asmiikhati of viridge tetank dhamandam aggaon akkhidvati, priests, whatsoever conditions there may be material or immaterial, of these conditions arhatalip is the chief (Db. 882; Pausboll here offers the conjectural amendment ydoomati, nom. pl. from (197), but the reading of the text is correct, comp. ydoond brdhassapagukapatid Zhithidyan polisamut).

YAVATAKO (má), As long, as far, as much, as many (comp. ideatake). Ydatake ass kdo to, as to a case vytmo, as long as his body is so long is the stretch of his arms (B. Lot. 570). Bornout has misunderstood the meaning of this passage, which clearly is that the height of Buddha was equal to the distance between the lips of his fingers when his arms were stretched out. I have more than once been told that in well-proportioned men this is generally found to be the case. Ydatake...

concludish... to take & postfieldputish, to provide as many (novices) as he is able to exhibit (P.L. xlv), Fem; alid; Ydeutik ydassass Shdmi ydassass qumted, going in her carriage as far as there was room for a carriage, or as the ground permitted (Dh. 231, y. of course agree with Shdmi). In one instance (P.L. 2) I have met with a manc form ydastiko.

YAVATATIYAM (ads.), Up to the third time [qun + qiu]. Y. edwind, having thrice endeavoured to prevent him (Dh. 172). Tutid's i.y., this happened three times (Mah. 45). Pit. 5, 66; Das. 4. With affix m, ydostatiyako, a name of the last four Sanghadlaena offences; because before the punishment is inflicted warning must have been thrice given (P64. 6).

— YAVATAYUKAM (adv.), As long as life should last [चम्बिया + चम्बिया + मी], In the phrase y. siiffhati, to live out one's span of life, Le, not have it shortened by evil karma required in the present or a previous existence. When used of a human being it means to live to a good old age; when used of a devu, to live the period allotted to devas of the devaloks in question (in some of the devas lokas life is of enormous length, see Man, B. 90). F. Jét, 8; Ten J. 52; Dh. 117, 252 (y. puffaiz kated), 229, 839 (line 4); Mah. 14 (read -kash).

YĀVATIḫAM (adv.), As many days as [some derivative of qīqīq + qīqīq]. Y. jámāḫ patīṭṭādītā tōqutāḫ... for as many days as he know- ingly conceals his sin, for so many days... (Pāt. 6). YAVO, Ḥarīy [qūy], Ab. 450; F. Jāt. 15.



YAYI (adj.), Going [qīng] [zheng], Sighay, going quietly. Nagaray, going to the city (See, K. 502).

YEAHUYYABIKA (f). Name of one of the Adhikarsapmanathas. It is properly an adj. In agreement with kirgyd undersood. The second part of the compound is  $  \pi^{2} + \pi^{3}  $, while in ye I think we have the relative pronoun  $  \pi^{2}  $. (comp. ergygoth = so-yath). Yij. sends me the full explanation of this term, “It means purdig to the vote and deciding by a majority; this is done by drawing tickets (salddh): a good orthodox priest must be selected as saldkgadhépaka or ticket-issner, who should be careful to have the votes taken when there is a majority of the orthodox (chammanddi).” He quotes, gasad kirgydo dhammaddidno behutard, and gedehyyachammaddino stassa yebhayyadid.

YEBHUYYO (adj.), Abundant, numerous [probably up+ up). Ab. 703 (I have never met with it elsewhere as an adj.). Instr. yebhuygena (adv.), generally, mostly, as a general rule, frequently, numerously, entirely (Dh. 169, 277, 288, 385). /To therea conkunanaite yebhuygena spaj-flkns, those (insects) as the priest welked up and down parished in great numbers (Dh. 88, comp. village he approaches, via all the villages he approaches (Mah, 43). Yari had even had a sariatish skokiteyya tush and even hareyya, should make whatever sort of vessel he requires (84m. 8.). Next, Yash yad sva and yari fad eve, whatsoever. Yash yas pabbajitnam spakhtdys samovafjati tsh sabbham sapertind, whatsoever conditions to the advantage of asceties having created it all (Jst. 8). Yo yo paftamam amatav adhiguzehati so droveris, whichever of us first attalus amata let him announce it (Db. 123). Yam yash padamah bhajati tattha tatth' eva pijilo, whatever country he dwells in therein he is honored (Dh. 53). Yenam yam skdroma lechat, in whatever way he wishes (Ten J. 89). Sometimes the second yo is used in the sense of "any one, some one:" Ye adna yasa attono sentike vassah na receti terma gadiiti atkarilabbo, he who does not like the presence near him of anybody, by him he (the intarloper) should be dismissed with the words, "Be off" (Ten J. 88).

The next, sing, yeah is used advertially with the meanings "that, as, because, seeing that, since, if, when" (Ab. 1140). Toak bahush yam pi jiasul, it's a wonder that you are alive (F. J. 13). Yon safta poadni mamduxbondhish (man amboadhi?), considering that you have hunted me for seven years (Ten J. 116). Andhan tamari told koi yash rago sahoto sarash, thick darkness is the result when last overcomes a man (A.W. I. 107). Hoti kho so bhikkhape samaya yasi, the time will come, prants, when... (Gog. Ev. 15, 20). Thaknais kho par' cladi bijiati yash, this is a reason why... (Dh. 143). Amaachariyam kho pan' etah yam... somena aipah vinicchimeyydha, it is not wonderful that you should judge a case justly (Ten J. 1). Labbid eata me gach mama santikan samundambadha... pahil, it is fortunate for me that Buddha sent to me (Dh. 434). In the phrase yam tariff dekkhasti I think we have the adverbs yam and tani, if so it would mean "as the sainta point out." With fol. ce: Ya'ee, than If, even If. Seyyo cyagulo bhuto tuto... yah ce bhijeyya, better a red-hot iron ball swallowed than that he should eat (Dh. 54, comp. 20, 329); Ya'ee soena saighafftamata yeva, even if at the moment of contact with the ear (A.W. I. cvii). For ya'ee at Dh. v. 339, see p. 602, line 25. With fol. fama: Yon nishak imari bhikkhaish upo-sankamited paccakypai, what if I were to go to this mock and qneadon him (Dh. 122, comp. 104, 121, Tea J. 37); Yon nishak Adrassa Edd-massa pothasain dhammah desaypah, let me first preach the Law to A.K. (Gog. Ev. 11). With fut. Yon nishak inca santike dhammah suissadmi, come, I will hear the Law from him, or "perhaps I shall bear the Law from him" (Ras. 21).

Yena Bhagood ten' apasnikami, went to Buddha, lit. when B. was there approached (Kh. 4; Dh. 106; Alw. I. 92). Yena Párligyakam itad acaari, went to P. (Dh. 105). Yena Bhagood ten' ajjalim popmedot, bendlug bis clasped hands towards B. (Gog. Rv. 8). Yena yena' eva pakkamati, whichever way he goes, wherever he goes. Yena ad tena ed paikamati, go this way or that, "go their respective ways" (Trenzkner).

Caus.yojjeti, to fix, apply, devote; to unite, mix; to try, adopt, use, prepare; to yoke, harness; to appoint, commission, employ; to furish, provide; to urge, induce. Yojetka Morath poindoukhena, let him grapple Mira with the weapon of wisdom (Dh. 8). Attidman yogassim (loc.) yojjaysah, not devoting himself to zeal (Dh. 38). Yojayi rathe, bound them to his chartot (Mah. 218). Sappimadhu sakkhardhi yojjet, having mixed it with ghee, howey and sugar (Dh. 196). Visant phalem yojjet, having applied poison to the fruit (Mah. 229). Hondahsh viryusamatkam yojjami, let me adopt, or try, the calming of my zeal (Br. J. 8.A.). Bahá monasse yojjet, having engaged a number of men (to make bricks, Mah. 107). Aharathati yojjami, ordered them to bring them, lit commisioned them, saying, Bring ye them (Mah. 179). parsing_res_list.block_content: #### MY CRITICS.

I went to Ceylon as a member of the Civil Service at the end of 1860, and for three years was private secretary to the then Governor, Sir C. MacCarthy. In 1863 I received an appointment in the Civil Service, but after a few months' work my health broke down, and I returned to Europe in March, 1864. During my stay in Ceylon I enjoyed the friendship of that gifted Frenchman, the late M. Paul Orblot, who first drew my attention to the importance and interest of Buddhist literature. Shortly before my health failed I made an effort to learn Pali under a native paydit, but met with indifferent success, and I did no more until the autumn of 1868, when Dr. Rost induced me to take up the study of Pali to earnest. I am conscious of many imperfections in this dictionary, but the fact that it contains more than thirteen thousand words, and nearly forty thousand references and quotations, and that seven years ago I hardly knew a word either of Pali or Sanskrit, entites me, I think, to be treated tenderly by my critics. At the end of 1869 Mr. Truhoer liberally offered to publish my dictionary at his own expense, and the first part (pp. 1-270) appeared with a temporary preface in October, 1872. During the course of the next few months it received most friendly and favourable reviews—for which I beg to return my sincere thanks—from Dr. Kern in the Bijdragen tot de Trail-Land... Ned. Indie for 1873; from M. Léon Feer in the Revue Critique (Dec. 7, 1872); from Mr. Pincott in the Oriental (Sept. 1873); from Mr. J. F. Dickson in the Ceylon Times (Jan. 6, 1873), and from unknown reviewers in the Church Missionary Intelligencer, the Homeward Mail, and (oddly enough) the Derby Mercury. In reply to one of M. Feer's friendly criticisms, I would point out that he quotes me incorrectly as saying that "le commun des Buddhistes aspire non au néant comme but supreme, mais au svarge." What I said was that Buddhists who are not Arhats look immediately to savage as the reward of a virtuous life. I ought perhaps to have added then, and I add now explicitly, that all true Buddhists "aspire" to Nirvāya as an ultimate reward, though of course only Arhats expect Nirvāya immediately after death and without further transmigration.

In the Revue Bibliographique for June 15, 1874, M. Foucaux published an article of four pages, in which he takes up a position of strong antagonism to my view of Nirvāna as expressed in my article Nibbaanā. His criticisms are expressed in temperate and courteous language, and I have read them with the attention which they merit as coming from a scholar of M. Foucaux's eminence; but I am bound to my that they do not in the slightest degree shake my confidence in my own view. How little common ground of discussion there is between us may be seen at the outset, where M. Foucaux quotes against me the Lalita Vistara, and calls it a "canonical text"! However, the passage quoted is not irreconcilable with orthodox Buddhism, and I am very willing to accept it. But when M. Foucaux says, "Et comme il faut, pour arriver au Nirvāna, se délivrer de tout composé, la comparaison de la lampe qui s'éteint ne nous montre que la disparition d'un composé, et ouflemment l'embolisation de l'esprit," it is clear that he is under the belief that mind is not a samskārni. I venture therefore to refer him to my article Saikkāro, which will show him that mind is a most important samskārna, and afford a complete answer to his argument. Further, M. Foucaux brings against me the eight Vimutti's. Had his reading not been limited to North Buddhist texts, he would have known that the Vimutti's belong to the ecstatic meditation, and are not "degrees of perfection to which a saint may attain." For an answer to his argument I must refer him to my article Viññāṇācātyatanam (also Akāṇaṇācātyatanam, etc.), from which he will see that Durnouf has absurdly mistranslated the Pali text. Vijñāna exists just as much in the eighth Vimutti as in the fourth or fifth, only it is in a state of trance (see art. Nirādhō).
Seo Prefee p. 12.

parsing_res_list.block_content: MY CHITICS.

I shall make no attempt to reply at full length to Dr. A. Weber's criticisms upon me in the Centralblatt of Feb. 8, 1873. In the first place, a considerable portion of his critique is directed against the form of plan, of my work as being unscientific; and I may reply generally, first that I purposely adopted an unscientific form to suit the convenience of non-Sanskritists (who prove to be about two-thirds of my subscribers); secondly that, in a first edition at least, I have a right to be judged by the matter and not the form of my work; and thirdly that Dr. Weber has really put himself out of court in this matter by bestowing, in this identical number of the Centralblatt, the warmest praise upon Monier Williams' Sanskrit Dictionary, which is also on an unscientific plan. Dr. Weber thinks Professor Williams' plan "convenient": exactly so, and that is the advantage I claim for mine. Dr. Weber complains that I have not brought under the simple root the various compounds of the root with prepositions. It is easy to see that had I done so I could not have begun to print until the whole dictionary was finished, in other words I should have been delayed about two years. Another section of Dr. Weber's criticisms deals with the deficiencies of my dictionary, and here again I am not careful to answer him, the mere size of the work being a sufficient answer, not to speak of the Addenda. Dr. Weber has made no allowance for the exceptional difficulties I have had to deal with, as the total absence of previous dictionaries, or even the merest vocabulary, to guide me, and the incredible blunders with which almost all the texts I had to incorporate abounded. The remainder of Dr. Weber's paper is taken up with philological criticisms. I have to thank him for three or four slight corrections, which I have adopted, but some of his criticisms simply show how ill even the best Sanskrit scholarship qualifies one to lay down the law about Pali. I shall give only one example. I said that appamafida represents the Sanskrit spramaya + ya, and Dr. Weber summarily brushes away this etymology with the words "appamañfa Demath, Bescheidenheit, aus alpamanya." To prove that I was right, and that the word has nothing to do with "humility," I will here print the text of the first appamafid: I don't know bhikkhu mettidaagatena cetaed ekam disam pharited viharati tatth dityak tathd tatiyam tathd catutthith, situudham adho tirigam sabbadhi sabbatatadiya sabbovantam lokala upekhāsahagatena cetad nipalena mahaggotena apramānena avera amydapjajhena pharited siharati. I trust that Dr. Weber will forgive me if I have proved restive under his somewhat heavy lash, and will believe me when I say that I entertain towards him unaltered feelings of friendship and respect.

For the benefit of Sanskritists I propose to compile a work on the plan of Wentergaard's Radios, giving the Sanskrit roots in the Nagari character, and grouping around them all the Fali verbal derivatives.
THE END.
PEPPHI AND BOPP, MHTONO,
